knowledge_statements.title: Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued convexity on a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space, let \(C\subseteq X\) be convex, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). The function \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(\lambda\in(0,1)\), \[f\bigl(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y\bigr)\leq \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in C:f(x)<+\infty\}\). The function is proper when \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\); otherwise it is identically \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function on a convex set is convex when, for any two points and any strictly intermediate convex-combination weight, its value at their convex combination does not exceed the corresponding weighted average of their values. Its effective domain consists of the points where it is finite, and it is proper when that domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex exactly when \(f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and all \(\lambda\in(0,1)\).

notation.meaning: Effective domain where the function has a finite value.
Extended-real value used to exclude points from the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Is Equivalent to Gradient Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order characterization for continuously differentiable functions on convex Euclidean domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. Then \(f\in\mathcal F^1(Q)\), equivalently \(f\) is convex on \(Q\), if and only if \[\langle \nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq 0\qquad\text{for all }x,y\in Q.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable function on a convex set is convex if and only if its gradient is a monotone mapping on that set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathcal F^1(Q)\iff \forall x,y\in Q,\quad \langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq 0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Minimax Linearization Parameter for Two Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition for arbitrary real-valued functions on a nonempty set; convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\neq\varnothing\), let \(f_1,f_2:Q\to\mathbb R\), and set \(f(x)=\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\). A scalar \(\lambda^*\in[0,1]\) is a minimax linearization parameter for \((f_1,f_2)\) over \(Q\) if
\[
\min_{x\in Q}\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=\min_{x\in Q}\bigl(\lambda^*f_1(x)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x)\bigr),
\]
with both sides interpreted in \(\mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two real-valued functions on a nonempty set, a minimax linearization parameter is a weight between zero and one for which minimizing the weighted sum gives the same extended-real value as minimizing their pointwise maximum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in Q}\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=\min_{x\in Q}\left(\lambda^*f_1(x)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x)\right)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ray-Extrapolation Characterization of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For a function whose domain is convex, convexity is equivalent to the stated inequality at every feasible ray extrapolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) have a convex domain. Then \(f\) is convex if and only if, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(\beta\geq0\) such that \(y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[f\bigl(y+\beta(y-x)\bigr)\geq f(y)+\beta\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a function with convex domain, convexity is equivalent to requiring every feasible extrapolation from y away from x to lie above the corresponding affine extrapolation of the values at x and y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff\bigl[\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall\beta\geq0\text{ with }y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ f(y+\beta(y-x))\geq f(y)+\beta(f(y)-f(x))\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strongly Convex Objective with Lipschitz-Continuous Hessian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the smooth strongly convex problem class used for the subsequent method analysis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb E}f(x)\), where \(f\in\mathbb C^3(\mathbb E)\), \(\sigma_2(f)>0\), and, for every \(x,y\in\mathbb E\),
\[f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac12\sigma_2(f)\|y-x\|^2\]
and
\[\|\nabla^2f(x)-\nabla^2f(y)\|\le L_3(f)\|x-y\|.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The problem class consists of minimizing a three-times continuously differentiable function on E that is strongly convex with positive modulus sigma_2(f) and has a globally Lipschitz-continuous Hessian with constant L_3(f).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \min_{x\in\mathbb E}f(x)\text{ is a strongly convex }C^3\text{ minimization problem with Lipschitz-continuous Hessian}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment for Some Convex Combination of Two Level-Bounded Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion is existential: it asserts attainment for at least one parameter \(\lambda^*\in[0,1]\), not for every parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Let \(f_1,f_2:Q\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\) be proper, closed, and convex. Assume that, for every \(i\in\{1,2\}\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\),
\[
L_i(\alpha):=\{x\in Q:f_i(x)\le\alpha\}
\]
is bounded whenever it is nonempty. Define
\[
\phi(\lambda):=\inf_{x\in Q}\bigl(\lambda f_1(x)+(1-\lambda)f_2(x)\bigr),\qquad \lambda\in[0,1].
\]
Then there exist \(\lambda^*\in[0,1]\) and \(x^*\in Q\) such that
\[
\phi(\lambda^*)=\lambda^*f_1(x^*)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x^*).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For two proper closed convex functions on a nonempty closed convex set, if every nonempty constrained level set of each function is bounded, then at least one convex combination of the functions attains its infimum over the set.
assumptions_latex: Q\text{ is closed and convex in a finite-dimensional Euclidean space}
f_i:Q\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is proper, closed, and convex for }i\in\{1,2\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda^*\in[0,1]\ \exists x^*\in Q:\ \phi(\lambda^*)=\lambda^*f_1(x^*)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x^*).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Combination Maximum Bound
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise upper bound for a convex function at a finite convex combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and suppose \(x=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\), where \(\alpha_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\). Then \[f(x)\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The value of a convex function at a finite convex combination is no greater than its largest value among the generating points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f(x_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extrapolation Characterization of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Both conditions are domain-conditional: interpolation or extrapolation is required only when the constructed point belongs to the function's domain; convexity here does not separately assert that the domain is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ have domain $\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. The condition $f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)$ for all $x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$ such that $\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ holds if and only if, for all $x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $\beta\geq0$ such that $y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f$, one has $f(y+\beta(y-x))\geq f(y)+\beta(f(y)-f(x))$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The domain-conditional chord inequality is equivalent to an extrapolation inequality: whenever extending from x through y remains in the domain, the function value at the extended point is at least the corresponding affine extrapolation of the two endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in[0,1])\;\bigl[\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\in\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\bigr]\\ &\iff (\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\beta\geq0)\;\bigl[y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow f(y+\beta(y-x))\geq f(y)+\beta(f(y)-f(x))\bigr].\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity under Partial Minimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The minimization variable is corrected to \(\mathbb V\), consistently with the declared product domain and the preceding quantified condition; the extract's \(\mathbb E\) occurrence is type-inconsistent. The minimum-based formulation implicitly requires the displayed marginal to be defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb E\times\mathbb V\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be convex and suppose that, for every \(x\in\mathbb E\), there exists \(y\in\mathbb V\) with \(f(x,y)<\infty\). If \[g(x)=\min_{y\in\mathbb V}f(x,y)\] defines \(g:\mathbb E\to[-\infty,\infty)\), then \(g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained partial minimum of a jointly convex function is convex when every parameter value admits a finite function value and the displayed marginal function is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is convex on }\mathbb E

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial minimization preserves convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of a marginal function on the projection of a convex feasible set. No attainment or closedness conclusion is asserted, and the infimum can equal minus infinity without an additional lower-boundedness assumption.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) be convex, let \(\phi:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex, and assume \(Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}\phi\). Define \(\widehat Q=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^m,\ (x,y)\in Q\}\) and, for \(x\in\widehat Q\), \(f(x)=\inf\{\phi(x,y):(x,y)\in Q\}\), allowing the value \(-\infty\). Then for all \(x_1,x_2\in\widehat Q\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \[f(\alpha x_1+(1-\alpha)x_2)\leq \alpha f(x_1)+(1-\alpha)f(x_2).\] Hence \(f\) is convex on \(\widehat Q\) in the extended-real sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a jointly convex function over one variable subject to a convex joint constraint produces a convex marginal function on the projected feasible set. The theorem does not guarantee attainment, closedness, or a finite lower value.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\inf\{\phi(x,y):(x,y)\in Q\}\) for \(x\in\widehat Q\), with no lower-boundedness or attainment assumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(\widehat Q\); no closedness or attainment conclusion follows.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous Subgradient Selection Implies Differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity is required of a subgradient selection at the specified interior-domain point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be convex and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Suppose there exists a selection \(g\), with \(g(x)\in\partial f(x)\), that is continuous at \(x_0\). Then \(f\) is differentiable at \(x_0\) and
\[
\nabla f(x_0)=g(x_0).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is differentiable at an interior-domain point if it admits a subgradient selection continuous there, and its gradient equals the selected subgradient at that point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regularity, Level Sets, and Attainment for Closed Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Five consequences of closed convexity, with the separate constrained hypotheses retained for the attainment and level-boundedness clauses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be closed and convex. Then: (i) for every sequence \(\{x_k\}\subset\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(\liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\geq f(\bar x)\); (ii) for every sequence \(\{x_k\}\subset\operatorname{dom}f\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\); and (iii) every level set of \(f\) is empty or closed and convex. Moreover, if \(f\) is closed and convex on \(Q\) and its constrained level sets are bounded, then \(\min_{x\in Q}f(x)\) is attained. If \(f\) is closed and convex on \(Q\) and \(X^*=\arg\min_{x\in Q}f(x)\) is nonempty and bounded, then every constrained level set of \(f\) on \(Q\) is empty or bounded.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone convex composition preserves convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar outer composition on the convex domain of the inner function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(\psi:\operatorname{dom}\psi\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval containing \(\operatorname{Im}\psi\), and let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and nondecreasing on \(\operatorname{Im}\psi\). Define \(f(x)=\phi(\psi(x))\). Then \(f\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the image of a convex function lies in the interval of definition of a convex scalar function, and the outer function is nondecreasing on that image, then their composition is convex on the inner function's convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\phi(\psi(x))\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Segment-Inequality Characterization of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A characterization for continuously differentiable real-valued functions on convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. Then \(f\in\mathcal F^1(Q)\), equivalently \(f\) is convex on \(Q\), if and only if, for every \(x,y\in Q\) and every \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \[f\bigl(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y\bigr)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuously differentiable function on a convex set is convex if and only if its value at every convex combination of two domain points is at most the corresponding convex combination of their function values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathcal F^1(Q)\iff \forall x,y\in Q\;\forall\alpha\in[0,1],\quad f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Involutive Polarity Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric bijection induced by polarity on the normalized closed convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On the class
\[
\mathcal F=\{f:\ f\text{ is nonnegative, closed, and convex, and }f(0)=0\},
\]
the map \(f\mapsto f^{\circ}\) is a symmetric one-to-one correspondence; equivalently, it maps \(\mathcal F\) bijectively to itself and satisfies \(f^{\circ\circ}=f\) for every \(f\in\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Polarity is an involutive bijection on the class of nonnegative closed convex functions that vanish at the origin.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal F=\{f:\ f\ge0,\ f\text{ closed and convex},\ f(0)=0\}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{\circ}\in\mathcal F,\qquad f^{\circ\circ}=f,\qquad f\mapsto f^{\circ}\ \text{is bijective on }\mathcal F.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex, Strictly Convex, and Concave Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and strict convexity require a convex effective domain. Strictness applies only to distinct points and interpolation coefficients in the open interval; concavity is defined by sign reversal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ and $\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)<+\infty\}$. The function $f$ is convex if $\operatorname{dom}f$ is convex and $f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)$ for every $x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $\alpha\in[0,1]$. It is strictly convex if $\operatorname{dom}f$ is convex and the inequality is strict whenever $x\neq y$ and $\alpha\in(0,1)$. It is concave if $-f$ is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is convex when its effective domain is convex and its value at every segment interpolation is at most the corresponding interpolation of the endpoint values. It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct endpoints and an interior coefficient, and it is concave when its negative is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}f\text{ convex}&\iff \operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }(\forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in[0,1])\;f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\leq\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y),\\ f\text{ strictly convex}&\iff \operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }(\forall x\neq y\in\operatorname{dom}f)(\forall\alpha\in(0,1))\;f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)<\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y),\\ f\text{ concave}&\iff -f\text{ is convex}.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weighted Squared-Norm Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Valid for every norm on \(\mathbb R^n\), including the endpoint weights \(\alpha=0\) and \(\alpha=1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\|\cdot\|\) be a norm on \(\mathbb R^n\). For every \(x,y\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\),
\[
\alpha\|x\|^2+(1-\alpha)\|y\|^2
\ge \alpha(1-\alpha)(\|x\|+\|y\|)^2
\ge \alpha(1-\alpha)\|x-y\|^2.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted sum of two squared norms dominates the weighted square of the sum of their norms, which in turn dominates the same weight times the squared distance between the vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \alpha\|x\|^2+(1-\alpha)\|y\|^2\ge\alpha(1-\alpha)(\|x\|+\|y\|)^2\ge\alpha(1-\alpha)\|x-y\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity via the Segment Inequality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: For proper extended-real-valued functions, records both the whole-space and effective-domain formulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper function \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\) is convex if and only if, for all \(x,y\in\mathbb E\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).\] Equivalently, \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and the same inequality holds for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real-valued function is convex exactly when it satisfies the two-point convex-combination inequality. Equivalently, its effective domain is convex and the inequality need only be checked on that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff \bigl(\forall x,y\in\mathbb E,\ \forall\lambda\in[0,1],\ f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\bigr)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Strict Convexity, and Concavity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definitions for an extended-real-valued function using its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\). The function \(f\) is convex if \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and, for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in[0,1]\), \(f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\le \alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\). It is strictly convex if \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex and, for every distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), \(f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)<\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\). It is concave if \(-f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity requires a convex effective domain and the convex-combination inequality. Strict convexity requires strict inequality for distinct domain points and interior weights. Concavity is defined by convexity after negating the function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}f\text{ convex}&\iff \operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)\le\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\quad(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ \alpha\in[0,1]),\\f\text{ strictly convex}&\iff \operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex and }f(\alpha x+(1-\alpha)y)<\alpha f(x)+(1-\alpha)f(y)\quad(x\ne y,\ \alpha\in(0,1)),\\f\text{ concave}&\iff -f\text{ is convex.}\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and multiplier subgradients of an affine-fiber value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General convex marginalization along the fibers of a full-row-rank linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex, let \(Q\subset\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) be closed and convex, and assume that the level sets of \(f\) on \(Q\) are bounded. Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(n>m\), have full row rank, and define \(\phi(u)=\min\{f(x):x\in Q,\ Ax=u\}\). Then \(\phi\) is convex. If \(\{x\in\operatorname{int}(Q):Ax=u\}\neq\varnothing\), then every \(y^*\) for which there exist \(x^*\in Q\) and \(g^*\in\partial f(x^*)\) satisfying \(Ax^*=u\) and \(\langle g^*-A^Ty^*,x-x^*\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in Q\) belongs to \(\partial\phi(u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal value obtained by minimizing a convex function over affine fibers is convex. At fibers meeting the interior of Q, every equality multiplier satisfying the associated subgradient variational inequality is a subgradient of the value function.
assumptions_latex: \text{the level sets of }f\text{ on }Q\text{ are bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \phi(u):=\min_{x\in Q,\ Ax=u}f(x)\text{ is convex},\qquad \{y^*:\exists x^*,g^*,\ Ax^*=u,\ g^*\in\partial f(x^*),\ \langle g^*-A^Ty^*,x-x^*\rangle\geq0\ \forall x\in Q\}\subseteq\partial\phi(u)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum of a Convex Function on a Finite Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The generators need not be distinct or extreme; the equality concerns the convex hull of the stated finite family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex, let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and set \[\Delta=\operatorname{Conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i:\alpha_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\right\}.\] Then \[\max_{x\in\Delta}f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of a convex function over the convex hull of finitely many domain points equals the largest function value among those generating points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\in\Delta}f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f(x_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence of a Minimax Linearization Weight
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-family theorem under closedness, convexity, and bounded constrained-level-set assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Q\) be a nonempty closed convex set and let \(f_i:Q\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be closed convex functions. Assume that for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\),
\[
\{x\in Q:\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\le\alpha\}
\]
is bounded. If \(F(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\), then there exists
\[
\lambda_*\in\Delta_m:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:\textstyle\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\}
\]
such that
\[
\min_{x\in Q}F(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\sum_{i=1}^m(\lambda_*)_i f_i(x).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many closed convex functions on a nonempty closed convex set, if every sublevel set of their pointwise maximum is bounded, then some simplex weight makes the minimum of their weighted sum equal the minimum of their pointwise maximum.
assumptions_latex: f_i:Q\to\mathbb R\text{ is closed and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R,\ \{x\in Q:\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)\le\alpha\}\text{ is bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda_*\in\Delta_m:\quad \min_{x\in Q}\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\sum_{i=1}^m(\lambda_*)_i f_i(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structure and lower bound of a convex directional derivative
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The base point must lie in the interior of the effective domain; the lower bound applies to every point of the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and let \(x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then the map \(d\mapsto f'(x;d)\) is convex and positively homogeneous of degree one. Moreover, for every \(y\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \[f(y)\geq f(x)+f'(x;y-x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At an interior-domain point of a convex function, the directional derivative is a convex, degree-one positively homogeneous function of the direction and supplies a global first-order lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'(x;\cdot)\text{ is convex and positively homogeneous of degree one, and }(\forall y\in\operatorname{dom}f)\ f(y)\geq f(x)+f'(x;y-x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear pullback and infimal image preserve convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The infimal image is interpreted as an extended-real-valued function, with the infimum over an empty fiber equal to +\infty; properness or attainment is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be linear. If g is convex on \mathbb{R}^m, then (g\circ A)(x)=g(Ax) is convex on \mathbb{R}^n. If h is convex on \mathbb{R}^n, then (Ah)(y)=\inf\{h(x)\mid Ax=y\} is convex on \mathbb{R}^m.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing a convex function with a linear transformation preserves convexity. Taking the infimum of a convex function over each fiber of a linear transformation also produces a convex function, although the resulting function need not be proper or attain its fiberwise infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\circ A\text{ is convex on }\mathbb{R}^n\quad\text{and}\quad y\mapsto\inf\{h(x)\mid Ax=y\}\text{ is convex on }\mathbb{R}^m.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Convex Combination with Positive Coefficients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Under the source's convention, every listed coefficient must be strictly positive; representations with zero coefficients are excluded unless redundant points are removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ be points in a real vector space. A point $x$ is a convex combination of $\{x_i\}_{i=1}^m$ if there exist $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_m$ such that $x=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i$, $\alpha_i>0$ for every $i$, and $\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-Function Convex Maximum Scalarization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion is equality of optimal values; it does not assert equality of minimizer sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f_1\) and \(f_2\) be closed and convex on \(Q\), and suppose their constrained level sets on \(Q\) are bounded. Define \(f(x)=\max\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}\). Then there exists \(\lambda^*\in[0,1]\) such that
\[
\min_{x\in Q} f(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\bigl(\lambda^*f_1(x)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x)\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two functions are closed and convex on Q and their constrained level sets are bounded, the minimum value of their pointwise maximum equals the minimum value of a suitable convex combination of them.
assumptions_latex: f_1,f_2\text{ are closed and convex on }Q
\text{The constrained level sets of }f_1\text{ and }f_2\text{ on }Q\text{ are bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\lambda^*\in[0,1]:\quad \min_{x\in Q}f(x)=\min_{x\in Q}\{\lambda^*f_1(x)+(1-\lambda^*)f_2(x)\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian Characterization of Strong Convexity in an Arbitrary Norm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An if-and-only-if second-order test on the interior of a convex set, retaining continuity on the full domain and allowing $\mu=0$.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be convex with nonempty interior, let $\|\cdot\|$ be a norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $\mu\geq0$. If $f:Q\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous on $Q$ and twice continuously differentiable on $\operatorname{int}Q$, then $$f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu}^{2}(Q,\|\cdot\|)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \langle\nabla^2f(x)h,h\rangle\geq\mu\|h\|^2$$ for every $x\in\operatorname{int}Q$ and every $h\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function continuous on a convex set and twice continuously differentiable on its nonempty interior belongs to the mu-strongly convex class exactly when every interior Hessian quadratic form is bounded below by mu times the squared chosen norm; the characterization includes mu equal to zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\in\mathcal{S}_{\mu}^{2}(Q,\|\cdot\|)\iff \forall x\in\operatorname{int}Q,\ \forall h\in\mathbb{R}^n,\quad \langle\nabla^2f(x)h,h\rangle\geq\mu\|h\|^2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Taxonomy of Convex-Function Encodings
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(\overline{\mathbb R}=\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty,+\infty\}\). A function is a map \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional taxonomy collecting four exact representations; it is an organizing definition rather than a claim that every representation is computationally finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\mathcal E(f)=\bigl(\operatorname{dom}f,\operatorname{epi}f,(L_f(\alpha))_{\alpha\in\mathbb R},\mathcal S_f\bigr),\quad \operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\},\quad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\},\quad L_f(\alpha)=\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] Here \(\mathcal S_f\) denotes any exact set-generated description, such as \(f=g+\delta_C\), a support representation, a gauge representation, or an auxiliary-variable epigraph lift. The four encoding classes are respectively extended-value, epigraphical, level-family, and set-generated encodings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The encoding profile of \(f\) consists of its effective domain, epigraph, complete family of lower level sets, and any exact representation generated from sets. Extended values encode domain restrictions; the epigraph records every inequality \(f(x)\le t\); the level family records every threshold test \(f(x)\le\alpha\); and a set-generated encoding describes the same function through indicators, support or gauge constructions, or a projected lifted set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal E(f)=\left(\{f<+\infty\},\{(x,t):f(x)\le t\},(\{f\le\alpha\})_{\alpha\in\mathbb R},\mathcal S_f\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=\inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x\in L_f(\alpha)\},\] whenever the relevant vertical fibers or level index sets have the standard endpoint property.
special_cases_latex: \[f=g+\delta_C\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dom}f=C\cap\operatorname{dom}g.\]
immediate_consequences_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcup_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}L_f(\alpha)\times[\alpha,+\infty)\] after taking the upward closure in the second coordinate.
boundary_notes: The four-way classification is a synthesized taxonomy and was not found as a named definition in the inspected sources.
Incomplete collections of level sets need not determine a function uniquely.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotone convex composition rule
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar outer composition, with monotonicity required only on the image of the inner function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(\psi:\operatorname{dom}\psi\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) be an interval containing \(\operatorname{Im}\psi\), and let \(\phi:I\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and nondecreasing on \(\operatorname{Im}\psi\). Then \(f=\phi\circ\psi\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex scalar function composed with a convex function remains convex when the outer function is nondecreasing on the inner function's image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}\psi\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity of a Pointwise Supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise supremum of an arbitrarily indexed family of closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\Delta$ be an arbitrary index set and define
\[
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y).
\]
If, for every $y\in\Delta$, the function $\phi(\cdot,y)$ is closed and convex on $Q$, then $f$ is closed and convex on
\[
\widehat Q=\left\{x\in Q:\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)<+\infty\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of an arbitrarily indexed family of closed convex functions is closed and convex on the subset of the common domain where the supremum is finite.
assumptions_latex: \forall y\in\Delta,\quad \phi(\cdot,y)\text{ is closed and convex on }Q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex on }\widehat Q=\{x\in Q:\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)<+\infty\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Maximum Rule for Closed Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite pointwise maxima of extended-real closed convex functions, including the exact active-function subdifferential formula at interior-domain points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $m\in\mathbb N$ and let $f_i$, $i=1,\ldots,m$, be closed convex functions. Define $f(x)=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x)$ and $I(x)=\{i:f_i(x)=f(x)\}$. Then $f$ is closed and convex, $\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)$, and, for every $x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)$, $$\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right).$$
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite pointwise maximum of closed convex functions is closed and convex. Its domain interior is the intersection of the component domain interiors, and at every such interior point its subdifferential is the convex hull of the subdifferentials of the active component functions.
assumptions_latex: f_i\text{ is closed and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex},\quad \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f_i),\quad \partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\!\left(\bigcup_{i\in I(x)}\partial f_i(x)\right)\ \forall x\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Active-Index Subgradients of a Pointwise Supremum
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Possibly infinite pointwise suprema of closed convex functions on a common convex set, with the source's one-sided relative-subdifferential rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\Delta$ be any set, let $Q$ be convex, and suppose that $\phi(\cdot,y)$ is closed and convex on $Q$ for every $y\in\Delta$. Define $$f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y),\qquad \widehat Q=\{x\in Q:f(x)<+\infty\},$$ and $I(x)=\{y\in\Delta:\phi(x,y)=f(x)\}$. At every point of that restriction, its relative subdifferential contains the convex hull of the relative subdifferentials of the active functions; equality is not asserted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of Log-Sum-Exp Aggregation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite log-sum-exp aggregation of convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $m\ge 1$, and let $f_i$, $i=1,\ldots,m$, be convex functions on a common domain. Then
\[
\phi(x)=\log\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m e^{f_i(x)}\right)
\]
is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extrapolation Characterization of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A necessary and sufficient ray-extrapolation inequality for convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f\) is convex if and only if, for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and every \(\beta\ge 0\) such that \(y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f\), one has \[f\bigl(y+\beta(y-x)\bigr)\ge f(y)+\beta\bigl(f(y)-f(x)\bigr).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is convex exactly when every admissible extrapolation beyond y away from x lies above the corresponding extrapolation of the secant values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff \forall x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\ \forall\beta\ge0,\ y+\beta(y-x)\in\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow f(y+\beta(y-x))\ge f(y)+\beta(f(y)-f(x))

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Real Representation of Objectives and Constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\overline{\mathbb R}=[-\infty,+\infty]\). An extended-real function is a map \(f:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convention allowing both infinite values; most optimization applications subsequently restrict attention to proper functions with values in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in X:f(x)<+\infty\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le t\}.\] A real-valued function \(g:C\to\mathbb R\) on \(C\subseteq X\) has the canonical extension \[\widetilde g(x):=\begin{cases}g(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] This extension has \(\operatorname{dom}\widetilde g=C\) and encodes minimization over \(C\) as unconstrained minimization of \(\widetilde g\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function may take finite values as well as \(-\infty\) or \(+\infty\). Its effective domain is the set where its value is below \(+\infty\), and its epigraph contains exactly the finite-height points lying above its values. A function defined only on \(C\) is extended to the ambient space by assigning \(+\infty\) outside \(C\), thereby encoding the domain restriction without changing the original epigraph over finite heights.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x\in C}g(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\widetilde g(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}g(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\widetilde g(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_X(\operatorname{epi}f).\]
Restricting \(f\) to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), or extending its declared domain by assigning \(+\infty\) elsewhere, leaves its finite-height epigraph unchanged.
special_cases_latex: \[\widetilde g=g+\delta_C\] when \(g\) is already defined on the ambient space.
immediate_consequences_latex: Hard feasibility conditions and objective values can be manipulated within one function class.
boundary_notes: The sum \(+\infty+(-\infty)\) is undefined, so arithmetic involving improper functions requires an explicit convention.
Allowing \(-\infty\) is useful for formal completeness but is excluded by properness.

notation.meaning: Ambient-space extension of g by positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient and Relative Strata of an Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) and \(D:=\operatorname{dom}f\). The affine hull of \(D\) is \(\operatorname{aff}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional domain geometry. Relative interior is used because a nonempty convex domain may be lower-dimensional and have empty ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\operatorname{int}D:=\{x\in D:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\subseteq D\},\] \[\operatorname{ri}D:=\{x\in D:\exists\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}D\subseteq D\}.\] The ambient boundary and relative boundary are \[\operatorname{bd}D:=\operatorname{cl}D\setminus\operatorname{int}D,\qquad \operatorname{rbd}D:=\operatorname{cl}D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D.\] The domain is full-dimensional when \(\operatorname{aff}D=\mathbb R^n\), and lower-dimensional otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain is stratified into ambient interior, relative interior, and boundary portions. Ambient interior uses neighborhoods in \(\mathbb R^n\), whereas relative interior uses neighborhoods only inside \(\operatorname{aff}D\). Thus a convex domain contained in a proper affine subspace can have no ambient interior while still having a nonempty relative interior. Its relative boundary is the closure of the domain with the relative interior removed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{int}D\subseteq\operatorname{ri}D\subseteq D\subseteq\operatorname{cl}D,\qquad \operatorname{aff}D=\mathbb R^n\Longrightarrow\operatorname{int}D=\operatorname{ri}D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{ri}D\iff x\text{ is interior to }D\text{ in the subspace topology of }\operatorname{aff}D.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(D\) is an affine set, then \(\operatorname{ri}D=D\) and \(\operatorname{rbd}D=\varnothing\).
For a nondegenerate line segment in \(\mathbb R^2\), its ambient interior is empty, its relative interior excludes the endpoints, and its relative boundary consists of the endpoints.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every nonempty convex set in finite dimensions has nonempty relative interior.
Continuity statements for proper convex functions naturally use \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), not necessarily \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
boundary_notes: The closure in the relative-boundary formula is the ambient closure; the resulting set lies in \(\operatorname{aff}D\).
Infinite-dimensional relative-interior notions may be empty and often require quasi-relative interior substitutes.

knowledge_statements.title: Every Convex Set Is an Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex set is the effective domain of its indicator, and the indicator is proper exactly when the set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every convex set \(C\subseteq X\), define \[\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Then \(\delta_C\) is convex and \(\operatorname{dom}\delta_C=C\). It is proper exactly when \(C\neq\varnothing\). Consequently, the effective domains of extended-real convex functions are precisely the convex subsets of \(X\), including the empty set when improper functions are admitted.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}\delta_C=C,\quad \delta_C\text{ is convex},\quad \delta_C\text{ is proper}\iff C\ne\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse realization of convex effective domains by extended-value convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domain Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The points where a convex extended-value function is finite form a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The effective domain is \[\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in X\mid f(x)<+\infty\}.\] For every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), one has \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Thus \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is a convex subset of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective domains of extended-real-valued convex functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Effective domain of an extended-value convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the effective-domain portion of the compound extract; its epigraph, affine-function, and whole-space-convention components belong to separate foundational branches.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and f:S\to[-\infty,+\infty]. With \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,\mu)\in S\times\mathbb{R}:\mu\geq f(x)\}, the effective domain is \operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\{x\in S:f(x)<+\infty\}. If f is convex, then \operatorname{dom}f is convex. Its dimension is called the dimension of f, and f is convex if and only if its restriction to \operatorname{dom}f is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain is the projection of the epigraph onto the argument space, equivalently the set where the function is below positive infinity. For a convex function this domain is convex; its dimension defines the dimension of the function, and restricting the function to this domain does not change convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}f=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^n}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\{x\in S:f(x)<+\infty\},\qquad f\text{ convex}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{dom}f\text{ convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative-Interior Value Structure of an Improper Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General extended-real-valued convex functions in finite-dimensional space, including the relative-boundary exception.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be an improper convex function. Then \(f(x)=-\infty\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Consequently, finite values, if any, can occur only on \(\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An improper convex function equals negative infinity throughout the relative interior of its effective domain. Since it equals positive infinity outside its effective domain, any finite values can occur only on the relative boundary of that domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f),\ f(x)=-\infty;\qquad \{x:f(x)\in\mathbb{R}\}\subseteq\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}f).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Arbitrary pointwise suprema preserve closed convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An arbitrary nonempty index family, restricted to the points where its supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $\Delta\ne\varnothing$, let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, and let $\phi:Q\times\Delta\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$. Define
\[
f(x)=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y),\qquad
\widehat Q=\{x\in Q:\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)<+\infty\}.
\]
If, for every $y\in\Delta$, the function $x\mapsto\phi(x,y)$ is convex on $Q$ and has a closed epigraph, then $f$ is convex and closed on $\widehat Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of any nonempty family of closed convex functions is closed and convex on the subset of the common domain where the supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x):=\sup_{y\in\Delta}\phi(x,y)\text{ is convex and closed on }\widehat Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Common-Zero-Subgradient Characterization of a Minimizer Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes when every point of a prescribed nonempty closed convex set is a global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f have domain \operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, let X^*:=\arg\min_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}f(x), and let \varnothing\ne X_*\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f be closed and convex. Then X_*\subseteq X^* if and only if 0\in\widehat{\partial f}(X_*):=\bigcap_{x\in X_*}\partial f(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty closed convex set X_* consists entirely of global minimizers of f exactly when zero is a subgradient of f at every point of X_*.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: X_*\subseteq X^*\iff 0\in\widehat{\partial f}(X_*)=\bigcap_{x\in X_*}\partial f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Graph Domain and Effective Domain of a Convex Bifunction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the joint and parameter domains and states their projection, convexity, and proper-slice properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex bifunction \(F\) with graph function \(\Gamma_F\), the graph domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\Gamma_F=\{(u,x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m+n}:\Gamma_F(u,x)<+\infty\}\), and \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:Fu\not\equiv +\infty\}\). Consequently, \(\operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^m}(\operatorname{dom}\Gamma_F)\), and this set is convex. If \(F\) is proper, then \(\operatorname{dom}F=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^m:Fu\text{ is proper}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph domain is the effective domain of the joint graph function. The bifunction domain consists of parameters whose slices are not identically positive infinity. It is the parameter projection of the graph domain and is convex. For a proper bifunction, its elements are exactly the parameters with proper slices.
assumptions_latex: F\text{ is a convex bifunction from }\mathbb{R}^m\text{ to }\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}F=\operatorname{proj}_{\mathbb{R}^m}(\operatorname{dom}\Gamma_F)\text{ is convex};\qquad F\text{ proper}\Longrightarrow\operatorname{dom}F=\{u:Fu\text{ is proper}\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value Dichotomy for a Relatively Open Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real-valued convex functions whose effective domain is relatively open; the second alternative allows positive or negative infinity at different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, and suppose \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is relatively open. Then either \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), or \(f(x)\in\{-\infty,+\infty\}\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). In particular, the hypothesis holds if \(\operatorname{dom}f=\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function has a relatively open effective domain, then it either never takes the value negative infinity or has no finite values anywhere. Having full effective domain is a special case of the relative-openness hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ f(x)>-\infty\right)\ \lor\ \left(\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ f(x)\in\{-\infty,+\infty\}\right).

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Hull Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The affine hull of a nonempty effective domain is any domain point plus the span of all domain-point displacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any \(x_0\in C\), define the direction space \(L_C:=\operatorname{span}(C-x_0)\). Then \[\operatorname{aff}C=x_0+L_C=x_0+\operatorname{span}(C-x_0).\] Both \(L_C\) and the affine space on the right are independent of the selected base point \(x_0\). For an extended-value function, taking \(C=\operatorname{dom}f\) identifies the smallest affine subspace containing every point where \(f\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}C=x_0+\operatorname{span}(C-x_0)\), independently of \(x_0\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional affine geometry of an effective domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Invariance of Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative interior is dense in the closure of a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set, and taking closure does not alter its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty convex \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C,\qquad \operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.\] Moreover, \(C\), \(\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(\operatorname{cl}C\) have the same affine hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{ri}C)=\operatorname{cl}C\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{cl}C)=\operatorname{ri}C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closure identities for nonempty convex sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior is the interior within the affine hull. Every nonempty finite-dimensional convex set has nonempty relative interior, which equals the ordinary interior when the affine hull is the whole space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\operatorname{ri}C:=\{x\in C\mid \exists\varepsilon>0,\ B(x,\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{aff}C\subseteq C\}.\] Then \(\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\). Moreover, if \(\operatorname{aff}C=\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C\neq\varnothing\), and \(\operatorname{ri}C\) is the interior of \(C\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative interior, including lower-dimensional domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Inclusion and Regularity Are Not Forced by Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function may include or exclude domain-boundary points, and an included finite boundary value need not be lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\delta_C\) denote the extended-value indicator of \(C\). The functions \[f_1=\delta_{[0,1]},\qquad f_2=\delta_{(0,1)},\qquad f_3(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&0<x\leq1,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\] are convex on \(\mathbb R\). The first includes both relative-boundary points in its domain, the second excludes both, and the third is finite but not lower semicontinuous at the included boundary point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Convexity alone implies neither relative-boundary inclusion nor boundary lower semicontinuity.}

knowledge_statements.title: Domain Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function's domain is the disjoint union of its relative interior and the domain points on its relative boundary; outside the domain its value is positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\operatorname{rbd}C:=\operatorname{cl}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\setminus\operatorname{ri}C.\] Then \[C=\operatorname{ri}C\,\dot\cup\,(C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C).\] Every point outside \(C\) satisfies \(f(x)=+\infty\). If \(C\) is relatively closed, then \(C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C=\operatorname{rbd}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=\operatorname{ri}C\,\dot\cup\,(C\cap\operatorname{rbd}C)\), while \(f=+\infty\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\setminus C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Does Not Determine Boundary Inclusion or Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional examples separating finite included boundaries, excluded boundaries, and discontinuous finite boundary values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Convexity alone does not prescribe behavior at a relative boundary. On \(\mathbb R\), the functions \[f_1=\delta_{[0,1]},\qquad f_2=\delta_{(0,1)},\qquad f_3(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&0<x\le1,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}\] are convex. The first includes both boundary points in its domain, the second excludes them, and the third is finite but not lower semicontinuous at the included boundary point \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function may include or exclude domain-boundary points, and an included finite boundary value need not be continuous or lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Convexity alone implies neither relative-boundary inclusion nor boundary lower semicontinuity.}

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard extended-real properness convention; convexity and lower semicontinuity are separate attributes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is proper precisely when \[\operatorname{dom}f

otin f(X)\). It is improper otherwise. The two elementary improper regimes are the empty-domain regime \(f\equiv+\infty\) and the negative-infinite regime \((\exists x)\ f(x)=-\infty\), which may coexist with positive-infinite values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is proper when it is finite somewhere and never equals \(-\infty\). It is improper if it is identically \(+\infty\), or if it assumes \(-\infty\) at any point. Properness does not mean that the function is finite everywhere, convex, continuous, closed, or bounded below by a finite constant.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Extended-Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-value function is proper when it is finite somewhere and never equals negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is proper when it never takes the value \(-\infty\) and is finite somewhere: \[f(x)>-\infty\quad(\forall x\in X),\qquad \operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in X\mid f(x)<+\infty\}\neq\varnothing.\] Equivalently, \(f\not\equiv+\infty\) and \(f\) has no negative-infinite value. Otherwise \(f\) is improper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is proper exactly when \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\) and \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard properness convention for extended-real-valued functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Proper extended-value convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes properness epigraphically, pointwise, through the effective domain, and as positive-infinity extension from a finite convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty] is proper if and only if \operatorname{epi}f\neq\varnothing and \operatorname{epi}f contains no vertical line. Equivalently, (\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n)\,f(x)<+\infty and (\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n)\,f(x)>-\infty. Equivalently, C=\operatorname{dom}f is nonempty and f|_C is finite; in that case C is convex and f is the extension to \mathbb{R}^n of a finite convex function on C obtained by setting f(x)=+\infty for x\notin C. A convex function that is not proper is improper.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex extended-value function is proper exactly when its epigraph is nonempty and contains no vertical line, or equivalently when it is finite somewhere and never equals negative infinity. This is also equivalent to having a nonempty effective domain on which the function is finite, with positive infinity assigned outside that domain. A convex function failing these conditions is improper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ proper}\iff\bigl[(\exists x)\,f(x)<+\infty\ \land\ (\forall x)\,f(x)>-\infty\bigr]\iff\bigl[\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\ \land\ f|_{\operatorname{dom}f}\text{ is finite}\bigr].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is a proper convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\), then there exist \(b\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\) such that \[f(x)\geq \langle x,b\rangle-\beta\qquad\text{for every }x\in\mathbb R^n.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper convex function on Euclidean space admits a finite affine function lying below it everywhere.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Epigraph Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identically positive-infinite function has an empty epigraph and is the indicator of the empty set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), \[f\equiv+\infty\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{epi}f=\varnothing.\] Equivalently, the identically positive-infinite function is the indicator \(\delta_{\varnothing}\) of the empty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\equiv+\infty\iff\operatorname{epi}f=\varnothing\iff f=\delta_{\varnothing}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-geometric characterization of the identically positive-infinite function.

notation.meaning: extended-value indicator of the empty set

knowledge_statements.title: Identically Infinite Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is identically positive infinite exactly when its effective domain is empty; under the standard convention it is convex but improper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The identically positive-infinite regime is characterized by \[f(x)=+\infty\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\] Equivalently, \[\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in X\mid f(x)<+\infty\}=\varnothing.\] Under the standard extended-value convention, this function is convex and improper.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\equiv+\infty\) if and only if \(\operatorname{dom}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The empty-effective-domain improperness regime.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Negative Infinity Need Not Reach Every Domain Boundary Point
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epigraph-convex function can equal negative infinity on almost all its domain while remaining finite at a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f(x)=\begin{cases}-\infty,&0\le x<1,\\0,&x=1,\\+\infty,&x\notin[0,1].\end{cases}\] Then \(f\) has a convex epigraph, \(\operatorname{dom}f=[0,1]\), and \(f(1)=0\). Thus a negative-infinite value need not propagate to every boundary point of the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is convex},\quad \{x:f(x)=-\infty\}=[0,1),\quad f(1)=0.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary limitation of relative-interior propagation.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Collapse to Negative Infinity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a finite-dimensional convex extended-value function takes negative infinity anywhere, it equals negative infinity throughout the relative interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be finite-dimensional and let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex with nonempty effective domain. If \(f(x_0)=-\infty\) for some \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), then \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\subseteq\{x\in X:f(x)=-\infty\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=-\infty\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional strengthening of negative-infinity propagation on the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Infinity Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard extended-real convexity convention, a negative-infinite value propagates along half-open segments toward every point whose value is below positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(t\in[0,1)\), \[f((1-t)x_0+ty)=-\infty.\] Thus a negative-infinite value propagates along each half-open segment from \(x_0\) toward a point \(y\) satisfying \(f(y)<+\infty\), and \(f\) is improper.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex under the standard extended-real convexity convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f((1-t)x_0+ty)=-\infty\) for every \(t\in[0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation of a negative-infinite value under convexity.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Conjugates of Improper Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identically positive-infinite function conjugates to negative infinity, while any negative-infinite value forces the conjugate to be identically positive infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[f^*(x^*):=\sup_{x\in X}\bigl(\langle x^*,x\rangle-f(x)\bigr).\] Under the standard rules \(a-(+\infty)=-\infty\) and \(a-(-\infty)=+\infty\) for finite \(a\), \[f\equiv+\infty\Longrightarrow f^*\equiv-\infty,\qquad (\exists x_0\in X\; f(x_0)=-\infty)\Longrightarrow f^*\equiv+\infty.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
Fenchel conjugates are permitted to be improper.
Standard subtraction of an infinite extended-real value from a finite pairing value is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\equiv+\infty\Rightarrow f^*\equiv-\infty,\qquad f(x_0)=-\infty\Rightarrow f^*\equiv+\infty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fenchel-conjugate behavior under the standard convention allowing improper conjugates.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Subdifferential in the Empty-Domain Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identically positive-infinite function has no domain point and therefore has an empty subdifferential everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the standard convention \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) whenever \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\), \[f\equiv+\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial f(x)=\varnothing\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
The convex subdifferential is empty outside the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\equiv+\infty\Longrightarrow(\forall x\in X)\ \partial f(x)=\varnothing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of supporting-subgradient certificates for the identically positive-infinite function.

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at x

knowledge_statements.title: Undefined Mixed-Infinity Arithmetic
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Opposite or cancelling infinite values make pointwise arithmetic undefined, so unrestricted convex calculus is unavailable without compatibility assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In standard extended-real arithmetic, \((+\infty)+(-\infty)\) and \((+\infty)-(+\infty)\) are undefined. A pointwise sum or difference producing either form is therefore not an extended-real-valued function there unless an additional convention is imposed. Convex-calculus formulas involving such operations require compatibility assumptions that exclude these forms.
assumptions_latex: Standard extended-real arithmetic is used, with no value assigned to indeterminate mixed-infinity forms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (+\infty)+(-\infty)\text{ and }(+\infty)-(+\infty)\text{ are undefined.}
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic obstruction to unrestricted pointwise calculus for improper extended-value functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Improperness Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneration of Fenchel conjugacy in the two principal improper extended-value regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(f^*(y)=\sup_{x\in X}(\langle y,x\rangle-f(x))\) on the algebraic dual \(X^*\). With the usual extended-real conventions, \[f\equiv+\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^*\equiv-\infty,\] whereas \[f(x_0)=-\infty\text{ for some }x_0\in X\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^*\equiv+\infty.\] Hence allowing either improperness regime makes the conjugate degenerate and places the function outside the proper convex duality framework.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An everywhere-infinite function has conjugate negative infinity, while any negative-infinite value makes the conjugate positive infinity everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space with algebraic dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Improper positive- or negative-infinity regimes produce an identically infinite conjugate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empty Subdifferential of the Identically Infinite Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of supporting-subgradient calculus in the empty-domain regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the standard convex subdifferential definition, \[\partial f(x):=\{x^*:\ f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle x^*,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\},\] with \(\partial f(x)=\varnothing\) whenever \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\). Hence \[f\equiv+\infty\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\partial f(x)=\varnothing\quad\text{for every }x\in X.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The identically positive-infinite function has no domain point and therefore has an empty subdifferential everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space paired with \(X^*\).
The subdifferential is defined only at finite-valued domain points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\equiv+\infty\Longrightarrow(\forall x\in X)\ \partial f(x)=\varnothing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-Real Indicator Encoding of Feasibility
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(C\subseteq X\), and \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimization-oriented indicator convention, assigning positive infinity outside the feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-real indicator of \(C\) is \[\delta_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] The constrained objective associated with \(g\) and \(C\) is \[F:=g+\delta_C,\qquad F(x)=\begin{cases}g(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] whenever the extended-real sum is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of \(C\) assigns zero to feasible points and \(+\infty\) to infeasible points. Adding it to an objective preserves objective values on \(C\) and excludes points outside \(C\) from finite-valued minimization. Thus a hard set constraint becomes part of an extended-real objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\inf_{x\in C}g(x)=\inf_{x\in X}(g+\delta_C)(x),\qquad \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}g(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}(g+\delta_C)(x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty).\]
\[\operatorname{dom}(g+\delta_C)=C\cap\operatorname{dom}g.\]
special_cases_latex: \[g\equiv0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname*{argmin}\delta_C=C\] when \(C\ne\varnothing\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \[C\text{ convex}\iff\delta_C\text{ convex}.\]
\[C\ne\varnothing\iff\delta_C\text{ proper}.\]
\[C\text{ closed}\iff\delta_C\text{ closed}.\]
boundary_notes: This is not the zero-one indicator used in probability or combinatorics.
If \(g(x)=-\infty\) outside \(C\), the expression \(g(x)+\delta_C(x)\) requires care because \(-\infty+(+\infty)\) is undefined.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph and Closedness of a Set Indicator
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a set indicator is the product of the set and the nonnegative vertical ray, so the indicator is lower semicontinuous exactly when the set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological vector space and \(C\subseteq X\). For the positive-infinity indicator \(\iota_C\), \[\operatorname{epi}\iota_C=C\times[0,+\infty).\] Consequently, \(\iota_C\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}\iota_C=C\times[0,+\infty)\), and \(\iota_C\) is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological structure of the positive-infinity indicator encoding.

notation.meaning: epigraph of the indicator of C

knowledge_statements.title: Convex-Set Indicators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A set indicator is zero on the set and positive infinity outside; it is convex exactly for a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The indicator of \(C\) is the extended-value function \[\iota_C(x):=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\iota_C=C\). The function \(\iota_C\) is convex exactly when \(C\) is convex; moreover, it is proper exactly when \(C\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\iota_C\) is convex if and only if \(C\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-infinity indicator convention for hard constraints.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Multiple Constraints as a Sum of Indicators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite collection of hard constraints is encoded by summing their indicators, which equals the indicator of their intersection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For sets \(F_1,\ldots,F_m\subseteq X\), with \(m\ge1\), \[\sum_{i=1}^m\iota_{F_i}=\iota_{\bigcap_{i=1}^mF_i}.\] Hence, for any objective \(g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), minimizing \(g\) subject to \(x\in F_i\) for every \(i\) is represented by minimizing \(g+\sum_{i=1}^m\iota_{F_i}\) over \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sum_{i=1}^m\iota_{F_i}=\iota_{\cap_{i=1}^mF_i}\), so the constrained and indicator-encoded minimization problems have identical values and minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-family variant of hard feasibility encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasibility Encodings
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an objective that never takes negative infinity, adding the feasible-set indicator converts constrained minimization into an equivalent unconstrained extended-value problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\iota_F(x)=0\) for \(x\in F\) and \(\iota_F(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\notin F\). Then \[\inf_{x\in F}g(x)=\inf_{x\in X}\bigl(g(x)+\iota_F(x)\bigr).\] The two formulations have the same minimizers whenever minimizers exist. If \(g\) is convex and \(F\) is convex, then \(g+\iota_F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in F}g(x)=\inf_{x\in X}(g(x)+\iota_F(x))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encoding a hard feasibility constraint in the objective.

notation.meaning: indicator function of the feasible set

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Closed Convex Restriction Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function to a closed convex set preserves lower semicontinuity and convexity, and preserves properness exactly when the set meets the original domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological vector space, let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(C\subseteq X\) be closed and convex. Then \(f+\iota_C\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, and \[f+\iota_C\text{ is proper}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\ne\varnothing.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f+\iota_C\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, and it is proper if and only if \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Properness and preservation properties for restriction to a closed convex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Restriction Encodings
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a set indicator restricts a function's effective domain to its intersection with that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The extended-value restriction of \(f\) to \(C\) is \[(f+\iota_C)(x)=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C.\end{cases}\] Its effective domain is \[\operatorname{dom}(f+\iota_C)=\operatorname{dom}f\cap C.\] If \(f\) is convex and \(C\) is convex, then the restricted encoding \(f+\iota_C\) is convex, provided the extended-real sum is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(f+\iota_C)=\operatorname{dom}f\cap C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-value representation of restricting a function to a set.

notation.meaning: restriction of f encoded by positive infinity

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex-Set Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a nonconvex set is nonconvex, so hard indicator encoding does not preserve convexity for a nonconvex feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is not convex, then its indicator \(\iota_C\) is not convex. Equivalently, indicator-based hard-constraint encoding preserves convexity only when the encoded set is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\iota_C\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact failure of convex indicator encoding for nonconvex sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity Defined Through the Epigraph
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convexity, including improper functions, is defined geometrically so that undefined arithmetic involving both infinities is avoided.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is convex if and only if \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le t\}\] is a convex subset of \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\). For a proper function this is equivalent to \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\] for every \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Extended-real convexity is the convexity of the epigraph. For proper functions, this is equivalent to the usual Jensen inequality restricted to the effective domain. The epigraph formulation remains meaningful even when direct extended-real arithmetic could contain the undefined sum \(+\infty+(-\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For proper \(f\), convexity is equivalent to convexity of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) together with the two-point Jensen inequality on that domain.
\[f\text{ concave}\iff -f\text{ convex}\iff\operatorname{hypo}f\text{ convex}.\]
special_cases_latex: \[C\text{ convex}\iff\delta_C\text{ convex}.\]
A real-valued function on a convex set satisfies the standard chord inequality exactly when its epigraph is convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every lower level set of a convex function is convex.
Linear images and intersections of epigraphs provide set-geometric tools for recognizing convexity.
boundary_notes: Convex lower level sets alone characterize quasiconvexity, not convexity.
For improper functions the epigraph definition is primary because an inequality containing both infinities may be undefined.

children.title: Ordinary Epigraphs
children.top_down_role: Epigraph geometry for real-valued functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Vertical-Fiber Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every ordinary epigraph fiber is a nonempty upward ray whose minimum recovers the function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \[\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}=[f(x),+\infty),\qquad f(x)=\min\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\] Thus every vertical line meets the epigraph in a nonempty ray with a least point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=\min\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\quad(\forall x\in X).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph reconstruction in the everywhere-finite regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph consists of points on or above a real-valued function's graph. The function is convex exactly when this set is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The ordinary epigraph of \(f\) is
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\leq t\}.\]
It contains every point lying vertically above the graph of \(f\). Moreover, \(f\) satisfies
\[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\leq \lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y)\]
for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\) if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a convex subset of \(X\times\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is convex in \(X\times\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-valued epigraph and its convexity characterization.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function is lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}.
