knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extended-real-valued functions, arithmetic conventions, and effective domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Records only the arithmetic and order conventions explicitly specified in the extract; operations such as \(\infty+(-\infty)\) are not defined here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-real-valued function is a function \(f:\mathbb E\to[-\infty,\infty]\) defined on all of \(\mathbb E\). For every finite \(a\), \(a+\infty=\infty+a=\infty\) and \(a-\infty=-\infty+a=-\infty\). If \(a>0\), then \(a\infty=\infty a=\infty\) and \(a(-\infty)=(-\infty)a=-\infty\); if \(a<0\), then \(a\infty=\infty a=-\infty\) and \(a(-\infty)=(-\infty)a=\infty\). Moreover, \(0(\pm\infty)=(\pm\infty)0=0\), \(-\infty<a<\infty\) for every finite \(a\), and \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in\mathbb E:f(x)<\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is defined everywhere on the underlying space and may take finite values or either infinity. The stated conventions govern addition of finite values to infinity, multiplication of infinity by positive, negative, or zero scalars, and the ordering of finite and infinite values. Its effective domain consists of the points where its value is strictly below positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in\mathbb E:f(x)<\infty\},\quad -\infty<a<\infty,\quad 0(\pm\infty)=(\pm\infty)0=0,\text{ with the stated sign-dependent infinite arithmetic rules.}

children.title: Extended-Value Epigraphs
children.top_down_role: Epigraph geometry incorporating effective domains and infeasible points.

knowledge_statements.title: Vertical Fibers and Epigraph Reconstruction
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite domain points have upward-ray epigraph fibers, infeasible points have empty fibers, and taking each fiber's infimum recovers the function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(x\in X\), let \(E_x:=\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\). Then \(E_x=[f(x),+\infty)\) when \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), while \(E_x=\varnothing\) otherwise. With \(\inf\varnothing:=+\infty\), \[f(x)=\inf E_x.\] Thus \(\operatorname{epi}f\) determines \(f\) uniquely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb R:(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstruction of a function taking only finite values and positive infinity from its epigraph.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Epigraph Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-value function is lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\) if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in the product space \(X\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological characterization for functions taking finite values or positive infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended-value epigraph records finite feasible values, while assigning positive infinity removes infeasible points from every finite-height slice. Convexity is equivalent to epigraph convexity, and under this codomain convention the function is proper exactly when its effective domain is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in X:f(x)<+\infty\},\qquad \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb{R}:f(x)\leq t\}.\]
Thus an infeasible point \(x\notin\operatorname{dom}f\) has no finite-height point in the epigraph. The extended-value function \(f\) is convex precisely when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is convex. It is proper precisely when \(\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\) under the stated codomain convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is convex; points outside \(\operatorname{dom}f\) contribute no finite-height epigraph points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convention using only finite values and \(+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primitive Operations on Epigraph Representations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) are extended-real functions on \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(F:X\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact identities for upper envelopes and marginal functions, with an explicit closure boundary for projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph transformation calculus consists of the identities \[\operatorname{epi}\Bigl(\sup_{i\in I}f_i\Bigr)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i\] and, for \(f(x):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,z)\), \[P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F),\quad P(x,z,t)=(x,t).\] An exact projected epigraph representation occurs when \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An upper envelope is represented by intersecting all constituent epigraphs. Eliminating auxiliary variables by partial minimization corresponds to projecting a higher-dimensional epigraph. Projection can omit boundary points, so the projected set is always contained in the marginal epigraph and its closure always contains that epigraph; exact equality requires additional attainment or closedness conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{epi}(\sup_i f_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i,\qquad P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}(\inf_zF(\cdot,z))\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x,t)\in P(\operatorname{epi}F)\iff(\exists z)\ F(x,z)\le t.\]
Exactness at a finite \(x\) includes the boundary point \((x,f(x))\) precisely when the infimum over \(z\) is attained.
special_cases_latex: For a finite maximum, \(\operatorname{epi}(\max_i f_i)=\bigcap_i\operatorname{epi}f_i\).
If \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, then it equals \(\operatorname{epi}f\).

If \(F\) is convex, its marginal \(f\) is convex, although closedness may fail without further hypotheses.

children.title: Epigraph Intersections
children.top_down_role: Intersection geometry associated with upper envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Intersection Can Be Empty Despite Common Domains
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The constant functions f_n=n are all proper closed convex functions with the same full domain, but their supremum is identically positive infinity and their epigraph intersection is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(n\in\mathbb N\), let \(f_n(x)=n\) on a nonempty real vector space \(X\). Every \(f_n\) is finite, proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and all effective domains equal \(X\). Nevertheless,
\[\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}f_n(x)=+\infty\quad(x\in X),\qquad
\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}\operatorname{epi}f_n=\varnothing.\]
Thus common-domain membership does not ensure properness of an infinite supremum; pointwise boundedness above is necessary.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a nonempty real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_n f_n\equiv+\infty\) and \(\bigcap_n\operatorname{epi}f_n=\varnothing\), although \(\operatorname{dom}f_n=X\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp properness failure for an infinite upper envelope.

knowledge_statements.title: Closedness and Properness of Epigraph Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary supremum of lower-semicontinuous functions is lower semicontinuous because its epigraph is an intersection of closed sets. Its effective domain consists of points where the family is pointwise bounded above.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=\sup_{i\in I}f_i\). If every \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i\]
is closed, so \(f\) is lower semicontinuous. Moreover,
\[\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)<+\infty\}.\]
Under the codomain convention \(f_i:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), the supremum \(f\) is proper exactly when this set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If every \(f_i\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(f=\sup_i f_i\) is lower semicontinuous; moreover, \(f\) is proper iff \(\{x:\sup_i f_i(x)<+\infty\}\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological and properness consequences for arbitrary upper envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a pointwise supremum is the intersection of the individual epigraphs. Hence arbitrary upper envelopes preserve convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the pointwise upper envelope \(f(x)=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)\), one has
\[\operatorname{epi}f=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i.\]
Consequently, an arbitrary pointwise supremum of convex functions is convex whenever it is interpreted as an extended-real function.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real vector space and \(I\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\sup_{i\in I}f_i)=\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{epi}f_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrary pointwise upper envelopes of extended-real functions.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(I\ne\varnothing\), and each \(f_i:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is defined on the same set \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).

A pair \((x,t)\) lies above the supremum exactly when it lies above every constituent function. The identity applies to arbitrary index sets and remains valid when the supremum is \(+\infty\).

If every epigraph is closed, the intersection epigraph is closed, so \(f\) is closed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal Functions and Projected Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f(x):=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,z)\), and \(P(x,z,t)=(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional projection correspondence, explicitly distinguishing exact projection, missing boundary points, and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projected epigraph set is \[E:=P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\{(x,t):(\exists z\in\mathbb R^m)\ F(x,z)\le t\}.\] It satisfies \[E\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}E.\] The representation is exact when \(E=\operatorname{epi}f\), and closed-exact when additionally \(E\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph image obtained by deleting auxiliary variables contains those thresholds attained by some auxiliary point. The marginal epigraph also contains limiting thresholds arising from unattained infima. Consequently, the projected epigraph may miss its lower boundary, but its closure contains the entire marginal epigraph. Exactness means no such boundary points are missing.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(f(x)\in\mathbb R\), \((x,f(x))\in P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) if and only if \(\inf_zF(x,z)\) is attained.
If \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, then both inclusions become equalities.
special_cases_latex: When \(m=0\), \(P\) is the identity and exactness is automatic.
If a compactness condition ensures attainment for every finite-valued fiber, the projection contains every lower-boundary point.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(F\) is convex, then \(f\) is convex.
Closedness of \(F\) alone does not ensure closedness of \(f\), because projection need not preserve closedness.
boundary_notes: The closure inclusion is not a claim that \(\operatorname{epi}f=\operatorname{cl}E\) in every improper case.
Projection preserves convexity but may destroy closedness.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure of a Linear Epigraph Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear epigraph image and the epigraph of its fiber infimum have the same closure. Lower semicontinuity recovers the marginal epigraph after closure, while equality before closure additionally requires attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax=y\}\), with the empty-fiber infimum equal to \(+\infty\), and suppose \(g\) never equals \(-\infty\). If
\[E=(A\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})(\operatorname{epi}f),\]
then
\[E\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\overline E,
\qquad \overline E=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}.\]
In particular, if \(g\) is lower semicontinuous, then \(\overline E=\operatorname{epi}g\), even when unattained fiber infima prevent \(E=\operatorname{epi}g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{(A\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})(\operatorname{epi}f)}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure-level epigraph identity when fiber minima need not be attained.

notation.meaning: linear image of the source epigraph

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Epigraph Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear epigraph image lies inside the epigraph of the fiber infimum. Equality holds exactly when every finite fiber minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Set \(g(y)=\inf\{f(x):Ax=y\}\), with the infimum of an empty set equal to \(+\infty\). Then
\[(A\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})(\operatorname{epi}f)=\{(y,t):\exists x,\ Ax=y,\ f(x)\leq t\}\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g.\]
The inclusion is equality if and only if, for every \(y\) with \(g(y)\in\mathbb{R}\), the problem \(\inf_{Ax=y}f(x)\) attains its infimum. Without attainment, the image can omit boundary points \((y,g(y))\).
assumptions_latex: \(X,Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
\(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and its fiber infimum never equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((A\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})(\operatorname{epi}f)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g\), with equality exactly when every finite fiber infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional linear images and fiberwise infimal projection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Obverse of a Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the obverse through polar-conjugate composition and an equivalent positive-scaling formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be nonnegative, closed, and convex with \(f(0)=0\), and define \(f_{\lambda}(x)=\lambda f(\lambda^{-1}x)\) for \(\lambda>0\). The obverse of \(f\) is
\[
g=(f^*)^{\circ},
\]
and it admits the representation
\[
g(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\ f_{\lambda}(x)\le1\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonnegative closed convex function vanishing at the origin, its obverse is the polar of its conjugate. Equivalently, at each point it is the infimum of the positive scales for which the scaled perspective value is at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g:=(f^*)^{\circ},\qquad g(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:\lambda f(\lambda^{-1}x)\le1\}.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Epigraphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting out an auxiliary variable produces points supported by feasible witnesses. It gives the entire marginal epigraph precisely when all finite marginal infima are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define \(g(x)=\inf_{z\in Z}F(x,z)\) and \(P(x,z,t)=(x,t)\). Then
\[P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\{(x,t):\exists z\in Z,\ F(x,z)\leq t\}\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g.\]
Equality holds if and only if each finite value \(g(x)\) is attained by some auxiliary variable \(z\). If \(F\) is convex, the projected set is convex, so exact projection implies that \(g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g\), and equality holds exactly when every finite marginal infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraph projection for marginal functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure-Level Marginal Epigraph Formula
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact closure relation for elimination when marginal infima may be unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)>-\infty\) and \(E=P(\operatorname{epi}F)\). Then
\[E\subseteq\operatorname{epi}g\subseteq\overline E,
\qquad \overline E=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}.\]
Hence, when \(g\) is lower semicontinuous,
\[\overline{P(\operatorname{epi}F)}=\operatorname{epi}g.\]
Attainment is needed only to remove the closure and obtain exact equality with the projection itself.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected epigraph and the marginal epigraph always have the same closure. If the marginal is lower semicontinuous, closing the projection recovers its epigraph; attainment is needed for equality before closure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{P(\operatorname{epi}F)}=\overline{\operatorname{epi}g}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Level Marginal Epigraph Formula
Local Level-Boundedness Closed-Projection Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform local level-boundedness in the eliminated variable prevents escaping witnesses and makes the projected epigraph exact and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\times Z\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Suppose that for every \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a compact set \(K\subset Z\) such that
\[\{z:F(x,z)\leq\alpha\}\subseteq K\qquad(x\in U).\]
If \(g(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)>-\infty\) for every \(x\), then every finite marginal value is attained, \(g\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, and
\[P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}g\]
is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(F\) is locally level-bounded in \(z\), uniformly for nearby \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every finite marginal infimum is attained and \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}g\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compactness condition preventing auxiliary witnesses from escaping near retained points.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Closed-Image Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection preserves a finite-dimensional polyhedral epigraph's polyhedrality and closedness; finite fiber infima are attained, so the projection is exactly the marginal epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:X\times Z\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper polyhedral convex and let \(g(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)>-\infty\) for every \(x\). Then \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is a polyhedron and hence is closed. Every finite value \(g(x)\) is attained, so
\[P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}g,\]
and \(g\) is polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}g\) is a closed polyhedron and \(g\) is polyhedral convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness and attainment for finite-dimensional polyhedral epigraph projection.

notation.meaning: coordinate projection deleting the auxiliary variable

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Image Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the epigraph has no nonzero recession direction invisible to the projection, its projected image is closed and exactly represents the marginal epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g(x)=\inf_{z\in Z}F(x,z)\). A sufficient closed-image condition is
\[\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker P=\{0\}.\]
Under this condition the linear image \(P(C)\) is closed. Its vertical sections are upward closed, and every finite fiber infimum is attained; consequently,
\[P(C)=\operatorname{epi}g.\]
Thus \(g\) is lower semicontinuous and convex. The condition is sufficient rather than necessary; other compactness or coercivity hypotheses can also ensure closedness and attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times Z\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\operatorname{rec}C\cap\ker P=\{0\}\), then \(P(C)\) is closed and equals \(\operatorname{epi}g\) for \(g(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient finite-dimensional recession condition for closed projection.

notation.meaning: projection onto the retained variable and height

knowledge_statements.title: Escaping-Witness Characterization of Projection Nonclosedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed finite-dimensional lifted set, a missing limit point of its projection forces every compatible auxiliary-witness sequence to escape to infinity; any bounded witness subsequence restores membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\times Z\) be closed, where \(X,Z\) are finite-dimensional, and let \(P(x,z)=x\). Suppose \(x_n\to\bar x\), with \(x_n\in P(C)\) and \(\bar x\notin P(C)\). Then every witness sequence \((z_n)\) satisfying \((x_n,z_n)\in C\) has no bounded subsequence. Conversely, the existence of a bounded witness subsequence implies \(\bar x\in P(C)\). Thus a missing projected limit requires all compatible witnesses to escape to infinity.
assumptions_latex: \(x_n\to\bar x\), with \(x_n\in P(C)\) and \(\bar x\notin P(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \((z_n)\) with \((x_n,z_n)\in C\) has no bounded subsequence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential mechanism behind failure of closedness under coordinate elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Closure Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex epigraph of one-over-x on the positive axis projects to the open positive axis, showing that linear projections need not preserve closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set
\[C=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x>0,\ t\geq 1/x\}\]
is the epigraph of the extended-value function equal to \(1/x\) for \(x>0\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. It is closed and convex. Nevertheless, under \(P(x,t)=x\),
\[P(C)=(0,+\infty),\]
which is not closed. Hence a linear projection of a closed convex epigraph need not be closed; escaping auxiliary or height coordinates can hide convergence to a missing boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex, but \(P(C)=(0,+\infty)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete finite-dimensional failure of closedness under linear projection.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact, Attained, and Closure-Exact Epigraph Lifts
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R\), and \(P(x,z,t)=(x,t)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional auxiliary-variable epigraph representations; the taxonomy records projection exactness rather than a particular cone or modeling language.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An auxiliary-variable lift of \(f\) is a set \(K\) satisfying at least \[P(K)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(K).\] It is exact when \(P(K)=\operatorname{epi}f\), closure-exact when \(\operatorname{cl}P(K)=\operatorname{epi}f\), and fiber-attained when every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) admits \(z\) with \((x,z,f(x))\in K\). For a lifted function \(F\), the canonical choice is \(K=\operatorname{epi}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lift represents an epigraph using extra variables and projection. An exact lift projects to the epigraph itself. A closure-exact lift may omit boundary points but recovers the epigraph after closure. A fiber-attained lift contains an auxiliary witness at every finite lower-boundary point. These distinctions isolate the modeling issue caused by unattained partial infima.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K=\operatorname{epi}F,\quad f(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P(K)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(K).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[(x,t)\in P(K)\iff(\exists z)\ (x,z,t)\in K.\]
For canonical epigraph lifts, fiber attainment implies inclusion of every finite lower-boundary point.
special_cases_latex: A conic lift has \(K\) described by affine equations and membership in a convex cone.
An inequality lift has \(K=\{(x,z,t):G_j(x,z,t)\le0,\ j=1,\ldots,r\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity of \(K\) implies convexity of its projection.
Closed convex \(K\) need not have closed projection, so exact and closure-exact lifts are distinct.
boundary_notes: This taxonomy does not assert finite representability or computational tractability.
The inspected source supports projection and attainment distinctions but does not present this exact three-name taxonomy.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph Characterization of Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to extended-real-valued functions on finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}, let \operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)<+\infty\}, and define \operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ t\ge f(x)\}. Then f is convex if and only if \operatorname{epi}f is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real-valued function on Euclidean space, the usual convexity inequality holds on its effective domain if and only if its epigraph is a convex subset of the product space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff \operatorname{epi}f\text{ is convex}.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraphical Lifts
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An epigraphical lift represents an epigraph as the projection of a higher-dimensional feasible set. Convex lifts preserve convexity, but closed lifts may have nonclosed projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The set \(K\) is an exact epigraphical lift of \(f\) if
\[\operatorname{epi}f=P(K)=\{(x,t):\exists z\in Z,\ (x,z,t)\in K\}.\]
The variable \(z\) is auxiliary and disappears under projection. If \(K\) is convex, then \(P(K)\), and therefore \(\operatorname{epi}f\), is convex. If \(K\) is also closed, its projection need not be closed without an additional closed-image condition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is an exact epigraphical lift of \(f\) when \(\operatorname{epi}f=P(K)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact auxiliary-variable representation of an epigraph.

notation.meaning: projection onto original variables and epigraph height

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Characterization of Full Graphs
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The full graph of a mapping between real vector spaces is convex exactly when the mapping is affine; every genuinely nonlinear full-domain graph equality is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X,Z\) be real vector spaces and \(h:X\to Z\). Then
\[\operatorname{gra}h\text{ is convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h\text{ is affine}.\]
Consequently, the full-domain equality constraint \(z=h(x)\) is convex precisely when \(h\) is affine.
assumptions_latex: \(h:X\to Z\) is defined on all of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{gra}h\) is convex if and only if \(h\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp convexity boundary for graph equalities defined on an entire real vector space.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph-Based Lifts
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A graph-based lift introduces a variable constrained to equal a mapping of the original variable. The representation is exact; when the spaces are real vector spaces, nonlinear graph equalities can destroy convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
One has the exact identity
\[\operatorname{epi}f=P\bigl(\{(x,z,t)\in X\times Z\times\mathbb{R}:z=h(x),\ \Phi(x,z)\leq t\}\bigr).\]
Thus the equality \(z=h(x)\) gives a graph-based lift. If \(h\) is affine and \(\Phi\) is convex, the lifted set is convex. For a general nonlinear \(h\), the identity remains exact, but the graph constraint can be nonconvex even when the composite function \(f\) happens to be convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is the projection of the lifted constraints \(z=h(x)\) and \(\Phi(x,z)\leq t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifts imposing an auxiliary variable through a graph equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Auxiliary-Variable Formulations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exact lift converts minimizing a function into minimizing the height variable over lifted constraints. Lifted optima project to original optima, and every finite-valued original minimizer has a lifted boundary witness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Exactness of the lift yields
\[\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\exists x\in S,\ \exists z\in Z,\ (x,z,t)\in K\},\]
where the infimum of the empty set is \(+\infty\). If the lifted problem attains an optimum \((x^\star,z^\star,t^\star)\), then \(x^\star\) solves the original problem and \(t^\star=f(x^\star)\). Conversely, if \(x^\star\in S\) is an original minimizer and \(f(x^\star)\in\mathbb{R}\), exactness provides \(z^\star\in Z\) such that \((x^\star,z^\star,f(x^\star))\in K\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\subseteq X\times Z\times\mathbb{R}\) is an exact epigraphical lift of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in S}f(x)=\inf\{t\in\mathbb{R}:\exists x\in S,\ \exists z\in Z,\ (x,z,t)\in K\}\), with the infimum of the empty set equal to \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization reformulation induced by an exact epigraphical lift.

knowledge_statements.title: Lift Exactness Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality after closure may preserve the optimal infimum but can lose boundary witnesses and minimizers. Exactness requires the projected lift itself to equal the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Writing \(E=P(K)\), exactness means
\[E=\operatorname{epi}f.\]
If only \(\overline{E}=\operatorname{epi}f\), the lift is closure-exact but not necessarily exact. In that case minimizing the continuous height coordinate over \(E\) has the same infimum as minimizing it over \(\operatorname{epi}f\), provided the infimum is finite, yet \(E\) may omit every point \((x,f(x))\) at an optimal boundary. Hence optimal values can agree while lifted minimizers or boundary certificates fail to exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The lift is exact iff \(P(K)=\operatorname{epi}f\); equality only after closure is insufficient for boundary-witness and minimizer equivalence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact projection from equality merely after closure.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concavity as Convexity Under Sign Reversal
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The sign reversal uses \(-(+\infty)=-\infty\) and \(-(-\infty)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real sign reversal connecting convex epigraph geometry with concave hypograph geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is concave by definition when \(-f\) is convex. Equivalently, \[\operatorname{hypo}f:=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb R:t\le f(x)\}\] is convex. The reflection \(R(x,t)=(x,-t)\) satisfies \[R(\operatorname{hypo}f)=\operatorname{epi}(-f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Concavity is convexity after multiplying function values by \(-1\). Geometrically, reflecting the hypograph of \(f\) across the zero-height hyperplane produces the epigraph of \(-f\). Thus convex-function statements based solely on epigraph geometry have sign-reversed concave counterparts based on hypographs.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ concave}\iff -f\text{ convex}\iff\operatorname{hypo}f\text{ convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite-valued \(f\), concavity is equivalent to \[f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\ge\lambda f(x)+(1-\lambda)f(y).\]
\[\{x:f(x)\ge\alpha\}=\{x:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{hypo}f\}.\]
special_cases_latex: Affine functions are both convex and concave.
Maximizing a concave function \(f\) is equivalent to minimizing the convex function \(-f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Upper level sets of a concave function are convex.
Upper semicontinuity of \(f\) corresponds to lower semicontinuity of \(-f\).
boundary_notes: Negating an extended-real function exchanges positive and negative infinity, so properness conventions must be transformed consistently.
A function can be both convex and concave only under additional domain and finiteness conditions before the usual affine conclusion applies.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Partial Closure Preserves Saddle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the curvature and closedness properties of the two variablewise closure operations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every concave-convex function K on \mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n, both \operatorname{cl}_1K and \operatorname{cl}_2K are concave-convex; moreover, \operatorname{cl}_1K is concave-closed and \operatorname{cl}_2K is convex-closed. Analogously, the corresponding partial closures of a convex-concave function preserve convex-concavity and have the respective closedness properties.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closing a concave-convex function in either variable preserves its saddle structure. Closure in the first, concave variable yields a concave-closed function, while closure in the second, convex variable yields a convex-closed function. The curvature-reversed version also holds.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Characterization of Concavity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is concave exactly when its hypograph is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a function \(g:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) on a convex subset \(C\) of a real vector space, define \[\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb R:t\leq g(x)\}.\] Then \(g\) is concave on \(C\) if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
Extended-real concavity uses the established lower-infinite convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is concave on }C\iff\operatorname{hypo}g\text{ is convex}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Function-height geometry without duplicating the sibling's sign-reversal correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Hypographs and Upper Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Upper semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of the hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a topological space and \(g:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Then \(g\) is upper semicontinuous if and only if \[\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:t\leq g(x)\}\] is closed in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: The height coordinate carries its usual topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\text{ is upper semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{hypo}g\text{ is closed}.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological hypograph characterization for extended-real functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypograph Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric characterization of concavity and upper semicontinuity by the hypograph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be a real topological vector space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be convex with its subspace topology, and let \(g:C\to[-\infty,+\infty)\). Define \[\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t)\in C\times\mathbb R:t\le g(x)\}.\] Then \(g\) is concave on \(C\) if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) is convex. Moreover, \(g\) is upper semicontinuous relative to \(C\) if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) is closed in \(C\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is concave exactly when its hypograph is convex, and it is upper semicontinuous on its domain exactly when its hypograph is relatively closed in the domain times the real line.
assumptions_latex: \(E\) is a real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq E\) is convex and has the subspace topology.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is concave if and only if \(\operatorname{hypo}g\) is convex, and it is upper semicontinuous relative to \(C\) if and only if its hypograph is closed in \(C\times\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of the Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper concave function has a nonempty convex effective domain and is finite-valued and concave there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g:C\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) is proper and concave, then \[\operatorname{dom}g=\{x\in C:g(x)>-\infty\}\] is a nonempty convex set, and the restriction of \(g\) to \(\operatorname{dom}g\) is finite-valued and concave.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is proper concave under the lower-infinite convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{dom}g\text{ is nonempty and convex}.

knowledge_statements.title: Concave Function Class
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A concave function lies above every chord of its graph. It is proper when it never equals positive infinity and is finite somewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(g:C\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) is concave if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), whenever the right-hand side is defined, \[g((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\geq(1-\lambda)g(x)+\lambda g(y).\] It is proper concave if \(g\) never takes \(+\infty\) and is not identically \(-\infty\). Equivalently, its effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{x\in C:g(x)>-\infty\}\) is nonempty and it is finite or \(-\infty\) everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\geq(1-\lambda)g(x)+\lambda g(y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real concavity with the usual lower-infinite value convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Concave-Convex and Convex-Concave Saddle Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines saddle functions through separate concavity and convexity in their two arguments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m, D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, and K:C\times D\to[-\infty,+\infty]. The function K is concave-convex if u\mapsto K(u,v) is concave on C for every v\in D and v\mapsto K(u,v) is convex on D for every u\in C. A convex-concave function is defined by reversing the two curvature requirements. Functions of either type are called saddle functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function on a product domain is concave-convex when every slice in the first variable is concave and every slice in the second variable is convex. Reversing the curvature requirements gives a convex-concave function; both types are saddle functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is concave-convex}\iff(\forall v\in D,\ K(\cdot,v)\text{ is concave on }C)\land(\forall u\in C,\ K(u,\cdot)\text{ is convex on }D).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate and Closure Invariance of a Convex–Concave Pairing

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be convex and g be concave on \mathbb{R}^n. If \langle f,g\rangle exists, then \langle f^*,g^*\rangle exists and \langle f^*,g^*\rangle=-\langle f,g\rangle. Moreover, \langle\operatorname{cl}f,\operatorname{cl}g\rangle exists and equals \langle f,g\rangle.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient of a Concave Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the source's concave subgradient convention, commonly called a supergradient; the defining affine function is a global upper bound on the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f\) be concave and \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). A vector \(g\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) in the concave convention if
\[
f(y)\le f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in\operatorname{dom}f.
\]
Under this notation one may write \(g\in\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a concave function, a subgradient at a domain point is a vector whose affine support through that point globally upper-bounds the function on its domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: g\in\nabla f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f(y)\le f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\quad\forall y\in\operatorname{dom}f.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Reversal Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negating function values bijectively converts concave functions to convex functions, preserves properness, and reflects the hypograph into the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), define \(f=-g\) pointwise using \(-(-\infty)=+\infty\) and \(-(+\infty)=-\infty\). Then \[g\text{ is concave on }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f=-g\text{ is convex on }C.\] Properness is preserved under this correspondence. Moreover, under the reflection \(R:X\times\mathbb R\to X\times\mathbb R\) given by \(R(x,t)=(x,-t)\), one has \[R(\operatorname{hypo}g)=\operatorname{epi}(-g).\] Thus hypograph convexity and closedness translate into the corresponding epigraph properties.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\text{ is concave}\iff -g\text{ is convex}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise sign reversal between extended-real concave and convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Value Concave Conventions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-value concave function may equal negative infinity outside its nonempty effective domain, but never positive infinity; negation gives the usual proper convex convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-value concave function is written \(g:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), with \(\operatorname{dom}g=\{x\in X:g(x)>-\infty\}\). It is proper when \(\operatorname{dom}g\neq\varnothing\) and \(g(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\in X\); hence a proper concave function may take \(-\infty\) but not \(+\infty\). Its hypograph is \[\operatorname{hypo}g=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:t\leq g(x)\}.\] Under sign reversal, \(-(-\infty)=+\infty\), so \(-g\) follows the standard proper extended-value convex convention.
assumptions_latex: Extended-real arithmetic is used only when the resulting expression is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is proper concave exactly when \(-g\) is proper convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conventions compatible with sign reversal and proper convex analysis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Threshold-Indexed Level-Set Encoding
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete real-threshold families. A single level set or a sparse threshold sample generally loses information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The weak and strict lower level sets of \(f\) at height \(\alpha\) are \[L_f(\alpha):=\{x\in X:f(x)\le\alpha\},\qquad L_f^{<}(\alpha):=\{x\in X:f(x)<\alpha\}.\] The weak upper level set is \[U_f(\alpha):=\{x\in X:f(x)\ge\alpha\}.\] The complete lower-level representation is the indexed family \((L_f(\alpha))_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A level-set representation records which points pass each threshold. Weak lower levels use \(f(x)\le\alpha\), strict lower levels use \(f(x)<\alpha\), and upper levels reverse the inequality. The complete weak lower-level family is nested and, with all real thresholds present, determines every extended-real value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\alpha\le\beta\Longrightarrow L_f(\alpha)\subseteq L_f(\beta),\qquad f(x)=\inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x\in L_f(\alpha)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[L_f(\alpha)=\{x:(x,\alpha)\in\operatorname{epi}f\}.\]
\[L_f^{<}(\alpha)=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}L_f(\beta).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f(x)=+\infty\), then \(x\) belongs to no finite lower level set.
If \(f(x)=-\infty\), then \(x\) belongs to every finite lower level set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity of \(f\) implies convexity of all lower level sets.
Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of all weak lower level sets on \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: Convexity of every lower level set defines quasiconvexity and does not imply convexity.
Reparameterizing function values by a strictly increasing map preserves the ordering of levels but changes their numerical labels.

knowledge_statements.title: Sublevel-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel sets grow with their threshold. Convex functions have convex sublevels, and convexity of every sublevel exactly characterizes quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), let \(L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\). These sets are nested: if \(\alpha\leq\beta\), then \(L_\alpha(f)\subseteq L_\beta(f)\). If \(f\) is convex, every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is convex. More generally, \(f\) is quasiconvex if and only if every sublevel set is convex, equivalently if \[f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\] for all \(x,y\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconvex exactly when every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested convex sublevels for convex and quasiconvex functions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nested Sublevel Geometry and Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is convex and \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak lower level sets; convexity of the family characterizes quasiconvexity, while convex functions form a stricter subclass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), define \[L_f(\alpha):=\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}.\] The family is increasing: \(\alpha\le\beta\Rightarrow L_f(\alpha)\subseteq L_f(\beta)\). The function \(f\) is quasiconvex precisely when every \(L_f(\alpha)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sublevel sets form a nested family indexed by height. Quasiconvexity means that every member of this family is convex. Equivalently, the value at an interior point of any segment does not exceed the larger endpoint value. Every convex function is quasiconvex, but sublevel geometry alone does not retain the linear interpolation bound that distinguishes convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ quasiconvex}\iff(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\ L_f(\alpha)\text{ is convex}\iff f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\] for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(\lambda\in(0,1)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[L_f(\alpha)=\operatorname{proj}_C\bigl(\operatorname{epi}f\cap(C\times\{\alpha\})\bigr).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then all \(L_f(\alpha)\) are convex.
For an indicator \(\delta_D\), the nonempty finite-height sublevel sets at \(\alpha\ge0\) equal \(D\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The intersection of any collection of sublevel sets at fixed threshold remains convex when \(f\) is quasiconvex.
Pointwise suprema of quasiconvex functions are quasiconvex because their sublevel sets are intersections.
boundary_notes: Quasiconvexity does not imply convexity; nonlinear increasing transformations can preserve sublevel geometry.
Strict sublevel sets and weak sublevel sets have different topological behavior at threshold values.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of strict and nonstrict sublevel sets

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed, Bounded, Compact, and Recession Level Regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(L_f(\alpha)=\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional topology and asymptotics of weak lower level sets; compactness is equivalent to closedness plus boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The level family is closed when \((\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\ L_f(\alpha)\) is closed, level-bounded when every \(L_f(\alpha)\) is bounded, and level-compact when every \(L_f(\alpha)\) is compact. The function is coercive when \[\|x_k\|\to\infty\Longrightarrow f(x_k)\to+\infty.\] For a closed proper convex \(f\), every nonempty level has the common recession cone \(R_f:=\operatorname{rec}L_f(\alpha)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Level-set topology separates closedness from boundedness. Closed levels encode lower semicontinuity; bounded levels encode coercive asymptotic growth; in finite dimensions their conjunction gives compact levels. For a closed proper convex function, all nonempty levels share one recession cone, which records directions along which the function does not force escape from a level.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ lower semicontinuous}\iff(\forall\alpha)\ L_f(\alpha)\text{ closed},\qquad f\text{ coercive}\iff(\forall\alpha)\ L_f(\alpha)\text{ bounded}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity plus coercivity is equivalent to level compactness.
For closed proper convex \(f\), \(R_f=\{0\}\) is equivalent to boundedness of every nonempty level set.
special_cases_latex: An empty level set is both closed and bounded.
If one nonempty level of a closed proper convex function is compact, then all its nonempty level sets are compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: A lower-semicontinuous level-bounded proper function attains its minimum in finite dimensions.
Nonzero directions in \(R_f\) identify asymptotic nonascent directions.
boundary_notes: The equivalence between compactness and closedness plus boundedness is finite-dimensional.
The common-recession-cone assertion requires closed proper convexity and nonempty levels.

notation.meaning: Common recession cone of the nonempty lower level sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Semicontinuity Does Not Open Strict Sublevels
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a closed half-line is lower semicontinuous and convex, yet its strict sublevel at level one is not open.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=[0,+\infty)\subset\mathbb R\) and \(f=\iota_C\), where \(\iota_C(x)=0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) otherwise. Then \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, but \[\{x:f(x)<1\}=C=[0,+\infty)\] is not open. Thus lower semicontinuity does not imply openness of strict sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex while \(\{f<1\}=[0,+\infty)\) is not open.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp topological boundary for strict sublevels of lower-semicontinuous convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Sublevel Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strict sublevel is the union of all ordinary sublevels at smaller thresholds. Convexity preserves its convexity, while upper semicontinuity makes it open.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the strict sublevel set is \(S_\alpha^{<}(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)<\alpha\}\). It satisfies the exact threshold representation \[S_\alpha^{<}(f)=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\beta\}=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}L_\beta(f).\] If \(f\) is convex, then \(S_\alpha^{<}(f)\) is convex. If \(f\) is upper semicontinuous, strict sublevels are open; lower semicontinuity alone instead controls the closedness of ordinary sublevels and does not generally make strict sublevels open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S_\alpha^{<}(f)=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}L_\beta(f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict sublevels and their relation to ordinary sublevels.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Sublevel Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of every sublevel set, or equivalently of the epigraph. Convexity additionally makes those sublevels convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), its sublevel set \[L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\] is closed in \(X\). Equivalently, its epigraph \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,t)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq t\}\) is closed in the product topology. Consequently, a lower-semicontinuous convex function has closed convex sublevel sets at every real threshold.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is lower semicontinuous exactly when every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological characterization of lower semicontinuity by sublevels.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity Is Preserved by Closed Convex Restriction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The restricting set must be a closed convex subset of the original domain set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n and let f:Q\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} have a closed convex epigraph \operatorname{epi}(f;Q)=\{(x,t)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}:x\in Q,\ t\ge f(x)\}. If Q_1\subseteq Q is closed and convex, then f|_{Q_1} is closed and convex on Q_1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restricting a function with a closed convex epigraph on Q to a closed convex subset of Q preserves closed convexity.
assumptions_latex: \operatorname{epi}(f;Q)\text{ is a closed convex subset of }\mathbb{R}^{n+1}
Q_1\subseteq Q\text{ is closed and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f|_{Q_1}\text{ is closed and convex on }Q_1.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment on Closed Sets under Coercivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum attainment for a proper closed coercive function over a closed feasible set; neither the function nor the feasible set is assumed convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{E}\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper, closed, and coercive. Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{E}\) be nonempty and closed with \(S\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Then there exists \(\bar x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}f\) such that \(f(\bar x)=\min_{x\in S}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed coercive extended-real-valued function attains its minimum on every nonempty closed set intersecting its effective domain.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar x\in S\cap\operatorname{dom}f:\ f(\bar x)=\min_{x\in S}f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Consequences of Closed Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A compound theorem with separate additional hypotheses for its optimization consequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be a closed convex function. Then: (i) if x_k\in\operatorname{dom}f and x_k\to\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f, then \liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\ge f(\bar x); (ii) if x_k\in\operatorname{dom}f and x_k\to\bar x\notin\operatorname{dom}f, then f(x_k)\to+\infty; (iii) for every \beta\in\mathbb{R}, \{x:f(x)\le\beta\} is empty or closed and convex; (iv) if f is closed and convex on Q and every set \{x\in Q:f(x)\le\beta\} is bounded, then \min_{x\in Q}f(x) has an optimal solution; (v) if f is closed and convex on Q and X^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in Q}f(x) is nonempty and bounded, then every set \{x\in Q:f(x)\le\beta\} is empty or bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function is sequentially lower semicontinuous at points of its domain, diverges to positive infinity along domain sequences converging outside the domain, and has empty or closed convex sublevel sets. On a set where it is closed and convex, boundedness of all constrained sublevel sets guarantees attainment. Conversely, a nonempty bounded minimizer set guarantees that every constrained sublevel set is empty or bounded.
assumptions_latex: f\text{ is a closed convex function}
\text{For (iv), }f\text{ is closed and convex on }Q\text{ and }\{x\in Q:f(x)\le\beta\}\text{ is bounded for every }\beta\in\mathbb{R}
\text{For (v), }f\text{ is closed and convex on }Q\text{ and }X^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in Q}f(x)\text{ is nonempty and bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Properties (i)--(v) in the statement hold under their stated hypotheses.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity on a Convex Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines relative closed convexity through the constrained epigraph and the full-domain specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be extended-real-valued and let Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be convex with Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f. Define \operatorname{epi}_Q(f)=\{(x,t)\in Q\times\mathbb{R}:t\ge f(x)\}. The function f is closed and convex on Q when \operatorname{epi}_Q(f) is a closed convex subset of \mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}. If Q=\operatorname{dom}f, then f is called a closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is closed and convex on a convex subset of its effective domain when its epigraph restricted to that set is closed and convex. Taking the set to be the effective domain gives the definition of a closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and convex on }Q\iff\operatorname{epi}_Q(f)\text{ is closed and convex};\quad Q=\operatorname{dom}f\Rightarrow f\text{ is a closed convex function}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent Characterizations of Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional characterization for an arbitrary extended-real-valued function; convexity is not assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(f\) is lower semicontinuous on \(\mathbb{R}^n\); (ii) \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is closed for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\); and (iii) \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in \(\mathbb{R}^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any extended-real-valued function on finite-dimensional Euclidean space, lower semicontinuity, closedness of every real sublevel set, and closedness of the epigraph are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\bigl(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb{R},\ \{x:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\text{ is closed}\bigr)\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sequential, Level-Set, and Attainment Properties of Closed Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Collects five regularity and level-boundedness consequences, including their distinct conditional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be a closed convex function. (i) If x_k\in\operatorname{dom}f and x_k\to\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f, then \liminf_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)\ge f(\bar x). (ii) If x_k\in\operatorname{dom}f and x_k\to\bar x\notin\operatorname{dom}f, then \lim_{k\to\infty}f(x_k)=+\infty. (iii) For every \alpha, \{x:f(x)\le\alpha\} is empty or closed and convex. (iv) If f is closed and convex on Q and every constrained level set \{x\in Q:f(x)\le\alpha\} is bounded, then \operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in Q}f(x)\ne\varnothing. (v) If f is closed and convex on Q and X^*=\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in Q}f(x) is nonempty and bounded, then every constrained level set is empty or bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed convex function is sequentially lower semicontinuous on its domain and diverges to positive infinity along domain sequences approaching a point outside the domain. Its level sets are empty or closed and convex. On a set Q, boundedness of every constrained level set guarantees attainment; conversely, a nonempty bounded optimal set guarantees that every constrained level set is empty or bounded.
assumptions_latex: \text{The attainment and boundedness clauses use their stated additional assumptions on }Q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \liminf f(x_k)\ge f(\bar x)\text{ inside the domain},\quad f(x_k)\to+\infty\text{ at exterior limits},\quad \text{and clauses (iii)--(v) hold}

knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Level Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All sublevels strictly above the infimum have the same recession directions, namely directions where the recession function is nonpositive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) with \(\inf f<\alpha<+infty\). Then the asymptotic directions of this nonempty sublevel set are independent of \(\alpha\) and satisfy \[\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha(f)=\{d\in X:f^\infty(d)\leq0\},\] where \(f^\infty(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}(f(x+d)-f(x))\) is the recession function. Hence every direction along which \(f\) is nonincreasing at infinity is precisely a recession direction of each sublevel strictly above \(\inf f\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha(f)=\{d:f^\infty(d)\leq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession geometry of nonminimal sublevels in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Classification at the Infimum Threshold
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite infimum the strict sublevel is empty and the ordinary sublevel is the minimizer set, so a closure gap occurs exactly when a minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(m=\inf_X f\in\mathbb R\). Then \(\{x:f(x)<m\}=\varnothing\) and \(\{x:f(x)\le m\}=\operatorname{argmin}f\). Consequently, \[\overline{\{f<m\}}=\{f\le m\}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing.\] Hence a closure gap at the finite infimum occurs exactly when the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\{f<m\}}=\{f\le m\}\) if and only if \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Completes the seed's minimal-threshold failure boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Threshold Closure Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Above the infimum, closing a strict sublevel gives the ordinary sublevel. At the minimum threshold this can fail, as for the squared function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha>\inf f\), convexity and lower semicontinuity give \[\overline{\{x\in X:f(x)<\alpha\}}=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}.\] The restriction \(\alpha>\inf f\) is essential. For example, if \(f(x)=x^2\) on \(\mathbb R\) and \(\alpha=\inf f=0\), then \(\{x:f(x)<0\}=\varnothing\), while \(\{x:f(x)\leq0\}=\{0\}\). Thus closed and strict sublevels can exhibit a closure gap exactly at a minimal threshold.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\{f<\alpha\}}=\{f\leq\alpha\}\) for \(\alpha>\inf f\), but this may fail at \(\alpha=\inf f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp closure equality above the infimum and its failure at the minimum level.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Levels of the Reconstructed Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The strict sublevel of a function reconstructed from a nested family is exactly the union of the family members below that threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((C_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\) be increasing and define \(f_C(x)=\inf\{\alpha:x\in C_\alpha\}\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Then, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[\{x:f_C(x)<\alpha\}=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}C_\beta.\] Thus reconstruction automatically left-regularizes the family when viewed through strict sublevels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{f_C<\alpha\}=\bigcup_{\beta<\alpha}C_\beta\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complements the seed's non-strict-level reconstruction formula.

knowledge_statements.title: Reconstruction from Level Families
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nested family reconstructs a function by the first threshold containing each point. Exact recovery requires right-continuity under intersection; convex or closed family members respectively yield quasiconvexity or lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f_C:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f_C(x)=\inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x\in C_\alpha\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Then, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \[\{x\in X:f_C(x)\leq\alpha\}=\bigcap_{\beta>\alpha}C_\beta.\] Consequently, the original family is recovered exactly as the sublevel family of \(f_C\) if and only if \[C_\alpha=\bigcap_{\beta>\alpha}C_\beta\] for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). If every \(C_\alpha\) is convex, then \(f_C\) is quasiconvex; if every \(C_\alpha\) is closed in a topology on \(X\), then \(f_C\) is lower semicontinuous in that topology.
assumptions_latex: \((C_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\) is an increasing family of subsets of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:f_C(x)\leq\alpha\}=\bigcap_{\beta>\alpha}C_\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical reconstruction from nested families and the required right-continuity condition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reconstruction from a Compatible Nested Level Family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(X\) is a set and \((C_\alpha)_{\alpha\in\mathbb R}\) is a family of subsets of \(X\). Adopt \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\) and allow an infimum of \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-theoretic reconstruction from all real thresholds; convexity or closedness is inherited only when imposed on the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family is lower-level compatible when \[\alpha\le\beta\Longrightarrow C_\alpha\subseteq C_\beta,\qquad C_\alpha=\bigcap_{\beta>\alpha}C_\beta\quad(\alpha\in\mathbb R).\] Its reconstructed function is \[f_C(x):=\inf\{\alpha\in\mathbb R:x\in C_\alpha\}.\] Under the compatibility conditions, \[C_\alpha=\{x\in X:f_C(x)\le\alpha\}\quad(\alpha\in\mathbb R).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete nested family reconstructs a function by assigning each point the first threshold at which it enters the family. Right-continuity in the threshold variable, expressed as \(C_\alpha=\bigcap_{eta>\alpha}C_\beta\), ensures that entry at a limiting threshold is recorded by the weak level set. With that condition, the reconstructed function has exactly the prescribed family as its weak lower levels.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_C(x)=\inf\{\alpha:x\in C_\alpha\},\qquad L_{f_C}(\alpha)=C_\alpha.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in C_\alpha\iff f_C(x)\le\alpha.\]
The family epigraph \(E_C:=\{(x,\alpha):x\in C_\alpha\}\) is upward closed in its second coordinate and equals \(\operatorname{epi}f_C\) when every vertical fiber contains its lower endpoint.
special_cases_latex: If every \(C_\alpha\) is convex, then \(f_C\) is quasiconvex.
If every \(C_\alpha\) is closed in a topological space, then \(f_C\) is lower semicontinuous under the usual level-set characterization.
immediate_consequences_latex: Two extended-real functions with identical weak lower level sets at every real threshold are equal.
If \(x\) belongs to no \(C_\alpha\), then \(f_C(x)=+\infty\); if it belongs to every \(C_\alpha\), then \(f_C(x)=-\infty\).
boundary_notes: Nestedness without threshold right-continuity may reconstruct only a regularized family and can fail to reproduce boundary membership.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge-Like Extended-Real-Valued Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines gauge-likeness through the origin minimum and proportionality of every finite sublevel set strictly above that minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An extended-real-valued function \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) is gauge-like if \(f(0)=\inf_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) and there exists a set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) such that, for every \(\alpha\) with \(f(0)<\alpha<+\infty\), there exists \(t_\alpha>0\) satisfying \(\{x\in\mathbb R^n\mid f(x)\le \alpha\}=t_\alpha C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real-valued function is gauge-like when its value at the origin is its infimum and every finite sublevel set strictly above that value is a positive rescaling of one fixed set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is gauge-like}\iff f(0)=\inf f\text{ and }\exists C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\ \forall\alpha\in(f(0),+\infty)\ \exists t_\alpha>0:\ \{f\le\alpha\}=t_\alpha C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical set-generated convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, and write \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) and \(\|\cdot\|\) for its inner product and norm. Extended-real functions take values in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space definition collecting the principal convex functions canonically encoded by a set; the gauge requires a closed convex set containing the origin, and metric projection requires closed convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The canonical set-generated functions associated with \(C\) are the indicator \[\iota_C(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\in C,\\+\infty,&x\notin C,\end{cases}\] the support function \[\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{c\in C}\langle c,u\rangle,\] and the distance function \[d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|.\] If \(C\) is closed, convex, and \(0\in C\), its gauge is \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] If \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, the infimum defining \(d_C\) is attained at the unique metric projection \(P_Cx\), so \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|\). These constructions encode membership, linear optimization values, radial scaling, and metric displacement, respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty subset \(C\) of a Hilbert space, its indicator is zero on \(C\) and positive infinity elsewhere; its support function is the supremum of the inner product with points of \(C\); and its distance function is the infimum of the norm distance to \(C\). When \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains the origin, its gauge is the least positive scaling factor whose dilation of \(C\) contains the argument. When \(C\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, the distance is attained at the unique metric projection.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\mapsto(\iota_C,\sigma_C,d_C)\), together with \(C\mapsto\gamma_C\) when \(C\) is closed, convex, and contains \(0\), is the canonical family of set-generated convex-function encodings.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For nonempty \(C\), \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\); hence the support function retains exactly the closed convex hull of \(C\).
For nonempty closed convex \(C\), \(d_C(x)=0\iff x\in C\), and \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C=\{c\}\), then \(\sigma_C(u)=\langle c,u\rangle\) and \(d_C(x)=\|x-c\|\).
If \(C\) is a closed linear subspace, \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|\) is the norm of the orthogonal residual.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\iota_C\) is convex exactly when \(C\) is convex, and lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed.
\(\sigma_C\) is convex, lower semicontinuous, and positively homogeneous for every nonempty \(C\).
boundary_notes: The gauge may equal \(+\infty\) outside the cone generated by \(C\); it is finite everywhere when the origin is an interior point of \(C\).
For a nonclosed or nonconvex set, the distance remains defined but need not possess a unique nearest point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Set-generated indicator, support, gauge, and distance functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical extended-real, dual, positively homogeneous, and metric functions associated with subsets of Euclidean space; conditions are scoped separately to the relevant construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n, define \delta_C(x)=0 when x\in C and \delta_C(x)=+\infty when x\notin C. Then \operatorname{epi}\delta_C=C\times[0,+\infty), and C is convex if and only if \delta_C is convex. For convex C, define \delta_C^*(x)=\sup_{y\in C}\langle x,y\rangle and d(x,C)=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|. If, in addition, C\ne\varnothing, define \gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda\geq0:x\in\lambda C\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of a set is zero on the set and positive infinity outside it; its epigraph is the half-cylinder over the set, and the indicator is convex exactly when the set is convex. For a convex set, the support function maximizes a linear functional over the set and the distance function takes the infimum of Euclidean distances to it. For a nonempty convex set, the gauge is the least nonnegative dilation containing the point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A convex function on a closed disk need not be closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A family showing that convexity and a closed effective domain do not by themselves imply lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $S=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$ and let $\phi:S\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $\phi\ge 0$. Define
\[
f(x,y)=\begin{cases}
0,&x^2+y^2<1,\\
\phi(x,y),&x^2+y^2=1,\\
+\infty,&x^2+y^2>1.
\end{cases}
\]
Then $f$ is convex, $\operatorname{dom}f=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le 1\}$, and $f$ is closed, equivalently lower semicontinuous, if and only if $\phi\equiv0$ on $S$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign zero inside the unit disk, arbitrary nonnegative values on its boundary, and positive infinity outside. The resulting function is convex and has the closed unit disk as its effective domain, but it is lower semicontinuous exactly when every boundary value is zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex},\quad \operatorname{dom}f=\{(x,y):x^2+y^2\le1\},\quad f\text{ is closed}\iff \phi\equiv0\text{ on }S

knowledge_statements.title: Finiteness and Boundedness of Support Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty set has an everywhere-finite support function exactly when it is bounded; in that case the support function is globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function \(\sigma_C\) is finite-valued on all of \(X^*\) if and only if \(C\) is norm bounded. If \(R=\sup_{x\in C}\|x\|<+\infty\), then \[|\sigma_C(x^*)-\sigma_C(y^*)|\le R\|x^*-y^*\|\qquad(x^*,y^*\in X^*).\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=X^*\iff C\) is norm bounded, and boundedness by \(R\) makes \(\sigma_C\) \(R\)-Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-boundedness characterized by finiteness of the support function on the whole continuous dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function records every continuous-linear supremum over a set. These values determine its closed convex hull and exactly recover a closed convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function of \(C\) is \[\sigma_C:X^*\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad \sigma_C(x^*)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x^*,x\rangle.\] It is convex, positively homogeneous, and lower semicontinuous. It depends only on the closed convex hull: \[\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}.\] If \(C\) is closed and convex, then it is recovered by \[C=\bigcap_{x^*\in X^*}\{x\in X:\langle x^*,x\rangle\leq\sigma_C(x^*)\}.\] Thus linear optimization values over \(C\) constitute a dual representation of its closed convex hull.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real normed space with continuous dual \(X^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(x^*)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x^*,x\rangle\), and a closed convex \(C\) is recovered from these values.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support values and half-space recovery of closed convex sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support function of a nonempty set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty. The supremum is taken in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\), so unboundedness in a direction is permitted.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space support function; no convexity, closedness, or boundedness is required for the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The support function of \(C\) is the extended-real function \[\sigma_C:H\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad \sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle.\] Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\{u\in H:\sigma_C(u)<+\infty\}\). For each \(u\ne0\) with finite support value, the closed half-space \[H_u=\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}\] is the smallest closed half-space with outward normal \(u\) containing \(C\). The function depends only on the closed convex hull: \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\). Consequently, if \(C\) is closed and convex, it is recovered by \[C=\bigcap_{u\in H}\{x\in H:\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a nonempty set \(C\) maps each direction \(u\) to the supremum of the linear functional \(x\mapsto\langle x,u\rangle\) over \(C\). It may be positive infinity. For a finite support value, the corresponding inequality defines the tightest containing half-space with that normal. The support function is unchanged by taking the closed convex hull, and a closed convex set is the intersection of all half-spaces specified by its support function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma_C(u)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,u\rangle\) for every \(u\in H\), with \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\overline{\operatorname{conv}}C}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\sigma_C=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,\cdot\rangle\) pointwise.
If \(C\) is closed and convex, \(x\in C\iff (\forall u\in H)\;\langle x,u\rangle\leq\sigma_C(u)\).
special_cases_latex: \(\sigma_{\{c\}}(u)=\langle c,u\rangle\).
For the closed unit ball \(B\), \(\sigma_B(u)=\|u\|\).
If \(C\) is bounded, then \(\sigma_C\) is finite everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sigma_C(0)=0\), \(\sigma_C(\lambda u)=\lambda\sigma_C(u)\) for \(\lambda>0\), and \(\sigma_C(u+v)\leq\sigma_C(u)+\sigma_C(v)\).
The support function is lower semicontinuous and convex as a pointwise supremum of continuous linear functions.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is unbounded, \(\sigma_C\) can equal \(+\infty\) in some directions.
The definition for the empty set requires a separate convention and is excluded here.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Perspective as a Support Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents the closed perspective, including its recession-function value at zero scale and its negative-scale failure boundary, as a support function.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed perspective of a closed proper convex function equals the support function of the hypograph of the negative conjugate. Its zero-scale value is the recession function, and it is infinite at negative scales.
