knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support-function order determines set inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order and uniqueness properties of support functions for nonempty closed convex subsets of finite-dimensional Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty closed convex sets, with $\xi_{Q_i}(g)=\sup_{x\in Q_i}\langle g,x\rangle\in(-\infty,+\infty]$ and $\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_i}=\{g:\xi_{Q_i}(g)<+\infty\}$. Then
\[
\bigl(\forall g\in\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2},\ \xi_{Q_1}(g)\leq\xi_{Q_2}(g)\bigr)\Longrightarrow Q_1\subseteq Q_2.
\]
Moreover, if $\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_1}=\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2}$ and the support functions agree throughout this common domain, then $Q_1=Q_2$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For nonempty closed convex sets, domination of the first support function by the second on the effective domain of the second implies inclusion of the first set in the second. Equality of both effective domains and of the support functions there implies equality of the sets.
assumptions_latex: Q_1,Q_2\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are nonempty, closed, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[\forall g\in\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2},\ \xi_{Q_1}(g)\leq\xi_{Q_2}(g)\right]\Rightarrow Q_1\subseteq Q_2;\quad \left[\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_1}=\operatorname{dom}\xi_{Q_2},\ \xi_{Q_1}=\xi_{Q_2}\text{ on this domain}\right]\Rightarrow Q_1=Q_2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Function and Its Basic Set Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded definition and elementary identities for the support function of a convex set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), its support function is \(\sigma_C(x^*)=\delta^*(x^*\mid C):=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle\). For every \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\), \(\inf_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle=-\sigma_C(-x^*)\). For every \(x^*\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\), \(C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,x^*\rangle\leq\beta\}\) if and only if \(\beta\geq\sigma_C(x^*)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{dom}\sigma_C\) is the barrier cone of \(C\), and \(\sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}C}=\sigma_{\operatorname{ri}C}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function records the supremum of each linear functional over a convex set. It recovers linear infima by sign reversal, characterizes containing closed half-spaces, has the barrier cone as its effective domain, and is unchanged by closure or relative interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_C(x^*)=\sup_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle,\quad \inf_{x\in C}\langle x,x^*\rangle=-\sigma_C(-x^*),\quad C\subseteq\{x:\langle x,x^*\rangle\leq\beta\}\iff\beta\geq\sigma_C(x^*),\quad \operatorname{dom}\sigma_C=\operatorname{barrier}(C),\quad \sigma_C=\sigma_{\operatorname{cl}C}=\sigma_{\operatorname{ri}C}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Homogeneity, subadditivity, and set-operation calculus for support functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The assertions at \(\alpha=0\) use the nonnegative extended-real convention \(0\cdot(+\infty)=0\). No closedness, convexity, or boundedness assumption on the generating sets is required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subdifferential of a support-function composition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and active-maximizer subdifferential formula for a nonnegative support function composed with differentiable convex components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne\Lambda\subset\mathbb R_+^m\) be bounded and convex, \(\psi(g)=\max_{\lambda\in\Lambda}\langle\lambda,g\rangle\), and \(F(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\), where every \(f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) is convex and differentiable. Then \(f=\psi\circ F\) is convex and, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda^{(i)}\nabla f_i(x):\lambda\in\operatorname*{Arg\,max}_{\mu\in\Lambda}\langle\mu,F(x)\rangle\right\}.\] Consequently, each displayed weighted gradient associated with an active maximizer belongs to \(\partial f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let Λ be a nonempty bounded convex subset of the nonnegative orthant and let ψ be its support function. If the components of F are differentiable convex functions, then ψ composed with F is convex. At every point, its subdifferential is the convex hull of the component-gradient combinations generated by maximizers active in the support-function evaluation; every such combination is therefore a subgradient.
assumptions_latex: F=(f_1,\ldots,f_m),\quad f_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\text{ convex and differentiable}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\psi\circ F\text{ is convex, and }\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}\left\{\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda^{(i)}\nabla f_i(x):\lambda\in\operatorname*{Arg\,max}_{\mu\in\Lambda}\langle\mu,F(x)\rangle\right\}\quad(\forall x\in\mathbb R^n).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gauge and unit-sublevel-set representation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^n\) be closed and convex with \(0\in C\). For \(\lambda>0\), write \(\lambda C=\{\lambda c:c\in C\}\), and adopt \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex gauge representation; the set need not be bounded or absorbing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge, or Minkowski functional, generated by \(C\) is \[\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\},\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}^n.\] It is a nonnegative, lower-semicontinuous, positively homogeneous convex function. Its radial set representation is \[C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\},\qquad rC=\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq r\}\quad(r>0).\] Conversely, if \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to[0,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and sublinear and \(C_p=\{x:p(x)\leq1\}\), then \(C_p\) is closed, convex, contains \(0\), and \(p=\gamma_{C_p}\). Thus closed convex sets containing the origin and nonnegative closed sublinear functions form a representation pair under \(C\mapsto\gamma_C\) and \(p\mapsto\{p\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex set \(C\) containing the origin, the gauge of a point is the least positive dilation factor needed to place that point in a dilate of \(C\), with value positive infinity if no dilation works. The original set is the unit sublevel set of its gauge, and every positive sublevel set is the corresponding dilation. Conversely, every nonnegative lower-semicontinuous sublinear function is the gauge of its unit sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{\lambda>0:x\in\lambda C\}\) and \(C=\{\gamma_C\leq1\}\); conversely \(p=\gamma_{\{p\leq1\}}\) for every nonnegative closed sublinear \(p\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(t>0\), \(\gamma_C(x)\leq t\iff x\in tC\).
The epigraph of \(\gamma_C\) is the closure of the conical hull generated by \(C\times\{1\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\) is the unit ball of a norm, then \(\gamma_C\) is that norm.
If \(C\) is symmetric and \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\), then \(\gamma_C\) is a norm.
If \(C\) is a closed convex cone, then \(\gamma_C\) is \(0\) on \(C\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(C\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere exactly when \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
The zero set \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}\) is the recession cone of \(C\).
boundary_notes: Without symmetry, a finite gauge need not be a norm because \(\gamma_C(x)\) and \(\gamma_C(-x)\) may differ.
Closedness is material to the exact identity \(C=\{\gamma_C\leq1\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Zero Set and Recession Cone
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex generator, the zero set of its gauge is exactly the generator's recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty closed convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space with \(0\in C\). Then \[\{x:\gamma_C(x)=0\}=\operatorname{rec}C.\] Thus the generated gauge vanishes on a nonzero direction exactly when the generator has a nonzero recession direction.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C^{-1}(0)=\operatorname{rec}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact degeneracy set for a closed convex gauge generator.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective Domain of a Gauge
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gauge is finite exactly on the positive radial hull of its generator; for a convex generator that domain is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq X\) contain \(0\), and let \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\). Then \[\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\{x:\gamma_C(x)<+\infty\}=\bigcup_{t>0}tC.\] If \(C\) is convex, this effective domain is a convex cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}\gamma_C=\bigcup_{t>0}tC\), which is a convex cone when \(C\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain geometry of an extended-valued gauge.

knowledge_statements.title: Gauge Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gauge of a set is the smallest positive dilation needed to contain a point. Convex sets yield convex gauges, while absorbing sets yield finite gauges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The gauge generated by \(C\) is the extended-real function \[\gamma_C:X\to[0,+\infty],\qquad \gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). It is positively homogeneous: \(\gamma_C(\lambda x)=\lambda\gamma_C(x)\) for every \(\lambda>0\). If \(C\) is convex, then \(\gamma_C\) is subadditive and hence convex. If \(C\) is absorbing, then \(\gamma_C\) is finite everywhere. No symmetry, closedness, or boundedness is required for the definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\gamma_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-valued gauge generated by a set containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Minkowski Functional Convention
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minkowski functional is another name for gauge. A convex set containing the origin lies between its strict and non-strict unit sublevels; a closed or open set is recovered by the corresponding unit sublevel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Minkowski functional of \(C\) is its gauge \(p_C=\gamma_C\), defined by \[p_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Under this convention, \[\{x\in X:p_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C\subseteq\{x\in X:p_C(x)\leq1\}.\] If additionally \(C\) is closed, then \[C=\{x\in X:p_C(x)\leq1\}.\] If instead \(C\) is open, then \[C=\{x\in X:p_C(x)<1\}.\] Thus boundary regularity determines whether the strict or non-strict unit sublevel recovers \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real topological vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x:\gamma_C(x)<1\}\subseteq C\subseteq\{x:\gamma_C(x)\leq1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology and unit-sublevel convention for the Minkowski functional.

knowledge_statements.title: Absorption and Algebraic Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex set containing zero, absorption is equivalent to zero being an algebraic interior point; in finite dimensions this is equivalent to ordinary interior membership.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be convex with \(0\in C\). Then \(C\) is absorbing if and only if \(0\in\operatorname{core}C\), where \(\operatorname{core}C\) denotes the algebraic interior. If \(X\) is finite-dimensional with its usual vector-space topology, this is further equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is absorbing}\iff0\in\operatorname{core}C\), and in finite dimensions this is equivalent to \(0\in\operatorname{int}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic geometric characterization of absorption for convex origin-containing sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Absorbing-Set Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex set containing zero absorbs every vector exactly when its Minkowski functional is finite everywhere; the functional is then sublinear.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is absorbing if, for every \(x\in X\), there exists \(t>0\) such that \(x\in tC\). Its Minkowski functional is \[p_C(x)=\inf\{t>0:x\in tC\},\] with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\). Thus \(C\) is absorbing if and only if \(p_C(x)<+\infty\) for every \(x\in X\). Moreover, convexity and \(0\in C\) imply that \(p_C\) is positively homogeneous and subadditive wherever it is finite.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, convex, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is absorbing exactly when \(p_C\) is finite-valued on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic absorbing geometry for a convex set containing the origin.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Norm Unit-Ball Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, a closed convex absorbing symmetric generator produces a norm exactly when it is bounded, and it is then that norm's closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be closed, convex, absorbing, centrally symmetric, and contain \(0\). Then its Minkowski functional \(p_C\) is a norm if and only if \(C\) is bounded. In that case \[C=\{x:p_C(x)\le1\}\] is the closed unit ball of \(p_C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and centrally symmetric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p_C\text{ is a norm}\iff C\text{ is bounded}\), with \(C=\{p_C\le1\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundedness boundary within the symmetric gauge regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Gauge Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed convex absorbing set containing zero, central symmetry is equivalent to evenness of its gauge. The gauge is then a seminorm, and it is a norm when its zero set is trivial, as occurs when the set is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(C\) is closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\), it is recovered from its gauge by \[C=\{x\in X:p_C(x)\leq 1\}.\] Consequently, \[C=-C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p_C(-x)=p_C(x)\ \text{for every }x\in X.\] In this symmetric regime, sublinearity makes \(p_C\) a seminorm. It is a norm if \(p_C(x)=0\) implies \(x=0\); in particular, this definiteness holds when \(C\) is bounded.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a Hausdorff real topological vector space.
\(C\subseteq X\) is nonempty, closed, convex, absorbing, and contains \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C=-C\) if and only if \(p_C(-x)=p_C(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetry and definiteness properties of Minkowski gauges for closed absorbing convex sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance, projection, and powered-distance hierarchy
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(C\subset H\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. Denote by \(P_Cx\) the unique nearest point of \(C\) to \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space metric hierarchy for nonempty closed convex sets, using the norm induced by the Hilbert structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance to \(C\) is \[d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|=\min_{c\in C}\|x-c\|=\|x-P_Cx\|.\] For \(p\geq1\), the powered-distance member of the hierarchy is \[D_{C,p}(x)=\frac1p d_C(x)^p.\] The most common smooth member is the half squared distance \[q_C(x)=D_{C,2}(x)=\frac12\|x-P_Cx\|^2.\] Each \(d_C\) and \(D_{C,p}\) is finite and convex; \(d_C\) is \(1\)-Lipschitz. The zero-level set of every member is \(C\): \[C=\{x:d_C(x)=0\}=\{x:D_{C,p}(x)=0\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonempty closed convex subset \(C\) of a Hilbert space, the distance function is the minimum norm distance from a point to \(C\), attained uniquely at its metric projection. Raising this distance to a power \(p\geq1\) and dividing by \(p\) gives the powered-distance hierarchy. The half squared distance is the standard quadratic member. All members are finite and convex, while the basic distance is globally one-Lipschitz and every member vanishes exactly on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_C(x)=\|x-P_Cx\|\) and \(D_{C,p}(x)=d_C(x)^p/p\) for \(p\geq1\), with \(\operatorname{zer}D_{C,p}=C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P_Cx=\operatorname*{argmin}_{c\in C}\|x-c\|\).
\(d_C=\iota_C\mathbin{\square}\|\cdot\|\), where \(\square\) denotes infimal convolution.
\(q_C=\iota_C\mathbin{\square}(\tfrac12\|\cdot\|^2)\).
special_cases_latex: For a closed linear subspace \(V\), \(d_V(x)=\|P_{V^\perp}x\|\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \(|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\leq\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in H\).
The conjugate satisfies \(d_C^*=\sigma_C+\iota_{B(0,1)}\).
boundary_notes: For a nonclosed set, the distance can vanish outside the set, namely on its closure.
For a nonconvex closed set, nearest points may fail to be unique and the distance need not be convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance Sublevels as Parallel Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sublevel sets of distance to a closed convex set are exactly its closed metric offsets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\overline B=\{u\in H:\|u\|\le 1\}\). For every \(r\ge0\), \[\{x\in H:d_C(x)\le r\}=C+r\overline B.\] In particular, the zero sublevel set recovers \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{d_C\le r\}=C+r\overline B\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sublevel-set representation for distance to a nonempty closed convex set in a real Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Distance-to-Set Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance to a nonempty set is finite and 1-Lipschitz; it is convex for convex sets and vanishes precisely on the closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The distance-to-set function generated by \(C\) is \[d_C:H\to[0,+\infty),\qquad d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|.\] It is everywhere finite and \(1\)-Lipschitz: \[|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\leq\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in H).\] If \(C\) is convex, then \(d_C\) is convex. Furthermore, \(d_C(x)=0\) holds exactly when \(x\in\overline C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_C(x)=\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|\) and \(|d_C(x)-d_C(y)|\leq\|x-y\|\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric distance in a Hilbert space, with convexity when the generating set is convex.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Sets Destroy Squared-Distance Convexity and Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a two-point set, half squared distance is neither convex nor differentiable at the midpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R\), \[q_C(x)=\frac12\min\{(x-1)^2,(x+1)^2\}.\] Since \(q_C(-1)=q_C(1)=0\) and \(q_C(0)=\tfrac12\), it is not convex. Its left and right derivatives at \(0\) are \(1\) and \(-1\), respectively, so it is not differentiable there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_C=\tfrac12d_C^2\) is nonconvex and nondifferentiable at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convex smooth squared-distance theory without convexity of the generating set.

knowledge_statements.title: Squared-Distance Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Half the squared distance to a closed convex set is differentiable and convex; its gradient is the residual from the metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[q_C(x)=\frac12d_C(x)^2=\frac12\inf_{c\in C}\|x-c\|^2.\] Then \(q_C\) is finite, continuous, and convex on \(H\). It is Fréchet differentiable everywhere, and its gradient is \[\nabla q_C(x)=x-P_Cx.\] Moreover, this gradient is \(1\)-Lipschitz, equivalently \(q_C\) is a convex function with a nonexpansive gradient.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q_C=\tfrac12d_C^2\) is convex and Fréchet differentiable with \(\nabla q_C=\operatorname{Id}-P_C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Half squared distance to a nonempty closed convex set in Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Fixed-Point Membership Certificate
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point belongs to the set exactly when it is fixed by the metric projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), \[x\in C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_Cx=x.\] Thus \(x-P_Cx\) vanishes exactly at feasible points.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\in C\iff P_Cx=x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Membership test for a nonempty closed convex set using its metric projection.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Essential for Unique Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed nonconvex two-point set has two nearest points to its midpoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{-1,1\}\subset\mathbb R\), both \(-1\) and \(1\) minimize \(|0-c|\) over \(c\in C\). Hence the nearest point to \(0\) is not unique and \(P_C0\) is not single-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The metric projection of \(0\) onto \(C\) is not unique.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniqueness for projection onto a closed nonconvex set.

knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Firm Nonexpansiveness and Pythagorean Inequality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projection gives a Pythagorean inequality, and its complementary residual map is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p=P_Cx\). For every \(c\in C\), \[\|x-c\|^2\ge \|x-p\|^2+\|p-c\|^2.\] Moreover, \(R_C=\operatorname{Id}-P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive: \[\|R_Cx-R_Cy\|^2\le \langle R_Cx-R_Cy,x-y\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pythagorean inequality holds and \(\operatorname{Id}-P_C\) is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additional metric geometry of projection onto a nonempty closed convex set in a real Hilbert space.

notation.meaning: projection residual map Id minus P_C

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every point has a unique nearest point in a nonempty closed convex set, characterized by a variational inequality; the projection is firmly nonexpansive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), there exists a unique \(p=P_Cx\in C\) satisfying \[\|x-p\|=d_C(x).\] A point \(p\in C\) equals \(P_Cx\) if and only if \[\langle x-p,c-p\rangle\leq0\qquad\text{for every }c\in C.\] The projection is firmly nonexpansive: \[\|P_Cx-P_Cy\|^2\leq\langle P_Cx-P_Cy,x-y\rangle\qquad(x,y\in H).\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq H\) is nonempty, closed, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=P_Cx\) is uniquely determined by \(p\in C\) and \(\langle x-p,c-p\rangle\leq0\) for every \(c\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space projection theorem and variational characterization.

notation.meaning: unique metric projection of x onto C

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Set Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distance cannot distinguish a set from its closure. For the open interval, boundary points have zero distance but no nearest point in the set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every nonempty subset \(S\) of a metric space, distance ignores nonclosedness: \[d_S=d_{\overline S}.\] Consequently, zero distance implies only membership in \(\overline S\), and a nearest point need not exist in \(S\). Concretely, for \(C=(0,1)\subset\mathbb R\), \[d_C=d_{[0,1]},\qquad d_C(0)=0,\] yet no \(c\in C\) satisfies \(|0-c|=0\). Thus closedness is essential for the projection theorem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_C=d_{[0,1]}\), but \(d_C(0)=0\) is not attained by any point of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of nearest-point attainment when closedness is removed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Closed Function with an Open Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The reciprocal function separates lower semicontinuity of an extended-value function from closedness of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function f:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R},\ f(x)=1/x, is convex. Its extension \widetilde f:\mathbb{R}\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} defined by \widetilde f(x)=1/x for x>0 and \widetilde f(x)=+\infty for x\le0 is closed, equivalently lower semicontinuous, while \operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=(0,\infty) is open.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal function is convex on the positive half-line. Extending it by positive infinity outside that half-line gives a closed, lower-semicontinuous function whose effective domain is open.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex},\qquad \widetilde f\text{ is closed (lower semicontinuous)},\qquad \operatorname{dom}\widetilde f=(0,\infty)\text{ is open}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Topological and asymptotic regularity profile
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Strong convergence is norm convergence; weak convergence is denoted by \(\rightharpoonup\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of a regularity profile for proper convex functions on Hilbert space, separating topological, local, minorization, and recession components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The topological-asymptotic regularity profile of \(f\) is the tuple \[\mathcal R(f)=\bigl(\operatorname{epi}f,\operatorname{cont}f,\mathcal A(f),\operatorname{rec}f\bigr),\] where \(f\) is lower semicontinuous when \(x_n\to x\) implies \(f(x)\leq\liminf_n f(x_n)\); \(\operatorname{cont}f\) is the set of points where \(f\) is finite and continuous; \[\mathcal A(f)=\{(u,\alpha)\in H\times\mathbb R:\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha\leq f(x)\ \forall x\in H\}\] is the family of continuous affine minorants; and the recession function is \[\operatorname{rec}f(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).\] For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), the epigraph is closed, \(\mathcal A(f)\ne\varnothing\), and \(f\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The topological-asymptotic regularity profile of a proper convex function records four objects: its epigraph, its finite continuity set, its continuous affine lower supports, and its recession function. Lower semicontinuity is the liminf inequality under norm convergence. The affine-minorant family consists of all continuous affine functions lying below the function everywhere. The recession function records the largest increment produced by a fixed displacement. For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, the epigraph is closed, at least one continuous affine minorant exists, and the function is continuous throughout the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R(f)=(\operatorname{epi}f,\operatorname{cont}f,\mathcal A(f),\operatorname{rec}f)\) defines the topological-asymptotic regularity data of \(f\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Lower semicontinuity is equivalent to closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) and to closedness of every lower level set.
For closed proper convex \(f\), \(f(x)=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal A(f)}(\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha)\).
special_cases_latex: In finite dimensions, every proper convex function is continuous on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
If \(f\) is finite and lower semicontinuous on all of \(H\), it is continuous everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: For convex \(f\), strong, weak, sequential, and weak sequential lower semicontinuity coincide.
\(\operatorname{rec}f\) is positively homogeneous and convex when \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\).
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional spaces, an everywhere-finite convex function need not be continuous without lower semicontinuity or local boundedness.
Continuity at boundary points of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is not guaranteed.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower semicontinuity and real level sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes only the definitions in this extract. The closing sentence announces a subsequent theorem, whose three-way equivalence is independently extracted and should not be duplicated here.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb E\to[-\infty,\infty]\). The function \(f\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x\in\mathbb E\) if, for every sequence \((x_n)\subseteq\mathbb E\) satisfying \(x_n\to x\), one has \(f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)\). It is lower semicontinuous if it is lower semicontinuous at every \(x\in\mathbb E\). For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), \(\operatorname{Lev}(f,\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbb E:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is lower semicontinuous at a point when its value there does not exceed the limit inferior along every sequence converging to that point. It is lower semicontinuous when this holds everywhere. Its alpha-level set consists of the points where its value is at most alpha.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is l.s.c. at }x\iff\bigl(\forall(x_n)\subseteq\mathbb E,\ x_n\to x\Rightarrow f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(x_n)\bigr),\qquad \operatorname{Lev}(f,\alpha)=\{x\in\mathbb E:f(x)\leq\alpha\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equi-Lipschitz, Equicontinuous, and Bounded Function Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines common Lipschitz control for a function family, its uniform-equicontinuity consequence, and pointwise and uniform boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and let \(\{f_i:S\to\mathbb{R}\mid i\in I\}\) be a family. It is equi-Lipschitzian relative to \(S\) if there exists \(\alpha\geq0\) such that \(|f_i(y)-f_i(x)|\leq\alpha\lVert y-x\rVert\) for all \(x,y\in S\) and \(i\in I\). This implies uniform equicontinuity: for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f_i(y)-f_i(x)|\leq\varepsilon\) for all \(i\in I\) whenever \(x,y\in S\) and \(\lVert y-x\rVert\leq\delta\). The family is pointwise bounded on \(S\) if \(\{f_i(x):i\in I\}\) is bounded for every \(x\in S\), and uniformly bounded on \(S\) if there exist \(\alpha_1,\alpha_2\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\alpha_1\leq f_i(x)\leq\alpha_2\) for all \(x\in S\) and \(i\in I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family is equi-Lipschitz when one Lipschitz constant works for every member and every pair of points in S; this implies uniform equicontinuity. Pointwise boundedness allows bounds to depend on the point, while uniform boundedness uses common lower and upper bounds for all points and family members.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\exists\alpha\geq0\;\forall i\in I\;\forall x,y\in S:\ |f_i(y)-f_i(x)|\leq\alpha\lVert y-x\rVert\right)\Longrightarrow\{f_i\}_{i\in I}\text{ is uniformly equicontinuous on }S,\quad\text{with pointwise and uniform boundedness defined as stated}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Regularity Inherited under Convex Domination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States an order-inheritance principle within the class of finite convex functions on Euclidean space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex and Lipschitzian relative to \(\mathbb{R}^n\). If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(f(x)\leq g(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(f\) is Lipschitzian relative to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a finite globally Lipschitz convex function dominates another finite convex function everywhere, the dominated function is also globally Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is Lipschitzian relative to }\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Provides a sufficient global Lipschitz condition through finite lower asymptotic growth along every direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex. If \(\liminf_{\lambda\to\infty}f(\lambda y)/\lambda<+\infty\) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(f\) is Lipschitzian relative to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex function is globally Lipschitz if the lower asymptotic value of its scaled values along every ray is not positive infinity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\alpha\geq0\;\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ |f(y)-f(x)|\leq\alpha\lVert y-x\rVert.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuity Relative to a Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines Lipschitz continuity for a real-valued function on an arbitrary Euclidean subset and records the resulting uniform continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\). The function \(f\) is Lipschitzian relative to \(S\) if there exists \(\alpha\geq0\) such that \(|f(y)-f(x)|\leq\alpha\lVert y-x\rVert\) for all \(x,y\in S\). Every function satisfying this condition is uniformly continuous relative to \(S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on S is Lipschitz relative to S if one nonnegative constant bounds every difference in function values by the corresponding Euclidean distance. This condition implies uniform continuity on S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left(\exists\alpha\geq0\;\forall x,y\in S:\ |f(y)-f(x)|\leq\alpha\lVert y-x\rVert\right)\Longrightarrow f\text{ is uniformly continuous relative to }S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Semicontinuity of block derivatives and the saddle subdifferential
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local result on an open convex set where the concave-convex function is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C\times D be open and convex, and let K be concave in u, convex in v, and finite on C\times D. For every fixed u'\in\mathbb{R}^m, (u,v)\mapsto K'(u,v;u',0) is lower semicontinuous on C\times D; for every fixed v'\in\mathbb{R}^n, (u,v)\mapsto K'(u,v;0,v') is upper semicontinuous there. Moreover, for every (u,v)\in C\times D and \varepsilon>0, there exists \delta>0, which may be chosen with (u,v)+\delta B\subset C\times D, such that \partial K(x,y)\subseteq\partial K(u,v)+\varepsilon B for every (x,y)\in(u,v)+\delta B.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each fixed first-block directional derivative is lower semicontinuous in the base point, while each fixed second-block directional derivative is upper semicontinuous. The saddle subdifferential mapping is locally outer semicontinuous in the stated Euclidean-enlargement sense.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower semicontinuity–epigraph closedness correspondence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological space and let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Equip \(X\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General Hausdorff-space correspondence; sequences suffice in metrizable spaces, while nets express the fully topological definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq r\},\qquad \operatorname{lev}_{\leq r}f=\{x\in X:f(x)\leq r\}.\] The function \(f\) is lower semicontinuous if, for every net \((x_a)\) converging to \(x\), \[f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a).\] The epigraphical closedness correspondence is the equivalence \[f\text{ is lower semicontinuous}\iff\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is closed in }X\times\mathbb R\iff (\forall r\in\mathbb R)\;\operatorname{lev}_{\leq r}f\text{ is closed in }X.\] In a metric space, the net condition may equivalently be tested on all convergent sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real function on a Hausdorff space, lower semicontinuity means that its value at the limit of every convergent net does not exceed the net's lower limiting values. This is equivalent to the epigraph being closed in the product space, and also equivalent to every lower level set being closed. In metric spaces, convergent sequences provide an equivalent test.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed, if and only if every \(\operatorname{lev}_{\leq r}f\) is closed.
equivalent_formulations_latex: At \(x\), lower semicontinuity is equivalent to \((\forall \alpha<f(x))(\exists V\in\mathcal V(x))\;f(V)\subset(\alpha,+\infty]\).
In metric spaces, \(f(x)\leq\liminf_n f(x_n)\) for every \(x_n\to x\) is equivalent to lower semicontinuity.
special_cases_latex: The indicator \(\iota_C\) is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(C\) is closed.
For a convex function on a Hilbert space, norm-lower-semicontinuity is equivalent to weak lower semicontinuity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Arbitrary pointwise suprema of lower-semicontinuous functions are lower semicontinuous.
A lower-semicontinuous function has closed sublevel sets at every real height.
boundary_notes: Sequential lower semicontinuity need not imply lower semicontinuity on a nonsequential topological space.
The correspondence itself does not require convexity or properness.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Closedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function is lower semicontinuous exactly when its epigraph is closed, equivalently when every real sublevel set is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq r\},\] where \(X\times\mathbb R\) has the product topology. Then \(f\) is lower semicontinuous on \(X\) if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed. Equivalently, every sublevel set \[\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\] is closed for each \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is lower semicontinuous if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in \(X\times\mathbb R\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed extended-real function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff topological space and let \(f:X\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). The epigraph is a subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\) with the product topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topological definition of a closed function through its epigraph; convexity is an independent property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is called epigraphically closed, or simply closed, when \[\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in X\times\mathbb R:f(x)\leq r\}\] is a closed subset of \(X\times\mathbb R\). Equivalently, for every net \(x_a\to x\), \[f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a),\] or, equivalently, every lower level set \(\{x:f(x)\leq r\}\) is closed for each \(r\in\mathbb R\). If \(X\) is a normed space and \(f\) is convex, the adjective closed therefore means lower semicontinuous in the ambient norm topology, not merely lower semicontinuous relative to \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real function is epigraphically closed when its epigraph is a closed subset of the product of its domain space and the real line. This is equivalent to the lower-semicontinuity liminf inequality and to closedness of every lower level set. For a convex function on a normed space, closedness refers to the ambient topology over the whole space, including approaches from outside the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is closed exactly when \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is closed in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is closed \(\iff (\forall r\in\mathbb R)\;\{f\leq r\}\) is closed.
In a metric space, \(f\) is closed \(\iff (\forall x_n\to x)\;f(x)\leq\liminf_n f(x_n)\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\), epigraphical closedness is equivalent to closedness of \(C\).
A continuous real-valued function is epigraphically closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(f\) is closed and convex, then \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a closed convex set.
The pointwise supremum of any family of closed functions is closed.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(\operatorname{dom}f\) is neither required nor sufficient for epigraphical closedness.
Relative lower semicontinuity on \(\operatorname{dom}f\) does not control approaches to its boundary from the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Norm–Weak Equivalence Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The unit-sphere indicator is norm-lower-semicontinuous but not weakly lower-semicontinuous, showing that convexity is essential.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, \(S=\{x\in H:\|x\|=1\}\), and \(f=\iota_S\). The set \(S\) is norm closed, so \(f\) is norm-lower-semicontinuous. If \((e_n)\) is orthonormal, then \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\), but \[f(0)=+\infty>0=\liminf_n f(e_n).\] Hence \(f\) is not weakly lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\iota_S\) is norm-lower-semicontinuous but not weakly lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional counterexample showing the necessity of convexity.

notation.meaning: weak convergence of an orthonormal sequence to zero

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Sequential Criterion for Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For convex functions on a Banach space, norm and weak lower semicontinuity agree, and each may be tested sequentially.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a convex \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) on a Banach space, the following are equivalent: norm lower semicontinuity, sequential norm lower semicontinuity, weak lower semicontinuity, and sequential weak lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is norm-lower-semicontinuous iff norm-sequentially lower-semicontinuous iff weakly lower-semicontinuous iff weakly sequentially lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential and topological equivalence for convex functions on Banach spaces.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuity Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity may be relative or sequential. For convex functions on Banach spaces, norm and weak lower semicontinuity coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Lower semicontinuity relative to a subset \(D\subseteq X\) means lower semicontinuity for the subspace topology on \(D\). Since the norm topology is metrizable, norm lower semicontinuity is equivalent to \[x_n\to x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}f(x_n).\] Weak lower semicontinuity implies norm lower semicontinuity. Conversely, for convex \(f\), every norm-closed sublevel set is convex and therefore weakly closed; hence norm and weak lower semicontinuity are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Norm lower semicontinuity and weak lower semicontinuity of \(f\) are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential, relative, norm, and weak lower-semicontinuity regimes.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strong, weak, sequential, and relative lower semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(D\subset H\), and let \(f:H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space taxonomy distinguishing ambient versus relative topology, strong versus weak topology, and nets versus sequences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At \(x\in H\), \(f\) is strongly lower semicontinuous if every net \(x_a\to x\) in norm satisfies \(f(x)\leq\liminf_a f(x_a)\); it is weakly lower semicontinuous if every net \(x_a\rightharpoonup x\) satisfies the same inequality. Replacing nets by sequences defines strong sequential and weak sequential lower semicontinuity. Relative lower semicontinuity on \(D\) means that the corresponding condition is imposed only on nets or sequences contained in \(D\), with convergence in the subspace topology. Global lower semicontinuity means the selected condition holds at every point of \(H\). For convex \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the four ambient regimes—strong, strong sequential, weak, and weak sequential—are equivalent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower semicontinuity has several regimes. Strong lower semicontinuity uses norm-convergent nets, while weak lower semicontinuity uses weakly convergent nets. Sequential variants test only sequences. Relative lower semicontinuity restricts the approaching points to a specified subset and uses its subspace topology. A regime is global when it holds at every ambient point. For convex extended-real functions on a Hilbert space that never take negative infinity, all four ambient strong, weak, net, and sequential regimes coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected convergence class determines the lower-semicontinuity regime through \(f(x)\leq\liminf f(x_a)\); for convex \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), the four ambient Hilbert-space regimes coincide.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong lower semicontinuity is equivalent to norm-closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\).
Weak lower semicontinuity is equivalent to weak closedness of \(\operatorname{epi}f\) in \(H\times\mathbb R\).
special_cases_latex: In metric spaces, strong lower semicontinuity and strong sequential lower semicontinuity coincide for arbitrary functions.
For convex functions on Hilbert space, norm-closed convex level sets are also weakly closed.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak lower semicontinuity implies strong lower semicontinuity because norm convergence implies weak convergence.
For convex Hilbert-space functions, verifying any one of the four ambient regimes verifies them all.
boundary_notes: Relative lower semicontinuity on \(D\) need not imply ambient lower semicontinuity at boundary points of \(D\).
Outside sequential spaces, sequential lower semicontinuity can be strictly weaker than net-based lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Proper Lower-Semicontinuous Convex Class
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The class Gamma-zero consists exactly of proper, lower-semicontinuous convex extended-real functions on a Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class \(\Gamma_0(H)\) consists of all functions \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) that are convex, lower semicontinuous, and proper. Properness means \[\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in H:f(x)<+\infty\}\neq\varnothing\] and \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in H\). Thus members of \(\Gamma_0(H)\) have nonempty effective domain and closed convex epigraphs, without taking the value \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Gamma_0(H)=\{f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]:f\text{ is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard Hilbert-space class used in conjugacy and proximal analysis.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession criterion for closed exact infimal convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness, properness, and pointwise attainment of an infimal convolution under strict recession compatibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,f_2:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be closed proper convex functions. If f_1^{0+}(z)+f_2^{0+}(-z)>0 for every z\neq 0, then f_1\square f_2 is closed, proper, and convex. Moreover, for every x\in\mathbb{R}^n there exists y\in\mathbb{R}^n such that (f_1\square f_2)(x)=f_1(x-y)+f_2(y)=\inf_{u\in\mathbb{R}^n}\{f_1(x-u)+f_2(u)\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If two closed proper convex functions have strictly positive combined recession value in every nonzero pair of opposite directions, their infimal convolution is closed, proper, and convex, and its defining infimum is attained at every point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_1\square f_2\text{ is closed, proper, and convex, and }\forall x\in\mathbb{R}^n\;\exists y\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ (f_1\square f_2)(x)=f_1(x-y)+f_2(y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and recession calculus for finite convex sums
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two finite-sum regimes: closed summands, and possibly nonclosed summands satisfying a common relative-interior condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper convex functions. If every f_i is closed and \sum_{i=1}^m f_i\not\equiv+\infty, then \sum_{i=1}^m f_i is closed, proper, and convex, and \left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)^{0+}=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^{0+}. If the f_i are not all closed but \bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing, then \operatorname{cl}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}f_i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite sum of proper closed convex functions is closed and proper when it is not identically positive infinity, and its recession function is the sum of the recession functions. When the summands are not all closed, a common relative-interior domain point makes closure commute with the finite sum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex primitive of an extended-real nondecreasing function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes existence, identification of both one-sided derivatives, and uniqueness up to an additive real constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a\in\mathbb{R}, and let \varphi:\mathbb{R}\to[-\infty,+\infty] be nondecreasing with \varphi(a)\in\mathbb{R}. If \varphi_- and \varphi_+ denote its left and right limits, then f(x)=\int_a^x\varphi(t)\,dt is a well-defined closed proper convex function on \mathbb{R} satisfying f'_- =\varphi_-\leq\varphi\leq\varphi_+=f'_+. If g is any closed proper convex function on \mathbb{R} such that g'_-\leq\varphi\leq g'_+, then g=f+\alpha for some \alpha\in\mathbb{R}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-real nondecreasing function that is finite at a chosen base point has a well-defined integral primitive that is closed, proper, and convex. Its left and right derivatives are the corresponding one-sided limits of the integrand and bracket the integrand. Any other closed proper convex function whose one-sided derivatives bracket the same integrand differs from this primitive by a real constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(x)=\int_a^x\varphi(t)\,dt\text{ is well-defined, closed, proper, and convex},\quad f'_- =\varphi_-\leq\varphi\leq\varphi_+=f'_+,\quad [g'_-\leq\varphi\leq g'_+]\Rightarrow(\exists\alpha\in\mathbb{R})\ g=f+\alpha.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity and one-sided continuity of convex derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Includes the extended-real conventions outside the effective domain and all four one-sided limit identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty] be closed, proper, and convex. Extend f'_+ and f'_- by assigning -\infty at points strictly to the left of \operatorname{dom}f and +\infty at points strictly to its right. Then f'_+ and f'_- are nondecreasing on \mathbb{R} and finite on \operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f). Whenever z_1<x<z_2, one has f'_+(z_1)\leq f'_-(x)\leq f'_+(x)\leq f'_-(z_2). Moreover, for every x\in\mathbb{R}, \lim_{z\downarrow x}f'_+(z)=\lim_{z\downarrow x}f'_-(z)=f'_+(x) and \lim_{z\uparrow x}f'_+(z)=\lim_{z\uparrow x}f'_-(z)=f'_-(x).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed proper convex function on the real line, extend both one-sided derivatives by minus infinity strictly to the left of its domain and plus infinity strictly to the right. Both derivatives are nondecreasing and finite in the domain interior. The left derivative at a point is no greater than the right derivative, derivatives at earlier and later points provide the stated bounds, and the right- and left-hand limits of either derivative equal the right and left derivatives, respectively.

f'_\pm(x)=-\infty\text{ strictly to the left of }\operatorname{dom}f
f'_\pm(x)=+\infty\text{ strictly to the right of }\operatorname{dom}f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f'_\pm\text{ are nondecreasing and finite on }\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f),\quad f'_+(z_1)\leq f'_-(x)\leq f'_+(x)\leq f'_-(z_2)\ (z_1<x<z_2),\quad \lim_{z\downarrow x}f'_\pm(z)=f'_+(x),\ \lim_{z\uparrow x}f'_\pm(z)=f'_-(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative Continuity on the Domain in One Dimension
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The result is specific to extended-real proper closed convex functions on the real line. It asserts sequential continuity relative to the effective domain, including its finite boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) be proper, closed, and convex, and let \(\bar x\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then, for every sequence \((x_k)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfying \(x_k\to\bar x\),

\]
Thus \(f\) is continuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(\operatorname{dom}f\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure formula for a generated positively homogeneous convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The notation \((f\lambda)(x)\) denotes the scaled perspective used in the generation construction, and \(\lambda=0^+\) denotes its recession-boundary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex with \(f(0)>0\), and let \(k\) be the positively homogeneous convex function generated by \(f\). Then \(k\) is proper and, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), \[(\operatorname{cl}k)(x)=\inf\{(f\lambda)(x):\lambda>0\text{ or }\lambda=0^+\},\] with the infimum attained. If \(0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), then \(k\) is closed and the \(\lambda=0^+\) term may be omitted, although the resulting infimum over \(\lambda>0\) need not be attained.

The closure of the generated function is the attained infimum of the scaled perspectives over positive scales and the recession-boundary scale. If the origin lies in the domain, the generated function is already closed and the boundary scale can be omitted, but attainment may then fail.

k\text{ is the positively homogeneous convex function generated by }f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Everywhere Supporting Subgradients Imply Convexity and Relative Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness of the epigraph is relative to $Q\times\mathbb{R}$. Ambient epigraph closedness follows if $Q$ is additionally closed; without that assumption the source's ambient-closedness parenthetical is not valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, and let $f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}$ be proper and finite throughout $Q$. If $\partial_Q f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in Q\}$ is nonempty for every $x\in Q$, then $f$ is convex and lower semicontinuous relative to $Q$. Equivalently, $\operatorname{epi}_Q f=\{(x,t)\in Q\times\mathbb{R}:t\ge f(x)\}$ is closed in $Q\times\mathbb{R}$. If $Q$ is closed, then $\operatorname{epi}_Q f$ is also closed in $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every point of a nonempty convex domain admits a supporting affine minorant valid throughout that domain, then the function is convex and lower semicontinuous relative to the domain. Ambient epigraph closedness additionally requires the domain to be closed.
assumptions_latex: f:Q\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\text{ is proper and finite on }Q
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex and lower semicontinuous relative to }Q,\qquad \operatorname{epi}_Qf\text{ is closed in }Q\times\mathbb{R}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Complete nondecreasing curve and its characterizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the curve by filling the interval between the left and right limits at every abscissa and records its order-theoretic and topological characterizations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \varphi:\mathbb{R}\to[-\infty,+\infty] be nondecreasing and have at least one finite value, and let \varphi_-,\varphi_+ be its left and right limits. A complete nondecreasing curve is \Gamma=\{(x,x^*)\in\mathbb{R}^2:\varphi_-(x)\le x^*\le\varphi_+(x)\}. If I=\{x:\exists x^*\ (x,x^*)\in\Gamma\}, then \Gamma may contain horizontal and vertical segments, the map (x,x^*)\mapsto x+x^* is a bijection from \Gamma onto \mathbb{R} and is continuous with continuous inverse, and \Gamma is equivalently a maximal totally ordered subset of \mathbb{R}^2 under the coordinatewise partial order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complete nondecreasing curve is obtained from an extended-real nondecreasing function having a finite value by including, at each real point, every finite ordinate between its left and right limits. Such a curve may have horizontal and vertical segments. Addition of the two coordinates gives a homeomorphism from the curve onto the real line, and these curves are exactly the maximal subsets of the plane that are totally ordered coordinatewise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (x,x^*)\mapsto x+x^*\text{ is a homeomorphism }\Gamma\to\mathbb{R},\quad \Gamma\text{ is a maximal coordinatewise totally ordered subset of }\mathbb{R}^2.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Level-set topology under a relatively open effective domain
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed proper convex functions whose effective domains are relatively open in their affine hulls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be closed, proper, and convex, and suppose \operatorname{dom}f is relatively open in \operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f); in particular, this holds when \operatorname{dom}f is affine. If \inf f<\alpha<+\infty, then
\[\operatorname{ri}\{x\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}=\{x\mid f(x)<\alpha\},\]
\[\operatorname{cl}\{x\mid f(x)<\alpha\}=\{x\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed proper convex function with relatively open effective domain, every finite level above the infimum has a non-strict level set whose relative interior is the strict level set, and the non-strict level set is the closure of the strict level set. An affine effective domain satisfies the domain hypothesis.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{ri}\{x\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}=\{x\mid f(x)<\alpha\},\quad \operatorname{cl}\{x\mid f(x)<\alpha\}=\{x\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed Convexity from Pointwise Subdifferential Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition placing a proper extended-real function in the closed convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q_1\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ and let $f:Q_1\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}$ be proper, with
\[
\operatorname{dom}f:=\{x\in Q_1:f(x)<+\infty\}.
\]
Suppose that for every $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$ there is a nonempty set $Y(x)$ satisfying
\[
\partial f(x)=\operatorname{conv}Y(x).
\]
Then $f$ is closed and convex on $Q_1$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper extended-real function is closed and convex if, at every point of its effective domain, its subdifferential is the convex hull of a nonempty chosen set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a closed convex function on }Q_1

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial limit identity for closed proper convex functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Radial recovery of values, including boundary and exterior values, within the closed proper convex class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] is closed, proper, and convex, then for every x\in\operatorname{dom}f and every y\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\[f(y)=\lim_{\lambda\uparrow 1}f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed proper convex function, approaching any point y along a segment from any point in the effective domain recovers f(y) as the radial limit.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(y)=\lim_{\lambda\uparrow 1}f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and Attainment of Linear Infimal Projection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional theorem for marginalizing a closed proper convex function along a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be closed, proper, and convex, let A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be linear, and define (Ah)(y)=\inf\{h(x)\mid Ax=y\}. Assume that Az\neq0 whenever h^{0+}(z)\leq0 and h^{0+}(-z)>0. Then Ah is closed, proper, and convex, (Ah)^{0+}=A(h^{0+}), where A(h^{0+})(y)=\inf\{h^{0+}(z)\mid Az=y\}, and for every y with (Ah)(y)\neq+\infty there exists x with Ax=y and h(x)=(Ah)(y).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function remains closed, proper, and convex after infimal projection along a linear map if the map annihilates no direction having nonpositive forward recession value and strictly positive reverse recession value. Recession commutes with this projection, and every marginal value below positive infinity is attained on its fiber.
assumptions_latex: h:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ah\text{ is closed, proper, and convex},\qquad (Ah)^{0+}=A(h^{0+}),\qquad (Ah)(y)\neq+\infty\implies\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \left(Ax=y\ \wedge\ h(x)=(Ah)(y)\right).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise constrained subgradients imply closedness on a convex set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient condition for closedness on a nonempty convex subset of the effective domain; the conclusion retains the source's set-relative formulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $Q\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be nonempty and convex, and let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ be proper and convex with $Q\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f$. For $x\in Q$, define
\[
\partial_Qf(x)=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in Q\}.
\]
If $\partial_Qf(x)\neq\varnothing$ for every $x\in Q$, then $f$ is a closed convex function on $Q$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a proper convex function has, at every point of a nonempty convex subset of its effective domain, an affine supporting slope valid throughout that subset, then the function is closed and convex on that subset.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a closed convex function on }Q

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closedness and recession calculus for pointwise suprema
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arbitrarily indexed pointwise suprema, including a relative-interior condition for commuting closure with the supremum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let I be an arbitrary index set, let f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper convex for every i\in I, and set f=\sup_{i\in I}f_i pointwise. If f is finite somewhere and every f_i is closed, then f is closed and proper and f^{0+}=\sup_{i\in I}f_i^{0+}. If the f_i are not all closed but there exists \bar x\in\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i) with f(\bar x)<+\infty, then \operatorname{cl}f=\sup_{i\in I}\operatorname{cl}f_i.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an arbitrary family of proper convex functions, a pointwise supremum that is finite somewhere is closed and proper when every member is closed, and its recession function is the supremum of their recession functions. If some members are nonclosed, a common relative-interior point where the supremum is finite makes closure commute with the supremum.
assumptions_latex: I\text{ is an arbitrary index set},\quad f_i:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is proper and convex for every }i\in I
\text{First regime: }f(x)<+\infty\text{ for some }x\text{ and every }f_i\text{ is closed}
\text{Second regime: the }f_i\text{ are not all closed and }\exists\bar x\in\bigcap_{i\in I}\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\text{ with }f(\bar x)<+\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \left[f\text{ is closed and proper and }f^{0+}=\sup_{i\in I}f_i^{0+}\right]\quad\text{or, in the second regime,}\quad\operatorname{cl}f=\sup_{i\in I}\operatorname{cl}f_i

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Co-finite Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the equivalent epigraphical and recession formulations and carefully qualifies the bounded-domain sufficient condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is co-finite if it is closed and proper and \(\operatorname{epi}f\) contains no nonvertical half-line. Equivalently, under those closedness and properness requirements, \[f^{0+}(y)=+\infty\qquad\text{for every }y\ne0.\] In particular, every closed proper convex function with bounded effective domain is co-finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function is co-finite when it is closed and proper and its epigraph contains no nonvertical half-line; equivalently, its recession function is infinite in every nonzero direction. A closed proper convex function with bounded effective domain is co-finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is co-finite}\iff\left(f\text{ is closed and proper and }\forall y\ne0,\ f^{0+}(y)=+\infty\right),\qquad \left(f\text{ closed and proper and }\operatorname{dom}f\text{ bounded}\right)\Longrightarrow f\text{ co-finite}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower-semicontinuous convex envelope and affine minorants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to[-\infty,+\infty]\). Pointwise ordering of extended-real functions is used.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space closed convex envelope, including the affine-minorant representation when continuous affine minorants exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\) is \[\breve f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}\}.\] It is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function majorized by \(f\), and \(\operatorname{epi}\breve f\) is closed and convex. Define the affine-minorant family \[\mathcal A_f=\{(u,\alpha)\in H\times\mathbb R:\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha\leq f(x)\ \forall x\in H\}.\] If \(f\) possesses a continuous affine minorant, then \[\breve f(x)=f^{**}(x)=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal A_f}\bigl(\langle x,u\rangle+\alpha\bigr).\] Thus closed convexification is equivalently the supremal calculus of all continuous affine lower supports.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of a function is the pointwise supremum of all lower-semicontinuous convex functions lying below it. It is therefore the largest closed convex minorant. When the original function admits at least one continuous affine minorant, the envelope equals its biconjugate and can be computed as the supremum of all continuous affine functions lying below the original function everywhere.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\breve f=\sup\{g\leq f:g\text{ is lower semicontinuous and convex}\}\), and, when \(\mathcal A_f\ne\varnothing\), \(\breve f=f^{**}=\sup_{(u,\alpha)\in\mathcal A_f}(\langle\cdot,u\rangle+\alpha)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\breve f\) is characterized by \(\breve f\leq f\) and \(g\leq\breve f\) for every lower-semicontinuous convex \(g\leq f\).
When an affine minorant exists, \(\operatorname{epi}\breve f=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}f)\) under the standard properness conditions.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is already lower semicontinuous and convex, then \(\breve f=f\).
For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, \(f\) is the supremum of its continuous affine minorants.
immediate_consequences_latex: The envelope operator is monotone: \(f\leq h\Rightarrow\breve f\leq\breve h\).
The envelope is idempotent: \(\breve{\breve f}=\breve f\).
boundary_notes: If no continuous affine minorant exists, the affine supremum may degenerate and must not be substituted for the defining envelope without qualification.
The envelope is a minorant of \(f\), despite occasional terminology calling it a hull.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex and closed-convex function hulls
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Assume that the indicated families of minorants are nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise hierarchy of convexification and lower-semicontinuous convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex envelope and lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(f\) are respectively \[\operatorname{conv}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex}\}\] and \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=\sup\{g:g\leq f,\ g\text{ convex and lower semicontinuous}\}.\] They satisfy the hull hierarchy \[\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\leq\operatorname{conv}f\leq f.\] Epigraphically, under the usual properness and affine-minorization condition, \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{conv}f)=\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{epi}f),\qquad \operatorname{epi}(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}(\operatorname{epi}f),\] with vertical completion implicit in the epigraph convention. The closed convex envelope is also \(f^{**}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex envelope of a proper function is the greatest convex function below it. The closed convex envelope is the greatest function below it that is both convex and lower semicontinuous. The closed convex envelope lies below the convex envelope, which lies below the original function. Under the standard affine-minorization condition, their epigraphs are the convex hull and closed convex hull of the original epigraph, and the closed convex envelope equals the Fenchel biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\leq\operatorname{conv}f\leq f\), with \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=f^{**}\) when \(f\) has a continuous affine minorant.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}f\) is the pointwise supremum of convex minorants of \(f\).
\(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f\) is the pointwise supremum of lower-semicontinuous convex minorants of \(f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{conv}f=f\).
If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), then \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=\operatorname{conv}f=f\).
For \(f=\iota_S\), the envelopes correspond to indicators of \(\operatorname{conv}S\) and \(\overline{\operatorname{conv}}S\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Both hull operators are monotone and idempotent on their respective fixed-point classes.
Closed convexification can change boundary values and can enlarge the effective domain to points represented by closed convex epigraph limits.
boundary_notes: The epigraph identities require attention to improper degeneracies and the existence of affine minorants.
Convexification alone need not produce a lower-semicontinuous function.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Laws for the Lower-Semicontinuous Hull
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower-semicontinuous hull formation is monotone, idempotent, and fixes exactly the lower-semicontinuous functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever the stated hulls remain \((-\infty,+\infty]\)-valued, \[f\le g\Longrightarrow \operatorname{cl}f\le\operatorname{cl}g,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\operatorname{cl}f.\] Moreover, \(\operatorname{cl}f=f\) if and only if \(f\) is lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) have hulls in the stated codomain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Hull formation is monotone and idempotent, with lower-semicontinuous functions as its fixed points.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic laws of lower-semicontinuous regularization without convexification.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Closure Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Subject to exclusion of minus-infinity degeneration, the epigraph of the lower-semicontinuous hull is the closure of the original epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the lower-semicontinuous hull does not take the value \(-\infty\), then \[\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\] in \(X\times\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: The greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant of \(f\) is \((-\infty,+\infty]\)-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}f)=\overline{\operatorname{epi}f}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Epigraphical representation of lower-semicontinuous regularization without convexification.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Semicontinuous Hulls
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower-semicontinuous hull is the greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant, obtained from neighborhood infima or, metrically, the limit inferior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The lower-semicontinuous hull of \(f\) is the envelope \[\operatorname{cl}f(x)=\sup_{U\in\mathcal N(x)}\inf_{y\in U}f(y).\] It satisfies \(\operatorname{cl}f\leq f\), is lower semicontinuous, and has the maximality property \[g\leq f\ \text{and }g\text{ lower semicontinuous}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad g\leq\operatorname{cl}f.\] In a metrizable space, \(\operatorname{cl}f(x)=\liminf_{y\to x}f(y)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}f\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous function majorized by \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Greatest lower-semicontinuous minorant in a general topological space.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Alone Need Not Close
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of an open interval is already convex, but closing its convex envelope adds the endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f=\delta_{(0,1)}:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Since \((0,1)\) is convex,
\[\operatorname{conv}f=f=\delta_{(0,1)},\]
but \(f\) is not lower semicontinuous and
\[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)=\delta_{[0,1]}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}f=\delta_{(0,1)}\neq\delta_{[0,1]}=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Example showing that the closure stage may strictly change the convex envelope.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexification Before Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, the convex envelope is represented by finite convex combinations. Taking its lower-semicontinuous hull then gives the closed convex envelope and the Fenchel biconjugate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: First form the convex envelope \[\operatorname{conv}f(x)=\inf\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i f(x_i):x_i\in X,\ \lambda_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^{n+1}\lambda_i x_i=x\right\}\qquad(x\in X).\] This is the greatest convex minorant of \(f\), but it need not be lower semicontinuous. Applying lower-semicontinuous closure afterward yields \[\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{conv}f)=\overline{\operatorname{conv}}f=f^{**}.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Hull Properness Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function has a proper closed convex hull exactly when it has a global affine lower bound; the function minus x squared shows failure otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed convex hull \(\operatorname{clconv}f\) is proper if and only if there exist \(a\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\langle a,x\rangle+b\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Thus properness of \(f\) alone does not ensure properness of its closed convex hull. For example, if \(f(x)=-x^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), then no finite affine function minorizes \(f\) globally, and \(\operatorname{clconv}f\equiv-\infty\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, but need not be convex or lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{clconv}f\) is proper exactly when \(f\) admits a finite affine minorant; without one, the hull may equal \(-\infty\) everywhere.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional criterion and a concrete loss-of-properness example.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discontinuous linear functional is a proper finite convex function with no continuous affine global minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space admitting a discontinuous linear functional \(\ell:H\to\mathbb R\). Then \(f=\ell\) is finite, proper, and convex, but it has no global minorant of the form \(x\mapsto\langle x,u\rangle+\beta\) with \(u\in H\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional real Hilbert space admitting a discontinuous linear functional \(\ell:H\to\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f=\ell\) has no continuous affine global minorant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional boundary for existence of continuous affine minorants.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Minorization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a real Hilbert space has a finite continuous affine lower bound valid everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
There exist \(u\in H\) and \(\beta\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
f(x)\geq \langle x,u\rangle+\beta\qquad\text{for every }x\in H.
\]
Equivalently, every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a real Hilbert space possesses a finite continuous affine global minorant.
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists u\in H,\ \exists\beta\in\mathbb{R},\ \forall x\in H:\ f(x)\geq\langle x,u\rangle+\beta\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global continuous affine minorization in a real Hilbert space.
