knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuous affine minorant and exact affine support
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global continuous affine lower bounds, with exactness at a specified point distinguished from mere minorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A continuous affine function \(a:H\to\mathbb R\) is an affine minorant of \(f\) if there exist \(u\in H\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \[a(y)=\langle y,u\rangle+\alpha\leq f(y)\qquad(\forall y\in H).\] It is exact at \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) if additionally \(a(x)=f(x)\), equivalently \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\qquad(\forall y\in H).\] In this case \(u\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\). Every \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\) possesses at least one continuous affine minorant, and if \(x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\), it possesses one exact at \(x\). Moreover, such an \(f\) is the pointwise supremum of all its continuous affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous affine minorant of a proper function is a continuous affine function lying below it at every point. It is exact at a point when it also matches the function there. Exact minorization is the subgradient inequality. Every proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a Hilbert space has at least one continuous affine minorant; at every interior point of its domain it has an exact one. The function itself is the pointwise supremum of all these affine minorants.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a(y)=\langle y,u\rangle+\alpha\) minorizes \(f\) exactly when \(a\leq f\); it is exact at \(x\) exactly when \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle y-x,u\rangle\) for all \(y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) has an affine minorant with slope \(u\) iff \(f-\langle\cdot,u\rangle\) is bounded below.
Exact affine minorization at \(x\) is equivalent to \(u\in\partial f(x)\).
special_cases_latex: A differentiable convex function has the exact affine minorant \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle y-x,\nabla f(x)\rangle\).
For \(f=\iota_C\), exact affine minorants at \(x\in C\) correspond to normal vectors to \(C\) at \(x\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous convex function is bounded below on every bounded subset of \(H\).
For \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), \(f=\sup\{a:a\text{ is a continuous affine minorant of }f\}\).
boundary_notes: Exact affine minorants need not exist at arbitrary boundary points of the effective domain.
A discontinuous linear functional on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space can have no continuous affine minorant.

if and only if \(u\in\partial f(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An affine global minorant touches a convex function at a point exactly when its slope is a subgradient there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugate Parameterization of Affine Minorants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed claim is sound but its canonical home is Fenchel conjugacy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

the inequality \(\langle x,u\rangle+\beta\leq f(x)\) for every \(x\in H\) holds if and only if \(\beta\leq-f^*(u)\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle\cdot,u\rangle+\beta\leq f\iff\beta\leq-f^*(u)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Closure Calculus for Function Operations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closure respects qualified convex sums, while a level-bounded closed convex function remains closed convex after minimization over fibers of a linear map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Under the relative-interior qualification,
\[
\operatorname{cl}(f+g)=\operatorname{cl}\bigl((\operatorname{cl}f)+(\operatorname{cl}g)\bigr).
\]
For the marginal operation, define \(h(y)=\inf\{F(z):Az=y\}\), with an empty infimum equal to \(+\infty\). Level-boundedness of \(F\) makes each finite feasible sublevel compact; consequently every finite infimum defining \(h\) is attained, and \(h\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on \(A(\operatorname{dom}F)\), extended by \(+\infty\) outside that set.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, convex, and level-bounded, and \(A:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to\mathbb{R}^p\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{cl}(f+g)=\operatorname{cl}(\operatorname{cl}f+\operatorname{cl}g)\), while \(h(y)=\inf_{Az=y}F(z)\) is closed convex and its finite infima are attained.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two finite-dimensional qualification rules for sums and linear marginalization.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closed realization of a convex function operation
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(\Phi\) be an operation producing an extended-real function from inputs \((f_i)_{i\in I}\), and let \(\breve g\) denote the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition of closure calculus as post-operation closed convex regularization; exact commutation laws require operation-specific qualification conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The closed realization of a function operation \(\Phi\) is defined by \[\overline{\Phi}(f_i:i\in I)=\breve{\bigl(\Phi(f_i:i\in I)\bigr)}.\] Thus \(\overline{\Phi}\) is the greatest lower-semicontinuous convex function lying below the raw output \(\Phi(f_i)\). For pointwise supremum, closure is unnecessary when every input is lower semicontinuous and convex: \[\sup_{i\in I}f_i\in\Gamma(H).\] For positive finite sums with compatible proper domains, the sum is likewise closed and convex. For operations involving infima, infimal convolution, linear images, or marginalization, the raw output can fail to be lower semicontinuous; its canonical closed value is therefore its envelope \(\breve{\Phi(f_i)}\), equivalently its biconjugate when a continuous affine minorant exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given any operation on extended-real functions, its closed realization is obtained by applying the lower-semicontinuous convex envelope to the operation's raw output. This produces the largest closed convex function below that output. Pointwise suprema of closed convex functions are already closed and convex, and compatible finite positive sums are also closed. Infimum-type operations, infimal convolutions, images, and marginal functions may lose closedness, so closure must generally be applied unless a qualification condition guarantees exact preservation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\Phi}(f_i)=\breve{\Phi(f_i)}\) defines the closure calculus for \(\Phi\); when \(\Phi(f_i)\in\Gamma(H)\), \(\overline{\Phi}(f_i)=\Phi(f_i)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\Phi(f_i)\) has a continuous affine minorant, then \(\overline{\Phi}(f_i)=\Phi(f_i)^{**}\).
Epigraphically, the closed realization replaces the raw epigraph by its closed convex hull under the standard properness conditions.
special_cases_latex: For \(g=\sup_i f_i\) with \(f_i\in\Gamma(H)\), \(\breve g=g\).
For a finite positive sum of lower-semicontinuous convex functions with nonempty common domain, the raw sum is lower semicontinuous and convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closed realization is idempotent: \(\breve{\breve g}=\breve g\).
No closure correction occurs precisely when the raw output is already lower semicontinuous and convex.
boundary_notes: Closure does not generally commute with infimum, image, or infimal convolution without additional assumptions.
The definition records the canonical regularized output and does not assert an unconditional algebraic identity between separate closures and the closure of an operation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalence Interval Between Lower and Upper Concave-Convex Closures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes the two iterated partial closures of a simple proper concave-convex function and every intermediate representative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K be a simple proper concave-convex function on \mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n. Then \operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\sim\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K,\qquad \operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\leq\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K. Moreover, the concave-convex functions H satisfying \operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\leq H\leq\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K form an equivalence class of closed proper concave-convex functions, and every such H has the same kernel as K.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a simple proper concave-convex function, the lower and upper iterated closures are equivalent and pointwise ordered. Every concave-convex function between them belongs to one equivalence class of closed proper functions and has the original kernel.
assumptions_latex: K\text{ is a simple proper concave-convex function on }\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\sim\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K,\quad \operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\leq\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K,\quad \{H:\operatorname{cl}_2\operatorname{cl}_1K\leq H\leq\operatorname{cl}_1\operatorname{cl}_2K\}\text{ is one closed proper equivalence class with kernel }\ker K

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugates of Linear Images and Precompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here Af denotes the infimal image of f under A, gA=g\circ A, and A^*g^* denotes the infimal image of g^* under the adjoint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let A:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be linear. For every convex f on \mathbb{R}^n, (Af)^*=f^*\circ A^*. For every convex g on \mathbb{R}^m, ((\operatorname{cl}g)\circ A)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*g^*). If A^{-1}(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g))\neq\varnothing, then (g\circ A)^*=A^*g^* and, for every x^*,\quad (g\circ A)^*(x^*)=\inf\{g^*(y^*):A^*y^*=x^*\}, where the infimum is attained unless its value is +\infty vacuously.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The conjugate of a convex function's linear image is its conjugate composed with the adjoint. The conjugate of a precomposition by a linear map is the closed infimal adjoint image of the conjugate. If the range of the map meets the relative interior of the function's domain, closure is unnecessary and the fiberwise infimum is attained, except for the vacuous positive-infinity case.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the closure-free and attainment conclusions: }\exists x\in\mathbb{R}^n\text{ with }Ax\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}g)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (Af)^*=f^*\circ A^*,\qquad ((\operatorname{cl}g)\circ A)^*=\operatorname{cl}(A^*g^*),\qquad (g\circ A)^*(x^*)=\min_{A^*y^*=x^*}g^*(y^*)\text{ under the stated qualification, with the stated }+\infty\text{ exception}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variablewise Closures of a Concave-Convex Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines convex closure in the second variable, concave closure in the first variable, and the associated closedness terminology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K be a concave-convex function on \mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n. The convex closure of K in its second variable, denoted \operatorname{cl}_vK or \operatorname{cl}_2K, is obtained by closing v\mapsto K(u,v) as a convex function for each fixed u. The concave closure of K in its first variable, denoted \operatorname{cl}_uK or \operatorname{cl}_1K, is obtained by closing u\mapsto K(u,v) as a concave function for each fixed v. The function K is convex-closed when K=\operatorname{cl}_2K and concave-closed when K=\operatorname{cl}_1K.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The second-variable closure closes every convex slice obtained by fixing the first variable, while the first-variable closure closes every concave slice obtained by fixing the second variable. Equality with the corresponding closure defines convex-closedness or concave-closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{cl}_2K:=\operatorname{cl}_vK,\qquad \operatorname{cl}_1K:=\operatorname{cl}_uK;\qquad K\text{ is convex-closed}\iff K=\operatorname{cl}_2K,\quad K\text{ is concave-closed}\iff K=\operatorname{cl}_1K.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support Functions of Minkowski Sums and Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support-function specialization of sum–infimal-convolution conjugacy for nonempty convex sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let C_1,\ldots,C_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n be nonempty convex sets. Then \sigma_{C_1+\cdots+C_m}=\sigma_{C_1}+\cdots+\sigma_{C_m} and \sigma_{\operatorname{cl}C_1\cap\cdots\cap\operatorname{cl}C_m}=\operatorname{cl}(\sigma_{C_1}\square\cdots\square\sigma_{C_m}). If \bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}C_i\neq\varnothing, closure can be omitted in the second identity and, for every x^*,\quad \sigma_{C_1\cap\cdots\cap C_m}(x^*)=\inf_{x_1^*+\cdots+x_m^*=x^*}\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_{C_i}(x_i^*), with the infimum attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The support function of a Minkowski sum is the sum of the individual support functions. The support function of the intersection of the closed sets is the closed infimal convolution of their support functions. If the sets' relative interiors have a common point, closure is unnecessary and the decomposition infimum is attained for every dual vector.
assumptions_latex: C_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is nonempty and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sigma_{\sum_i C_i}=\sum_i\sigma_{C_i},\qquad \sigma_{\bigcap_i\operatorname{cl}C_i}=\operatorname{cl}(\square_i\sigma_{C_i}),\qquad \sigma_{\bigcap_i C_i}(x^*)=\min_{\sum_i x_i^*=x^*}\sum_i\sigma_{C_i}(x_i^*)\text{ under the stated qualification}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Conjugacy Duality for Sums and Infimal Convolutions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite families of proper convex functions on a common finite-dimensional space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,\ldots,f_m be proper convex functions on \mathbb{R}^n. Then (f_1\square\cdots\square f_m)^*=f_1^*+\cdots+f_m^* and (\operatorname{cl}f_1+\cdots+\operatorname{cl}f_m)^*=\operatorname{cl}(f_1^*\square\cdots\square f_m^*). If \bigcap_{i=1}^m\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f_i)\neq\varnothing, closure can be omitted in the second identity and, for every x^*,\quad (f_1+\cdots+f_m)^*(x^*)=\inf_{x_1^*+\cdots+x_m^*=x^*}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(x_i^*), with the infimum attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conjugation exchanges finite infimal convolution with addition. Conversely, the conjugate of the sum of the closed envelopes is the closed infimal convolution of the conjugates. When all relative interiors of the domains meet, the closure is unnecessary and every dual decomposition problem attains its infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (\square_{i=1}^m f_i)^*=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*,\qquad \left(\sum_{i=1}^m\operatorname{cl}f_i\right)^*=\operatorname{cl}\left(\square_{i=1}^m f_i^*\right),\qquad \left(\sum_{i=1}^m f_i\right)^*(x^*)=\min_{\sum_i x_i^*=x^*}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i^*(x_i^*)\text{ under the stated qualification}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local convex continuity and boundedness regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, and fix \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise Hilbert-space correspondence for proper convex functions; local boundedness means boundedness on a norm neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The following four local regularity conditions at \(x_0\) define the same regime: \[(i)\ f\text{ is locally Lipschitz near }x_0;\qquad (ii)\ f\text{ is continuous at }x_0;\] \[(iii)\ f\text{ is bounded on a neighborhood of }x_0;\qquad (iv)\ f\text{ is bounded above on a neighborhood of }x_0.\] Explicitly, condition (iv) means that there exist \(\rho>0\) and \(M\in\mathbb R\) such that \(f(x)\leq M\) for every \(x\in B(x_0;\rho)\). Local Lipschitz continuity means that there exist \(r>0\) and \(L\geq0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in B(x_0;r)).\] If these equivalent conditions hold at one point, then \(f\) is locally Lipschitz throughout \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function on a Hilbert space, four pointwise notions coincide: local Lipschitz continuity, continuity, boundedness on a neighborhood, and boundedness above on a neighborhood. Local upper boundedness requires one finite upper bound on some norm ball around the point. Local Lipschitz continuity requires a uniform Lipschitz constant on a possibly smaller ball. Once this regime occurs, the function is locally Lipschitz at every point in the interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x_0\), local Lipschitz continuity, continuity, local boundedness, and local upper boundedness of proper convex \(f\) are equivalent.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x_0\in\operatorname{cont}f\iff(\exists\rho>0)\;\sup_{B(x_0;\rho)}f<+\infty\).
Under any equivalent condition, \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), then \(\operatorname{cont}f=\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
In finite dimensions, every proper convex function is continuous on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A locally upper-bounded convex function is automatically locally bounded below as well.
On compact subsets of the relative interior in finite dimensions, a proper convex function is Lipschitz.
boundary_notes: The correspondence is local and does not imply a global Lipschitz constant.
At boundary points of the effective domain, local boundedness and continuity can fail.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Automatic-Continuity Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A discontinuous linear functional is finite and convex on its whole infinite-dimensional normed space but is nowhere continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be an infinite-dimensional normed space and let \(\ell:X\to\mathbb R\) be a discontinuous linear functional. Then \(\ell\) is proper, finite-valued, and convex, with \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\ell)=X\), but it is nowhere continuous. Thus the finite-dimensional automatic-continuity theorem does not extend to arbitrary infinite-dimensional normed spaces.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell:X\to\mathbb R\) is a discontinuous linear functional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}\ell)=X\) while \(\ell\) is nowhere continuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of dimension-free automatic relative-interior continuity without a regularity hypothesis.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Continuity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper finite-dimensional convex function is automatically continuous throughout the relative interior of its effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x_0\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), the restriction of \(f\) to \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) is finite and continuous at \(x_0\) in the relative topology of \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Equivalently, for every sequence \((x_k)\) in \(\operatorname{dom}f\) satisfying \(x_k\to x_0\), one has \(f(x_k)\to f(x_0)\). Thus no lower-semicontinuity assumption is needed at relative-interior points in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_{\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)}\) is continuous in the relative topology of \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional continuity in the intrinsic topology of the effective domain.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity on the relative interior of the effective domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex. Let \(A=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), equipped with the relative Euclidean topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic-domain continuity; relative continuity is continuity of the restriction to the affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative interior of the effective domain is \[\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:(\exists\varepsilon>0)\;B(x;\varepsilon)\cap A\subset\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] The function \(f\) is relatively continuous at \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) when its restriction \(f|_A:A\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is continuous at \(x\). Every proper convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\) is finite and relatively continuous at each \(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). More strongly, for every nonempty compact \(K\subset\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists \(L_K\geq0\) such that \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L_K\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in K).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative interior of the effective domain consists of points having a neighborhood inside the domain when neighborhoods are taken within the domain's affine hull. Relative continuity means ordinary continuity after restricting the function to that affine hull. Every proper finite-dimensional convex function is relatively continuous throughout the relative interior of its effective domain and is Lipschitz on each compact subset contained there.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f|_A\) is continuous on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and it is Lipschitz on every compact subset of that relative interior.
equivalent_formulations_latex: After identifying \(A\) with a Euclidean space of dimension \(\dim A\), relative-interior continuity becomes ordinary interior continuity.
\(x\in\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) iff some relative ball \(B(x;\varepsilon)\cap A\) lies in \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
special_cases_latex: If \(\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\mathbb R^n\), then \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
If \(f\) is real-valued on \(\mathbb R^n\), then it is continuous everywhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: A lower-dimensional effective domain does not obstruct continuity when the correct relative topology is used.
All discontinuities of a proper finite-dimensional convex function are confined to the relative boundary of its domain.
boundary_notes: Relative continuity does not imply ambient continuity when the affine hull is a proper subspace and the function equals \(+\infty\) off that subspace.
No continuity conclusion is asserted at relative-boundary points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subsequence compactness of densely bounded saddle functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise boundedness is required only on a dense Cartesian subset, while convergence is uniform on every closed bounded subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, and let \((K_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite concave-convex functions on \(C\times D\). Suppose there are dense sets \(C'\subseteq C\) and \(D'\subseteq D\) such that \((K_i(u,v))_{i\ge1}\) is bounded for every \((u,v)\in C'\times D'\). Then some subsequence \((K_{i_j})_{j\ge1}\) converges uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\times D\) to a finite concave-convex function \(K\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sequence of finite saddle functions that is pointwise bounded on a dense Cartesian subset has a subsequence converging locally uniformly, in the closed-bounded-set sense, to a finite saddle function.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\text{ and }D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are relatively open and convex}
\forall i\ge1,\;K_i:C\times D\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is finite and concave-convex}
\exists C'\subseteq C,D'\subseteq D\text{ dense}:\forall(u,v)\in C'\times D',\;\sup_{i\ge1}|K_i(u,v)|<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists(i_j)_{j\ge1},\;\exists K:C\times D\to\mathbb{R}\text{ finite and concave-convex}:\quad \forall S\subseteq C\times D\text{ closed and bounded},\;\sup_{x\in S}|K_{i_j}(x)-K(x)|\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interior Local Boundedness and Lipschitz Regularity of Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional regularity theorem using the ball and norm notation stated in the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). Then \(f\) is locally bounded and locally Lipschitz continuous at \(x_0\). More precisely, there exist \(\epsilon>0\) and \(L>0\) such that \(B_1(x_0,\epsilon)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) and
\[
|f(y)-f(x_0)|\le L\|y-x_0\|_{(1)}\qquad\text{for all }y\in B_1(x_0,\epsilon).
\]
In particular, \(f\) is bounded on \(B_1(x_0,\epsilon)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every interior point of the effective domain of a finite-dimensional convex function, the function is locally bounded and locally Lipschitz. On a sufficiently small stated ball, its difference from the value at the center is bounded by a constant times the stated norm distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\epsilon,L>0:\ B_1(x_0,\epsilon)\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f,\ \forall y\in B_1(x_0,\epsilon),\ |f(y)-f(x_0)|\le L\|y-x_0\|_{(1)},\ \text{and }f\text{ is bounded on }B_1(x_0,\epsilon)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise bounded saddle families are locally uniformly bounded and equi-Lipschitz
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The pointwise control set must generate the whole product domain after closure and convexification.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, and let \(\{K_i\}_{i\in I}\) be finite concave-convex functions on \(C\times D\). Suppose \(C'\subseteq C\), \(D'\subseteq D\), \(\operatorname{conv}(\operatorname{cl}(C'\times D'))\supseteq C\times D\), and \(\{K_i(u,v):i\in I\}\) is bounded for every \((u,v)\in C'\times D'\). Then for every closed bounded \(S\subseteq C\times D\), there exist finite constants \(M_S,L_S\) such that \(|K_i(x)|\le M_S\) and \(|K_i(x)-K_i(y)|\le L_S\|x-y\|\) for all \(i\in I\) and \(x,y\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a family of finite saddle functions is pointwise bounded on a subset whose closed convex hull covers the product domain, then the family is uniformly bounded and equi-Lipschitz on every closed bounded subset of that domain.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\text{ and }D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are relatively open and convex}
\{K_i\}_{i\in I}\text{ is a family of finite concave-convex functions on }C\times D
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall S\subseteq C\times D\text{ closed and bounded},\;\exists M_S,L_S<\infty\;\forall i\in I:\;\sup_{x\in S}|K_i(x)|\le M_S,\quad |K_i(x)-K_i(y)|\le L_S\|x-y\|\;\forall x,y\in S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz Continuity and Boundedness of Convex Subgradients
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The bounded-subgradient condition always implies Lipschitz continuity on the specified set; openness of the set is required for the stated converse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(X\subseteq\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), and fix \(L\). Define \(\mathrm{(i)}\) by \(|f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\in X\), and \(\mathrm{(ii)}\) by \(\|g\|_*\le L\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(g\in\partial f(x)\). Then \(\mathrm{(ii)}\Rightarrow\mathrm{(i)}\). If \(X\) is open, then \(\mathrm{(i)}\Longleftrightarrow\mathrm{(ii)}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function on a subset of the interior of its domain, uniform boundedness by L of every subgradient on the set implies that the function is L-Lipschitz there. If the set is open, the Lipschitz and bounded-subgradient conditions are equivalent.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\text{ is proper and convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[\forall x\in X\;\forall g\in\partial f(x),\ \|g\|_*\le L\bigr]\Rightarrow\bigl[\forall x,y\in X,\ |f(x)-f(y)|\le L\|x-y\|\bigr],\quad\text{and if }X\text{ is open, the two conditions are equivalent.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Joint continuity of parameterized saddle functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity in the parameter may be imposed everywhere or only for primal-variable pairs in a dense Cartesian subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, let \(T\) be a locally compact topological space, and let \(K:C\times D\times T\to\mathbb{R}\). Then \(K\) is jointly continuous on \(C\times D\times T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued parameterized saddle function is jointly continuous when its parameter sections are continuous; it is enough to require this continuity for variable pairs in a dense Cartesian subset.

T\text{ is a locally compact topological space}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Best sampled value bounded by the pointwise continuity modulus
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an arbitrary real-valued function on a set when the infimum is attained; no convexity or algorithmic assumptions are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:Q\to\mathbb R\), let \(x_0,\ldots,x_k\in Q\), and suppose \(x^*\in Q\) attains \(f^*:=\inf_{x\in Q}f(x)\). Define \(f_k^*:=\min_{0\le i\le k}f(x_i)\), \(v_k^*:=\min_{0\le i\le k}\|x_i-x^*\|\), and \(\omega_f(x^*;t):=\sup\{|f(x)-f(x^*)|:x\in Q,\ \|x-x^*\|\le t\}\). knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many sampled points, the gap between the best sampled value and the attained minimum is at most the pointwise modulus of continuity evaluated at the distance of the closest sample to the minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_k^*-f^*\le \omega_f(x^*;v_k^*)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Continuity Relative to a Subset
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines continuity along a subset without imposing continuity under approaches from outside it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a function on \(\mathbb R^n\) and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). The function \(f\) is continuous relative to \(S\) if and only if its restriction \(f|_S\) is continuous; equivalently, for every \(x\in S\), \(\lim_{S\ni y\to x}f(y)=f(x)\). No condition is imposed on approaches to \(x\) from outside \(S\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is continuous relative to }S\iff f|_S\text{ is continuous}\iff \forall x\in S,\ \lim_{S\ni y\to x}f(y)=f(x)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense-set convergence determines a finite saddle-function limit
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The hypothesis requires a finite pointwise limit on a dense Cartesian subset of the relatively open product domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be relatively open convex sets, and let \((K_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite concave-convex functions on \(C\times D\). Suppose there are dense sets \(C'\subseteq C\) and \(D'\subseteq D\) such that \(\lim_{i\to\infty}K_i(u,v)\) exists and is finite for every \((u,v)\in C'\times D'\). Then this limit exists and is finite for every \((u,v)\in C\times D\); the function \(K(u,v)=\lim_{i\to\infty}K_i(u,v)\) is concave-convex; and \(K_i\to K\) uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\times D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite pointwise convergence of saddle functions on a dense Cartesian subset extends to the whole product domain, preserves the saddle property, and is uniform on each closed bounded subset.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^m\text{ and }D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ are relatively open and convex}
\forall i\ge1,\;K_i:C\times D\to\mathbb{R}\text{ is finite and concave-convex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall(u,v)\in C\times D,\;K(u,v):=\lim_{i\to\infty}K_i(u,v)\in\mathbb{R};\quad K\text{ is concave-convex};\quad \forall S\subseteq C\times D\text{ closed and bounded},\;\sup_{x\in S}|K_i(x)-K(x)|\to0.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise, interior, and compactly contained convex regularity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex on a real Hilbert space. For finite-dimensional relative statements, work in \(A=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Taxonomy of increasingly uniform local regularity regimes for convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Three local convex regularity regimes are distinguished. Pointwise regularity at \(x\) means that \(f\) is continuous at \(x\), equivalently locally Lipschitz or locally upper bounded there. Interior regularity means \[f\text{ is locally Lipschitz at every }x\in\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f.\] In finite dimensions, intrinsic interior regularity replaces the interior by \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) and uses the relative topology of \(A\). Compactly contained regularity means that for every nonempty compact \(K\subset\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\), there exists \(L_K<+\infty\) satisfying \[|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L_K\|x-y\|\qquad(\forall x,y\in K).\] The constant may depend on \(K\); no global Lipschitz bound is part of the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Local convex regularity has three useful scales. Pointwise regularity means continuity at one point, equivalently local Lipschitz continuity or local upper boundedness there. Interior regularity means local Lipschitz continuity at every interior point. In finite dimensions, the intrinsic version uses the relative interior and its affine-hull topology. Compactly contained regularity strengthens this to one Lipschitz constant on each compact subset of the relative interior, while allowing the constant to change from one compact set to another.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise, interior, and compactly contained regularity are defined by continuity at one point, local Lipschitz continuity throughout the intrinsic interior, and a uniform Lipschitz constant on each compact intrinsic-interior subset, respectively.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Pointwise regularity at \(x\) is equivalent to boundedness above on some neighborhood of \(x\).
Compactly contained regularity is local Lipschitz regularity made uniform over each fixed compact subset.
special_cases_latex: If \(f\in\Gamma_0(H)\), then interior regularity holds on \(\operatorname{int}\operatorname{dom}f\).
Every proper convex function on \(\mathbb R^n\) has compactly contained regularity on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: On each admissible compact \(K\), \(f\) is uniformly continuous.
Regularity constants can deteriorate as compact sets approach the relative boundary.
boundary_notes: Compact subsets touching the relative boundary are not covered.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, relative-interior statements require additional care because the relevant interior may be empty and finite-dimensional compactness arguments fail.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant associated with compact set \(K\)

knowledge_statements.title: Local Upper Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex function on an open convex set is continuous at a point exactly when it is locally bounded above there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is continuous at \(x_0\) if and only if there exist \(r>0\) and \(M\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(B(x_0,r)\subseteq U\) and
\[
f(x)\leq M\qquad\text{for every }x\in B(x_0,r).
\]
For convex functions, this one-sided local upper bound forces both local boundedness and continuity at the center.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and convex, and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is continuous at \(x_0\) if and only if it is bounded above on some neighborhood of \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise continuity criterion for finite convex functions on open domains.

notation.meaning: open Euclidean ball centered at x with radius r

knowledge_statements.title: Local Lower Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near every relative-interior point, a proper finite-dimensional convex function has a finite lower bound in the affine hull of its domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(L=\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\). There exist \(r>0\) and \(m\in\mathbb{R}\) such that
\[
f(x)\geq m\qquad\text{for every }x\in B(x_0,r)\cap L.
\]
The radius may be chosen so that this relative ball lies in \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\); continuity of the finite restriction then supplies a finite lower bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists r>0,\ \exists m\in\mathbb{R}: f(x)\geq m\) on \(B(x_0,r)\cap\operatorname{aff}(\operatorname{dom}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic local lower boundedness at relative-interior points.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompact Interior Sets Need Not Admit Uniform Control
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Interior containment alone does not ensure uniform boundedness or a common Lipschitz constant on a noncompact set, as the exponential function on the nonnegative ray shows.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in K}f(x)=+\infty\) and \(\sup_{x\ne y\in K}|f(x)-f(y)|/|x-y|=+\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Boundary-value failure regimes for convex functions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{rbd}D=\overline D\setminus\operatorname{ri}D\). Limits are taken with \(y\to x\) and \(y\in\operatorname{ri}D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic-boundary taxonomy based on the interior lower limit and the assigned boundary value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the intrinsic interior lower limit at \(x\) by \[\ell_f(x)=\liminf_{\substack{y\to x\\y\in\operatorname{ri}D}}f(y)\in[-\infty,+\infty].\] Boundary behavior is classified as follows. It is regular finite when \(x\in D\), \(\ell_f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(f(x)=\ell_f(x)\). It is a finite upward jump when \(x\in D\), \(\ell_f(x)\in\mathbb R\), and \(f(x)>\ell_f(x)\). It is excluded-boundary divergence when \(x\notin D\), so \(f(x)=+\infty\), with either finite approach value \(\ell_f(x)<+\infty\) or divergent approach \(\ell_f(x)=+\infty\). Finally, it is included divergent behavior when \(x\in D\) and \(f(x)=\ell_f(x)=+\infty\), which is impossible under the effective-domain convention and is therefore represented instead by exclusion from \(D\). Lower semicontinuity at \(x\) is exactly \(f(x)\leq\ell_f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a relative-boundary point, compare the assigned function value with the lower limiting values approached from the relative interior. A regular finite boundary point has a finite matching limit. A finite upward jump has a boundary value strictly above a finite interior limit. If the boundary point is outside the effective domain, its value is positive infinity; the interior values may either remain finitely bounded along some approaches or diverge to positive infinity. Lower semicontinuity is precisely the requirement that the assigned value not exceed the intrinsic lower limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pair \((f(x),\ell_f(x))\) classifies regular finite, upward-jump, finite-approach excluded, and divergent excluded boundary behavior; lower semicontinuity at \(x\) is \(f(x)\leq\ell_f(x)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A finite upward jump is characterized by \(x\in D\) and \(f(x)>\liminf_{y\to x,\,y\in\operatorname{ri}D}f(y)\).
A closed convex function excludes any boundary point whose finite assigned value would exceed the interior lower limit.
special_cases_latex: For a univariate convex function at an endpoint \(a\), the one-sided limit \(f(a+)\) exists in \(\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(f(a)\geq f(a+)\).
The indicator of a closed convex set has regular finite value \(0\) at included boundary points and value \(+\infty\) outside the set.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity guarantees interior continuity but does not prevent boundary jumps.
Closing a convex function lowers an upward-jump boundary value to the corresponding lower-semicontinuous envelope value.
boundary_notes: The taxonomy uses \(\liminf\); a full limit need not exist at a multidimensional boundary point.
The inequality direction \(f(x)\geq\ell_f(x)\) is specific to the one-dimensional endpoint result and is not asserted universally in higher dimensions.

notation.meaning: intrinsic interior lower limit at the boundary point

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Relative Boundary Continuity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite boundary continuity means convergence to the finite boundary value along every sequence in the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x_0\in D\cap\operatorname{rbd}D\), with \(f(x_0)\in\mathbb R\). The function is continuous at \(x_0\) relative to its domain when \[\lim_{\substack{x\to x_0\\x\in D}}f(x)=f(x_0).\] Equivalently, \(f(x_k)\to f(x_0)\) for every sequence \(x_k\in D\) converging to \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative continuity at \(x_0\) is equivalent to convergence along every domain sequence approaching \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and sequential formulation at a finite domain-boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Continuity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a finite boundary point, relative lower semicontinuity plus a local upper bound is sufficient for continuity along the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Write \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\). Suppose \(f(x_0)\in\mathbb{R}\), \(f\) is lower semicontinuous at \(x_0\) relative to \(D\), and there exist a neighborhood \(V\) of \(x_0\) and \(M\in\mathbb{R}\) such that \(f(x)\leq M\) for every \(x\in V\cap D\). Then
\[
\lim_{\substack{x\to x_0\\x\in D}}f(x)=f(x_0),
\]
so \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous at \(x_0\) in the relative topology.
assumptions_latex: \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\) may lie on the relative boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Local upper boundedness relative to \(\operatorname{dom}f\), together with lower semicontinuity at \(x_0\), implies relative continuity at \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient boundary-continuity criterion in the relative domain topology.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unique Continuous Convex Extension from the Relative Interior
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuous finite extension to the boundary of a locally simplicial convex set under bounded-on-bounded upper control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex and locally simplicial. Let \(f:\operatorname{ri}C\to\mathbb R\) be convex and bounded above on every bounded subset of \(\operatorname{ri}C\). Then there exists a unique finite convex function \(\bar f:C\to\mathbb R\), continuous relative to \(C\), such that \(\bar f|_{\operatorname{ri}C}=f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If C is a locally simplicial convex set and a finite convex function on its relative interior is bounded above on every bounded subset there, then the function has exactly one extension to a finite convex function continuous on all of C.
assumptions_latex: C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is convex and locally simplicial}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists!\,\bar f:C\to\mathbb R:\ \bar f\text{ is finite, convex, and continuous relative to }C,\quad \bar f|_{\operatorname{ri}C}=f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise limsup bounds become locally uniform upper bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The conclusion is one-sided and uniform only on closed bounded subsets lying inside the relatively open domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a relatively open convex set, let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be convex, and let \((f_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). If \(\limsup_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in C\), then for every closed bounded \(S\subset C\) and every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists \(i_0\) such that \(f_i(x)\le f(x)+\varepsilon\) for all \(i\ge i_0\) and all \(x\in S\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise asymptotic upper bound of finite convex functions by a finite convex function becomes a uniform eventual upper bound, with any positive tolerance, on each closed bounded subset of the relatively open domain.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a relatively open convex set}
S\subset C\text{ is closed and bounded}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists i_0\ \forall i\ge i_0\ \forall x\in S:\ f_i(x)\le f(x)+\varepsilon

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense pointwise convergence of convex functions is locally uniform
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves finiteness of the dense-set limits and the relative openness of the common domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a relatively open convex set and let \((f_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). Suppose there is \(C'\subset C\) with \(\operatorname{cl}C'\supset C\) such that \(\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\in\mathbb R\) exists for every \(x\in C'\). Then \(\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\) exists for every \(x\in C\); the function \(f(x)=\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\) is finite and convex on \(C\); and \(f_i\to f\) uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If finite convex functions on a relatively open convex set converge to finite values on a dense subset, their pointwise limit extends to the entire set, is finite and convex, and the convergence is uniform on every closed bounded subset.
assumptions_latex: C\text{ is a relatively open convex set}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall x\in C,\ f(x):=\lim_{i\to\infty}f_i(x)\in\mathbb R;\quad f\text{ is convex};\quad \forall S\subset C\text{ closed and bounded},\ \sup_{x\in S}|f_i(x)-f(x)|\to0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional and coordinate-partial criteria for saddle differentiability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization at a finite point of a concave-convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K be concave in u\in\mathbb{R}^m and convex in v\in\mathbb{R}^n, with K(u,v) finite. Then K is differentiable at (u,v) if and only if K is finite on a neighborhood of (u,v) and the directional-derivative mapping (u',v')\mapsto K'(u,v;u',v') is linear on \mathbb{R}^{m+n}. In particular, K is differentiable at (u,v) if all m+n two-sided coordinate partial derivatives at (u,v) exist and are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite saddle function is differentiable at a point exactly when it is locally finite and its directional derivative is linear in the direction. Existence and finiteness of all two-sided coordinate partial derivatives is sufficient.
assumptions_latex: K:\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is concave in }u\text{ and convex in }v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: K\text{ is differentiable at }(u,v)\iff\bigl[K\text{ is finite on a neighborhood of }(u,v)\text{ and }K'(u,v;\cdot,\cdot)\text{ is linear}\bigr];\quad\bigl[\text{all }m+n\text{ finite two-sided coordinate partial derivatives exist}\bigr]\Rightarrow K\text{ is differentiable at }(u,v).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Separate parameter continuity and convexity imply joint continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers the full hypothesis and the dense-set weakening of parameter continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be relatively open and convex, let \(T\) be locally compact, and let \(f:C\times T\to\mathbb R\). If \(f(\cdot,t)\) is convex on \(C\) for every \(t\in T\) and \(f(x,\cdot)\) is continuous on \(T\) for every \(x\in C\), then \(f\) is jointly continuous on \(C\times T\). It suffices that there exist \(C'\subset C\) with \(\operatorname{cl}C'\supset C\) such that \(f(x,\cdot)\) is continuous on \(T\) for every \(x\in C'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on a relatively open convex set times a locally compact parameter space is jointly continuous when it is convex in the first variable and continuous in the parameter. Parameter continuity need only be verified on a subset dense in the convex domain.
assumptions_latex: C\subset\mathbb R^n\text{ is relatively open and convex}
T\text{ is a locally compact topological space}
\forall t\in T,\ f(\cdot,t)\text{ is convex on }C
\forall x\in C,\ f(x,\cdot)\text{ is continuous on }T
\text{or, more weakly, }\exists C'\subset C:\operatorname{cl}C'\supset C\ \land\ \forall x\in C',\ f(x,\cdot)\text{ is continuous}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is continuous on }C\times T

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Existence and block decomposition of saddle-function directional derivatives
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional differentiability at points of an open convex region on which the saddle function is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let K:\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}} be concave in its first argument and convex in its second, and let C\times D be an open convex set on which K is finite. For every (u,v)\in C\times D, the directional derivative K'(u,v;u',v') exists and is finite for every (u',v')\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n. As a function of (u',v'), it is positively homogeneous, concave in u', and convex in v', and satisfies K'(u,v;u',v')=K'(u,v;u',0)+K'(u,v;0,v').
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every point of an open convex region where a concave-convex saddle function is finite, all directional derivatives exist and are finite. The derivative is positively homogeneous and concave-convex in the direction, and it equals the sum of its first-block and second-block directional derivatives.
assumptions_latex: K:\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\overline{\mathbb{R}}\text{ is concave in }u\text{ and convex in }v
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall (u',v')\in\mathbb{R}^m\times\mathbb{R}^n,\quad K'(u,v;u',v')\in\mathbb{R},\quad K'(u,v;u',v')=K'(u,v;u',0)+K'(u,v;0,v'),\text{ and }K'(u,v;\cdot,\cdot)\text{ is positively homogeneous and concave-convex}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Pointwise-bounded convex sequences have locally uniformly convergent subsequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise boundedness may be imposed on the whole domain or only on a dense subset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a relatively open convex set and let \((f_i)_{i\ge1}\) be finite convex functions on \(C\). Suppose either that \((f_i(x))_{i\ge1}\) is bounded for every \(x\in C\), or that there is a dense subset \(C'\subset C\) for which it is bounded at every \(x\in C'\). Then there exist indices \(i_1<i_2<\cdots\) and a finite convex function \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) such that \(f_{i_j}\to f\) uniformly on every closed bounded subset of \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sequence of finite convex functions that is pointwise bounded on its relatively open convex domain—or merely on a dense subset—has a subsequence converging uniformly on each closed bounded subset to a finite convex function.

\text{or, more weakly, }\exists C'\subset C\text{ dense}:\forall x\in C',\ \sup_{i\ge1}|f_i(x)|<\infty
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists i_1<i_2<\cdots\ \exists f:C\to\mathbb R\text{ finite and convex}\ \forall S\subset C\text{ closed and bounded}:\ \sup_{x\in S}|f_{i_j}(x)-f(x)|\to0

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Discontinuity Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite boundary discontinuity is failure of relative continuity at a boundary point where the function has a finite value; a domain sequence witnesses the failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(x_0\in D\cap\operatorname{rbd}D\), with \(f(x_0)\in\mathbb R\). A finite boundary discontinuity occurs when \(f\) is not continuous at \(x_0\) relative to \(D\). Equivalently, there are \(x_k\in D\), \(x_k\to x_0\), and \(\varepsilon>0\) such that \[|f(x_k)-f(x_0)|\ge\varepsilon\] for every \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Relative discontinuity is equivalent to a domain sequence whose values remain separated from \(f(x_0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition and sequential witness at a finite effective-domain boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Boundary Discontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite convex boundary value need not equal the limit of interior values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f(x)=\begin{cases}1,&x=0,\\0,&0<x\le1,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Its epigraph is convex, so \(f\) is proper and convex, and \(0\in\operatorname{rbd}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) has the finite value \(f(0)=1\). Nevertheless, \[\lim_{x\downarrow0}f(x)=0\ne f(0).\] Hence convexity and finiteness at a boundary point do not imply relative continuity there; in this example lower semicontinuity fails at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function can assign a finite elevated endpoint value while all nearby interior values are lower, producing boundary discontinuity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The proper convex function displayed above is finite but discontinuous at the boundary point \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Blow-Up Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary blow-up means universal divergence to positive infinity along relative-interior approaches to an excluded boundary point; equivalently, the positive-infinity extension is lower semicontinuous there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\), and \(\bar x\in\operatorname{rbd}D\setminus D\). Boundary blow-up at \(\bar x\) means \[x_k\in\operatorname{ri}D,\quad x_k\to\bar x\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f(x_k)\to+\infty.\] Equivalently, the extension already assigning \(f(\bar x)=+\infty\) is lower semicontinuous at \(\bar x\) relative to \(D\cup\{\bar x\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every relative-interior sequence approaching \(\bar x\) has values tending to \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential divergence at an excluded finite relative-domain boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Blow-Up
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex values may diverge to positive infinity when approaching a domain boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f(x)=\begin{cases}-\log x,&x>0,\\+\infty,&x\le0.\end{cases}\] Then \(f\) is proper, closed, and strictly convex, with \(\operatorname{dom}f=(0,+\infty)\). At the boundary point \(0\), \[\lim_{x\downarrow0}f(x)=+\infty.\] Thus continuity on \(\operatorname{ri}(\operatorname{dom}f)\) supplies no finite boundary extension and no upper bound on neighborhoods that meet points arbitrarily close to this boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The negative logarithm is convex and continuous inside its domain but diverges to positive infinity at the boundary zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\), so no finite continuous boundary extension exists at \(0\).

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Boundary Dependence Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directional boundary dependence occurs when two admissible interior approaches to the same finite boundary point produce different extended limits.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=\operatorname{dom}f\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(\bar x\in D\cap\operatorname{rbd}D\), with \(f(\bar x)\in\mathbb R\). Boundary behavior is directionally dependent at \(\bar x\) if there are sequences \(x_k,y_k\in\operatorname{ri}D\), both converging to \(\bar x\), for which the extended limits of \(f(x_k)\) and \(f(y_k)\) exist and are unequal. Consequently, no unique relative-interior boundary limit exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Unequal limits along two relative-interior sequences preclude a unique boundary limit.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonunique approach behavior at a finite effective-domain boundary point.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Boundary Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed convex function may have path-dependent finite or infinite behavior near a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb{R}^2\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[f(x,y)=\begin{cases}y^2/x,&x>0,\\0,&(x,y)=(0,0),\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] This quadratic-over-linear perspective is proper, closed, and convex. Although \(f(0,0)=0\), approaching through its domain gives \[f(t,0)=0,\qquad f(t,\sqrt{t})=1\quad(t>0).\] Both paths converge to \((0,0)\), but their function values have different limits. Thus lower semicontinuity at a finite boundary point does not imply relative continuity or path-independent boundary behavior.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratic-over-linear perspective has value zero at the origin, but approaches zero or one along two different interior paths.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The boundary limit of \(f\) at \((0,0)\) depends on the approach path, so \(f\) is not relatively continuous there.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Asymptotic geometry of a closed proper convex function
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Fix \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional closed convex analysis; the definition records both the recession function and the recession cone of the epigraph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The asymptotic function geometry of \(f\) is the pair \(\mathcal G_\infty(f)=(f^\infty,\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f))\), where \[f^\infty(d):=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}\in(-\infty,+\infty]\] and \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f):=\{(d,\beta)\in E\times\mathbb R:(x,r)+t(d,\beta)\in\operatorname{epi}f\ \text{for every }(x,r)\in\operatorname{epi}f, t\ge0\}.\] The limit is independent of \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and the defining geometric identity is \[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=\{(d,\beta):f^\infty(d)\le\beta\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function on a finite-dimensional space, its asymptotic geometry consists of its recession function and the recession cone of its epigraph. The recession value in direction \(d\) is the limiting growth rate \(\lim_{t\to\infty}[f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)]/t\), independent of the chosen base point in the effective domain. A pair \((d,\beta)\) is a recession direction of the epigraph exactly when translating every epigraph point by every nonnegative multiple of \((d,\beta)\) remains in the epigraph. Equivalently, this cone is the epigraph of \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal G_\infty(f)=(f^\infty,\operatorname{epi}f^\infty),\qquad \operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}f^\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.\]
\[f^\infty(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).\]
special_cases_latex: For an affine function \(f(x)=\langle a,x\rangle+b\), one has \(f^\infty(d)=\langle a,d\rangle\).
For an indicator \(f=\iota_C\) of a nonempty closed convex set, \(f^\infty=\iota_{\operatorname{rec}C}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The function \(f^\infty\) is lower semicontinuous, convex, and positively homogeneous.
The directions satisfying \(f^\infty(d)\le0\) are precisely the common recession directions of all nonempty sublevel sets of \(f\).
boundary_notes: The base-point limit formula need not define the appropriate horizon object for an arbitrary nonconvex function.
Infinite-dimensional variants require an explicitly selected topology and may involve noncompact bounded sublevel sets.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and localization without recession directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and boundedness of minimizers together with uniform localization of sufficiently accurate approximate minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex, and suppose that \(f\) has no nonzero direction of recession. Then \(\inf f\in\mathbb R\) is attained, and \(M=\operatorname{argmin}f\) is a nonempty closed bounded convex set. Moreover, for every \(\varepsilon>0\) there exists \(\delta>0\) such that \[f(x)\leq \inf f+\delta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \operatorname{dist}(x,M)<\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function with no nonzero recession direction has a finite attained minimum and a nonempty closed bounded convex minimum set. Given any neighborhood of that set, every sufficiently accurate approximate minimizer lies in the neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex}
f\text{ has no nonzero direction of recession}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \inf f\in\mathbb R,\quad \varnothing\ne M=\operatorname{argmin}f\text{ is closed, bounded, and convex, and }\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists\delta>0\ \forall x,\ f(x)\leq\inf f+\delta\Rightarrow\operatorname{dist}(x,M)<\varepsilon.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Sublinear Structure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function of a closed proper convex function is a proper lower-semicontinuous sublinear function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, then \(\operatorname{rec}f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and sublinear. Thus
\[(\operatorname{rec}f)(0)=0,\qquad (\operatorname{rec}f)(\lambda d)=\lambda(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)\quad(\lambda\geq0),\]
and
\[(\operatorname{rec}f)(d_1+d_2)\leq(\operatorname{rec}f)(d_1)+(\operatorname{rec}f)(d_2).\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, positively homogeneous, and subadditive.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic structure of the recession function in the closed proper convex regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph-Recession Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of the recession function is the recession cone of the original epigraph, and recession values bound global directional growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(d\in H\) and \(s\in\mathbb R\),
\[(d,s)\in\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\iff(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)\leq s.\]
Consequently,
\[\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)=\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}f),\]
and, for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\geq0\),
\[f(x+td)\leq f(x)+t(\operatorname{rec}f)(d).\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{rec}f)=\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric representation and global directional-growth inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function records the limiting slope of a closed proper convex function along each direction; the slope equals the supremum of the difference quotients and is independent of the chosen domain point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), the recession function of \(f\) is defined by
\[
(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},\qquad d\in X.
\]
For every \(d\in X\), the limit exists in \(\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), equals \(\sup_{t>0}(f(x+td)-f(x))/t\), and is independent of the selected \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}f\) is well defined independently of \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), and \((\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=\sup_{t>0}(f(x+td)-f(x))/t\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closed proper convex version on a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment under common-recession conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to an arbitrary finite or infinite family of consistent closed proper convex inequalities and includes a more general condition involving a finite polyhedral subfamily.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_0\) and \((f_i)_{i\in I}\) be closed proper convex functions on \(\mathbb R^n\), where \(I\) is arbitrary, and suppose \(F:=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f_i(x)\leq0\ \forall i\in I\}\neq\varnothing\). The infimum of \(f_0\) over \(F\) is attained if there is no direction of recession common to \(f_0\) and every \(f_i\). More generally, it is attained if there exists a finite \(I_0\subseteq I\) such that each \(f_i\), \(i\in I_0\), is polyhedral and every recession direction common to \(f_0\) and all \(f_i\) is a direction along which \(f_0\) and every \(f_i\), \(i\in I\setminus I_0\), are constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consistent, possibly infinite system of closed proper convex inequalities, the convex objective attains its constrained infimum when the functions have no common recession direction. More generally, attainment holds when finitely many constraint functions are polyhedral and every common recession direction leaves the objective and every remaining constraint function constant.
assumptions_latex: f_0,f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ are closed proper convex for every }i\in I
I\text{ is an arbitrary finite or infinite index set}
\text{Either no recession direction is common to }f_0\text{ and all }f_i,\text{ or the stated finite-polyhedral-subfamily condition holds}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in F}f_0(x)\neq\varnothing

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Representations and Regularity of the Recession Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural properties and increment-quotient representations of the recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\overline{\mathbb{R}} be proper and convex. Then f^{0+} is proper, convex, and positively homogeneous, and for every y\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\[f^{0+}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f} igl(f(x+y)-f(x) igr).\]
If f is closed, then f^{0+} is closed and, for every x\in\operatorname{dom}f and y\in\mathbb{R}^n,
\[f^{0+}(y)=\sup_{\lambda>0} rac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda}=\lim_{\lambda	o\infty} rac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function of a proper convex function is proper, convex, and positively homogeneous, and it equals the supremum of all unit-displacement increments in a given direction. If the function is closed, its recession function is closed and also equals the supremum and the limit at infinity of the corresponding directional difference quotients based at any domain point.
assumptions_latex: \text{For the closedness and difference-quotient conclusions, }f\text{ is closed}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f^{0+}\text{ is proper, convex, and positively homogeneous},\quad f^{0+}(y)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}(f(x+y)-f(x));\quad f\text{ closed}\Rightarrow f^{0+}\text{ is closed and }f^{0+}(y)=\sup_{\lambda>0}\frac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda}=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\frac{f(x+\lambda y)-f(x)}{\lambda}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least Global Increment Majorant
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise minimality characterization of the recession function among global displacement majorants.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let f:\mathbb{R}^n	o\overline{\mathbb{R}} be proper and convex. Then
\[f(z)\leq f(x)+f^{0+}(z-x)\qquad orall x,z\in\mathbb{R}^n.\]
Moreover, if a function h satisfies
\[f(z)\leq f(x)+h(z-x)\qquad orall x,z\in\mathbb{R}^n,\]
then f^{0+}\leq h pointwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The recession function itself globally bounds every increment of a proper convex function, and it is pointwise no larger than any other function having this global displacement-majorant property.
assumptions_latex: h\text{ is any function satisfying the displayed increment inequality for all }x,z\in\mathbb{R}^n
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f(z)\leq f(x)+f^{0+}(z-x)\ \forall x,z;\qquad \bigl[f(z)\leq f(x)+h(z-x)\ \forall x,z\bigr]\Rightarrow f^{0+}\leq h\text{ pointwise}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constancy Along a Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes constancy on every line parallel to a direction through the two oriented recession values, with a one-line sufficient condition in the closed case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a proper convex function and let \(y\) be a vector. Then \(\lambda\mapsto f(x+\lambda y)\) is constant on \(\mathbb R\) for every \(x\) if and only if \(f^{0+}(y)\leq 0\) and \(f^{0+}(-y)\leq 0\). If \(f\) is closed and there exist \(x\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \(f(x+\lambda y)\leq\alpha\) for every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), then these two recession inequalities hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function is constant on every line parallel to y exactly when its recession values in both directions are nonpositive. If the function is closed, boundedness above on one complete such line is sufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [\forall x\;\lambda\mapsto f(x+\lambda y)\text{ is constant on }\mathbb R]\iff[f^{0+}(y)\leq0\ \land\ f^{0+}(-y)\leq0],\quad [f\text{ closed}\ \land\ \exists x,\alpha\in\mathbb R\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R:\ f(x+\lambda y)\leq\alpha]\Rightarrow[f^{0+}(y)\leq0\ \land\ f^{0+}(-y)\leq0].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex hull of functions with a common recession function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The attainment conclusion concerns the convex-combination representation of the functional convex hull referenced by the source.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_m:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed proper convex functions with the same recession function \(k\). Then \[f=\operatorname{conv}\{f_1,\ldots,f_m\}\] is closed and proper and has recession function \(k\). Moreover, for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), the infimum in the convex-combination representation of \(f(x)\) is attained by some convex combination.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The functional convex hull of finitely many closed proper convex functions sharing one recession function is closed and proper and retains that recession function. Its pointwise convex-combination infimum is attained at every point.
assumptions_latex: f_i:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\text{ is closed, proper, and convex for }i=1,\ldots,m
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is closed and proper},\quad f^{0^+}=k,\quad \forall x\in\mathbb R^n\text{ the convex-combination infimum representing }f(x)\text{ is attained}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constrained attainment from common recession directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: General and polyhedral sufficient conditions for attainment of a constrained convex minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be closed, proper, and convex, and let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, closed, and convex. If \(h\) and \(C\) have no common nonzero direction of recession, then there exists \(\bar x\in C\) such that \[h(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}h(x).\] If \(C\) is polyhedral, the same conclusion holds under the weaker hypothesis that every common recession direction of \(h\) and \(C\) is a direction on which \(h\) is constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed proper convex function attains its infimum over a nonempty closed convex set if the function and set have no common nonzero recession direction. For a polyhedral feasible set, it suffices that the function be constant along every common recession direction.

\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\text{ is closed and convex}
\text{either }h\text{ and }C\text{ have no common nonzero recession direction, or }C\text{ is polyhedral and }h\text{ is constant along every common recession direction}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists\bar x\in C\quad h(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}h(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recession-Function Characterization of Global Uniform Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes global uniform continuity of a finite convex function by finiteness of its recession function and records the stronger global Lipschitz conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and let \(f^{0+}\) be its recession function. Then \(f\) is uniformly continuous relative to \(\mathbb{R}^n\) if and only if \(f^{0+}(y)<+\infty\) for every \(y\in\mathbb{R}^n\). When these equivalent conditions hold, \(f\) is Lipschitzian relative to \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex function on Euclidean space is uniformly continuous exactly when its recession function is finite in every direction. Under this condition, it is globally Lipschitz.
assumptions_latex: f^{0+}\text{ is the recession function of }f
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is uniformly continuous on }\mathbb{R}^n\iff\forall y\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ f^{0+}(y)<+\infty;\qquad \text{either condition implies that }f\text{ is Lipschitzian on }\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity Along a Recession Direction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes directions along which a proper convex function is globally nonincreasing, including the additional propagation property under closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a proper convex function and let \(y\) be a vector. If, for some \(x\), \(\liminf_{\lambda\to+\infty}f(x+\lambda y)<+\infty\), then \(\lambda\mapsto f(x+\lambda y)\) is nonincreasing on \(\mathbb R\). This monotonicity holds for every \(x\) if and only if \(f^{0+}(y)\leq0\). If \(f\) is closed, monotonicity for one \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) implies monotonicity for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper convex function, finite asymptotic liminf along a line forces the function to be nonincreasing along that entire line. Global nonincrease in direction y is equivalent to the recession value in direction y being nonpositive. For a closed function, nonincrease from one domain point propagates to every base point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda\mapsto f(x+\lambda y)\text{ is nonincreasing on }\mathbb R;\quad [\forall x\text{ this holds}]\iff f^{0+}(y)\leq0,\quad\text{with one-point propagation when }f\text{ is closed}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radial, recession, and horizon variants
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional, let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and choose \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). No convexity is imposed unless stated separately.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A variant family separating base-point radial growth, global recession inequalities, and lower-semicontinuous horizon growth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the radial lower asymptotic slope, the global recession majorant, and the horizon function by \[f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0}(d):=\liminf_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t},\] \[f^{\mathrm{rec}}(d):=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f,\ t>0}\frac{f(x+td)-f(x)}{t},\] and \[f^{\mathrm{hor}}(d):=\liminf_{\substack{t\to+\infty\\ d'\to d}}\frac{f(x_0+td')-f(x_0)}{t}.\] The asymptotic variant family is \(\mathcal V_\infty(f;x_0):=(f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0},f^{\mathrm{rec}},f^{\mathrm{hor}})\). These objects are kept distinct for a general proper function. If \(f\) is lower semicontinuous and convex, all three are independent of \(x_0\) and coincide with the closed convex recession function \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The asymptotic variant family distinguishes three constructions. The radial slope measures lower limiting growth along one ray from a selected base point. The global recession majorant takes the supremum of all difference quotients over every feasible base point and positive step. The horizon function additionally permits perturbations of the direction before taking the lower limit, thereby encoding lower-semicontinuous asymptotic behavior. For a general proper function these variants can differ and the radial object can depend on its base point. For a lower-semicontinuous convex function they coincide with the ordinary recession function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal V_\infty(f;x_0)=(f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0},f^{\mathrm{rec}},f^{\mathrm{hor}}),\qquad f\in\Gamma_0(E)\Longrightarrow f^{\mathrm{rad}}_{x_0}=f^{\mathrm{rec}}=f^{\mathrm{hor}}=f^\infty.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f^{\mathrm{rec}}(d)=\inf\{\beta\in\mathbb R:f(x+td)\le f(x)+t\beta\ \text{for all }x\in\operatorname{dom}f, t\ge0\}.\]
special_cases_latex: For a positively homogeneous lower-semicontinuous convex function \(p\), all variants equal \(p\).
For an indicator \(\iota_C\), the convex-case common value is \(0\) on \(\operatorname{rec}C\) and \(+\infty\) elsewhere.
immediate_consequences_latex: Coincidence of the three variants is a structural regularity furnished by closed convexity, not part of their general definition.
The perturbed-direction lower limit distinguishes horizon behavior from growth observed along a single fixed ray.
boundary_notes: Conventions for horizon functions vary with homogenization and base-point normalization; the convention must be matched to a source.
Without convexity, no equality among the three constructions is asserted.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: organizes commonly used radial, recession, and horizon constructions.
The exact horizon convention and the claimed convex-case coincidence require an inspected authoritative source.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational Horizon Function
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The variational horizon function is the lower-regularized linear-scale growth of a proper function; it is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a proper function \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define
\[
f^\infty(d)=\liminf_{\substack{t\to+\infty\\d'\to d}}\frac{f(td')}{t}
=\liminf_{\substack{\lambda\downarrow0\\d'\to d}}\lambda f(d'/\lambda).
\]
The function \(f^\infty\) is lower semicontinuous and positively homogeneous in the sense that
\[
f^\infty(\mu d)=\mu f^\infty(d)\qquad(\mu>0).
\]
