knowledge_statements.title: Asymptotic Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An asymptotic function records lower linear growth from a fixed domain point while allowing nearby directions; without closed convex structure, the result may depend on that point.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed-Convex Horizon–Recession Correspondence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed proper convex function, the variational horizon function equals the base-point-independent recession function and the support function of the conjugate domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then, for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\),
\[
f^\infty(d)=(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)
=\lim_{t\to+\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}
=\sup_{t>0}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}.
\]
The common value is independent of \(x_0\), and
\[
f^\infty=\operatorname{rec}f=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\infty=\operatorname{rec}f=\sigma_{\operatorname{dom}f^*}\), independently of \(x_0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between the variational horizon function and convex recession growth.

notation.meaning: support function of the conjugate domain

knowledge_statements.title: Recession-Variant Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality of standard asymptotic variants for proper closed convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, closed, and convex, then for every \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f\),
\[
f^\infty(d)=f^{\mathrm{rec}}(d)=\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{f(x_0+td)-f(x_0)}{t}=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}\bigl(f(x+d)-f(x)\bigr).
\]
Moreover,
\[
\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=(\operatorname{epi}f)^\infty=\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f).
\]
Thus the horizon, ray-slope, increment-supremum, and epigraph-recession constructions represent the same closed convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a proper closed convex function, horizon, recession, ray-slope, increment-supremum, and epigraph constructions all yield the same asymptotic function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\infty=f^{\mathrm{rec}}=f_{\mathrm{as}}\) and \(\operatorname{epi}f^\infty=\operatorname{rec}(\operatorname{epi}f)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Open-Half-Line Boundary Information Is Lost
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of the open positive half-line and the indicator of its closure have the same horizon function, so horizon regularization loses the missing boundary point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C=(0,+\infty)\subset\mathbb{R}\) and \(f=\delta_C\). Then \(f\) is proper and convex but not lower semicontinuous, and
\[
f^\infty(d)=
\begin{cases}
0,&d\geq0,\\
+\infty,&d<0
\end{cases}
=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}(d).
\]
Since \(\operatorname{cl}f=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}\), one also has
\[
f^\infty=(\operatorname{cl}f)^\infty.
\]
Thus the horizon construction does not retain whether the finite boundary point belonged to the original domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^\infty=\delta_{[0,+\infty)}=(\operatorname{cl}f)^\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coercivity, level-boundedness, and inf-compactness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((E,\|\cdot\|)\) be a normed space and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), write \(L_\alpha(f):=\{x\in E:f(x)\le\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definitions apply in normed spaces; compact-level conclusions are topology-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is coercive when \[\forall M\in\mathbb R\ \exists R>0\ \forall x\in E:\ \|x\|\ge R\Longrightarrow f(x)>M,\] equivalently \(f(x)\to+\infty\) as \(\|x\|\to+\infty\). It is level-bounded when \(L_\alpha(f)\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). It is inf-compact in a topology \(\tau\) when every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is \(\tau\)-compact. The coercivity-level-boundedness interface is the implication chain \[\text{inf-compactness}\Longrightarrow\text{level-boundedness}\Longleftrightarrow\text{coercivity},\] where the first implication presumes that compact sets are bounded. In finite-dimensional spaces, lower semicontinuity makes every sublevel closed, so coercivity is equivalent to inf-compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper function is coercive if its values eventually exceed every real threshold outside a sufficiently large norm ball. It is level-bounded if every real sublevel set is bounded. It is inf-compact in a chosen topology if every sublevel is compact in that topology. Coercivity and level-boundedness are equivalent directly from these quantifiers. Compact sublevels imply bounded sublevels whenever compact sets are bounded. In finite dimensions, lower semicontinuity closes the sublevels and bounded closed sets are compact, so a lower-semicontinuous coercive function is inf-compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ coercive}\Longleftrightarrow(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\ L_\alpha(f)\text{ bounded}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[f\text{ coercive}\Longleftrightarrow\inf_{\|x\|\ge R}f(x)\longrightarrow+\infty\quad(R\to+\infty).\]
\[f\text{ level-bounded}\Longleftrightarrow\text{every sequence }(x_n)\text{ with }\sup_n f(x_n)<+\infty\text{ is bounded}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(E\) is finite-dimensional and \(f\) is lower semicontinuous, coercivity is equivalent to compactness of all sublevel sets.
If additionally \(\inf f<+\infty\), any nonempty compact sublevel below a finite comparison value yields attainment of \(\inf f\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every minimizing sequence of a level-bounded function with finite infimum is bounded.
Lower semicontinuity and finite-dimensional coercivity provide the compactness mechanism used in existence arguments.
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional normed spaces, closed bounded sublevels need not be norm compact.
Coercivity alone does not assert lower semicontinuity or attainment.

notation.meaning: The closed-value sublevel set at height \(\alpha\).
The topology in which inf-compactness is evaluated.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Bounded Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is level-bounded when every set on which its value is at most a fixed finite threshold is bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is level-bounded if, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), its sublevel set
\[
\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\alpha}f=\{x\in X\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}
\]
is bounded in \(X\). Empty sublevel sets are regarded as bounded, so the definition concerns only heights at which the sublevel set is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is level-bounded exactly when \(\{x\in X:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global level-boundedness on a normed space.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive Growth
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is coercive when its values tend to positive infinity along every sequence whose norm tends to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is coercive if
\[
\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}f(x)=+\infty.
\]
Explicitly, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\) there exists \(R>0\) such that \(\|x\|\geq R\) implies \(f(x)>\alpha\). Equivalently, every sequence \((x_k)\) with \(\|x_k\|\to+\infty\) satisfies \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive when \(f(x_k)\to+\infty\) for every sequence satisfying \(\|x_k\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Norm-coercivity for extended-real-valued functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For an extended-real function on a normed space, coercivity is equivalent to boundedness of every finite sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The following conditions are equivalent:
\[
\lim_{\|x\|\to+\infty}f(x)=+\infty,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{lev}_{\leq\alpha}f=\{x\in X\mid f(x)\leq\alpha\}\text{ is bounded for every }\alpha\in\mathbb{R}.
\]
Thus norm-coercivity and global level-boundedness are equivalent; neither convexity nor lower semicontinuity is required for this equivalence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is coercive if and only if \(f\) is level-bounded.

knowledge_statements.title: Coercivity Need Not Give Attainment on a Nonreflexive Space
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A norm-nonattaining functional on a nonreflexive Banach space yields a continuous convex coercive function whose infimum is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a nonreflexive Banach space and choose \(\ell\in X^*\) with \(\|\ell\|=1\) that does not attain its norm on the closed unit ball. Define
\[
f(x)=\frac12\|x\|^2-\ell(x).
\]
Then \(f\) is finite, continuous, convex, and coercive, but
\[
\inf_{x\in X}f(x)=-\frac12,
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing.
\]
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\in X^*\), \(\|\ell\|=1\), does not attain its norm on the closed unit ball.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2-\ell(x)\) is coercive and convex but has no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp ambient-space boundary for the direct method.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflexive-Space Direct-Method Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a reflexive Banach space, a proper weakly lower-semicontinuous coercive function attains a finite minimum and has a weakly compact minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a reflexive Banach space and let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and coercive. Then
\[
\min_{x\in X}f(x)\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing.
\]
Moreover, \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is weakly compact; if \(f\) is convex, then \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, weakly lower semicontinuous, and coercive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min f\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Infinite-dimensional attainment under weak compactness and weak lower semicontinuity.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Dimensional Attainment from Level-Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous level-bounded function on finite-dimensional space attains a finite minimum and has a nonempty compact minimizer set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and level-bounded. Then
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x)\in\mathbb{R},
\qquad \operatorname{argmin}f\neq\varnothing,
\]
and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\min f\in\mathbb{R}\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is nonempty and compact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Weierstrass consequence; convexity is unnecessary.

knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence and compactness of minimizers under lower semicontinuity and level-boundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and level-bounded. Then \(f\) is bounded below, its infimum is finite, and there exists \(x^\star\in\mathbb{R}^n\) such that
\[
f(x^\star)=\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n}f(x).
\]
Moreover, the minimizer set
\[
\operatorname*{argmin}f=\{x:f(x)=\inf f\}
\]
is nonempty and compact. Convexity is unnecessary for existence; if \(f\) is convex, the minimizer set is additionally convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper lower-semicontinuous level-bounded function on finite-dimensional space attains its finite minimum, and its minimizer set is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}f\) is nonempty and compact.

notation.meaning: The set of global minimizers of f.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Descending, flat, and lineality directions
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be finite-dimensional and let \(f:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with recession function \(f^\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The taxonomy is based on the sign and two-sided vanishing of the recession function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the descending, nonascending, flat, and asymptotic-lineality direction sets by \[D_-(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)<0\},\qquad D_{\le0}(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)\le0\},\] \[D_0(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)=0\},\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty(f):=\{d:f^\infty(d)=f^\infty(-d)=0\}.\] A nonzero member of \(D_-(f)\) is an asymptotically descending direction; a nonzero member of \(D_0(f)\) is an asymptotically flat direction; and a nonzero member of \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)\) is a two-sided flat or asymptotic-lineality direction. For every nonempty sublevel \(L_\alpha(f)\), \[\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha(f)=D_{\le0}(f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The sign of the recession function separates asymptotic directions into descending directions, where the asymptotic slope is negative; nonascending directions, where it is nonpositive; and flat directions, where it vanishes. A two-sided flat direction is one on which the recession function vanishes in both orientations. The nonascending cone is exactly the recession cone of every nonempty sublevel set. Thus nonzero nonascending directions characterize unbounded rays that can remain inside a sublevel, while two-sided flat directions isolate asymptotic invariance along complete lines.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[D_-(f)\subseteq D_{\le0}(f),\qquad \operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)=D_0(f)\cap(-D_0(f)),\qquad \operatorname{rec}L_\alpha(f)=D_{\le0}(f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[d\in D_{\le0}(f)\Longleftrightarrow f(x+td)\le f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}f, t\ge0.\]
\[d\in\operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)\Longleftrightarrow f(x+td)=f(x)\quad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{dom}f, t\in\mathbb R.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_C\), \(D_{\le0}(f)=\operatorname{rec}C\) and \(\operatorname{lin}_\infty(f)=\operatorname{lin}C\).
If \(D_{\le0}(f)=\{0\}\), every nonempty sublevel is bounded.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero direction in \(D_{\le0}(f)\) forces every nonempty sublevel to be unbounded.
A direction in \(D_-(f)\) is incompatible with existence of a finite global minimum.
boundary_notes: A one-sided zero recession value does not imply invariance in the opposite direction.
Flatness of \(f^\infty\) is asymptotic and does not by itself imply multiple minimizers unless the corresponding ray or line meets the solution set.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: sign taxonomy induced by the recession function.
The asserted common recession cone of sublevels and the two-sided invariance formulation require source verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Conjugate-Domain Characterization of Recession Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession lineality is the orthogonal complement of the span of the conjugate domain, and it is nontrivial exactly when that span is not dense.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Then
\[
\operatorname{lin}(f)=(\operatorname{span}\operatorname{dom}f^*)^\perp
=\{d\in X:\langle d,u\rangle=0\text{ for every }u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.
\]
Consequently, \(\operatorname{lin}(f)\neq\{0\}\) exactly when \(\operatorname{span}(\operatorname{dom}f^*)\) is not dense in \(X\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(f)=(\operatorname{span}\operatorname{dom}f^*)^\perp\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual characterization for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions on a Hilbert space.

knowledge_statements.title: Recession Lineality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recession lineality consists of directions with zero recession slope in both signs; it is a subspace along which the function is translation invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The recession lineality space of \(f\) is
\[
\operatorname{lin}(f)=\{d\in X\mid(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=0\text{ and }(\operatorname{rec}f)(-d)=0\}.
\]
It is a vector subspace of \(X\). Every \(d\in\operatorname{lin}(f)\) is a two-sided invariant direction:
\[
f(x+td)=f(x)\qquad\text{for every }x\in X\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R},
\]
with equality understood in the extended-real sense.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{lin}(f)=\{d:(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=(\operatorname{rec}f)(-d)=0\}\) is a vector subspace, and \(f(x+td)=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\) and \(t\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lineality induced by zero recession in both directions.

source_witnesses.locator: 9.4 Recession Function p. 164

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine Directions and Epigraph Lineality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The extract prints \(\nu\) in condition (c); it is interpreted as the quantified scalar \(v\), as required by condition (a) and the closing sentence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be a proper convex function, \(y\) a vector, and \(v\in\mathbb R\). The following are equivalent: (i) \(f(x+\lambda y)=f(x)+\lambda v\) for every \(x\) and every \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\); (ii) \((y,v)\) belongs to the lineality space of \(\operatorname{epi}f\); and (iii) \(-f^{0+}(-y)=f^{0+}(y)=v\). If \(f\) is closed and there exists \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) for which \(\lambda\mapsto f(x+\lambda y)\) is affine on \(\mathbb R\), then these conditions hold with \(v=f^{0+}(y)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction produces the same affine change of a proper convex function from every base point exactly when the corresponding direction-slope pair lies in the epigraph's lineality space, equivalently when the two opposite recession values have matching slopes. For a closed function, affine behavior along one domain line suffices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: [\forall x\ \forall\lambda\in\mathbb R:\ f(x+\lambda y)=f(x)+\lambda v]\iff[(y,v)\in\operatorname{lin}(\operatorname{epi}f)]\iff[-f^{0+}(-y)=f^{0+}(y)=v],\text{ with one-line sufficiency when }f\text{ is closed}.

source_evidence.locator: Complete book / 8. Recession Cones and Unboundedness / Theorem 8.8

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Zero Recession Is Not Flatness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero recession slope in one orientation does not make a direction globally flat.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\max\{x,0\}\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \[f^{\infty}(-1)=0\qquad\text{but}\qquad f^{\infty}(1)=1.\] Moreover, \(f(1)=1\) while \(f(0)=0\), so translation in direction \(-1\) does not leave \(f\) invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(-1\notin F(f)\) although \(f^{\infty}(-1)=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a one-sided recession direction and a globally flat direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Dual-Annihilator Characterization of Flat Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The globally flat directions are exactly those annihilated by every dual vector where the conjugate is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the Hilbert-space identification of \(X\) with its continuous dual, \[F(f)=(\operatorname{dom}f^*)^{\perp}=\{d\in X:\langle u,d\rangle=0\text{ for every }u\in\operatorname{dom}f^*\}.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(f)=(\operatorname{dom}f^*)^{\perp}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Flat directions characterized by the effective domain of the Fenchel conjugate.

notation.meaning: annihilator of the effective domain of the conjugate

knowledge_statements.title: Quotient Representation by Flat Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factoring out the closed subspace of global flat directions yields a closed proper convex function without residual flat directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(F(f)\) is a closed linear subspace of \(X\). If \(Q:X\to X/F(f)\) is the quotient map, there is a unique function \(\widetilde f:X/F(f)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) such that \[f=\widetilde f\circ Q.\] The function \(\widetilde f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex and has no nonzero globally flat direction.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(f)\) is closed and linear, and \(f\) factors through \(X/F(f)\) with \(F(\widetilde f)=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural quotient induced by the global flat-direction space.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Function Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direction is globally flat exactly when translating by any real multiple leaves the function unchanged, equivalently when both recession slopes vanish.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the space of flat directions by
\[
F(f)=\{d\in X\mid f(x+td)=f(x)\text{ for every }x\in X\text{ and }t\in\mathbb{R}\}.
\]
Then
\[
F(f)=\operatorname{lin}(f)=\{d\in X\mid(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)=(\operatorname{rec}f)(-d)=0\}.
\]
Consequently, global translation invariance is equivalent to vanishing recession growth in both orientations.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(f)=\{d:f(x+td)=f(x)\ \forall x\in X,\forall t\in\mathbb{R}\}=\operatorname{lin}(f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global two-sided flatness for closed proper convex functions.

notation.meaning: space of globally flat directions of \(f\)

source_witnesses.locator: 9.4 Recession Function p. 164

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Extreme-Point Attainment on Line-Free Closed Convex Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Guarantees existence of an extreme-point maximizer only when the supremum is already known to be attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex and let \(C\subseteq\operatorname{dom}f\) be closed and convex. If \(C\) contains no lines and \(\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\), then there exists \(e\in\operatorname{ext}C\) such that \(f(e)=\sup_{x\in C}f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function attains its supremum on a closed convex set containing no lines, then some extreme point of that set also attains the supremum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists e\in\operatorname{ext}C:\quad f(e)=\sup_{x\in C}f(x)

knowledge_statements.title: Unboundedness Without a Recession Direction in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted ellipsoid in ℓ² is closed, convex, and unbounded but has a trivial recession cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In \(X=\ell^2\), let
\[
C=\left\{x=(x_n)\in\ell^2:\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{x_n^2}{n^2}\leq1\right\},\qquad f=\delta_C.
\]
The set \(C\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and unbounded, since \(n e_n\in C\) for every \(n\). Nevertheless,
\[
\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}.
\]
Thus a nonempty sublevel of a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function can be unbounded in infinite dimensions without possessing a nonzero recession direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is unbounded and \(\operatorname{rec}C=\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the finite-dimensional converse from unboundedness to a nonzero recession direction.

notation.meaning: the nth standard unit vector of \(\ell^2\)

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Level Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty convex sublevel set persists exactly along directions where the function's recession value is nonpositive; in finite dimensions, such directions characterize unboundedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The persistent directions of the nonempty sublevel set satisfy
\[
\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha=\{d\in X\mid(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)\leq0\}.
\]
Equivalently, \(d\in\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha\) precisely when
\[
x+td\in L_\alpha\qquad\text{for every }x\in L_\alpha\text{ and }t\geq0.
\]
Thus \(L_\alpha\) is unbounded whenever it has a nonzero recession direction; in finite dimensions the converse also holds.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a real Hilbert space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rec}L_\alpha=\{d\in X:(\operatorname{rec}f)(d)\leq0\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recession directions of nonempty convex sublevel sets.

notation.meaning: recession cone of a nonempty closed convex set

source_witnesses.locator: 9.4 Recession Function p. 164

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness Need Not Produce an Unbounded Minimizer Set
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function can have a bounded interval of minimizers without any nonzero zero-recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[f(x)=d_{[-1,1]}(x)^2=\bigl(\max\{|x|-1,0\}\bigr)^2.\] Then \(f\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, with \(\operatorname{argmin}f=[-1,1]\). Moreover, \(f^{\infty}(d)=+\infty\) for every \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f=[-1,1]\) is nonsingleton and bounded, while \(f^{\infty}(d)>0\) for every \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the converse from mere minimizer multiplicity to a nonzero zero-recession direction.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Minimizers Characterized by Zero Recession Directions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An attained minimizer set is unbounded exactly when the objective has a nonzero zero-recession direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\operatorname{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\). Then \[\operatorname{argmin}f\text{ is unbounded}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists d\ne0\text{ such that }f^{\infty}(d)=0.\] For every such \(d\) and every \(\bar x\in\operatorname{argmin}f\), \(\bar x+\mathbb R_+d\subseteq\operatorname{argmin}f\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}f\) is unbounded if and only if \(f^{\infty}(d)=0\) for some \(d\ne0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of unbounded attained minimizer sets in finite dimensions.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonuniqueness Consequences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonzero recession direction that cannot increase the value from an attained minimum generates an unbounded ray of minimizers, and two-sided recession generates a line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the recession function defined by \(f^{\infty}(d)=\sup_{x\in\operatorname{dom}f}(f(x+d)-f(x))\), the inequality \(f^{\infty}(d)\le0\) implies \(f(x+td)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\ge0\). Taking \(x=\bar x\), minimality gives \(f(\bar x+td)=f(\bar x)\). Thus the entire ray \(\bar x+\mathbb R_{+}d\) consists of minimizers. If both \(d\) and \(-d\) are recession directions, the full affine line \(\bar x+\mathbb Rd\) consists of minimizers.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bar x+td\in\operatorname{argmin}f\) for every \(t\ge0\); hence the minimizer is not unique and the solution set is unbounded.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Consequences of a nonzero nonincreasing recession direction at an attained minimum.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure sets for topological preservation claims
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal U\) and \(\mathcal V\) be classes of sets, functions, or optimization data, let \(T:\mathcal U\to\mathcal V\) be an operation, and let \(\tau\) and \(\sigma\) be specified topologies on the input and output spaces.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A formal framework for recording exactly where closedness, compactness, lower semicontinuity, or attainment fails under an operation or a topology change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a topological property predicate \(P_\tau\) on \(\mathcal U\) and its output analogue \(P_\sigma\), define the failure boundary of \(T\) for \(P\) by \[\operatorname{Fail}_P(T;\tau,\sigma):=\{u\in\mathcal U:P_\tau(u)\ \text{holds and }P_\sigma(Tu)\ \text{fails}\}.\] For a function \(f\), use \(P_{\mathrm{lsc},\tau}(f)\) for \(\tau\)-lower semicontinuity, and use \[P_{\mathrm{att}}(f):\Longleftrightarrow \operatorname*{argmin}f\ne\varnothing\quad\text{and}\quad\inf f> -\infty.\] The topological failure-boundary profile is \[\mathfrak F(T;\tau,\sigma):=(\operatorname{Fail}_{\mathrm{closed}},\operatorname{Fail}_{\mathrm{compact}},\operatorname{Fail}_{\mathrm{lsc}},\operatorname{Fail}_{\mathrm{att}}).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a chosen operation and specified input and output topologies, the failure boundary for a property is the class of inputs that possess the property before the operation but whose images lose it afterward. Applying this definition separately to closedness, compactness, lower semicontinuity, and attainment produces a topological failure profile. The topology is part of the definition: the same set or function can occupy different failure classes when norm, weak, relative, or quotient topologies are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[u\in\operatorname{Fail}_P(T;\tau,\sigma)\Longleftrightarrow P_\tau(u)\wedge\neg P_\sigma(Tu).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\operatorname{Fail}_P(T;\tau,\sigma)=\mathcal U_P^\tau\setminus T^{-1}(\mathcal V_P^\sigma),\] where \(\mathcal U_P^\tau:=\{u:P_\tau(u)\}\) and \(\mathcal V_P^\sigma:=\{v:P_\sigma(v)\}\).
special_cases_latex: For a linear map \(A\), \(\operatorname{Fail}_{\mathrm{closed}}(A)\) records closed sets whose linear images are not closed.
For a topology change \(T=\operatorname{id}\), the definition records properties not preserved by the identity map between the two topological structures.
immediate_consequences_latex: A preservation theorem for \(P\) on a subclass \(\mathcal C\) is equivalent to \(\mathcal C\cap\operatorname{Fail}_P(T;\tau,\sigma)=\varnothing\).
Any counterexample belongs to a uniquely specified failure set only after the operation, property, and both topologies are fixed.
boundary_notes: This is a classification definition, not a claim that the failure sets are themselves topological boundaries in the closure-minus-interior sense.
Attainment depends on objective values and feasible-domain conventions, not solely on the topology of a set.

notation.meaning: Inputs for which operation \(T\) fails to preserve property \(P\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formal sidecar definition tailored to the node blueprint.
The terminology is organizational rather than universally standardized and needs an exact supporting source or editorial confirmation.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure and attainment defects of infimal linear images
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) and \(Y\) be finite-dimensional real vector spaces, let \(A:E\to Y\) be linear, and let \(F:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variable elimination through a linear constraint; the definition separates loss of lower semicontinuity from failure of fiberwise attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the infimal linear image or marginal \[g(y):=\inf\{F(x):x\in E, Ax=y\},\qquad \inf\varnothing:=+\infty.\] Its closure-defect set and attainment-defect set are \[\Delta_{\mathrm{cl}}(A,F):=\{y:g(y)<\liminf_{z\to y}g(z)\}^{\complement}\cap\{y:g(y)>\liminf_{z\to y}g(z)\},\] equivalently and more directly, \[\Delta_{\mathrm{cl}}(A,F):=\{y:g(y)>(\operatorname{cl}g)(y)\},\] and \[\Delta_{\mathrm{att}}(A,F):=\{y:g(y)\in\mathbb R, \{x:Ax=y, F(x)=g(y)\}=\varnothing\}.\] The image-marginal closure failure boundary is \[\mathfrak M(A,F):=(\Delta_{\mathrm{cl}}(A,F),\Delta_{\mathrm{att}}(A,F)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginal of a function under a linear map assigns to each output point the infimum of the original function over its fiber. Its closure defect consists of output points where the marginal lies strictly above its lower-semicontinuous envelope, so the marginal is not closed there. Its attainment defect consists of output points with a finite marginal value for which no feasible point in the corresponding fiber realizes that value. Together these two sets distinguish loss of closedness under projection from nonattainment during variable elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak M(A,F)=(\{y:g(y)>(\operatorname{cl}g)(y)\},\{y:g(y)\in\mathbb R, \operatorname*{argmin}_{Ax=y}F(x)=\varnothing\}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\Delta_{\mathrm{cl}}(A,F)=\{y:(y,g(y))\notin\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}g)\ \text{at equality of values}\}.\]
The strict epigraph satisfies \[\{(y,r):g(y)<r\}=(A\times\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb R})\{(x,r):F(x)<r\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A=\operatorname{id}\), then \(g=F\), so both defects are empty.
If every relevant fiber sublevel \(\{x:Ax=y, F(x)\le\alpha\}\) is compact, the corresponding finite fiber infimum is attained.
immediate_consequences_latex: The marginal is lower semicontinuous exactly when \(\Delta_{\mathrm{cl}}(A,F)=\varnothing\).
Closedness of \(F\) alone does not, without a qualification condition, force its infimal linear image to be closed.
boundary_notes: Projection of the ordinary epigraph need not equal the ordinary epigraph of \(g\) at unattained boundary values; the strict-epigraph identity avoids this ambiguity.
The displayed defect definition uses finite-dimensional sequential lower limits.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: marginal functions are infimal images under linear maps.
The initial liminf expression is intentionally superseded by the direct envelope definition and should be checked editorially.
An inspected source is required for the epigraph and closure claims.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The epigraph formulation is false: since the lower-semicontinuous envelope satisfies \((\operatorname{cl}g)(y)\le g(y)\), every finite \((y,g(y))\) belongs to \(\operatorname{epi}(\operatorname{cl}g)\), including closure-defect points. No sources were supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Linear Images
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed convex epigraph of 1/x on the positive half-line has the nonclosed positive half-line as its image under first-coordinate projection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\ge 1/x\}\) and let \(P(x,y)=x\). Then \(C\) is a closed convex subset of \(\mathbb R^2\), while its linear image is \(P(C)=(0,+\infty)\), which is not closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex, whereas \(P(C)=(0,+\infty)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional counterexample showing that linear images need not preserve closedness.

notation.meaning: Closed convex set used in the counterexample.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Missing Projected Boundary Points Require Escape in Eliminated Variables
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approaching a missing boundary point of a closed set's finite-dimensional projection forces the eliminated variables to escape to infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^n\) be closed, let \(P(x,z)=x\), and suppose \(\bar x\in\overline{P(C)}\setminus P(C)\). For every sequence \((x_k,z_k)\in C\) with \(x_k\to\bar x\), one has \(\|z_k\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((x_k,z_k)\in C,\ x_k\to\bar x\Longrightarrow\|z_k\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sequential mechanism behind a nonclosed coordinate projection of a closed set.

notation.meaning: Coordinate projection onto the retained variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Projections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the closed convex epigraph of 1/x onto its domain produces the open positive half-line, so closedness is lost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is the epigraph of the convex function \(x\mapsto1/x\) on \((0,+\infty)\), extended by \(+\infty\) outside that interval, and is closed and convex in \(\mathbb R^2\). Its coordinate projection is \(\pi_x(C)=(0,+\infty)\): every positive coordinate occurs, while no nonpositive coordinate does. Since \(0\) belongs to the closure but not to the projection, projection of a closed convex set can be nonclosed even in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) is closed and convex whereas \(\pi_x(C)=(0,+\infty)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate projections are linear images but need not preserve closedness of convex sets.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Marginal Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginalizing the closed convex indicator of C produces the indicator of the open positive half-line, which is convex but not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x>0,\ y\ge 1/x\}\), let \(F=\iota_C\) and \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb R}F(x,y)\). Then \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, whereas \(g=iota_{(0,+\infty)}\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, but \(g=\iota_{(0,+\infty)}\) is convex and not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partial minimization can destroy closedness even when the joint function is closed convex.

notation.meaning: Convex indicator of the set C.

knowledge_statements.title: Closure-Restoration Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a lower-semicontinuous convex function over a fixed compact convex set preserves convexity and lower semicontinuity and attains each finite marginal value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). Convexity of \(F\) and convexity of \(Y\) imply convexity of \(g\). Compactness of \(Y\), together with lower semicontinuity of \(F\), ensures that for every \(x\) with finite marginal value there exists \(y_x\in Y\) such that \(g(x)=F(x,y_x)\). Moreover, compactness permits minimizing points along convergent sequences of parameters to have convergent subnets, yielding lower semicontinuity of \(g\). Thus compact marginalization restores both closedness and attainment.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a finite-dimensional real vector space and \(Y\) is a nonempty compact convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
\(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex on its convex domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is convex and lower semicontinuous, and whenever \(g(x)<+nfty\), the infimum is attained in \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-variable regime restoring attainment and lower semicontinuity of convex marginalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Mazur Strong Approximation of Weakly Convergent Sequences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex combinations of tails of a weakly convergent sequence can be chosen to converge in norm to the same limit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(x_n\rightharpoonup x\) in a Banach space \(X\), then there exist \(y_n\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_k:k\ge n\}\) such that \(\|y_n-x\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists y_n\in\operatorname{conv}\{x_k:k\ge n\}\text{ with }\|y_n-x\|\to0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexification bridge from weak convergence to norm convergence.

notation.meaning: Convex hull of the nth tail of the sequence.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak and Norm Topologies Coincide Exactly in Finite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak and norm topologies are identical exactly in finite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a normed space \(X\), the weak topology \(\sigma(X,X^*)\) equals the norm topology if and only if \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sigma(X,X^*)=\tau_{\|\cdot\|}\iff\dim X<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp dimensional boundary for equality of the two topologies.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak–Strong Topology Gap
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex lower semicontinuity is equivalent for weak and norm topologies, but weak compactness and convergence are strictly weaker in infinite-dimensional spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A convex subset of \(X\) has the same closure in the norm and weak topologies. Consequently, since \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is convex, it is norm closed if and only if it is weakly closed, so convex \(f\) is norm lower semicontinuous exactly when it is weakly lower semicontinuous. The compactness notions differ: norm-compact sets are weakly compact, but in an infinite-dimensional reflexive space the unit ball \(B_X\) is weakly compact and not norm compact. Weak convergence likewise need not imply norm convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is a real Banach space equipped with its norm and weak topologies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is norm lower semicontinuous if and only if it is weakly lower semicontinuous; weak and norm compactness, however, need not coincide.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex closedness is topology-invariant here, while compactness and convergence strength remain topology-dependent.

notation.meaning: Weak topology induced by the continuous dual.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak–norm topology gap profile
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. Write \(\tau_w:=\sigma(X,X^*)\) for the weak topology and \(\tau_s\) for the norm topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition records topology-sensitive differences for arbitrary sets and functions, while identifying the convex closedness regime where the gap vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C\subseteq X\) and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), define the weak–strong gap profile \[\mathfrak G_{w,s}(C,f):=(G_{\mathrm{cl}},G_{\mathrm{lsc}},G_{\mathrm{cmp}},G_{\mathrm{conv}}),\] where \[G_{\mathrm{cl}}:=\operatorname{cl}_{w}C\setminus\operatorname{cl}_{s}C,\qquad G_{\mathrm{lsc}}:=\{x:(\operatorname{cl}_{w}f)(x)<(\operatorname{cl}_{s}f)(x)\},\] \[G_{\mathrm{cmp}}:=\mathbf 1_{\{C\text{ weakly compact}\wedge C\text{ not norm compact}\}},\] and \[G_{\mathrm{conv}}:=\{(x_n,x):x_n\rightharpoonup x\text{ but }\|x_n-x\|\not\to0\}.\] Since \(\tau_w\subseteq\tau_s\), weak closedness implies norm closedness, norm compactness implies weak compactness, and norm convergence implies weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The weak–strong gap profile records four possible discrepancies: points added by weak rather than norm closure, values lowered by weak rather than norm lower-semicontinuous regularization, weakly compact sets that are not norm compact, and weakly convergent sequences that fail to converge in norm. Because the weak topology is coarser, weak closedness is stronger than norm closedness, while weak compactness is weaker than norm compactness. For convex sets and convex functions, separation collapses the closedness and lower-semicontinuity gaps even though compactness and convergence gaps can remain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\tau_w\subseteq\tau_s,\quad \operatorname{cl}_sC\subseteq\operatorname{cl}_wC,\quad C\text{ norm compact}\Longrightarrow C\text{ weakly compact}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For convex \(C\subseteq X\), \[\operatorname{cl}_wC=\operatorname{cl}_sC.\]
For convex \(f\), \[f\text{ is weakly lower semicontinuous}\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is norm lower semicontinuous}.\]
special_cases_latex: In an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space with orthonormal sequence \((e_n)\), one has \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) but \(\|e_n\|=1\).
In a reflexive Banach space, every norm-closed bounded convex set is weakly compact.
immediate_consequences_latex: Weak compactness can provide convergent subnets or subsequences when norm compactness is unavailable, subject to the relevant compactness theorem.
For convex optimization, changing from norm to weak topology does not change closed convex epigraphs, but it can change compactness arguments.
boundary_notes: For nonconvex sets or functions, norm closedness or norm lower semicontinuity need not imply the weak counterpart.
Compactness and sequential compactness require care in general nonmetrizable weak topologies.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard comparison of weak and norm topologies on Banach spaces.
Exact source support is required for the convex closure equivalence, reflexive compactness statement, and sequential qualifications.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-interior and compactness failure classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X\) be a Hausdorff locally convex space and let \(C\subseteq X\) be nonempty and convex. Closures are taken in the specified locally convex topology.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Designed for infinite-dimensional convex analysis, where ordinary interior and closed-bounded compactness criteria may fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the quasi-relative interior by \[\operatorname{qri}C:=\{x\in C:\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}\text{ is a linear subspace of }X\}.\] The ambient-interior failure class and compactness failure class are \[\mathcal I(X):=\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is convex}, \operatorname{int}_X C=\varnothing, \operatorname{qri}C\ne\varnothing\},\] \[\mathcal K(X):=\{C\subseteq X:C\text{ is closed and bounded but not compact}\}.\] The interior-compactness failure boundary of \(X\) is the pair \[\mathfrak B_{I,K}(X):=(\mathcal I(X),\mathcal K(X)).\] It records when a usable generalized interior survives despite empty ambient interior and when closed boundedness fails to yield compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasi-relative interior of a convex set consists of points from which the closed cone generated by the set is a linear subspace. The ambient-interior failure class contains convex sets with empty ordinary interior but nonempty quasi-relative interior. The compactness failure class contains closed bounded sets that are not compact. Their ordered pair formalizes two failure mechanisms common in infinite-dimensional spaces: ordinary interior-based qualification conditions can become vacuous, and finite-dimensional closed-bounded compactness arguments can cease to apply.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak B_{I,K}(X)=(\{C:\operatorname{int}_XC=\varnothing,\operatorname{qri}C\ne\varnothing\},\{C:C\text{ closed and bounded but noncompact}\}).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x\in\operatorname{qri}C\Longleftrightarrow\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}=-\overline{\operatorname{cone}(C-x)}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(X\) is finite-dimensional, every closed bounded set is compact, so \(\mathcal K(X)=\varnothing\).
In every infinite-dimensional normed space, its closed unit ball belongs to \(\mathcal K(X)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal I(X)\) shows that an ambient-interior qualification cannot be substituted blindly for a generalized-interior qualification.
Membership in \(\mathcal K(X)\) shows that bounded minimizing sequences need not possess norm-convergent subsequences.
boundary_notes: Quasi-relative interior is only one generalized-interior notion; core, intrinsic core, and relative interior are not interchangeable without hypotheses.
Weak compactness may still hold for a norm-closed bounded set even when norm compactness fails.

notation.meaning: All nonnegative scalar multiples of elements of \(C-x\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: combines quasi-relative interior and failure of Heine–Borel compactness.
The organizational term 'failure boundary' and the exact generalized-interior choice need source or editorial confirmation.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Ambient Interior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every convex set confined to a proper affine subspace has empty ambient interior, even when it has substantial interior relative to that subspace.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) lies in a proper affine subspace \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\) of \(\mathbb R^n\), no ambient open ball can be contained in \(A\), and therefore none can be contained in \(C\). Hence \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\). For example, every nondegenerate line segment in \(\mathbb R^2\) has empty ambient interior even though its open segment is nonempty in the topology induced on its affine line.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}_{\mathbb R^n}C=\varnothing\), although \(C\) may have nonempty relative interior in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient interior fails automatically for lower-dimensional convex sets.

notation.meaning: Interior in the ambient Euclidean topology.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Relative Interior May Be Empty in Infinite Dimensions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The positive cone in sequence space has full affine hull but empty relative interior, so finite dimensionality is essential to the nonemptiness replacement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In \(X=\ell^2\), the closed convex cone \(C=\{x=(x_i):x_i\ge0\ \forall i\}\) has \(\operatorname{aff}C=X\) but \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{aff}C=X,\quad\operatorname{ri}C=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensional limitation of the seed's nonemptiness assertion.

notation.meaning: Cone of coordinatewise nonnegative square-summable sequences.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Density and Closure Invariance
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite-dimensional convex set's relative interior is dense in its closure, and closure does not change its relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space, then \(\overline{\operatorname{ri}C}=\overline C\) and \(\operatorname{ri}(\overline C)=\operatorname{ri}C\).
assumptions_latex: The ambient vector space is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline{\operatorname{ri}C}=\overline C,\quad\operatorname{ri}(\overline C)=\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional structural properties supporting relative interior as an intrinsic replacement.

knowledge_statements.title: Segment Accessibility from Relative-Interior Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every nonterminal point on a segment from a relative-interior point toward a closure point remains in the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(C\) is a nonempty finite-dimensional convex set, \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\), and \(y\in\overline C\), then \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\) for every \(0\le t<1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((1-t)x+ty\in\operatorname{ri}C\quad(0\le t<1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic access from relative interior toward every closure point.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Replacement
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonempty finite-dimensional convex set always has nonempty interior relative to its affine hull, providing the intrinsic replacement for ambient interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The relative interior of \(C\) is its interior in the affine space \(\operatorname{aff}C\): \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\). Equivalently, \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) when some neighborhood of \(x\) relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\) is contained in \(C\). Every nonempty finite-dimensional convex set has \(\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\). Thus when ambient interior is empty solely because \(C\) is lower-dimensional, relative interior supplies the intrinsic nondegeneracy notion.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}C=\operatorname{int}_{\operatorname{aff}C}C\ne\varnothing\), so interior-based conditions may be formulated intrinsically in \(\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional intrinsic replacement for ambient interior.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine effective domain implies closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient closedness criterion for finite-dimensional proper convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty] be proper and convex. If \operatorname{dom}f is an affine set, then f is closed, equivalently f=\operatorname{cl}f. In particular, every proper convex function finite on all of \mathbb{R}^n is closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper convex function whose effective domain is affine is closed. In particular, a proper convex function finite everywhere on R^n is closed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f=\operatorname{cl}f

source_evidence.locator: Complete book / 7. Closures of Convex Functions / Corollary 7.4.2

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Valued Infimum Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite infimum is unattained when feasible values approach a real optimum but no feasible point realizes it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) with \(C\ne\varnothing\), finite infimum nonattainment means \(p=\inf_{x\in C}f(x)\in\mathbb R\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f=\varnothing\). Equivalently, \(f(x)>p\) for every \(x\in C\), while some sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) satisfies \(f(x_k)\to p\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}_{x\in C}f=\varnothing\iff[(\forall x\in C)\ f(x)>p\text{ and }(\exists x_k\in C)\ f(x_k)\to p]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates nonattainment from infeasibility and an infimum equal to minus infinity.

knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Lower-Semicontinuous Infima Force Escape
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a lower-semicontinuous objective on a closed finite-dimensional feasible set, every minimizing sequence escapes to infinity when the finite infimum is unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and closed, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous with finite unattained infimum \(p\). Every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\subset C\) satisfying \(f(x_k)\to p\) obeys \(\|x_k\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x_k)\to p\Longrightarrow\|x_k\|\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional compactness obstruction for lower-semicontinuous objectives.

knowledge_statements.title: Infimum Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exponential function is smooth and strictly convex, but its infimum is zero and is not attained on the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=e^x\) is finite, smooth, and strictly convex on \(\mathbb R\). It satisfies \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=0\), while \(f(x)>0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R\); hence \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is continuous and strictly convex, but \(\inf_{x\in\mathbb R}f(x)=0\) and \(\operatorname{argmin}f=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Continuity and strict convexity alone do not guarantee attainment on a noncompact domain.

notation.meaning: Set of points attaining the global infimum.

source_witnesses.locator: I. Convex Functions of One Real Variable p. 1

locator_traceability.matched_excerpt: - I. Convex Functions of One Real Variable p. 1

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Compactness Restores Attainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly lower-semicontinuous function attains its finite infimum when a near-optimal sublevel set is weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a Banach space and \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be weakly lower semicontinuous with \(\inf_X f\in\mathbb R\). If \(\{x:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is nonempty and weakly compact for some \(\alpha>\inf_X f\), then \(f\) attains its infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(\{f\le\alpha\}\ne\varnothing\) is weakly compact for some \(\alpha>\inf_X f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{argmin}_X f\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct-method replacement for norm compactness in Banach-space minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Riesz Finite-Dimensional Compactness Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The closed unit ball is norm compact exactly in finite-dimensional normed spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a normed space \(X\), the closed unit ball \(B_X\) is compact in the norm topology if and only if \(X\) is finite-dimensional.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_X\text{ is norm compact}\iff\dim X<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary for norm compactness of the closed unit ball.

notation.meaning: Closed unit ball of the normed space.

knowledge_statements.title: Reflexivity Characterizes Weak Compactness of the Unit Ball
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Banach space has a weakly compact closed unit ball exactly when it is reflexive.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a Banach space \(X\), the closed unit ball \(B_X\) is compact in the weak topology \(\sigma(X,X^*)\) if and only if \(X\) is reflexive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(B_X\text{ is weakly compact}\iff X\text{ is reflexive}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak-topology replacement for failed norm compactness of infinite-dimensional unit balls.

notation.meaning: Weak topology induced by the continuous dual.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite-Dimensional Compactness Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An orthonormal sequence converges weakly to zero but has no norm-convergent subsequence, so the unit ball is weakly compact but not norm compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in H\), Bessel's inequality implies \(\langle e_n,x\rangle\to0\), so \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\). However, for distinct indices \(m\ne n\), \(\|e_n-e_m\|=\sqrt2\); therefore \((e_n)\) has no norm-Cauchy subsequence. Since every \(e_n\) lies in the closed unit ball \(B_H\), that ball is not norm compact. Yet Hilbert spaces are reflexive, so \(B_H\) is weakly compact, exposing the infinite-dimensional compactness gap.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space with an orthonormal sequence \((e_n)_{n\ge1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_n\rightharpoonup0\) but no subsequence converges in norm; hence the closed unit ball is weakly sequentially compact but not norm compact.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded closed sets lose norm compactness in infinite dimensions, despite possible weak compactness.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Sound, complete, and exact convexity criteria
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space and let \(\mathcal F\) be a specified class of functions \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Let \(R\) be a predicate on \(\mathcal F\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A regime-aware definition of what qualifies as a convexity recognition criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The predicate \(R\) is a sound convexity criterion on \(\mathcal F\) if \[\forall f\in\mathcal F:\ R(f)\Longrightarrow f\text{ is convex}.\] It is complete if \[\forall f\in\mathcal F:\ f\text{ is convex}\Longrightarrow R(f),\] and exact if it is both sound and complete, equivalently \[\forall f\in\mathcal F:\ R(f)\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is convex}.\] A convexity recognition system is a family \(\mathscr R=\{(\mathcal F_i,R_i)\}_{i\in I}\) in which each criterion records its own applicability regime, such as arbitrary extended-valued functions, differentiable functions on open convex sets, or twice differentiable functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convexity recognition criterion is sound when every function satisfying it is convex, complete when every convex function in its declared class satisfies it, and exact when both directions hold. A recognition system is an indexed family of such predicates together with their function classes. Including the function class is essential: epigraph and chord criteria apply very broadly, whereas gradient-monotonicity and Hessian criteria require differentiability and domain assumptions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R\text{ exact on }\mathcal F\Longleftrightarrow(\forall f\in\mathcal F)\,[R(f)\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ convex}].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[R\text{ exact}\Longleftrightarrow R\text{ sound and }R\text{ complete}.\]
Using \(\mathcal C:=\{f\in\mathcal F:f\text{ is convex}\}\), exactness is \[\{f\in\mathcal F:R(f)\}=\mathcal C.\]
special_cases_latex: The epigraph predicate is exact on proper extended-real-valued functions over convex domains.
Positive-semidefiniteness of the Hessian is exact for twice continuously differentiable real-valued functions on an open convex domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: A criterion stated without its function class is mathematically incomplete because its soundness or completeness may depend on regularity assumptions.
Several exact criteria may recognize the same convexity class while furnishing different certificates.
boundary_notes: Midpoint convexity is not an exact criterion on unrestricted functions without a regularity hypothesis.
Second-order criteria are unavailable for nonsmooth functions and should not be treated as necessary conditions in that regime.

notation.meaning: The declared applicability class of functions.
A proposed recognition predicate evaluated at \(f\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: formalizes necessity, sufficiency, and equivalence of recognition predicates.
The framework is organizational; exact source support is required for the named special cases.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric convexity recognition profile
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space \(E\), and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zeroth-order geometric recognition through chords, epigraphs, and affine-line sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define the geometric recognition predicates \[R_{\mathrm{ch}}(f):\Longleftrightarrow f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le(1-\lambda)f(x)+\lambda f(y)\] for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\); \[R_{\mathrm{epi}}(f):\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq E\times\mathbb R\text{ is convex};\] and \[R_{\mathrm{line}}(f):\Longleftrightarrow[t\mapsto f(x+td)]\text{ is convex on }I_{x,d}:=\{t:x+td\in C\}\] for every \(x\in C\) and \(d\in E\). The geometric criterion profile is \(\mathscr G(f):=(R_{\mathrm{ch}},R_{\mathrm{epi}},R_{\mathrm{line}})\). Each component is exact: \[f\text{ is convex}\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{ch}}(f)\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{epi}}(f)\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{line}}(f).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The geometric recognition profile consists of three predicates. The chord predicate requires the graph value at every point of a segment to lie below the corresponding chord. The epigraph predicate requires the region above the graph to be convex. The line predicate requires every affine-line restriction, on its natural interval of definition, to be a one-dimensional convex function. For a proper extended-real-valued function on a convex domain, each predicate is equivalent to convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex}\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{ch}}(f)\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{epi}}(f)\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{line}}(f).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[R_{\mathrm{ch}}(f)\Longleftrightarrow\text{every chord joining two finite graph points lies on or above the graph}.\]
\[R_{\mathrm{line}}(f)\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{ch}}(f)\text{ on every affine line intersecting }C.\]
special_cases_latex: When \(E=\mathbb R\), the line predicate reduces to ordinary one-dimensional convexity.
For an indicator \(f=\iota_D\), the epigraph predicate is equivalent to convexity of \(D\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity can be checked on two-dimensional epigraph geometry or on one-dimensional affine sections.
No differentiability or topological assumption is required for these algebraic geometric criteria.
boundary_notes: Closedness of the epigraph characterizes lower semicontinuity, not convexity; convexity and closedness are separate properties.
Testing only coordinate-axis lines is generally insufficient to recognize multivariate convexity.

notation.meaning: The segment or chord inequality predicate.
The parameter interval on which the affine line remains in \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Epigraph Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex domain is convex exactly when the set of points lying on or above its graph is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\operatorname{epi}f=\{(x,r)\in C\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}\). Then \(f\) is convex precisely when, for every \(x_0,x_1\in C\), \(r_i\ge f(x_i)\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), one has \((1-\lambda)(x_0,r_0)+\lambda(x_1,r_1)\in\operatorname{epi}f\). Equivalently, \[f((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\le(1-\lambda)f(x_0)+\lambda f(x_1).\] Thus convexity of the function is exactly convexity of its epigraph.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}f\) is a convex subset of the product space.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric equivalence between functional convexity and convexity of the epigraph.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Epigraph criterion for convexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space \(E\), and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. Extend \(f\) by \(+\infty\) outside \(C\) when forming its epigraph in \(E\times\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely algebraic; no closedness, continuity, or finite-dimensional assumption is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The epigraph of \(f\) is \[\operatorname{epi}f:=\{(x,r)\in E\times\mathbb R:f(x)\le r\}.\] The epigraph convexity criterion is the equivalence \[f\text{ is convex}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{epi}f\text{ is a convex subset of }E\times\mathbb R.\] Explicitly, epigraph convexity means that for all \((x,r),(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y,(1-\lambda)r+\lambda s)\in\operatorname{epi}f.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph is the set of all points lying at or above the graph of an extended-real-valued function. The epigraph criterion says that the function is convex exactly when this set is convex in the product space. Thus every convex combination of two epigraph points must remain an epigraph point. This criterion concerns convexity only; whether the epigraph is closed is a separate lower-semicontinuity question.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex}\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{epi}f\text{ convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\forall x,y\in C,\lambda\in[0,1]:\ f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\le(1-\lambda)f(x)+\lambda f(y).\]
\[\forall(x,r),(y,s)\in\operatorname{epi}f,\lambda\in[0,1]:\ ((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y,(1-\lambda)r+\lambda s)\in\operatorname{epi}f.\]
special_cases_latex: For \(f=\iota_D\), \(\operatorname{epi}f=D\times[0,+\infty)\), so the criterion reduces to convexity of \(D\).
For an affine function, the epigraph is a half-space in \(E\times\mathbb R\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Set operations preserving convexity of epigraphs generate convexity-preserving operations on functions.
The effective domain \(\operatorname{dom}f\), being the projection of a convex epigraph, is convex whenever \(f\) is convex.
boundary_notes: A convex epigraph need not be closed.
The hypograph criterion corresponds to concavity rather than convexity.

notation.meaning: The indicator equal to \(0\) on \(D\) and \(+\infty\) outside \(D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Restriction-to-Lines Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex set is convex exactly when its restriction to every affine line is convex as a one-dimensional function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(a,d\in X\) with \(d\ne0\), define \(I_{a,d}=\{t\in\mathbb R:a+td\in C\}\) and \(\phi_{a,d}(t)=f(a+td)\). Then \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if every \(\phi_{a,d}:I_{a,d}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if, for every \(a,d\in X\) with \(d\ne0\), the function \(t\mapsto f(a+td)\) is convex on \(I_{a,d}=\{t\in\mathbb R:a+td\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recognition of multivariate convexity through all affine one-dimensional sections.

notation.meaning: Affine line through a in direction d.
Parameter interval of the line section lying in C.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine-line restriction criterion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space \(E\), and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper. For \(x\in C\) and \(d\in E\), define \(I_{x,d}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+td\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic reduction of multivariate convexity to all one-dimensional affine sections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \((x,d)\), define the line restriction \[\varphi_{x,d}:I_{x,d}\to(-\infty,+\infty],\qquad \varphi_{x,d}(t):=f(x+td).\] Because \(C\) is convex, \(I_{x,d}\) is an interval, possibly empty, a singleton, or unbounded. The restriction-to-lines criterion is \[f\text{ is convex on }C\Longleftrightarrow\varphi_{x,d}\text{ is convex on }I_{x,d}\quad\text{for every }x\in C, d\in E.\] Convexity of a restriction means that for all \(s,t\in I_{x,d}\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[\varphi_{x,d}((1-\lambda)s+\lambda t)\le(1-\lambda)\varphi_{x,d}(s)+\lambda\varphi_{x,d}(t).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict the function to any affine line and parameterize the part of that line lying in the domain by an interval. The original function is convex exactly when every such one-dimensional restriction is convex on its natural interval. All directions must be tested; restricting attention to a preferred finite collection of directions does not generally suffice.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex on }C\Longleftrightarrow(\forall x\in C)(\forall d\in E)\ \varphi_{x,d}\text{ convex on }I_{x,d}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: It suffices to require convexity of \(t\mapsto f(a+tb)\) for every affine map \(t\mapsto a+tb\) whose relevant interval maps into \(C\).
The criterion is equivalent to requiring the chord inequality on every segment contained in \(C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(d=0\), the restriction is constant and supplies no additional condition.
If \(E=\mathbb R^n\), arbitrary directions \(d\in\mathbb R^n\) are still required.
immediate_consequences_latex: Multivariate convexity questions may be reduced to one-dimensional slope or derivative criteria after restricting to a line.
Any violation of convexity is witnessed on the affine line through the two points violating the chord inequality.
boundary_notes: Separate convexity of coordinate slices is weaker than joint convexity.
The criterion does not imply continuity at boundary points of \(C\).

notation.meaning: The maximal parameter interval for the line section through \(x\) in direction \(d\).

children.top_down_role: One-dimensional recognition through ordered chord and slope geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordered secant-slope criterion
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) be a nonempty interval and let \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) be finite-valued. For \(x<y\), define the secant slope \(s_f(x,y):=[f(y)-f(x)]/(y-x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-dimensional finite-valued regime; derivative-free recognition by ordered chord slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The ordered-slope predicate is \[R_{\mathrm{slope}}(f):\Longleftrightarrow s_f(x,y)\le s_f(x,z)\le s_f(y,z)\quad\text{for every }x<y<z\text{ in }I.\] The one-dimensional slope recognition criterion is \[f\text{ is convex on }I\Longleftrightarrow R_{\mathrm{slope}}(f).\] Equivalently, for every fixed \(x\in I\), the map \(y\mapsto s_f(x,y)\) is nondecreasing for \(y>x\), and for every fixed \(z\in I\), the map \(x\mapsto s_f(x,z)\) is nondecreasing for \(x<z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a finite real-valued function on an interval, assign to each ordered pair of points its secant slope. The function is convex exactly when, for every three ordered points, the slope over the left subinterval does not exceed the slope over the full interval, and the full-interval slope does not exceed the slope over the right subinterval. This is a derivative-free recognition rule and also organizes the monotonicity of one-sided derivatives when they exist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex}\Longleftrightarrow(\forall x<y<z)\ s_f(x,y)\le s_f(x,z)\le s_f(y,z).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[s_f(x,y)\le s_f(y,z)\quad\text{for all }x<y<z.\]
\[\frac{f(y)-f(x)}{y-x}\le\frac{f(z)-f(x)}{z-x}\quad\text{for all }x<y<z.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable, the criterion is equivalent to monotonicity of \(f'\).
For an affine function, all secant slopes are equal.
immediate_consequences_latex: A convex function has finite one-sided derivatives at interior points whenever the corresponding slope bounds are finite.
At every interior point, the left slope bounds do not exceed the right slope bounds.
boundary_notes: Extended-real values require modified conventions and are excluded from this formulation.
Monotonicity of sampled slopes on only a discrete subset does not establish convexity on the whole interval without additional regularity.

notation.meaning: The secant slope of \(f\) between \(x\) and \(y\).

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical monotonic-secant characterization of one-dimensional convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Secant-Line Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real-valued function on an interval is convex exactly when its graph lies below every chord joining two points of its graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex on \(I\) if and only if, for every \(x<y<z\) in \(I\),
\[
f(y)\leq \frac{z-y}{z-x}f(x)+\frac{y-x}{z-x}f(z).
\]
Equivalently, over every interval \([x,z]\), the graph of \(f\) lies below the chord joining \((x,f(x))\) and \((z,f(z))\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(I\) if and only if \(f(y)\leq \frac{z-y}{z-x}f(x)+\frac{y-x}{z-x}f(z)\) for every \(x<y<z\) in \(I\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Chord characterization of finite real-valued convex functions on an interval.

notation.meaning: Real interval on which the function is defined.

source_witnesses.locator: I. Convex Functions of One Real Variable p. 1

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Secant Slopes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity on an interval is equivalent to the ordered increase of secant slopes across every three points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is convex on \(I\) if and only if, for every \(x<y<z\) in \(I\),
\[
s_f(x,y)\leq s_f(x,z)\leq s_f(y,z).
\]
Equivalently, for each fixed endpoint, every defined secant slope is nondecreasing as the other endpoint moves to the right, with comparisons made across all admissible ordered points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex if and only if \(s_f(x,y)\le s_f(x,z)\le s_f(y,z)\) whenever \(x<y<z\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-point slope criterion in one real dimension.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Derivative Recognition Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous function with an everywhere finite right or left derivative is convex exactly when that one-sided derivative is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) be an open interval and let \(f:I\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. If \(f'_+(x)\in\mathbb R\) exists for every \(x\in I\), then \[f\text{ is convex on }I\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\mapsto f'_+(x)\text{ is nondecreasing}.\] The analogous equivalence holds with the finite left derivative \(f'_-(x)\).
assumptions_latex: The selected one-sided derivative exists and is finite at every point of \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(I\) if and only if the selected one-sided derivative is nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse recognition from an everywhere finite monotone one-sided derivative, with continuity excluding jump discontinuities.

notation.meaning: Finite right derivative of f at x.
Finite left derivative of f at x.

knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Slope Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function has ordered, nondecreasing one-sided derivatives, and every secant slope lies between the adjacent one-sided slopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At every \(x\in I\), the finite one-sided derivatives \(f'_-(x)\) and \(f'_+(x)\) exist and satisfy \(f'_-(x)\leq f'_+(x)\). Each of the maps \(x\mapsto f'_-(x)\) and \(x\mapsto f'_+(x)\) is nondecreasing. More strongly, whenever \(x<y\),
\[
f'_+(x)\leq s_f(x,y)\leq f'_-(y).
\]
Consequently, \(f\) is differentiable except at at most countably many points.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f'_-(x)\le f'_+(x)\), both one-sided derivatives are nondecreasing, and \(f'_+(x)\le f'_-(y)\) for \(x<y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite one-sided derivatives at interior points of an open interval.

notation.meaning: Left derivative of the convex function.
Right derivative of the convex function.
