knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuous One-Sided-Derivative Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An everywhere zero right derivative does not imply convexity when jump discontinuities are allowed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x)=0\) for \(x<0\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x\geq0\). The finite right derivative exists everywhere and satisfies \(f'_+(x)=0\), hence is nondecreasing. However, \(f\) is discontinuous and therefore is not convex on the open interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Existence and monotonicity of an everywhere finite right derivative do not imply convexity without a regularity assumption excluding jumps.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convexity recognition from a monotone right derivative when continuity is omitted.

notation.meaning: Right derivative of the discontinuous step function.

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Endpoint Secant Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Secants from one endpoint can have increasing slopes even though the function is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:[0,1]\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(x)=2x^2-x^3\). For \(x>0\), \[s_f(0,x)=\frac{f(x)-f(0)}x=2x-x^2,\] which is nondecreasing on \([0,1]\). Nevertheless, \(f''(x)=4-6x<0\) for \(x>2/3\), so \(f\) is not convex. Thus monotonicity of secant slopes sharing one fixed endpoint is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Monotonicity of \(x\mapsto s_f(0,x)\) does not imply convexity of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth polynomial counterexample to recognition using only secants from one endpoint.

notation.meaning: Secant slope from the fixed endpoint zero to x.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Slope Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Secant monotonicity from only one fixed base point does not characterize convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:[0,2]\to\mathbb{R}\) be the continuous piecewise-affine function interpolating
\[
(0,0),\quad(1,1),\quad\left(\frac32,\frac{27}{10}\right),\quad(2,4).
\]
The fixed-base secant quotient \(x\mapsto(f(x)-f(0))/x=f(x)/x\) is nondecreasing on \((0,2]\). However, the slopes on \([1,3/2]\) and \([3/2,2]\) are respectively \(17/5\) and \(13/5\). Because these adjacent slopes decrease, \(f\) is not convex. Hence checking secants from one base point is insufficient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-linear function can have increasing secant slopes from one fixed origin while failing convexity because slopes decrease elsewhere.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is the stated continuous piecewise-affine interpolant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto f(x)/x\text{ is nondecreasing on }(0,2]\), but \(f\text{ is not convex}.\)

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jensen admissibility and Jensen gap
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real locally convex space \(E\), let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex, and let \(\mu\) be a probability measure for which an \(E\)-valued barycenter \(b_\mu\in C\) and the integral of \(f\) are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A unified definition covering finite barycenters and admissible measure-based averages; precise integration assumptions belong to each regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A pair \((f,\mu)\) is Jensen-admissible when \(b_\mu:=\int_Cx\,d\mu(x)\) exists in \(C\), the positive part of \(f\) is integrable or the extended integral is otherwise unambiguous, and \(f(b_\mu)\) is defined. Its Jensen gap is \[J_f(\mu):=\int_C f(x)\,d\mu(x)-f\!\left(\int_Cx\,d\mu(x)\right).\] The Jensen principle is the nonnegativity property \[J_f(\mu)\ge0\] for every measure in a declared admissible class. A Jensen equality regime is characterized by \(J_f(\mu)=0\), while strictness means \(J_f(\mu)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability measure is Jensen-admissible for a convex function when its barycenter exists in the domain and the function integral is meaningful. The Jensen gap is the average function value minus the function value at the barycenter. The Jensen principle is the assertion that this gap is nonnegative throughout the selected admissible measure class. Finite convex combinations arise from finitely supported probability measures, while probabilistic and integral versions require explicit measurability and integrability hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[J_f(\mu):=\int f\,d\mu-f(b_\mu),\qquad\text{Jensen property}\Longleftrightarrow J_f(\mu)\ge0\text{ for every admissible }\mu.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a random variable \(X\) with law \(\mu\), \[J_f(\mu)=\mathbb E[f(X)]-f(\mathbb E[X]).\]
For \(\mu=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i\delta_{x_i}\), \[J_f(\mu)=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i)-f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\right).\]
special_cases_latex: For an affine \(f\), every admissible Jensen gap is zero.
For strictly convex \(f\), a nondegenerate admissible distribution typically has a positive gap, subject to finiteness and support conditions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every measure-based regime contains the finite convex-combination regime when finitely supported measures are admissible.
The gap provides a single object for distinguishing inequality, equality, and strictness regimes.
boundary_notes: In infinite-dimensional spaces, existence of a barycenter depends on the integration notion and topology.
Expressions involving \(+\infty-+\infty\) are excluded as undefined.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Jensen gap unifying finite and measure-based forms.
The exact admissibility conditions and strict-equality annotations require an inspected source.
knowledge_statements.title: Jensen admissibility and Jensen gap

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum of a Convex Function over a Finite Convex Hull
knowledge_statements.scope_note: No topology or separate attainment assumption is needed: every generating point lies in the hull, and the finite convex-averaging bound supplies the reverse inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $x_1,\ldots,x_m$ lie in a real vector space and let $\Delta:=\operatorname{Conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}=\{\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i:\alpha_i\geq0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1\}$. If $C$ is convex, $\Delta\subseteq C$, and $f:C\to\mathbb{R}$ is convex, then $\max_{x\in\Delta}f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f(x_i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function maximized over the convex hull of finitely many points has the same maximum value as its maximum over those generating points.
assumptions_latex: x_1,\ldots,x_m\text{ are points in a real vector space}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\in\Delta}f(x)=\max_{1\leq i\leq m}f(x_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Jensen Inequality with Positive Weights
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This finite form assumes at least two domain points and strictly positive weights summing to one; it also concludes that their weighted average remains in the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $f$ be convex on $\operatorname{dom}f$, let $m\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\geq2$, and let $x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $\alpha_i>0$ for $i=1,\ldots,m$, with $\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i=1$. Then $\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f(x_i)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, a finite average of at least two domain points with strictly positive weights remains in the domain, and the function value at that average does not exceed the weighted average of the function values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\in\operatorname{dom}f\quad\text{and}\quad f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f(x_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex on \(\mathbb E\). For every integer \(k\ge1\), every \(x_1,\ldots,x_k\in\mathbb E\), and every \(\lambda\in\Delta_k=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^k:\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i=1\}\), \[f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function evaluated at any finite convex combination is at most the corresponding convex combination of its values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i f(x_i)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict upper-bound characterization of convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to functions that may take either infinite value and quantifies over real strict upper bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]. Then f is convex if and only if, for every x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n, every \alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}, and every \lambda\in(0,1), \[f(x)<\alpha\ \land\ f(y)<\beta\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)<(1-\lambda)\alpha+\lambda\beta.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An extended-value function is convex exactly when any two strict finite upper bounds on its endpoint values yield the correspondingly averaged strict upper bound at every strict convex combination of the endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff\forall x,y\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \forall\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}\ \forall\lambda\in(0,1),\ [f(x)<\alpha\land f(y)<\beta\Rightarrow f((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)<(1-\lambda)\alpha+\lambda\beta].

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite Jensen inequality and convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers arbitrary finite convex combinations for extended-real-valued functions that never take negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f:\mathbb{R}^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]. Then f is convex if and only if, for every integer m\geq1, all x_1,\ldots,x_m\in\mathbb{R}^n, and all \lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m\geq0 satisfying \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1, \[f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function that never takes negative infinity is convex exactly when Jensen's inequality holds for every finite collection of points and every collection of nonnegative weights summing to one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is convex}\iff f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i)\text{ for every finite convex combination}.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Real Finite Jensen Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite Jensen inequality extends to convex functions that may take positive infinity, with zero-weight terms omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex. For \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in C\) and \(\lambda_i\geq0\) with \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\), omit all indices with \(\lambda_i=0\). Then \[f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i\right)\leq\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i f(x_i)\] in the extended-real order. Conversely, validity for every two-point family is convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\sum_i\lambda_i x_i)\leq\sum_{i:\lambda_i>0}\lambda_i f(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Jensen inequality for proper extended-real-valued convex functions, with zero-weight terms omitted.

notation.meaning: Extended-real weighted sum with zero-weight terms omitted.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Convex-Combination Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is convex exactly when its value at every finite weighted barycenter does not exceed the corresponding weighted average of its values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\geq2\). The barycenter \(\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i\) belongs to \(C\), and finite Jensen inequality gives
\[
f(\bar{x})\leq\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f(x_i).
\]
Conversely, if this inequality holds for every such finite family and probability vector, then \(f\) is convex on \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
\(n\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\geq2\), \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in C\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\) for \(1\leq i\leq n\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i\right)\leq\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f(x_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite Jensen inequality in a real vector space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite barycentric Jensen property
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a convex subset of a real vector space and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Purely finite algebraic averaging; no topology, measurability, or integration theory is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\ge1\), points \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\), and weights \(\lambda=(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m)\) in the simplex \[\Delta_m:=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\},\] define the barycenter \(\bar x_\lambda:=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i\) and finite Jensen gap \[J_f(\lambda;x_1,\ldots,x_m):=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i f(x_i)-f(\bar x_\lambda),\] whenever the extended-real difference is defined. The finite convex-combination property is \[J_f(\lambda;x_1,\ldots,x_m)\ge0\] for every \(m\), every \(\lambda\in\Delta_m\), and every \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\). This property is equivalent to convexity of \(f\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convex combination is specified by finitely many domain points and nonnegative weights summing to one. Their weighted sum is the barycenter. The finite Jensen gap is the weighted average of the function values minus the value at that barycenter. Requiring this gap to be nonnegative for every finite collection is exactly the finite convex-combination form of convexity. The case of two points is the ordinary defining convexity inequality and already generates all finite cases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f\text{ convex}\Longleftrightarrow(\forall m,\lambda\in\Delta_m,x_i\in C)\quad f\!\left(\sum_i\lambda_i x_i\right)\le\sum_i\lambda_i f(x_i).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: It is sufficient to impose the displayed inequality for \(m=2\).
The property is Jensen nonnegativity for every finitely supported probability measure \(\mu=\sum_i\lambda_i\delta_{x_i}\).
special_cases_latex: For equal weights \(\lambda_i=1/m\), the inequality becomes \[f\!\left(\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m x_i\right)\le\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^m f(x_i).\]
If one weight equals \(1\), the Jensen gap is zero.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every finite barycenter remains in \(C\) because \(C\) is convex.
The finite regime supplies the algebraic core of measure-based Jensen inequalities.
boundary_notes: Midpoint inequalities alone require regularity before they imply full convexity for arbitrary functions.
Undefined extended-real differences are avoided by using the inequality form as the primary formulation.

notation.meaning: The simplex of nonnegative weights summing to one.

A precise inspected source locator remains required.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bochner-integral Jensen regime
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\Omega,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)\) be a probability space, let \(E\) be a separable Banach space, let \(C\subseteq E\) be convex, and let \(X:\Omega\to C\) be strongly measurable and Bochner integrable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Banach-space probabilistic regime with Bochner barycenters and an extended-real convex integrand.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex and Borel measurable. The pair \((f,X)\) is Bochner–Jensen admissible when \(\mathbb E[X]\in C\), \(f(X)^+\) is integrable, and the extended expectation \(\mathbb E[f(X)]\) is well-defined. Define \[J_f(X):=\mathbb E[f(X)]-f(\mathbb E[X])\] whenever this difference is defined. The Bochner measure-based Jensen property is \[f(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[f(X)]\] for every admissible \(X\). Equivalently, if \(\mu:=\mathbb P\circ X^{-1}\) is the law of \(X\), then \[f\!\left(\int_Cx\,d\mu(x)\right)\le\int_Cf(x)\,d\mu(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the Bochner regime, an integrable Banach-space-valued random variable has a barycenter given by its expectation. A convex measurable function and random variable are Jensen-admissible when this barycenter belongs to the domain and the extended expectation of the function is meaningful. The measure-based Jensen property compares the function value at the barycenter with the expected function value. The same statement may be written using the distribution of the random variable and its Bochner integral.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(\mathbb E[X])\le\mathbb E[f(X)]\quad\text{for every Bochner–Jensen admissible }(f,X).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For the law \(\mu=\mathbb P\circ X^{-1}\), \[f(b_\mu)\le\int f\,d\mu,\qquad b_\mu:=\int x\,d\mu.\]
Conditional Jensen takes the form \[f(\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G])\le\mathbb E[f(X)\mid\mathcal G]\] when the conditional expectations and measurability conditions are available.
special_cases_latex: When \(E=\mathbb R^n\), Bochner integration reduces to componentwise integration.
A finitely valued random variable recovers the finite convex-combination Jensen inequality.
immediate_consequences_latex: The expectation of an integrable random variable taking values in a closed convex set remains in that set.
Affine functions have zero Jensen gap whenever both expectations are finite.
boundary_notes: If \(C\) is not closed, the assumption \(\mathbb E[X]\in C\) cannot be omitted.
Pettis-integral, conditional, and nonseparable variants require distinct measurability and barycenter hypotheses.
No expression of the form \(+\infty-+\infty\) is admitted.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard Bochner-integral formulation of Jensen's inequality.
An inspected source is required for the exact extended-integrability assumptions and conditional variant.

knowledge_statements.title: Integral Jensen Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a probability measure, a convex function of an integrable barycenter is at most the integral of the function values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Closed convexity of \(C\) ensures that the barycenter \(\int_S g\,d\mu\) belongs to \(C\). Integral Jensen inequality then gives
\[
f\!\left(\int_S g\,d\mu\right)\leq\int_S f(g(s))\,d\mu(s).
\]
Both sides are finite under the stated integrability assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(g:S\to\mathbb{R}^d\) is Bochner integrable with \(g(s)\in C\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(s\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex and \(f\circ g\) is integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\!\left(\int_S g\,d\mu\right)\leq\int_S f(g(s))\,d\mu(s)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional integral Jensen inequality with finite integrals.

knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Jensen Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function of a random vector's expectation is no larger than the expected function value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The expectation \(\mathbb{E}X\) belongs to \(C\), and
\[
f(\mathbb{E}X)\leq\mathbb{E}[f(X)].
\]
Equivalently, applying integral Jensen inequality to the distribution \(\mathcal{L}(X)\) gives
\[
f\!\left(\int_C x\,d\mathcal{L}(X)(x)\right)\leq\int_C f(x)\,d\mathcal{L}(X)(x).
\]
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is an integrable \(C\)-valued random vector, where \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\mathbb{E}X)\leq\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional probabilistic Jensen inequality with finite expectations.

notation.meaning: Expectation under the underlying probability law.

knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Expectation Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Conditionally, a convex function of the conditional mean does not exceed the conditional mean of the function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A version of \(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]\) is \(C\)-valued almost surely because \(C\) is closed and convex. Conditional Jensen inequality states
\[
f\!\left(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]\right)
\leq \mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid\mathcal{G}]
\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P})\) is a probability space and \(\mathcal{G}\subseteq\mathcal{F}\) is a sub-\(\sigma\)-algebra.
\(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(X\) is an integrable random vector with \(X\in C\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\!\left(\mathbb{E}[X\mid\mathcal{G}]\right)\leq\mathbb{E}[f(X)\mid\mathcal{G}]\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional conditional Jensen inequality on a closed convex domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended-Real Jensen Beyond Transform Integrability
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex function admits extended-real Jensen for an integrable input even when its positive part is nonintegrable; a finite right-hand side requires extra assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and let \(X\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\) satisfy \(X\in\operatorname{dom}f\) almost surely and \(\mathbb EX\in\operatorname{dom}f\). Then \(f\) has an affine minorant, so \(f(X)^-\in L^1\) and \(\mathbb E[f(X)]\in(-\infty,+\infty]\) is well defined. Moreover,
\[
f(\mathbb EX)\leq \mathbb E[f(X)].
\]
Finiteness of \(\mathbb E[f(X)]\) is an additional requirement, not a consequence of \(X\in L^1\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R^d\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
\(X\in L^1(\Omega;\mathbb R^d)\), \(X\in\operatorname{dom}f\) almost surely, and \(\mathbb EX\in\operatorname{dom}f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(X)^-\in L^1\) and \(f(\mathbb EX)\leq\mathbb E[f(X)]\leq+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real expectation Jensen for proper lower-semicontinuous convex functions in finite dimensions.

notation.meaning: negative part of the extended-real random variable f(X)

knowledge_statements.title: Integrability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrable random variable may have a nonintegrable convex transform, so finite Jensen inequalities need additional integrability or growth assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Although \(X\) is integrable, \(f(X)=X^2\) is not integrable because \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=\infty\). Thus the finite-valued assertion
\[
f(\mathbb{E}X)\leq\mathbb{E}[f(X)]<\infty
\]
cannot be concluded from \(X\in L^1\) alone. Jensen remains meaningful with an extended right-hand side, but a finite formulation requires integrability of \(f(X)\), an appropriate growth bound on \(f\), or stronger moments of \(X\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\geq0\) is a random variable with \(\mathbb{E}X<\infty\) but \(\mathbb{E}X^2=\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Integrability of \(X\) alone does not ensure integrability of \(f(X)\); finite-valued Jensen formulations require an additional condition.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between finite and extended-real Jensen formulations.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative integrable random variable with infinite second moment.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jensen gap and its equality and strictness regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex, and let \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\in C\) and \(\alpha\in\Delta_m:=\{a\in\mathbb{R}_+^m:\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=1\}\). Put \(\bar x=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, finite convex-combination Jensen regimes. The definition distinguishes equality, strict separation, and the effect of zero weights; it does not cover measure-valued Jensen inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Jensen gap of \((f;x_i,\alpha_i)\) is
\[
J_f(\alpha;x_1,\ldots,x_m):=\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i f(x_i)-f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^m\alpha_i x_i\right)\geq0.
\]
The data are in the Jensen equality regime when \(J_f=0\), and in the strict-separation regime when \(J_f>0\). The strict Jensen regime for \(f\) means that for every such family whose positive-weight support \(\{x_i:\alpha_i>0\}\) contains at least two distinct points, \(J_f>0\). This is precisely the finite-combination form of strict convexity. Indices with \(\alpha_i=0\) do not affect either regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a convex function, the Jensen gap is the weighted average \(\sum_i\alpha_i f(x_i)\) minus the value at the barycenter \(f(\sum_i\alpha_i x_i)\), and it is nonnegative. Equality means that this gap is zero. Strict separation means it is positive. A function is in the strict Jensen regime when every finite convex combination having at least two distinct positive-weight points has positive gap; zero-weight points are irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(J_f:=\sum_i\alpha_i f(x_i)-f(\sum_i\alpha_i x_i)\geq0\); equality is \(J_f=0\), while strict Jensen separation is \(J_f>0\) whenever the positive-weight support is not a singleton.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(m=2\), the strict regime is \(f(tx+(1-t)y)<tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)\) for all distinct \(x,y\in C\) and all \(t\in(0,1)\).
The equality regime is equivalently \(f(\bar x)=\sum_i\alpha_i f(x_i)\).
special_cases_latex: If all positive-weight points equal \(x\), then \(\bar x=x\) and \(J_f=0\).
If \(f\) is affine on \(C\), then \(J_f=0\) for every finite convex combination.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity excludes Jensen equality whenever at least two distinct points receive positive weight.
Deleting all zero-weight indices leaves \(\bar x\), \(J_f\), and the equality classification unchanged.
boundary_notes: Convexity alone permits equality for distinct points, for example when the function is affine on their segment.
The definition concerns finite combinations; integral equality conditions require additional measure-theoretic hypotheses.

notation.meaning: The unit simplex of nonnegative weights in \(\mathbb{R}^m\).
The Jensen gap for the specified function, points, and weights.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Jensen Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity makes Jensen's inequality strict when the averaging distribution is not concentrated at one point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Closed convexity of \(C\) ensures that \(\mathbb{E}X\in C\). If the law of \(X\) is not concentrated at one point, strict convexity strengthens Jensen inequality to
\[
f(\mathbb{E}X)<\mathbb{E}[f(X)].
\]
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is nonempty, closed, and convex, and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is strictly convex.
\(X\) is an integrable random vector with \(X\in C\) almost surely, \(f(X)\) is integrable, and \(X\) is not almost surely constant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\mathbb{E}X)<\mathbb{E}[f(X)]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict probabilistic Jensen inequality for a nondegenerate finite-dimensional distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Equality Cases
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With positive weights, equality in finite Jensen occurs exactly when the convex function is affine on the convex hull of the weighted points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(K=\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\) and \(\bar{x}=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i\). Then
\[
f(\bar{x})=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f(x_i)
\]
holds if and only if the restriction \(f|_K\) is affine. Equivalently, there is an affine function \(a\) on \(\operatorname{aff}K\) such that \(f(x)=a(x)\) for every \(x\in K\).
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) with \(n\geq2\), \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in C\), \(\lambda_i>0\) for \(1\leq i\leq n\), and \(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i=1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i x_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i f(x_i)\) if and only if \(f\) is affine on \(\operatorname{conv}\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality characterization for finite positive-weight Jensen averaging.

notation.meaning: Convex hull of the positively weighted points.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Affine-Segment Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a convex function is affine on a segment, every distribution supported on that segment yields Jensen equality, including nonconstant distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Because \(f\) agrees with an affine function on \([x,y]\), every random vector \(Z\) supported on that segment satisfies
\[
f(\mathbb{E}Z)=\mathbb{E}[f(Z)].
\]
The equality may hold when \(x\neq y\) and \(Z\) is not almost surely constant. Thus distributional nondegeneracy alone does not imply strict Jensen inequality without strict convexity on the convex hull of the support.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb{R}^d\) is convex, \(x,y\in C\), and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is convex.
\(Z\) is a random vector satisfying \(Z\in[x,y]\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\mathbb{E}Z)=\mathbb{E}[f(Z)]\), including when \(Z\) is not almost surely constant.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of Jensen strictness for distributions supported on an affine segment.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributional Degeneracy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a strictly convex function, equality in Jensen's inequality occurs exactly when the random vector is almost surely constant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated assumptions, Jensen's inequality gives \(f(\mathbb{E}X)\leq \mathbb{E}[f(X)]\). Strict convexity makes equality equivalent to distributional degeneracy: \[\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=f(\mathbb{E}X)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \exists x_0\in C\;\mathbb{P}(X=x_0)=1.\] Thus every nondegenerate law supported in \(C\) for which the expectations exist yields strict inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is strictly convex on a convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(X\in C\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb{E}[f(X)]=f(\mathbb{E}X)\) if and only if there exists \(x_0\in C\) such that \(\mathbb{P}(X=x_0)=1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality characterization for strict Jensen inequality in finite dimensions.

children.title: First-Order Convexity Criteria
children.top_down_role: Recognition through supporting affine models and monotonicity of first-order mappings.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order certificate system for convexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. A finite-valued function \(f\) is assumed defined on an open neighborhood \(\Omega\supseteq C\) when gradients are used; an extended-real function is interpreted through its effective domain when subgradients are used.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional first-order recognition. Smooth criteria require differentiability on an open neighborhood; the subgradient criterion covers nonsmooth proper functions on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A first-order convexity certificate on \(C\) is either of the following equivalent smooth conditions:
\[
f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\quad(\forall x,y\in C),
\]
\[
\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq0\quad(\forall x,y\in C).
\]
For a possibly nonsmooth finite-valued function on an open convex set \(C\), the supporting-subgradient certificate is
\[
\forall x\in C\ \exists g_x\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \forall y\in C:\quad f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle.
\]
The vectors \(g_x\) are subgradients. In their respective regularity regimes, satisfaction of any displayed certificate is the first-order convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order convexity certificate says either that every tangent affine model formed from the gradient globally underestimates the function, that the gradient is a monotone mapping, or, in the nonsmooth setting, that every point admits a subgradient whose affine function globally underestimates the function. Under the stated domain and differentiability conditions, these are recognition criteria for convexity.
assumptions_latex: For gradient certificates, \(f\) is differentiable on an open set \(\Omega\supseteq C\).
For the nonsmooth certificate, \(C\) is open and convex and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is finite-valued.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The first-order certificate is the global supporting-affine inequality, equivalently gradient monotonicity in the differentiable regime, or existence of a supporting subgradient at every point in the nonsmooth regime.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the differentiable regime, \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if every gradient affine approximation is a global minorant on \(C\).
In the differentiable regime, \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\nabla f\) is monotone on \(C\).
For finite-valued \(f\) on open convex \(C\), convexity is equivalent to \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in C\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is affine, both smooth inequalities hold with equality.
If \(f\) is differentiable and convex, \(\partial f(x)=\{\nabla f(x)\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\nabla f(x_\star)=0\), the supporting inequality gives \(f(y)\geq f(x_\star)\) for all \(y\in C\).
Strict or strong variants are obtained by replacing the displayed inequalities with their strict or quadratic-growth forms.
boundary_notes: A monotone mapping need not be a gradient; monotonicity recognizes convexity only after the mapping is known to equal \(\nabla f\).
Gradient tests are unavailable at points where the relevant derivative does not exist.

notation.meaning: The convex subdifferential, consisting of global supporting slopes at \(x\).

children.title: Gradient Supporting-Hyperplane Criterion
children.top_down_role: Supporting-affine recognition in differentiable regimes.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Supporting-Hyperplane Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function is strictly convex exactly when each tangent affine function touches only at its base point and strictly underestimates the function elsewhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is strictly convex if and only if \(f(y)>f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\) for every distinct \(x,y\in C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ strictly convex}\iff f(y)>f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\quad(x\ne y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-convexity variant of differentiable supporting-affine recognition.

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Supporting-Hyperplane Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function on an open convex set is convex exactly when every tangent affine function globally underestimates it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if its tangent affine function at every point is a global minorant on \(C\): \[f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad (x,y\in C).\] Equivalently, every graph point \((x,f(x))\) admits the supporting hyperplane determined by \(\nabla f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\) for all \(x,y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional first-order characterization on an open convex domain.

notation.meaning: Euclidean gradient of the differentiable function.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gradient supporting-hyperplane condition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open with \(C\subseteq\Omega\), and let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable functions on a convex test set contained in an open differentiability domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gradient supporting-hyperplane condition on \(C\) is
\[
\forall x,y\in C:\qquad f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle.
\]
Thus, for each base point \(x\in C\), the affine function
\[
a_x(y):=f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle
\]
is a global minorant of \(f\) on \(C\) and satisfies \(a_x(x)=f(x)\). A differentiable function is convex on \(C\) exactly when this condition holds at every base point. The strict form requires strict inequality for every \(x\neq y\), and corresponds to strict convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At each point \(x\), form the affine approximation with slope \(\nabla f(x)\). The supporting-hyperplane condition requires this affine function to lie below \(f\) at every point \(y\) of the convex set and to touch \(f\) at \(x\). For a function differentiable on an open neighborhood of the set, this condition at every point is equivalent to convexity; its strict form is equivalent to strict convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open set \(\Omega\) containing \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) satisfies the criterion precisely when \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\) for every \(x,y\in C\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The graph of \(f\) lies above every tangent hyperplane based at a point of \(C\).
The first-order remainder \(r(x,y):=f(y)-f(x)-\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\) is nonnegative for every \(x,y\in C\).
special_cases_latex: For affine \(f\), \(r(x,y)=0\) for every pair.
For strongly convex \(f\) with modulus \(c>0\), the strengthened condition is \(r(x,y)\geq\tfrac c2\|y-x\|^2\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A stationary point \(x_\star\) with \(\nabla f(x_\star)=0\) is a global minimizer on \(C\).
Strict inequality away from the base point prevents a supporting affine model from touching the graph at two distinct points.
boundary_notes: Differentiability must be meaningful on a neighborhood of each tested point.
The condition is global over pairs in \(C\); a supporting inequality verified only locally is not this criterion.

notation.meaning: The affine first-order model of \(f\) based at \(x\).

knowledge_statements.title: Gradient Monotonicity Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function on an open convex set is convex exactly when its gradient is a monotone mapping.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if its gradient is monotone, meaning \[\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq0\qquad (x,y\in C).\] The condition is global over pairs of domain points; pointwise sign conditions on individual gradient components are neither required nor sufficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq0\) for all \(x,y\in C\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Monotonicity condition for a gradient mapping
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(\Omega\supseteq C\) be open, and let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be differentiable.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean finite-dimensional differentiable regime. The criterion concerns a known gradient field, not arbitrary monotone operators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The gradient monotonicity condition on \(C\) is
\[
\forall x,y\in C:\qquad \langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq0.
\]
The gradient is strictly monotone when the left side is positive for every \(x\neq y\), and strongly monotone with modulus \(c>0\) when
\[
\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq c\|x-y\|^2
\]
for every \(x,y\in C\). For a differentiable potential \(f\), monotonicity, strict monotonicity, and strong monotonicity of \(\nabla f\) correspond respectively to convexity, strict convexity, and strong convexity of \(f\) on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A gradient is monotone when the inner product between its change and the corresponding displacement is always nonnegative. Strict monotonicity requires positivity for distinct points, while strong monotonicity requires a uniform quadratic lower bound. When the mapping is the gradient of a differentiable function, these three regimes recognize convexity, strict convexity, and strong convexity, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable on an open set containing \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The criterion is \(\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\geq0\) for all \(x,y\in C\), with strict and strong variants obtained by the stated sharpenings.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Ordinary gradient monotonicity is equivalent to convexity of the differentiable potential \(f\) on \(C\).
Strong monotonicity with modulus \(c\) is equivalent to strong convexity with modulus \(c\) under the source convention.
special_cases_latex: For an affine function, the gradient is constant and the monotonicity pairing is zero.
For \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle Qx,x\rangle+\langle b,x\rangle\) with symmetric \(Q\), the pairing equals \(\langle Q(x-y),x-y\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict monotonicity implies ordinary monotonicity.
Strong monotonicity with \(c>0\) implies strict monotonicity.
boundary_notes: An arbitrary monotone mapping need not be a gradient; an integrability condition is needed before a convex potential can be inferred.
The criterion is pairwise on the entire convex set, not merely at a selected sample of points.

knowledge_statements.title: Subgradient Supporting-Affine Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite function on an open convex domain is convex exactly when every point has a global supporting affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x\in C\), define \[\partial f(x)=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n: f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\text{ for every }y\in C\}.\] Then \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in C\). Thus convexity is equivalent to the existence at every point of a globally supporting affine minorant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in C\), where each \(g\in\partial f(x)\) satisfies \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for all \(y\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-valued nonsmooth criterion on an open convex domain.

notation.meaning: Set of global supporting slopes of \(f\) at \(x\).
A subgradient at the base point.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Subgradient supporting-affine condition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open, nonempty, and convex, and let \(f:S\to\mathbb{R}\). Extend \(f\) by \(+\infty\) outside \(S\) when defining global subgradients.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth recognition for finite-valued functions on an open convex domain. Boundary subgradient existence is not asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x\in S\), a vector \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\) is a subgradient of \(f\) at \(x\) when
\[
f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\qquad\text{for every }y\in S.
\]
The set of all such vectors is
\[
\partial f(x):=\{g\in\mathbb{R}^n:f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\ \forall y\in S\}.
\]
The subgradient supporting-affine criterion is \(\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\) for every \(x\in S\). On an open convex domain, a finite-valued function is convex exactly when this criterion holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A subgradient at \(x\) is a slope whose affine function touches \(f\) at \(x\) and lies below \(f\) everywhere on the domain. The supporting-affine criterion requires at least one such slope at every point. For a finite-valued function on an open convex set, this pointwise existence condition is equivalent to convexity and does not require differentiability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The criterion is \(\forall x\in S:\partial f(x)\neq\varnothing\), where \(g\in\partial f(x)\) exactly when \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in S\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every point of the graph admits a nonvertical supporting hyperplane to the epigraph.
There exists a selection \(x\mapsto g_x\) such that \(f(y)-f(x)\geq\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\) for every ordered pair \((x,y)\in S^2\).
special_cases_latex: If \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\), then any convex subgradient there equals \(\nabla f(x)\).
At a global minimizer \(x_\star\), \(0\in\partial f(x_\star)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Each affine map \(y\mapsto f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) with \(g\in\partial f(x)\) is a global minorant.
The subdifferential \(\partial f(x)\) is a closed convex set, possibly with more than one element at a nonsmooth point.
boundary_notes: For convex functions, subgradients can fail to exist at boundary points of the effective domain.
Nonemptiness at only selected points is insufficient for this recognition criterion.

children.title: Second-Order Convexity Criteria
children.top_down_role: Recognition through Hessian, directional, and restricted-domain curvature.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order curvature certificate system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable. For \(x\in\Omega\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(I_{x,d}:=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:x+td\in\Omega\}\) and \(\varphi_{x,d}(t):=f(x+td)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional twice-differentiable recognition on an open convex domain. Restricted or lower-dimensional domains require relative-direction modifications.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The second-order convexity certificate is either of the equivalent conditions
\[
\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq0\qquad(\forall x\in\Omega),
\]
or
\[
\varphi_{x,d}''(t)=\langle\nabla^2 f(x+td)d,d\rangle\geq0
\quad(\forall x,d,\ t\in I_{x,d}).
\]
A twice-differentiable function is convex on \(\Omega\) exactly when this certificate holds. Positive definiteness at every point is sufficient for strict convexity, while the uniform bound \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq cI\) is equivalent to strong convexity with modulus \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Second-order recognition requires nonnegative curvature in every direction at every point. In matrix language, each Hessian must be positive semidefinite. In one-dimensional language, every restriction of the function to a feasible line must have nonnegative second derivative. On an open convex domain these conditions are equivalent to convexity. Positive-definite Hessians imply strict convexity, and a uniform eigenvalue lower bound characterizes strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The second-order certificate is \(\langle\nabla^2f(x)d,d\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), equivalently \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) everywhere.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every line restriction \(t\mapsto f(x+td)\) is convex on its feasible interval.
The smallest eigenvalue satisfies \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\geq0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\).
special_cases_latex: In one dimension, the criterion is \(f''(t)\geq0\) throughout an open interval.
For a quadratic function with symmetric Hessian \(Q\), the criterion reduces to \(Q\succeq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\) everywhere, then \(f\) is strictly convex.
If \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq cI\) everywhere for \(c>0\), then \(f\) is strongly convex with modulus \(c\).
boundary_notes: Pointwise positive definiteness is sufficient but not necessary for strict convexity.
On a nonopen or lower-dimensional set, ambient Hessian semidefiniteness need not be necessary.

notation.meaning: The interval of parameters for which the line through \(x\) in direction \(d\) stays in \(\Omega\).
The symmetric matrix or operator \(A\) is positive semidefinite.

knowledge_statements.title: Twice-Differentiable Hessian Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Existence of the Hessian everywhere is sufficient; continuity of the second derivatives is not required for the Hessian convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable. Then \[f\text{ is convex on }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\quad\forall x\in C.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp finite-dimensional Hessian criterion without continuity of the second derivatives.

knowledge_statements.title: Hessian Semidefiniteness Criterion
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable function on an open convex set is convex exactly when its Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point: \[\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2 f(x)v\geq0\text{ for every }v\in\mathbb{R}^n,\qquad x\in C.\] Convexity of the domain is essential for converting this pointwise curvature condition into a global convexity statement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical finite-dimensional criterion on an open convex set.

notation.meaning: Hessian matrix of second partial derivatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-semidefinite Hessian condition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable, with symmetric Hessian \(\nabla^2 f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical twice-differentiable Euclidean criterion on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The Hessian semidefiniteness condition is
\[
\forall x\in\Omega:\quad \nabla^2 f(x)\succeq0,
\]
meaning
\[
\forall x\in\Omega\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n:\quad
\langle\nabla^2f(x)d,d\rangle\geq0.
\]
For twice-differentiable \(f\) on an open convex set, this condition is equivalent to convexity of \(f\). The strict matrix condition \(\nabla^2f(x)\succ0\) everywhere is sufficient for strict convexity but is not necessary. The uniform condition \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq cI\) is equivalent to strong convexity with modulus \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hessian test requires the quadratic form generated by the Hessian to be nonnegative for every point and every direction. Equivalently, every Hessian is positive semidefinite. For a twice-differentiable function on an open convex domain, this is exactly the condition for convexity. Positive definiteness everywhere is a sufficient strictness condition, while a uniform positive lower eigenvalue bound characterizes strong convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The criterion is \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\), equivalently \(d^\top\nabla^2f(x)d\geq0\) for all \(x,d\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(\lambda_{\min}(\nabla^2f(x))\geq0\) for every \(x\in\Omega\).
Every directional curvature \(d^\top\nabla^2f(x)d\) is nonnegative.
special_cases_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^\top Qx+b^\top x+c\) with symmetric \(Q\), convexity is equivalent to \(Q\succeq0\).
For \(n=1\), the condition becomes \(f''(x)\geq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The lower bound \(\nabla^2f(x)\succeq cI\) yields a uniform curvature certificate.
A zero eigenvalue is compatible with convexity and may also be compatible with strict convexity.
boundary_notes: The ambient Hessian test is not necessary on arbitrary nonopen convex subsets.
Strict convexity does not require positive definiteness at every point; \(t\mapsto t^4\) is a standard boundary case.

notation.meaning: The smallest eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix \(A\).

children.title: Directional Second-Order Criteria
children.top_down_role: Recognition through curvature along feasible directions and lines.

knowledge_statements.title: Directional Second-Order Criteria
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Twice differentiable convexity is equivalent to nonnegative second directional curvature along every line through the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in C\) and \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(I_{x,v}=\{t\in\mathbb{R}:x+tv\in C\}\) and \(\phi_{x,v}(t)=f(x+tv)\). Then \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if every \(\phi_{x,v}\) is convex on \(I_{x,v}\), equivalently, \[D^2f(x)[v,v]=v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)v\geq0\] for all admissible \(x\) and \(v\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(D^2f(x)[v,v]\geq0\) for every \(x\in C\) and \(v\in\mathbb{R}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order recognition expressed through all line restrictions.

notation.meaning: Second directional derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) along \(v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative curvature along every feasible line
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be open and convex, let \(f:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}\) be twice differentiable, and for \(x\in\Omega\), \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), define \(I_{x,d}=\{t:x+td\in\Omega\}\) and \(\varphi_{x,d}(t)=f(x+td)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directional and line-restriction version of classical second-order recognition on an open convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The directional second-order condition is
\[
\forall x\in\Omega\ \forall d\in\mathbb{R}^n\ \forall t\in I_{x,d}:
\quad \varphi_{x,d}''(t)\geq0.
\]
Since
\[
\varphi_{x,d}''(t)=\langle\nabla^2f(x+td)d,d\rangle,
\]
the condition requires nonnegative curvature along every feasible line and every direction. It is equivalent to convexity of each line restriction \(\varphi_{x,d}\), and hence to convexity of \(f\) on \(\Omega\). A uniform directional bound \(\varphi_{x,d}''(t)\geq c\|d\|^2\) is the corresponding strong-convexity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Restrict the function to every line that remains in the domain. The directional second-order criterion requires every such one-dimensional function to have nonnegative second derivative throughout its feasible interval. This directional derivative equals the Hessian quadratic form in the chosen direction. Testing all feasible lines is equivalent to convexity on the open convex domain; a uniform positive lower bound gives strong convexity.
assumptions_latex: Each derivative is evaluated only for \(t\in I_{x,d}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\varphi_{x,d}''(t)=d^\top\nabla^2f(x+td)d\geq0\) for all feasible \((x,d,t)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Every restriction of \(f\) to a line intersected with \(\Omega\) is a convex univariate function.
For every \(z\in\Omega\) and \(d\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(d^\top\nabla^2f(z)d\geq0\).
special_cases_latex: It is enough to test unit directions because the quadratic form is homogeneous of degree two in \(d\).
In dimension one there is only the scalar condition \(f''\geq0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Testing all directions at a fixed point is equivalent to positive semidefiniteness of the Hessian at that point.
The uniform bound with \(c>0\) implies strict convexity.
boundary_notes: Testing only coordinate directions generally misses mixed-curvature directions.
A direction must be feasible in the domain; ambient directions are inappropriate for a lower-dimensional restriction.

notation.meaning: The restriction of \(f\) to the line through \(x\) in direction \(d\).

children.title: Restricted-Domain Curvature Tests
children.top_down_role: Curvature recognition on affine hulls, subspaces, and convex domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Curvature with Boundary Extension
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous function on a convex domain, nonnegative relative curvature throughout the relative interior is equivalent to convexity on the whole domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, set \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\) and \(L=A-A\), and suppose \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuous on \(C\) and twice differentiable relative to \(A\) on \(\operatorname{ri}C\). Then \[f\text{ is convex on }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad D^2f(x)[v,v]\geq0\quad\forall x\in\operatorname{ri}C,\ \forall v\in L.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is twice differentiable relative to \(\operatorname{aff}C\) on \(\operatorname{ri}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(D^2f(x)[v,v]\geq0\) for all \(x\in\operatorname{ri}C\) and \(v\in A-A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative Hessian recognition on an arbitrary convex domain, with continuity controlling values on its relative boundary.

notation.meaning: Direction space of the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Restricted-Domain Curvature Tests
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a relatively open convex domain, convexity requires nonnegative curvature only along directions in the domain's affine hull.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Only curvature tangent to the affine hull is relevant. Specifically, \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \[D^2f(x)[v,v]\geq0\qquad (x\in C,\ v\in L).\] If \(f\) is the restriction of a twice continuously differentiable ambient function, this becomes \(v^{\mathsf T}\nabla^2f(x)v\geq0\) for every \(v\in L\); curvature normal to \(A\) is immaterial.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and relatively open in its affine hull \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\).
\(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is twice continuously differentiable relative to \(A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if \(D^2f(x)[v,v]\geq0\) for every \(x\in C\) and \(v\in L\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative second-order test on a lower-dimensional convex domain.

notation.meaning: Linear space of feasible affine directions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Relative curvature test on a convex affine domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex, let \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\), and let \(V=A-A\) be its direction subspace. Assume \(f\) is twice differentiable on a relatively open convex neighborhood \(U\subseteq A\) containing \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional curvature recognition relative to an affine hull. Only directions tangent to the affine domain are tested.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The restricted-domain curvature condition is
\[
\langle \nabla_A^2f(x)d,d\rangle\geq0
\qquad(\forall x\in U,\ \forall d\in V),
\]
where \(\nabla_A^2f(x)\) is the Hessian of \(f|_A\) in the Euclidean structure of \(V\). Equivalently, for every affine line \(x+\mathbb{R}d\subseteq A\), the feasible restriction \(t\mapsto f(x+td)\) has nonnegative second derivative. This condition recognizes convexity relative to \(U\). Curvature in directions orthogonal to \(V\) is irrelevant to convexity of the restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a convex domain lies in a proper affine subspace, curvature must be tested only along directions parallel to that affine hull. The relative Hessian, or equivalently every feasible line restriction inside the affine hull, must have nonnegative quadratic form. Curvature normal to the domain does not affect convexity of the restricted function.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) is relatively open and convex in \(A=\operatorname{aff}C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relative criterion is \(d^\top\nabla_A^2f(x)d\geq0\) for all \(x\in U\) and all \(d\in V=A-A\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: After choosing \(x_0\in A\), the translated function \(h(v)=f(x_0+v)\) is convex on its open convex domain in \(V\) exactly when \(\nabla^2h(v)\succeq0\).
Every feasible line restriction within \(A\) is convex.
special_cases_latex: If \(A=\mathbb{R}^n\), the condition is the ordinary Hessian semidefiniteness test.
If \(C\) is contained in a line, only the second derivative along that line matters.
immediate_consequences_latex: An indefinite ambient Hessian can still induce a positive-semidefinite relative Hessian on \(V\).
Changing an extension of \(f|_A\) away from \(A\) does not change the relative criterion.
boundary_notes: Testing the full ambient Hessian is generally too strong for a lower-dimensional domain.
If \(C\) is not relatively open in \(A\), boundary values may require continuity or a separate limiting argument.

notation.meaning: The affine hull of the restricted domain.
The direction subspace parallel to the affine hull.
The Hessian of the restriction relative to \(A\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Applicability boundary of a convexity recognition test
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal{F}\) be a class of pairs \((C,f)\), and let a recognition test consist of a hypothesis predicate \(H(C,f)\) and a certificate predicate \(K(C,f)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes the boundary at which familiar first- or second-order tests cease to certify convexity because their domain, coverage, or regularity hypotheses fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The applicability region of a convexity test \((H,K)\) is
\[
\mathcal{A}_{H,K}:=\{(C,f)\in\mathcal{F}:H(C,f)\text{ holds and }[K(C,f)\Longleftrightarrow f\text{ is convex on }C]\}.
\]
Its recognition boundary is the complement \(\mathcal{F}\setminus\mathcal{A}_{H,K}\), partitioned into a hypothesis-failure region \(\{H\text{ false}\}\) and, if present, a coverage-failure region where the tested points or directions do not quantify over all objects required by \(K\). For the standard gradient and Hessian criteria, essential boundary variables include convexity of \(C\), differentiability on an open neighborhood, and complete pairwise or directional coverage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recognition test has an applicability region consisting of the function-domain pairs for which its hypotheses hold and its certificate is equivalent to convexity. The recognition boundary is everything outside that region. Typical causes are a nonconvex domain, a missing derivative, a nonopen lower-dimensional domain tested with an ambient Hessian, or checking only a restricted collection of points or directions.
assumptions_latex: A test is specified by explicit hypotheses \(H\) and a certificate \(K\).
Convexity is always understood relative to the stated domain \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{A}_{H,K}=\{(C,f):H(C,f)\wedge[K(C,f)\Longleftrightarrow\operatorname{Conv}_C(f)]\}\), and the recognition boundary is \(\mathcal{F}\setminus\mathcal{A}_{H,K}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A point lies beyond the test boundary when at least one required domain, regularity, or quantifier-coverage condition is absent.
For the ambient Hessian equivalence, openness and convexity of the domain and twice differentiability are part of the applicability region.
special_cases_latex: The gradient supporting-hyperplane test lies inside its applicability region when \(C\) is convex and \(f\) is differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(C\).
For a lower-dimensional \(C\), a relative Hessian test may be applicable even when the ambient Hessian equivalence is not.
immediate_consequences_latex: A certificate evaluated outside its applicability region cannot be promoted to a convexity equivalence without an additional argument.
The boundary definition separates failure of a theorem's hypotheses from actual nonconvexity of the function.
boundary_notes: Being outside a recognition test's applicability region does not imply that the function is nonconvex.
Different recognition tests have different applicability regions.

notation.meaning: The hypothesis predicate of a recognition test.
The mathematical certificate predicate of the test.
The applicability region of the test.

children.title: Nonconvex-Domain Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Failure of segment and local-to-global reasoning on nonconvex domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex-Domain Obstructions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A disconnected domain can support zero local curvature everywhere while global supporting inequalities between components fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function is smooth on the open set \(C\) and satisfies \(f''(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\). Nevertheless, taking \(x\in(1,2)\) and \(y\in(-2,-1)\) gives \[f(y)=0<1=f(x)+f'(x)(y-x).\] Thus the global supporting-affine inequality fails. Convexity of the domain, or an explicit restriction to segments contained in the domain, is indispensable in local-to-global recognition theorems.
assumptions_latex: \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is given by \(f(x)=0\) on \((-2,-1)\) and \(f(x)=1\) on \((1,2)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f''(x)=0\) throughout \(C\), the global supporting inequality fails for points in different components; hence local curvature does not imply a global first-order criterion on a nonconvex domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected-domain counterexample to local-to-global differential recognition.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Segment obstruction on a nonconvex domain
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). For \(x,y\in D\), write \([x,y]=\{(1-t)x+ty:t\in[0,1]\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain-level obstruction to ordinary convexity and to segment-based local-to-global recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The segment-obstruction set of \(D\) is
\[
\mathcal{O}(D):=\{(x,y,t)\in D\times D\times(0,1):(1-t)x+ty\notin D\}.
\]
The domain has a nonconvex-domain obstruction exactly when \(\mathcal{O}(D)\neq\varnothing\), equivalently when \(D\) is not convex. For every obstructed triple, the usual convexity inequality
\[
f((1-t)x+ty)\leq(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)
\]
is not even evaluable as an inequality for \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). Consequently, line-restriction and local-to-global arguments apply only within convex components or to pairs whose entire segment remains in \(D\), unless \(f\) and its domain are extended.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonconvex-domain obstruction is a pair of domain points together with an intermediate weight whose convex combination leaves the domain. Such an obstruction exists exactly when the domain is nonconvex. At that triple, the ordinary convexity inequality cannot be evaluated because the function has no value at the intermediate point. Segment-based recognition therefore cannot compare all pairs without restricting the domain or extending the function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal{O}(D)\neq\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow D\) is nonconvex, and every \((x,y,t)\in\mathcal{O}(D)\) blocks evaluation of the ordinary convexity inequality.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(D\) is convex if and only if \(\mathcal{O}(D)=\varnothing\).
The obstruction is equivalently the existence of \(x,y\in D\) with \([x,y]\nsubseteq D\).
special_cases_latex: If \(D\) is a union of two disjoint convex sets, cross-component pairs ordinarily generate obstructions.
A convex subset \(C\subseteq D\) has no internal segment obstruction even when \(D\) itself is nonconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Convexity can be assessed separately on convex subsets of \(D\), but those local assessments do not impose cross-subset inequalities.
A Hessian or gradient condition checked locally on disconnected pieces does not by itself supply a global convex-function structure on \(D\).
boundary_notes: Some authors study functions convex on every segment contained in a nonconvex domain; that is a restricted notion and is not ordinary convexity on a convex domain.
Extending \(f\) by \(+\infty\) does not yield a convex extended-real function unless its effective domain becomes convex.

notation.meaning: The set of triples witnessing failure of segment closure in \(D\).

knowledge_statements.title: Missing-Derivative Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex absolute-value function is not differentiable at zero, so gradient and Hessian tests must be replaced by subgradient criteria.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=|x|\) is convex on \(\mathbb{R}\), but \(f'(0)\) and \(f''(0)\) do not exist. Consequently, gradient monotonicity and Hessian semidefiniteness cannot be imposed pointwise on the whole domain. Nonsmooth recognition instead uses \[\partial f(0)=[-1,1],\] whose elements generate supporting affine minorants at the nondifferentiable point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The function \(f\) is convex but has neither a gradient nor a classical Hessian at \(0\), so classical derivative criteria are inapplicable there.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical nonsmooth boundary of gradient and Hessian tests.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First- and second-derivative inapplicability sets
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\). Derivatives are understood only at points having an appropriate open neighborhood on which \(f\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth boundary of gradient- and Hessian-based convexity recognition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the first- and second-derivative failure sets by
\[
N_1(f;C):=\{x\in C:f\text{ is not differentiable at }x\},
\]
\[
N_2(f;C):=\{x\in C:f\text{ is not twice differentiable at }x\}.
\]
The gradient recognition regime applies globally only when \(N_1(f;C)=\varnothing\) and differentiability holds on an open neighborhood of \(C\). The classical Hessian regime applies globally only when \(N_2(f;C)=\varnothing\) under the corresponding open-domain hypothesis. When these sets are nonempty, convexity remains meaningful, but the missing gradient or Hessian cannot be used at those points; subgradient or directional formulations are the appropriate replacements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The missing-gradient set contains points where the function is not differentiable, and the missing-Hessian set contains points where it is not twice differentiable. A global gradient test requires the first set to be empty, while a global classical Hessian test requires the second set to be empty, together with the relevant open-domain assumptions. Convexity itself does not require either derivative, so nonsmooth points call for subgradients or directional derivatives rather than rejection of convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Gradient and Hessian criteria are inapplicable respectively on \(N_1(f;C)\) and \(N_2(f;C)\); these failures do not imply nonconvexity.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(x\in N_1(f;C)\) when no single linear map gives the first-order approximation required by differentiability at \(x\).
\(x\in N_2(f;C)\) when the classical Hessian needed by the second-order criterion is undefined at \(x\).
special_cases_latex: For \(f(t)=|t|\), \(0\in N_1(f;\mathbb{R})\), although \(f\) is convex.
A differentiable convex function can still belong to the missing-Hessian regime at points where it is not twice differentiable.
immediate_consequences_latex: At a convex nonsmooth point, \(\partial f(x)\) may replace the missing gradient.
For convex functions, one-sided directional derivatives exist throughout the interior of the effective domain even when the gradient does not.
boundary_notes: Almost-everywhere differentiability does not justify a gradient inequality at exceptional points.
A Hessian condition holding wherever the Hessian exists needs additional regularity before it becomes a global convexity criterion.

notation.meaning: The set of points at which the gradient regime fails.
The set of points at which the classical Hessian regime fails.

children.title: Restricted Convexity-Test Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Insufficient evidence confined to restricted points, directions, or boundary regions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coverage boundary for restricted convexity tests
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be nonempty and convex. Let \(P\subseteq C\times C\) be a set of tested ordered pairs and let \(Q\subseteq C\times\mathbb{R}^n\) be a set of tested point-direction pairs.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formalizes insufficiency caused by checking supporting inequalities or curvature only on restricted points, directions, or boundary regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pairwise first-order test has complete coverage when \(P=C\times C\); otherwise its coverage gap is
\[
G_P:=(C\times C)\setminus P.
\]
A directional second-order test has complete coverage when, for every \(x\in C\), it includes every direction required by the relevant tangent or affine-hull space \(V_x\); its gap is
\[
G_Q:=\{(x,d):x\in C,\ d\in V_x\}\setminus Q.
\]
The restricted convexity-test failure boundary is reached when \(G_P\neq\varnothing\) or \(G_Q\neq\varnothing\): satisfaction of the certificate on \(P\) or \(Q\) alone is then a restricted certificate, not the universally quantified convexity criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A first-order convexity test is fully covering only when it checks every ordered pair of points required by the criterion. A directional curvature test is fully covering only when it checks every required feasible direction at every point. Any omitted pair or direction forms a coverage gap. Passing a test on a set with a nonempty gap is only restricted evidence and is not, by itself, the standard global convexity certificate.
assumptions_latex: The full first- or second-order criterion being approximated is specified.
\(V_x\) is the ambient direction space on an open domain or the appropriate relative tangent space on a restricted domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A restricted test crosses its failure boundary when \(G_P\neq\varnothing\) or \(G_Q\neq\varnothing\); passing such a test does not equal the full universally quantified certificate.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Complete first-order coverage means every inequality \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g_x,y-x\rangle\) required by the criterion is tested.
Complete Hessian coverage means the quadratic form is nonnegative for every required direction, not merely for a spanning list of directions.
special_cases_latex: Testing only coordinate directions can miss a negative quadratic-form direction with mixed coordinates.
Testing only interior points does not automatically control arbitrary boundary values without a continuity or closure argument.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonempty coverage gap identifies exactly which universal quantifiers remain uncertified.
Additional structure may close a coverage gap, but that structure must be stated as a separate hypothesis.
boundary_notes: Testing a basis of directions is insufficient for a general quadratic inequality; all directions or an equivalent matrix certificate are required.
Dense-set testing can be sufficient under continuity, but density alone is not the standard certificate.

notation.meaning: The omitted ordered point pairs in a first-order test.
The omitted feasible point-direction pairs in a curvature test.

knowledge_statements.title: Incomplete Local Tests
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive curvature on a tested subset does not certify convexity when an untested region contains negative curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Direct differentiation yields \(f''(x)=12x^2-2\), so \(f''(x)>0\) for every \(x\in S\). However, \(f''(0)=-2<0\). Equivalently, since \(f(-1/2)=f(1/2)=-3/16\), one has \[f(0)=0>\frac{f(-1/2)+f(1/2)}{2}=-\frac{3}{16},\] which violates midpoint convexity. Hence curvature verified only on \(S\) cannot certify global convexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f''(x)>0\) on \(S\), the function is not convex on \(\mathbb{R}\); therefore a curvature test that omits part of the domain is incomplete.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A positive-curvature test on an incomplete region misses nonconvexity elsewhere.

notation.meaning: Subset on which curvature is inspected.
