knowledge_statements.title: Separate Convexity Does Not Imply Joint Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The bilinear function xy is convex in each coordinate separately but is not jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(h(x,y)=xy\). Every slice obtained by fixing one coordinate is affine and hence convex. Nevertheless, \(h\) is not jointly convex, since \(h(1,-1)=h(-1,1)=-1\) whereas \(h(0,0)=0>-1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every one-coordinate slice is convex, but \(h\) is not jointly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Converse failure for convexity of all one-coordinate slices.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinate Slices
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing any subset of coordinates of a convex function leaves a convex function of the remaining coordinates, provided the resulting slice meets the original domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: After identifying \(\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(\mathbb{R}^{J}\times\mathbb{R}^{J^c}\), define \(g:\mathbb{R}^{J}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(g(u)=f(u,\bar x_{J^c})\). The embedding \(u\mapsto(u,\bar x_{J^c})\) is affine, so \(g\) is convex. Its effective domain is \[\operatorname{dom}g=\{u\in\mathbb{R}^{J}:(u,\bar x_{J^c})\in\operatorname{dom}f\}.\] Therefore the slice is proper exactly when the corresponding coordinate-affine set meets \(\operatorname{dom}f\).
assumptions_latex: \(J\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and coordinates outside \(J\) are fixed at \(\bar x_{J^c}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coordinate slice \(u\mapsto f(u,\bar x_{J^c})\) is convex on its induced domain.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity on coordinate slices formed by fixing complementary variables.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Interior Qualification for Affine Domain Intersections
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an affine set meets the relative interior of a convex domain, restriction commutes with relative interior and closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a finite-dimensional real vector space and let \(M\) be affine. If \(M\cap\operatorname{ri}C\ne\varnothing\), then \[\operatorname{ri}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{ri}C\cap M,\qquad \operatorname{cl}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{cl}C\cap M.\] Without this relative-interior intersection hypothesis, neither identity is guaranteed.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is nonempty and convex in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ri}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{ri}C\cap M\) and \(\operatorname{cl}(C\cap M)=\operatorname{cl}C\cap M\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional relative-interior and closure calculus for a qualified affine restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: Domain-Intersection Effects
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine restriction intersects the effective domain with the affine set; convexity survives, but properness is lost exactly when that intersection is empty.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the restriction \(g=f|_M\), one has \[\operatorname{dom}g=M\cap\operatorname{dom}f.\] This intersection is convex because both \(M\) and \(\operatorname{dom}f\) are convex. Since \(f\) never takes \(-\infty\), the restricted function \(g\) is proper if and only if \(M\cap\operatorname{dom}f\neq\varnothing\). Thus affine restriction preserves convexity but can destroy properness when the affine set misses the effective domain; it can also reduce the domain's affine dimension.
assumptions_latex: \(f:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is a proper convex function on a real vector space.
\(M\subseteq X\) is a nonempty affine set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The restricted domain is \(\operatorname{dom}(f|_M)=M\cap\operatorname{dom}f\), and restriction is proper exactly when this intersection is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effective-domain and properness effects caused by affine restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Below Fibers Can Produce Minus Infinity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper source function may yield minus infinity after fiber minimization if a fiber is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A proper convex source function need not have a proper linear-image value function: if \(F\) is unbounded below on a nonempty fiber \(A^{-1}(y)\), then \(g(y)=-\infty\). For example, with \(A:\mathbb{R}\to\{0\}\) the zero map and \(F(x)=x\), one has \(g(0)=-\infty\). Thus exclusion of unbounded-below fibers is necessary when \(g\) is required to take values only in \(( -\infty,+\infty]\).
assumptions_latex: Some nonempty fiber is unbounded below for \(F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The corresponding value is \(-\infty\), so the value function is not proper in the usual extended-real convex class.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Codomain and properness boundary for fiber infima.

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible Image, Domain, and Epigraph Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasible parameters form the image of the original domain; strict epigraph points always lift, while finite boundary points lift exactly at attained fiber minima.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and define \(g(y)=\inf\{F(x):Ax=y\}\). The set of parameters having a feasible finite-valued point is \(A(\operatorname{dom}F)\). If no such fiber is unbounded below, then \(\operatorname{dom}g=A(\operatorname{dom}F)\). Every strict epigraph point \((y,t)\) with \(g(y)<t\) equals \((Ax,t)\) for some \((x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}F\), while a finite boundary point \((y,g(y))\) has such a lift exactly when the fiber infimum is attained. Consequently \((A\times\operatorname{id})(\operatorname{epi}F)=\operatorname{epi}g\) exactly when every finite fiber value is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is represented by \(A(\operatorname{dom}F)\), and epigraph-image equality is equivalent to attainment of every finite fiber value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Image representation distinguishing feasibility, finite values, and attained boundary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Inf-Compactness Ensures Closed Attained Fiber Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform level-boundedness over compact parameter sets makes fiber minima attained and the value function proper and closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X,Y\) be finite-dimensional, let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper lower-semicontinuous convex, and let \(A:X\to Y\) be linear. Suppose that for every compact \(K\subseteq Y\) and every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the set \[\{x\in X:Ax\in K,\ F(x)\leq\alpha\}\] is compact. Then \(g(y)=\inf\{F(x):Ax=y\}\) is a proper lower-semicontinuous convex function, and every finite value \(g(y)\) is attained.
assumptions_latex: The displayed parameterized sublevel sets are compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is proper lower-semicontinuous convex and attains every finite value.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional sufficient condition for lower semicontinuity and attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Image Value Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimum of a convex function over each fiber of a linear map is a convex value function, without guaranteeing attainment or lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(y\in Y\), define \[g(y)=\inf\{f(x):x\in C,\ Ax=y\},\qquad \inf\varnothing=+\infty.\] Then, for all \(y_0,y_1\in Y\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[g((1-\lambda)y_0+\lambda y_1)\leq (1-\lambda)g(y_0)+\lambda g(y_1).\] Thus optimization over the affine fibers of a linear mapping preserves convexity, although the infimum need not be attained and \(g\) need not be lower semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, \(C\subseteq X\) is convex, and \(A:X\to Y\) is linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is convex on \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional algebraic convexity; attainment and lower semicontinuity are not asserted.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Value function over fibers of a linear mapping
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(A:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is linear and \(g:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex analysis; values are obtained by infimizing over equality-constrained linear fibers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The linear image of \(g\) under \(A\) is \[(Ag)(x):=\inf\{g(y):Ay=x\},\qquad \inf\varnothing:=+\infty.\] Its effective domain is \(A(\operatorname{dom}g)\) when all nonempty fibers have finite infimum. If \(g\) is convex and bounded below on every fiber \(A^{-1}(x)\), then \(Ag\) is convex and nowhere equals \(-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear-image value function assigns to each target point the infimum of the original function over all points mapped to that target. Empty fibers have value positive infinity. Convexity passes to this value function when the original function is convex and its value is bounded below on every fiber.
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(g\) is bounded below on \(\{y:Ay=x\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ag\) is an extended-real convex function on \(\mathbb{R}^{n}\), with \(\operatorname{dom}(Ag)=A(\operatorname{dom}g)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an indicator \(g=\delta_C\), \(Ag=\delta_{A(C)}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) is invertible, \((Ag)(x)=g(A^{-1}x)\).
If \(A(x,y)=x\), then \((Ag)(x)=\inf_y g(x,y)\), the marginal function.
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear images of convex sets are convex through the indicator-function specialization.
Equality-constrained optimal values inherit convexity in their right-hand side.
boundary_notes: The infimum need not be attained.
Closedness is not guaranteed by convexity alone under a linear image.
Without fiberwise lower boundedness, the value may equal \(-\infty\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Domain and Epigraph of a Linear-Image Value Function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact image representation, including the distinction between strict epigraph points and attained boundary points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and \(A:X\to Y\) be linear, and define \(g(y)=\inf\{F(x):Ax=y\}\). For every \(y\) with \(g(y)>-\infty\), \(g(y)<t\) holds exactly when there exists \(x\) with \(Ax=y\) and \(F(x)<t\). Moreover, \[(y,g(y))\in\{(Ax,t):(x,t)\in\operatorname{epi}F\}\] exactly when the fiber infimum is attained. Thus the linear image of \(\operatorname{epi}F\) contains every strict epigraph point of \(g\), and it equals \(\operatorname{epi}g\) precisely when every finite fiber value is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The epigraph of a fiber value function is the linear image of the original epigraph except that an unattained finite infimum can omit its boundary point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strict epigraph points always lift through \((x,t)\mapsto(Ax,t)\), and a finite boundary point lifts exactly when its fiber infimum is attained.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity of four infimal combination constructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The operation (f_i\lambda_i) is retained with the source's previously established functional-scaling convention, including its interpretation at \lambda_i=0. The last infimum ranges over every convex-combination representation of x.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f_1,\ldots,f_m be proper convex functions on \mathbb{R}^n. Then the following functions are convex:\quad f(x)=\inf_{x_1+\cdots+x_m=x}\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i(x_i),\quad g(x)=\inf_{\substack{\lambda_i\ge 0\\\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1}}\sum_{i=1}^m(f_i\lambda_i)(x),\quad h(x)=\inf_{\substack{\lambda_i\ge 0\\\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1}}\max_{1\le i\le m}(f_i\lambda_i)(x),\quad k(x)=\inf_{\substack{\lambda_i\ge 0,\ \sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i=1\\x=\sum_{i=1}^m\lambda_i x_i}}\max_{1\le i\le m}\lambda_i f_i(x_i).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For finitely many proper convex functions, four value-function constructions remain convex: minimizing a maximum over additive decompositions; minimizing a sum or maximum of the source-defined scaled-function terms over simplex weights; and minimizing a weighted maximum over convex-combination representations. The formulas allow zero weights and therefore depend on the source's scaling convention at zero.
assumptions_latex: f_i\text{ is a proper convex function on }\mathbb{R}^n\text{ for }i=1,\ldots,m
(f_i\lambda_i)\text{ is interpreted using the source's functional-scaling convention, including }\lambda_i=0
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f,\ g,\ h,\text{ and }k\text{ defined above are convex functions on }\mathbb{R}^n.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex composition calculus
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(h:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\) and \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k):C\to\mathbb{R}^{k}\), where \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth finite-dimensional composition; curvature propagation is controlled by outer convexity and coordinatewise monotonicity on the relevant extended domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The composition is \[F(x):=(h\circ g)(x)=h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_k(x)),\qquad\operatorname{dom}F=\{x\in C:g(x)\in\operatorname{dom}h\}.\] A convex composition regime is specified by a convex outer function \(h\) and, for each coordinate, either: \(h\) is nondecreasing in that coordinate and \(g_i\) is convex; or \(h\) is nonincreasing in that coordinate and \(g_i\) is concave. Under the compatible domain condition, \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition calculus determines the curvature of a composite from the outer function's curvature and monotonicity together with each inner component's curvature. Increasing coordinates accept convex inner functions, while decreasing coordinates accept concave inner functions. The composite domain must also be convex.
assumptions_latex: For every coordinate \(i\), the extended-value outer function has a fixed monotonicity direction compatible with the curvature of \(g_i\).
\(\operatorname{dom}F\) is nonempty and the extended-domain monotonicity condition makes it convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=h\circ g\) is convex on \(\operatorname{dom}F\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With sign vector \(s_i\in\{+1,-1\}\), require \(h\) to be nondecreasing in \(s_i z_i\) and \(s_i g_i\) to be convex.
The scalar rule is recovered when \(k=1\).
special_cases_latex: Affine inner components require no monotonicity restriction because they are both convex and concave.
A coordinatewise nondecreasing convex outer function composed with convex inner functions is convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Many norm, maximum, and log-sum-exp constructions follow from the vector rule.
Domain compatibility is part of the calculus, not an optional regularity condition.
boundary_notes: Outer convexity without compatible monotonicity does not generally preserve convexity.
Monotonicity merely on a truncated declared domain can be insufficient if the extended-value domain condition fails.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Scalar monotone composition regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(g:C\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), \(h:I\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\), and \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\), \(I\subseteq\mathbb{R}\) are convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth scalar compositions in finite dimensions; both increasing and decreasing outer regimes are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[F(x):=h(g(x)),\qquad \operatorname{dom}F=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}g:g(x)\in\operatorname{dom}h\}.\] The scalar monotone composition rule has two convex regimes: (i) \(h\) is convex and nondecreasing while \(g\) is convex; or (ii) \(h\) is convex and nonincreasing while \(g\) is concave. With the corresponding extended-domain monotonicity condition, \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A scalar monotone composition applies a one-variable outer function to a scalar inner function. A convex increasing outer function preserves convex inner curvature, while a convex decreasing outer function reverses the required inner curvature to concavity. Domain compatibility is required in both regimes.
assumptions_latex: Either \(h\) is nondecreasing and \(g\) is convex, or \(h\) is nonincreasing and \(g\) is concave.
The monotonicity holds for the relevant extended-value extension, or on an interval containing every comparison value used by the composition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=h\circ g\) is convex on its effective domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Regime (ii) is regime (i) applied after replacing \(g\) by \(-g\) and \(h(t)\) by \(h(-t)\).
For differentiable functions, the compatible signs are \(h''\geq0\) and \(h'g''\geq0\).
special_cases_latex: If \(h\) is affine, either inner curvature may be handled according to the sign of its slope.
If \(g\) is affine, convexity of \(h\) alone suffices.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(g\) is convex, then \(\exp(g)\) is convex.
If \(g>0\) is concave, then \(1/g\) is convex.
boundary_notes: The rule is sufficient, not necessary.
Failure of the outer-domain monotonicity condition can make the composite domain nonconvex.

knowledge_statements.title: Nondecreasing Outer-Function Regime
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex nondecreasing outer function composed with a convex scalar inner function is convex, provided all inner values lie in the outer domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(F(x)=\phi(f(x))\). For every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), convexity of \(f\), monotonicity of \(\phi\), and convexity of \(\phi\) give the valid propagation pattern summarized by \[F((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\leq(1-\lambda)F(x)+\lambda F(y).\] Hence a convex nondecreasing outer function preserves the convex curvature of its scalar inner function.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and \(f:C\to I\) is convex, where \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) is an interval.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise monotone vector composition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n}\) is convex, \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k):C\to\mathbb{R}^{k}\), and \(h:\mathbb{R}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth vector composition with coordinate-dependent curvature and monotonicity directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[F(x):=h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_k(x)),\qquad \operatorname{dom}F=\{x\in C:g(x)\in\operatorname{dom}h\}.\] Suppose \(h\) is convex. Partition \(\{1,\ldots,k\}=I_{+}\cup I_{-}\). If the extended-value extension of \(h\) is nondecreasing in each coordinate \(i\in I_{+}\) and nonincreasing in each coordinate \(i\in I_{-}\), while \(g_i\) is convex for \(i\in I_{+}\) and concave for \(i\in I_{-}\), then \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vector composition applies a multivariate convex outer function to several scalar inner functions. Each outer coordinate has its own monotonicity direction. Increasing coordinates require convex inner functions, and decreasing coordinates require concave inner functions. Under the compatible extended-domain condition, the resulting scalar function is convex.
assumptions_latex: \(I_{+}\) and \(I_{-}\) form a partition of the coordinate indices.
For \(i\in I_{+}\), \(h\) is coordinatewise nondecreasing and \(g_i\) is convex.
For \(i\in I_{-}\), \(h\) is coordinatewise nonincreasing and \(g_i\) is concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=h(g_1,\ldots,g_k)\) is convex on its effective domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(s_i=1\) on \(I_{+}\) and \(s_i=-1\) on \(I_{-}\), require \(s_i g_i\) convex and \(h\) nondecreasing in the transformed coordinate \(s_i z_i\).
If every coordinate is increasing, \(I_{-}=\varnothing\) and all \(g_i\) are convex.
special_cases_latex: The maximum outer function gives pointwise maxima of convex functions.
The log-sum-exp outer function composed with convex components is convex.
Affine inner components may be assigned either direction.
immediate_consequences_latex: Mixed convex and concave inner components can coexist when the outer monotonicities are compatible.
The scalar monotone composition rule is the case \(k=1\).
boundary_notes: Convexity of \(h\) alone does not control nonlinear inner components.
Coordinatewise monotonicity must hold on the relevant extended domain or a rigorously controlled attainable region.

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Monotonicity Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly convex outer function preserves convexity when each nonaffine argument coordinate has the appropriate monotonicity and inner curvature, while affine coordinates need no monotonicity condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(F(x)=h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_m(x))\). Then, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[F((1-\lambda)x+\lambda y)\leq(1-\lambda)F(x)+\lambda F(y).\] Hence \(F\) is convex on \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space, \(m\in\mathbb N\), and \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):C\to\mathbb R^m\).

The index set \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) is partitioned into \(P\), \(N\), and \(A\). For \(i\in P\), \(h\) is nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is convex; for \(i\in N\), \(h\) is nonincreasing in coordinate \(i\) and \(g_i\) is concave; for \(i\in A\), \(g_i\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\circ g\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard vector composition rule on the full argument space, with an explicit curvature–monotonicity assignment for every coordinate.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinatewise monotonicity regimes for vector composition
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^k\), let \(h:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and partition \(\{1,\ldots,k\}=I_+\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_-\mathbin{\dot\cup}I_0\). The three index sets designate nondecreasing, nonincreasing, and unrestricted argument slots.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real convex composition; monotonicity is imposed only along comparisons that remain in the effective domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) has coordinatewise monotonicity regime \((I_+,I_-,I_0)\) on \(D\) when, for every \(u,v\in D\) that agree outside one coordinate \(i\), \(u_i\le v_i\) implies \(h(u)\le h(v)\) if \(i\in I_+\), and \(u_i\le v_i\) implies \(h(u)\ge h(v)\) if \(i\in I_-\); no order condition is imposed for \(i\in I_0\). Equivalently, define \(u\preceq_I v\) by \(u_i\le v_i\) for \(i\in I_+\), \(u_i\ge v_i\) for \(i\in I_-\), and \(u_i=v_i\) for \(i\in I_0\). Then the regime condition is \(u\preceq_I v\Rightarrow h(u)\le h(v)\) for all \(u,v\in D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function has regime \((I_+,I_-,I_0)\) if it is nondecreasing in each coordinate indexed by \(I_+\), nonincreasing in each coordinate indexed by \(I_-\), and unrestricted in coordinates indexed by \(I_0\), with all comparisons taken inside its domain. Equivalently, it is order preserving for the mixed coordinate order \(\preceq_I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[u\preceq_I v\quad\Longrightarrow\quad h(u)\le h(v).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: When \(h\) is differentiable on an open convex domain, the regime is equivalent to \(\partial_i h(z)\ge0\) for \(i\in I_+\) and \(\partial_i h(z)\le0\) for \(i\in I_-\), for every \(z\in D\).
For convex extended-value composition rules, the relevant condition is monotonicity of the extended-value extension of \(h\), not merely monotonicity on a non-order-complete displayed domain.
special_cases_latex: If \(I_+=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), the regime is ordinary coordinatewise nondecreasing monotonicity.
If \(I_-=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), the regime is ordinary coordinatewise nonincreasing monotonicity.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(h\) is convex with this regime, then \(x\mapsto h(g_1(x),\ldots,g_k(x))\) satisfies the standard convex-composition certificate when each \(g_i\) is convex for \(i\in I_+\), concave for \(i\in I_-\), and affine for \(i\in I_0\), subject to domain compatibility.
boundary_notes: Coordinatewise monotonicity is weaker than monotonicity for arbitrary partial orders not generated by the designated coordinate signs.
Failure of this regime invalidates the stated composition certificate but does not by itself prove that a particular composition is nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Sets of nondecreasing, nonincreasing, and unrestricted coordinates.
Mixed coordinate order determined by the regime partition.

\(g_i\) is affine. Every nonaffine slot \(j\neq i\) satisfies the appropriate coordinatewise curvature–monotonicity condition: convex with nondecreasing, or concave with nonincreasing.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Affine slots in a vector composition certificate
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k):C\to\mathbb R^k\), and let \(h:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), where \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^k\) is convex and \(g(C)\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional convex composition with affine inner components; the definition concerns individual argument slots rather than joint affinity of the whole vector map.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An index \(i\in\{1,
\ldots,k\}\) is an affine argument slot of the composition \(h\circ g\) on \(C\) when there exist \(a_i\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b_i\in\mathbb R\) such that \(g_i(x)=a_i^Tx+b_i\) for every \(x\in C\). In a convex vector-composition certificate, no coordinatewise monotonicity of \(h\) is required in such a slot: affinity gives both \(g_i(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)=\theta g_i(x)+(1-\theta)g_i(y)\) and simultaneous convexity and concavity of \(g_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The \(i\)-th argument is an affine slot when its inner component is \(g_i(x)=a_i^Tx+b_i\) throughout the convex input set. Because this component preserves convex combinations exactly and is both convex and concave, a convex outer function need not have a prescribed monotonicity direction in that coordinate for the standard composition rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[g_i(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)=\theta g_i(x)+(1-\theta)g_i(y),\qquad x,y\in C,\ \theta\in[0,1].\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A slot is affine precisely when both \(g_i\) and \(-g_i\) are convex on \(C\).
For every segment contained in \(C\), the restriction of \(g_i\) to that segment is affine in the segment parameter.
special_cases_latex: A constant component \(g_i(x)=b_i\) is an affine argument slot with \(a_i=0\).
If every component is affine, then \(g(x)=Ax+b\) and convexity of \(h\) alone makes \(h(Ax+b)\) convex on its natural domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(h\) is convex, the remaining nonaffine components obey the appropriate curvature–monotonicity rules, and \(g(C)\subseteq D\), then affine slots introduce no additional directional monotonicity requirement.
boundary_notes: A component that is merely separately affine in several blocks need not be jointly affine in all variables.
Domain compatibility remains necessary: the natural domain \(\{x\in C:g(x)\in D\}\) must be used.

knowledge_statements.title: Separate Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is separately convex when each one-coordinate slice is convex after all other coordinates are fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\), where each \(C_i\) is convex. A function \(h:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is separately convex if, for every \(i\) and every fixed choice \(u_j\in C_j\) for \(j\ne i\), the slice \[t\mapsto h(u_1,\ldots,u_{i-1},t,u_{i+1},\ldots,u_m)\] is convex on \(C_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate convexity is convexity of every one-coordinate slice of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition through convexity of every one-coordinate slice on a product convex domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Convexity Implies Separate Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every jointly convex function is separately convex, but separate convexity is strictly weaker.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h:C_1\times\cdots\times C_m\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is jointly convex, then \(h\) is separately convex. The converse fails, as shown by the seed example \(h(u,v)=uv\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h\) is separately convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hierarchy between joint convexity and coordinate-slice convexity on product convex domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint versus Separate Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The separately affine function uv is not jointly convex, and composing it with x and −x gives the nonconvex function −x².
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h(u,v)=uv\) is affine, hence convex, in either variable when the other variable is fixed, but it is not jointly convex. For the affine inner functions \(g_1(x)=x\) and \(g_2(x)=-x\), \[h(g_1(x),g_2(x))=-x^2,\] which is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: \(g_1,g_2:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) are defined by \(g_1(x)=x\) and \(g_2(x)=-x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Separate convexity of \(h\) does not imply convexity of \(h(g_1,g_2)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete counterexample showing that separate convexity cannot replace joint convexity in the general vector-composition rule.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

children.title: Composition Failure Regimes
children.top_down_role: Curvature mismatch, nonmonotonicity, and hidden-domain obstructions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Failure regimes for curvature-based composition certificates
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_k):C\to\mathbb R^k\), let \(h:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and define \(f=h\circ g\) on \(F=\{x\in C:g(x)\in D\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition classifies failure of a standard sufficient convexity certificate, not necessarily failure of convexity of the resulting function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The composition data \((h,g,C,D)\) are in a composition-failure regime when at least one of the following holds: \(F\) is not convex; \(h\) lacks the required convexity or concavity on the attainable region; some nonaffine inner component has curvature opposite to the monotonicity direction required of its outer slot; the necessary monotonicity holds only on a displayed domain but fails for the relevant extended-value extension; or the attainable set \(g(F)\) is not known well enough to certify the preceding properties on a convex order-stable set containing it. Formally, relative to a proposed certificate \(\mathcal C\), the failure set is \(\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}=\{(h,g,C,D):\text{at least one predicate in }\mathcal C\text{ is false or uncertified}\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A composition-failure regime is a set of outer and inner functions for which a proposed curvature-composition certificate has a false or uncertified premise. Typical causes are a nonconvex natural domain, an outer-curvature failure, a curvature–monotonicity mismatch, extended-domain monotonicity failure, or inability to control the attainable range. Membership means the certificate cannot establish convexity; it does not assert that the composition itself is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}=\bigcup_{P\in\mathcal C}\{(h,g,C,D):P\text{ is false or uncertified}\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: A composition lies outside the certificate's validity region exactly when the conjunction of its domain, curvature, and monotonicity predicates is not established.
For extended-real compositions, failure of convexity of the natural domain \(F\) is itself sufficient to place the data in the failure regime.
special_cases_latex: For scalar \(h\circ g\), convex \(g\) paired with a convex but decreasing outer function is a curvature–monotonicity mismatch unless additional structure is available.
If \(h\) is constant on a disconnected displayed domain, monotonicity there does not repair nonconvexity of the natural composition domain.
immediate_consequences_latex: A sound verifier must return an uncertified status whenever the data belong to \(\mathfrak F_{\mathcal C}\); it may not infer nonconvexity without an independent violation or counterexample.
boundary_notes: The listed predicates are sufficient-rule boundaries and are not necessary conditions for convexity in every structured example.
Accidental cancellation can make a composition convex even when the generic certificate fails.

children.title: Curvature–Monotonicity Mismatch
children.top_down_role: Compositions outside valid curvature propagation patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Curvature Balance for Scalar Compositions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Hessian chain rule gives the exact smooth curvature balance; a negative outer derivative on the attained range can reverse positive inner curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex, let \(f\in C^2(C)\), and let \(\phi\in C^2(I)\) on an open interval \(I\supset f(C)\). Then
\[
\nabla^2(\phi\circ f)(x)=\phi''(f(x))\nabla f(x)\nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}+\phi'(f(x))\nabla^2f(x).
\]
Consequently, \(\phi\circ f\) is convex on \(C\) if and only if this matrix is positive semidefinite for every \(x\in C\).
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\in C^2(I)\) for an open interval \(I\supset f(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(\phi\circ f\) is convex exactly when \(\phi''(f)
abla f
abla f^{\mathsf T}+\phi'(f)
abla^2f\succeq0\) throughout \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-differentiable scalar compositions on an open convex Euclidean domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature–Monotonicity Mismatch
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex functions x²−1 and t² have the nonconvex composite (x²−1)² because the outer function decreases on part of the attainable inner range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Both \(f\) and \(\phi\) are convex, and \(f(\mathbb R)=[-1,+\infty)\), where \(\phi\) is not nondecreasing. Their composite is \[F(x)=(x^2-1)^2.\] It is not convex on \(\mathbb R\); for example, \[F(0)=1>\frac{F(-1/\sqrt{2})+F(1/\sqrt{2})}{2}=\frac14.\]
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(\phi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) are defined by \(f(x)=x^2-1\) and \(\phi(t)=t^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Although \(f\) and \(\phi\) are convex, \(\phi\circ f\) is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure when a convex outer function decreases on part of the attainable inner range.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Curvature–monotonicity mismatch in a composition slot
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(g_i:C\to\mathbb R\), and let \(h:D\subseteq\mathbb R^k\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be an outer function used in \(h(g_1,\ldots,g_k)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional nonsmooth composition certificates; mismatch is defined relative to the desired convex or concave conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a desired convex conclusion, slot \(i\) has a curvature–monotonicity mismatch when \(g_i\) is nonaffine and either \(g_i\) is convex while the relevant extended-value outer function is not nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\), or \(g_i\) is concave while that outer function is not nonincreasing in coordinate \(i\). For a desired concave conclusion, the matched pairs are reversed: a concave inner function requires a nondecreasing concave outer slot, while a convex inner function requires a nonincreasing concave outer slot. An affine inner slot is excluded because it admits either curvature designation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A slot is mismatched when the inner function bends in a direction that the outer function's monotonicity does not safely propagate. For convex compositions, convex inner curvature pairs with a nondecreasing outer coordinate and concave inner curvature pairs with a nonincreasing coordinate. The sign-dual pairings apply to concave compositions. Affine slots are not mismatches.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{convex target:}\quad (g_i\text{ convex},\ h\uparrow_i)\ \text{or}\ (g_i\text{ concave},\ h\downarrow_i),\] with failure of the applicable monotonicity predicate defining mismatch for a nonaffine slot.
equivalent_formulations_latex: In the twice-differentiable scalar case, the term \(h'(g(x))g''(x)\) has an uncertified sign when the signs of \(h'\) and \(g''\) are mismatched.
The mismatch disappears if \(g_i\) is affine, because its curvature contribution vanishes.
special_cases_latex: A convex inner function composed with a convex nonincreasing outer function is mismatched for the standard convex-composition rule.
A concave inner function composed with a concave nondecreasing outer function is matched for a concave conclusion.
immediate_consequences_latex: A mismatch prevents use of the generic coordinatewise composition rule, while leaving open the possibility that special algebraic structure makes the particular composition convex or concave.
boundary_notes: Monotonicity must be checked on the relevant extended-value domain or an adequate attainable-range extension.
Mismatch is a certificate classification, not a necessary-and-sufficient test for the actual curvature of every composition.

notation.meaning: The extended outer function is nondecreasing in coordinate i.
The extended outer function is nonincreasing in coordinate i.

children.title: Implicit Attainable-Range Boundary
children.top_down_role: Validity or certifiability depending on implicit attainable ranges.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainable-range boundary for composition certification
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(g:C\to\mathbb R^k\), let \(h:D\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\), and set \(F=\{x\in C:g(x)\in D\}\) and \(R=g(F)\subseteq D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The definition separates properties needed only on attainable outer arguments from properties imposed on a larger explicit domain for a tractable certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The implicit attainable-range boundary is the relative boundary \(\partial_D R=\operatorname{cl}_D R\setminus\operatorname{ri}_D R\) of the set \(R=g(F)\) inside the outer domain \(D\). A range-restricted composition certificate is valid only if its curvature, monotonicity, and domain-stability conditions hold on a specified set \(U\) satisfying \(R\subseteq U\subseteq D\), with \(U\) convex and stable under every coordinate-order comparison used by the certificate. The boundary is implicit when membership in \(R\), or the required order-stable convex enlargement \(U\), is unavailable in an explicit certifiable form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attainable range consists of outer arguments actually produced by feasible inputs. Its implicit boundary is the relative boundary of that image inside the outer domain. A certificate restricted to attainable values must identify a convex, order-stable set containing the image and verify the outer conditions there. If that set or its boundary cannot be characterized, the range-restricted certificate is not established.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[R=g(F),\qquad \partial_D R=\operatorname{cl}_D R\setminus\operatorname{ri}_D R,\qquad R\subseteq U\subseteq D.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an extended-value outer function, domain compatibility is encoded by the natural domain \(F=\{x:g(x)\in D\}\); convexity of \(F\) cannot be omitted.
An order-stable set for a nondecreasing coordinate contains every smaller coordinate value used when comparing the inner function at convex combinations.
special_cases_latex: If \(g(C)\subseteq\operatorname{ri}D\) and a convex order-stable neighborhood of \(g(C)\) is explicit, no hidden attainable-range boundary obstructs the local certificate.
For scalar composition, a convex nondecreasing outer function whose extended domain is a lower ray has the domain stability required by the standard rule.
immediate_consequences_latex: Monotonicity verified only pointwise on \(R\) is insufficient if the composition argument also uses convex combinations or coordinatewise comparison points outside \(R\).
boundary_notes: The image of a convex set under a nonlinear map need not be convex.
The definition concerns certifiability; it does not state that an implicit range makes the composition nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Relative boundary of the attainable range in D.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Domain Preimage Test for Compositions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The composite domain is the preimage of the outer effective domain; if that preimage is nonconvex, the extended-real composite cannot be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex, let \(g:C\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). For \(F=\phi\circ g\),
\[
\operatorname{dom}F=C\cap g^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}\phi).
\]
Since the effective domain of every extended-real convex function is convex, nonconvexity of this set certifies that \(F\) is not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(\phi\circ g)=C\cap g^{-1}(\operatorname{dom}\phi)\), and nonconvexity of this set implies nonconvexity of \(\phi\circ g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain obstruction for extended-real scalar compositions.

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Domain Restrictions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composing the extended-real negative logarithm with x²−1 creates the disconnected effective domain |x|>1, preventing extended-real convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\phi\circ f\). Its effective domain is \[\operatorname{dom}F=(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,+\infty),\] which is not convex. Therefore \(F\) is not convex as an extended-real function.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi:\mathbb R\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is defined by \(\phi(t)=-\log t\) for \(t>0\) and \(\phi(t)=+\infty\) for \(t\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The effective domain of \(\phi\circ f\) is nonconvex, so \(\phi\circ f\) is not an extended-real convex function.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: An outer effective domain can induce a nonconvex effective domain through an incompatible inner function.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Hidden Range Restrictions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squaring preserves convexity for a convex inner function whose values are nonnegative, even though squaring is not globally nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The outer function \(\phi(t)=t^2\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\) and nondecreasing on \([0,+\infty)\), but not on all of \(\mathbb R\). If \(f(C)\subseteq[0,+\infty)\), then \[F(x)=\phi(f(x))=f(x)^2\] is convex on \(C\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space, \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) is convex, and \(f(C)\subseteq[0,+\infty)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f\) is convex on \(C\), although \(\phi\) is not globally nondecreasing.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global nonmonotonicity is harmless when the inner function attains values only in a monotone region of the outer function.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of the Coordinatewise Upper Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A componentwise convex map may have a nonconvex exact range, but adding nonnegative coordinatewise slack produces a convex upper image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(C\) be convex and let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m):C\to\mathbb R^m\) have convex components. Although \(g(C)\) need not be convex, its coordinatewise upper image
\[
\mathcal U=g(C)+\mathbb R_+^m=\{y\in\mathbb R^m:\exists x\in C,\ g_i(x)\leq y_i\text{ for all }i\}
\]
is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(C)+\mathbb R_+^m\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-image geometry generated by a finite vector of convex functions.

notation.meaning: coordinatewise upper image of the attainable range

knowledge_statements.title: Attainable-Range Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Componentwise convexity does not make a vector map's attainable range convex; the map x↦(x,x²) has a parabolic, nonconvex range.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(C=\mathbb R\) and \(g(x)=(x,x^2)\), both component functions are convex, while \[g(C)=\{(u,v)\in\mathbb R^2:v=u^2\}\] is not convex; it contains \((-1,1)\) and \((1,1)\) but not their midpoint \((0,1)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space and \(g:C\to\mathbb R^m\) is a vector-valued mapping with convex component functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The attainable set \(g(C)\) need not be convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A vector mapping can have a curved, nonconvex attainable range even when all component functions are convex.

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Global-Certificate Gaps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard coordinatewise rule does not certify h(x²,x²)=x²−x² because the second slot has the wrong curvature, but cancellation makes the composite identically zero and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(h\) is nondecreasing in its first coordinate and nonincreasing in its second, while both \(g_1\) and \(g_2\) are convex and \(g_2\) is not concave. Thus the standard coordinatewise certificate does not apply. Nevertheless, \[F(x)=h(g_1(x),g_2(x))=0\] for every \(x\in\mathbb R\), so \(F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The composite \(h(g_1,g_2)\) is convex although the standard coordinatewise curvature–monotonicity certificate does not apply.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient coordinatewise composition certificate can miss convexity caused by dependence and cancellation between argument slots.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variable-elimination and nonnegative aggregation operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(X=\mathbb R^n\), \(Y=\mathbb R^m\), let \(C\subseteq Y\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(F:X\times Y\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\). Also let \((A,\mu)\) be a measure space and \(F_a:X\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be indexed functions.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional partial minimization together with deterministic or measure-indexed nonnegative aggregation; closedness and attainment are not built into the basic operation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The variable-elimination operator sends a jointly convex function \(F\) to its marginal \((\mathcal M_C F)(x)=\inf_{y\in C}F(x,y)\), with effective domain \(\{x:\exists y\in C,\ F(x,y)<+\infty\}\), provided the infimum is never \(-\infty\). The nonnegative aggregation operator sends an indexed family to \((\mathcal A_\mu F)(x)=\int_A F_a(x)\,d\mu(a)\) whenever the extended integral is well defined. Finite sums correspond to atomic \(\mu\). Joint convexity is preserved by \(\mathcal M_C\), and pointwise convexity in \(x\) is preserved by \(\mathcal A_\mu\) for a nonnegative measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable elimination takes the infimum of a jointly convex function over a convex block of variables. Nonnegative aggregation takes a weighted sum or integral of functions convex in the retained variable. The basic calculus consists of these two operations and their compositions. Convexity is preserved when partial infima do not equal minus infinity and integrals are well defined, but closedness and attainment require separate conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(\mathcal M_C F)(x)=\inf_{y\in C}F(x,y),\qquad (\mathcal A_\mu F)(x)=\int_A F_a(x)\,d\mu(a).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Variable elimination is projection of the epigraph up to possible missing boundary points caused by nonattainment.
A finite nonnegative weighted sum \(\sum_{j=1}^r w_jF_j(x)\), \(w_j\ge0\), is aggregation with an atomic measure.
special_cases_latex: If \(C=Y\), \(\mathcal M_C\) is unrestricted partial minimization.
An expectation \(\mathbb E[F_\xi(x)]\) is aggregation under a probability measure.
immediate_consequences_latex: Repeated elimination may be represented as a single infimum over a product of convex feasible sets when the constraints separate appropriately.
Positive integration and partial minimization can generate value functions used in stochastic and parametric convex optimization.
boundary_notes: Partial minimization need not preserve closedness, and its infimum need not be attained.
Signed weights or signed measures do not generally preserve convexity.
Undefined expressions such as \(+\infty-\infty\) are excluded.

notation.meaning: Partial minimization over the eliminated variable in C.

children.title: Marginal Value-Function Calculus

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Marginal value function and its epigraph projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) and let \(P:\mathbb R^{n+m+1}\to\mathbb R^{n+1}\) be \(P(x,z,r)=(x,r)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional extended-real marginalization; convexity is separated from closedness and attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal value function of \(F\) with respect to \(z\) is \(f:\mathbb R^n\to[-\infty,+\infty]\) defined by \(f(x)=\inf_{z\in\mathbb R^m}F(x,z)\). Its effective domain is \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:\inf_zF(x,z)<+\infty\}\). If \(F\) is convex and \(f(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\), then \(f\) is convex. In general its epigraph satisfies \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F)\). The marginal is attained at \(x\) when \(\operatorname{Argmin}_zF(x,z)=\{z:F(x,z)=f(x)\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The marginal value at \(x\) is the infimum of the joint function over the eliminated variable \(z\). For a jointly convex function, the marginal is convex unless it takes minus infinity. Its epigraph lies between the projection of the joint epigraph and the closure of that projection. Attainment means that at least one eliminated-variable value realizes the infimum.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f(x)=\inf_zF(x,z),\qquad P(\operatorname{epi}F)\subseteq\operatorname{epi}f\subseteq\operatorname{cl}P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For finite \(f(x)\), attainment at \(x\) is equivalent to \((x,f(x))\in P(\operatorname{epi}F)\).
If the infimum is attained for all finite marginal values, then \(\operatorname{epi}f=P(\operatorname{epi}F)\).
special_cases_latex: Constraining \(z\) to a convex set \(C\) is represented by replacing \(F(x,z)\) with \(F(x,z)+\delta_C(z)\).
An infimal convolution is a marginal after introducing variables constrained by a linear sum relation.
immediate_consequences_latex: Closedness of \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) implies both closedness of the marginal and attainment at every \(x\) with finite \(f(x)\).
boundary_notes: A linear projection of a closed convex set need not be closed.
Convexity of \(f\) alone neither guarantees attainment nor lower semicontinuity.

notation.meaning: Projection that eliminates z from epigraph coordinates.
Set of minimizers in the eliminated variable.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity of Attained Minimizer Fibers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each attained fiber-minimizer set of a jointly convex integrand is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every fixed \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\) at which the infimum is attained, \[M(x)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y)=\{y:F(x,y)=p(x)\}\] is a nonempty convex subset of \(Y\).
assumptions_latex: The finite value \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\) is attained at the fixed \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(x)\) is nonempty and convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry of realized minimizers within a fixed fiber.

notation.meaning: minimizers in the fiber over x

knowledge_statements.title: Attained Marginals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A jointly convex function has a convex marginal; attained fiber minima furnish representatives satisfying the marginal convexity inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). Then \(p\) is convex. More precisely, for all \(x_0,x_1\in\operatorname{dom}p\), \(y_i\in M(x_i)\), and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), \[p((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq F((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1,(1-\lambda)y_0+\lambda y_1)\leq(1-\lambda)p(x_0)+\lambda p(x_1).\]
assumptions_latex: For every \(x\in\operatorname{dom}p\), the set \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is convex, with its convexity inequality represented by attained fiber minimizers.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real convex marginalization with attained fiber infima.

children.title: Marginal Attainment-Closure Failure Boundary
children.top_down_role: Projection-induced attainment and closedness failures.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and closure defect of a marginal projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), let \(f(x)=\inf_zF(x,z)\), and let \(P(x,z,r)=(x,r)\). Assume \(f(x)>-\infty\) where considered.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional marginalization; the boundary records projection defects even when the joint function is closed and convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The marginal attainment defect set is \(B_{\mathrm{att}}=\{x\in\operatorname{dom}f:(x,f(x))\notin P(\operatorname{epi}F)\}\). The marginal closure defect set is \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}=\operatorname{epi}f\setminus P(\operatorname{epi}F)\). Thus \(x\in B_{\mathrm{att}}\) exactly when the infimum defining \(f(x)\) is finite but not attained, while \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}\ne\varnothing\) records boundary points added when the projected epigraph is completed. The attainment-closure failure boundary is \(B=B_{\mathrm{cl}}\cap\partial P(\operatorname{epi}F)\), with the boundary taken in \(\mathbb R^{n+1}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attainment defect contains parameters whose finite marginal values are approached but never achieved. The closure defect consists of epigraph points missing from the projection of the joint epigraph. Their boundary portion is the marginal attainment-closure failure boundary. It identifies precisely where projection can lose minimizing points or closedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[B_{\mathrm{att}}=\{x:(x,f(x))\notin P(\operatorname{epi}F)\},\qquad B_{\mathrm{cl}}=\operatorname{epi}f\setminus P(\operatorname{epi}F).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(x\in\operatorname{dom}f\), \(x\notin B_{\mathrm{att}}\) if and only if \(\operatorname{Argmin}_zF(x,z)\ne\varnothing\).
If \(P(\operatorname{epi}F)\) is closed, then \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}=B_{\mathrm{att}}=\varnothing\).
special_cases_latex: When all relevant sublevel sets in the eliminated variable are compact under a standard level-boundedness condition, the marginal is closed and its minima are attained.
A nonclosed projected epigraph can omit exactly the points \((x,f(x))\) while containing every \((x,r)\) with \(r>f(x)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Nonemptiness of \(B_{\mathrm{att}}\) certifies failure of exact epigraph projection.
Nonemptiness of \(B_{\mathrm{cl}}\) prevents identifying the marginal epigraph with the unclosed projection.
boundary_notes: The two defects are related but conceptually distinct: a projection may fail to be closed beyond the lower graph.
Closedness of \(F\) alone does not force closedness of its epigraph projection.

notation.meaning: Parameter set where the marginal infimum is not attained.
Epigraph points absent from the projected joint epigraph.

source_refs.locator: §3.3, Proposition 3.3.1(b), equation (3.1), Figure 3.3.1, and discussion immediately preceding Proposition 3.3.2, pp. 124–126

knowledge_statements.title: Unattained Marginal Values
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the continuous jointly convex function that is exponential in the eliminated variable, every marginal value is zero but no finite fiber point attains it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^2\to\mathbb{R}\) be defined by \(F(x,y)=e^y\), and let \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y)\). Then \(F\) is continuous and jointly convex, while for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), \[p(x)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y)=\varnothing.\] Thus finite convex marginal values need not be attained in their fibers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p(x)=0\) for every \(x\), but \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{y\in\mathbb{R}}F(x,y)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment can fail even for finite continuous convex integrands.

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed Marginal Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The indicator of this closed convex set marginalizes to the indicator of the open interval of positive real numbers, giving a convex but nonclosed marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is closed and convex, and \(F=\iota_C\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Its marginal satisfies \[p(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}}\iota_C(x,y)=\begin{cases}0,&x>0,\\+\infty,&x\leq0.\end{cases}\] Hence \(p=\iota_{(0,\infty)}\) is convex but is not lower semicontinuous at \(0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p=\iota_{(0,\infty)}\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A closed convex integrand may have a nonclosed convex marginal.

notation.meaning: indicator taking zero on the set and positive infinity outside

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Projection-Induced Closure Loss
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Marginalizing the indicator of a closed convex set gives the indicator of its coordinate projection; a nonclosed projection therefore produces a nonclosed marginal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \[\inf_{y\in Y}\iota_C(x,y)=\iota_{\pi_X(C)}(x).\] Therefore, if the coordinate projection \(\pi_X(C)\) is not closed, the marginal \(\iota_{\pi_X(C)}\) is convex but not lower semicontinuous. Closed convex sets in finite-dimensional product spaces can have nonclosed coordinate projections.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is closed and convex, and \(F=\iota_C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)=\iota_{\pi_X(C)}(x)\); if \(\pi_X(C)\) is not closed, the marginal is not lower semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure loss for indicator marginals is identified with nonclosed coordinate projection of a closed convex feasible set.

notation.meaning: coordinate projection onto the retained space

source_witnesses.locator: 3.3 Image and Marginal Functions p. 118

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Closure Recovery by Local Uniform Level-Boundedness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, local uniform level-boundedness in the eliminated variable prevents escaping minimizers and makes the marginal proper, closed, convex, and attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p(x)=\inf_{y\in Y}F(x,y)\). If \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex and is locally uniformly level-bounded in \(y\), then \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Every finite value \(p(x)\) is attained, and \[\operatorname{epi}p=\{(x,r):\exists y\in Y,\ F(x,y)\le r\}\] is closed.
assumptions_latex: \(F:X\times Y\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex.
For every \(\bar x\in X\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), some neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and bounded set \(B\subseteq Y\) satisfy \(\{y:F(x,y)\le\alpha\}\subseteq B\) for all \(x\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex; every finite fiber infimum is attained; and the displayed epigraphical projection is closed and equals \(\operatorname{epi}p\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional recovery of properness, closedness, and fiber attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginal Closure Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local level-boundedness recovers attainment and lower semicontinuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex, and define \(p(x)=\inf_yF(x,y)\). Suppose \(p\) is proper and, for every compact \(K\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) and every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the set
\[\{(x,y):x\in K,\ F(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\]
is bounded. Then every finite fiber infimum is attained, and \(p\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex. Equivalently, its epigraph is closed and equals the projection of \(\operatorname{epi}F\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A proper closed convex integrand with locally uniform bounded sublevel fibers has an attained, proper, closed convex marginal.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and convex
Fiber sublevel sets are locally uniformly bounded
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\) is closed convex and each finite value \(p(x)\) is attained.

notation.meaning: compact subset of the parameter space

children.title: Infimal Convolution
children.top_down_role: Variable-splitting construction linking marginalization, conjugacy, and smoothing.

knowledge_statements.title: Order Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing either input pointwise cannot decrease the infimal convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1\leq f_2\) and \(g_1\leq g_2\) pointwise, then \(f_1\square g_1\leq f_2\square g_2\) pointwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_1\square g_1\leq f_2\square g_2\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise order preservation in both arguments.

knowledge_statements.title: Commutativity and Identity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution is commutative, with the indicator of the origin as its identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For extended-real functions \(f,g:X\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), \(f\square g=g\square f\). Moreover, if \(\iota_{\{0\}}(0)=0\) and \(\iota_{\{0\}}(x)=+\infty\) for \(x\ne0\), then \(f\square\iota_{\{0\}}=f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\square g=g\square f\) and \(f\square\iota_{\{0\}}=f\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic algebraic laws of binary infimal convolution.

knowledge_statements.title: Effective-Domain Sum
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The infimal convolution is below positive infinity exactly at sums of points from the two effective domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x:f(x)<+\infty\}\), \[\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(f\square g)=\operatorname{dom}f+\operatorname{dom}g\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility of additive decompositions underlying the binary operation.

notation.meaning: Minkowski sum of two subsets of X

knowledge_statements.title: Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Infimal convolution assigns to each point the infimum of the total cost over all decompositions into one argument for each function; for convex inputs it is convex when it does not take negative infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The infimal convolution of \(f\) and \(g\) is the extended-real function \[(f\square g)(x)=\inf\{f(u)+g(v):u,v\in X,\ u+v=x\}=\inf_{y\in X}\bigl(f(y)+g(x-y)\bigr).\] If \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and \((f\square g)(x)>-\infty\) for every \(x\in X\), then \(f\square g\) is convex. Lower semicontinuity and attainment require additional hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((f\square g)(x)=\inf_{y\in X}(f(y)+g(x-y))\); if \(f\) and \(g\) are convex and \(f\square g\) never takes \(-\infty\), then \(f\square g\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary infimal convolution on a common vector space, together with its basic convexity property.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Distance to a convex set as an infimal convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The infimum representation holds for every nonempty convex set. The source's minimum notation additionally requires attainment, which nonempty convexity alone does not guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\varnothing\ne C\subseteq\mathbb E\) be convex, let \(\delta_C\) be its indicator function, and let \(h_1(u)=\|u\|\). Then, for every \(x\in\mathbb E\), \[d_C(x):=\inf_{y\in C}\|x-y\|=\inf_{y\in\mathbb E}\{\delta_C(y)+\|x-y\|\}=(\delta_C\square h_1)(x).\] Consequently, \(d_C\) is convex. The infima may be written as minima when they are attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The distance to a nonempty convex set is the infimal convolution of its indicator function with the norm, and hence is convex. Minimum notation requires attainment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_C=\delta_C\square h_1\quad\text{and}\quad d_C\text{ is convex}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Binary Infimal Convolution
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preserves the extract's minimum-based convention. Properness alone does not guarantee attainment, so this definition does not supply a general existence theorem for the displayed minimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_1,h_2:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper. Under the extract's attained-minimum convention, their infimal convolution is defined by \[(h_1\square h_2)(x)=\min_{u\in\mathbb E}\bigl\{h_1(u)+h_2(x-u)\bigr\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the source's minimum convention, the binary infimal convolution assigns to a point the minimum total value over all decompositions into u and x minus u; properness by itself does not ensure that this minimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (h_1\square h_2)(x)=\min_{u\in\mathbb E}\{h_1(u)+h_2(x-u)\}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation for the binary infimal convolution of a proper extended-real-valued convex function with a finite-valued convex function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h_1:\mathbb E\to(-\infty,\infty]\) be proper and convex, and let \(h_2:\mathbb E\to\mathbb R\) be convex. Define \[(h_1\square h_2)(x)=\inf_{y\in\mathbb E}\{h_1(y)+h_2(x-y)\}.\] Then \(h_1\square h_2\) is convex.

children.top_down_role: Aggregation of convex integrands under deterministic and probabilistic indexing.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Nonnegative aggregation of convex integrands
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((A,\Sigma,\mu)\) be a measure space with \(\mu\ge0\), let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, and let \(\varphi:C\times A\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be measurable in \(a\) for every \(x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic sums, integrals, and expectations; existence of the integral is imposed separately from pointwise convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The convex-integrand aggregation generated by \((\varphi,\mu)\) is \(G(x)=\int_A\varphi(x,a)\,d\mu(a)\) on the set of \(x\in C\) for which the extended integral is well defined and does not contain the indeterminate form \(+\infty-\infty\). The integrand is convex for aggregation when \(x\mapsto\varphi(x,a)\) is convex on \(C\) for \(\mu\)-almost every \(a\). Under these conditions, \(G\) is convex on its effective domain. An expectation is the case in which \(\mu\) is a probability measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex-integrand aggregate is a nonnegative integral of functions that are convex in the decision variable for almost every index. The aggregate is defined wherever the integral exists without an infinity ambiguity. It is convex there. Finite nonnegative weighted sums and probabilistic expectations are special cases of the same operation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[G(x)=\int_A\varphi(x,a)\,d\mu(a),\qquad \varphi(\cdot,a)\text{ convex for }\mu\text{-a.e. }a.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For an atomic measure \(\mu=\sum_{j=1}^r w_j\delta_{a_j}\), the aggregate is \(G(x)=\sum_{j=1}^r w_j\varphi(x,a_j)\) with \(w_j\ge0\).
For a random element \(\xi\), \(G(x)=\mathbb E[\varphi(x,\xi)]\) whenever the expectation exists.
special_cases_latex: A positive scalar multiple of one convex function is aggregation over a one-point index set.
An infinite series of convex functions with nonnegative coefficients is covered when its sum is well defined.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity is inherited when a positive-measure portion of the integrands supplies strict curvature in every nonzero direction, subject to finiteness.
Affine terms may be aggregated with arbitrary nonnegative weights without changing convexity.
boundary_notes: Negative weights can destroy convexity.
Pointwise convexity does not by itself guarantee measurability, integrability, lower semicontinuity, or interchange of integration with minimization.
The effective domain of \(G\) can be smaller than the intersection of the pointwise domains because of integrability.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Under Expectation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expectation of an almost-surely convex integrand is convex under measurable sections and a common integrable lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\). If the random sections are measurable, the decision sections are convex almost surely, and an integrable random lower bound makes the expectations well-defined, then \(F\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(f:C\times\Omega\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(\omega\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is measurable for every \(x\in C\).
Outside one \(\mathbb P\)-null set, \(x\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is convex.
There exists an integrable random variable \(G\) such that \(f(x,\omega)\geq G(\omega)\) almost surely for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-measure specialization of convex integrand aggregation.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregation of Strong-Convexity Moduli
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Expectation averages nonnegative random strong-convexity moduli.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f(\cdot,\omega)\) is \(m(\omega)\)-strongly convex almost surely and every random section \(f(x,\cdot)\) is integrable, then \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is \(\mathbb E[m]\)-strongly convex.
assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(X\) is a real Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\mathbb E[f(\cdot,\omega)]\) is \(\mathbb E[m]\)-strongly convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-weighted strengthening of convexity preservation.

assumptions_latex: \((\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\) is a probability space and \(X\) is a real vector space.
For every \(x\in X\), \(\omega\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is measurable, and for almost every \(\omega\), \(x\mapsto f(x,\omega)\) is convex.
The expectations used below are well-defined and never have the indeterminate form \(+\infty-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: expectation preserves pointwise convex inequalities under measurability and well-defined integration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation by probability-weighted integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x_0,x_1\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), almost-sure convexity gives \[f((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1,\omega)\leq(1-\lambda)f(x_0,\omega)+\lambda f(x_1,\omega).\] Monotonicity and linearity of expectation, under the stated well-definedness convention, imply \[F((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)F(x_0)+\lambda F(x_1).\] Thus the expectation aggregate \(F(x)=\mathbb E[f(x,\omega)]\) is convex. This conclusion alone does not assert finiteness, lower semicontinuity, or interchange of expectation with minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The expectation of an almost-surely convex integrand is convex when its sections are measurable and the relevant extended expectations are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Aggregation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property kind fits expectation aggregation, but no citation is supplied. In addition, the integrand's codomain and the precise extended-expectation convention are not fully specified, so the hypotheses supporting linearity and the claimed codomain of the aggregate remain uncertain.

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Under Deterministic Integration
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating almost-everywhere convex decision sections preserves convexity when the sections are measurable and a common integrable lower bound makes every integral well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\). If the decision sections are convex almost everywhere, the parameter sections are measurable, and \(f\) has a common integrable lower bound, then \(I:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is convex.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
\(f:T\times C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), and \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is measurable for every \(x\in C\).
Outside one \(\mu\)-null set, \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is convex.
There exists \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) such that \(f(t,x)\geq g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation for a general measure-space aggregate under a well-defined extended-integral regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Semicontinuity Under an Integrable Lower Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Almost-everywhere lower-semicontinuous sections with a common integrable lower bound produce a lower-semicontinuous integral aggregate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated measurability and common-lower-bound assumptions, if \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is lower-semicontinuous for almost every \(t\), then \[I(x)\leq\liminf_{n\to\infty}I(x_n)\quad\text{whenever }x_n\to x.\] Hence \(I\) is lower-semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(X\) is a finite-dimensional normed space.
For every \(x\in X\), \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is measurable.
For almost every \(t\), \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is lower-semicontinuous.
There exists \(g\in L^1(\mu)\) such that \(f(t,x)\geq g(t)\) for almost every \(t\) and every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is lower-semicontinuous.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fatou-type closedness regime for deterministic integral aggregation.

assumptions_latex: \((T,\Sigma,\mu)\) is a measure space and \(X\) is a real vector space.
For each \(x\in X\), \(t\mapsto f(t,x)\) is measurable, and for almost every \(t\), \(x\mapsto f(t,x)\) is convex.
All displayed integrals are well-defined, with no \(+\infty-\infty\) ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I(x)=\int_T f(t,x)\,d\mu(t)\) is convex.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: integration preserves almost-everywhere pointwise convex inequalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity preservation under deterministic measure integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For arbitrary \(x_0,x_1\in X\) and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\), pointwise convexity holds for almost every \(t\): \[f(t,(1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)f(t,x_0)+\lambda f(t,x_1).\] Integrating this inequality and using linearity on the well-defined terms yields \[I((1-\lambda)x_0+\lambda x_1)\leq(1-\lambda)I(x_0)+\lambda I(x_1).\] Therefore \(I\) is convex. Additional domination, normal-integrand, or compactness hypotheses are required for conclusions about continuity, differentiation, or interchange with optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating functions that are convex in the decision variable almost everywhere preserves convexity, provided the sections are measurable and all integrals are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.title: Deterministic Integral Aggregation
