knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quasiconvex function via the max-Jensen inequality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space and let \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scalar extended-real quasiconvexity on a convex domain; no continuity or ordinary convexity is assumed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\) when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\]
for every \(x,y\in C\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\). Thus values at interior points of a segment cannot exceed the larger endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function on a convex domain is quasiconvex when its value at every interior convex combination of two points is at most the maximum of its two endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall x,y\in C\ \forall t\in(0,1):\quad f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\), the sublevel set \(\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) is convex.
Every restriction of \(f\) to a line segment is a one-dimensional quasiconvex function.
special_cases_latex: Every convex function is quasiconvex.
Every monotone real-valued function on an interval is quasiconvex, even when it is not convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: The minimizer set \(\operatorname{argmin}_C f\), when nonempty, is convex.
Quasiconvexity is preserved under increasing scalar reparameterizations and pointwise suprema under the standard domain conditions.
boundary_notes: Quasiconvexity does not require a convex epigraph.
A sum of quasiconvex functions need not be quasiconvex.
Quasiconvexity is distinct from quasiconcavity; satisfying both gives quasilinearity.

children.title: Level-Set Quasiconvexity
children.top_down_role: Primary organization through convex sublevel sets.

knowledge_statements.title: Differentiable First-Order Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function is quasiconvex exactly when its gradient at x pairs nonpositively with every direction toward a point of no larger value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(f\) is quasiconvex if and only if \[f(y)\le f(x)\Longrightarrow \nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)\le0\qquad(x,y\in C).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff[f(y)\le f(x)\Rightarrow\nabla f(x)^\top(y-x)\le0].\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional differentiable test for quasiconvexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Line-Restriction Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is quasiconvex exactly when every affine-line restriction is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A function \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) on a convex set \(C\) is quasiconvex if and only if every function \(t\mapsto f(x+td)\) is quasiconvex on \(\{t\in\mathbb R:x+td\in C\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff\text{ every affine-line restriction is quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of quasiconvexity to one-dimensional affine restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconvexity Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nondecreasing step function is quasiconvex but not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) defined by \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\le0\) and \(f(x)=1\) for \(x>0\) is nondecreasing and hence quasiconvex, but it is not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex but not convex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates ordinary level-set quasiconvexity from convexity without duplicating the strict-quasiconvex cubic example.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Effective Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The effective domain of an extended-real quasiconvex function is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is quasiconvex, then \(\operatorname{dom}f=\{x\in C:f(x)<+\infty\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}f\text{ is convex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequence for extended-real quasiconvex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Sublevel Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quasiconvexity is equivalently characterized by convexity of every strict sublevel set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\). Then \(f\) is quasiconvex if and only if \(\{x\in C:f(x)<\alpha\}\) is convex for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex}\iff(\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R)\ \{f<\alpha\}\text{ is convex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent formulation using strict sublevels.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is quasiconvex exactly when all its sublevel sets are convex, equivalently when values along segments do not exceed the endpoint maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\) if and only if, for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the set \(L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in C:f(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is convex. Equivalently, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)\leq\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\] These two formulations use the same extended-real ordering convention.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is quasiconvex exactly when every sublevel set \(L_\alpha(f)\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the extended-real, convex-sublevel-set characterization of quasiconvexity.

notation.meaning: Sublevel set of f at height alpha

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-sublevel-set characterization
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\) be a nonempty convex subset of a real vector space, let \(f:C\to[-\infty,+\infty]\), and define \(L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\) for \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The level-set encoding of scalar quasiconvexity, including empty and full sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is level-set quasiconvex when
\[L_\alpha(f)=\{x\in C:f(x)\le\alpha\}\]
is convex for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). The sublevel family is nested: if \(\alpha\le\beta\), then \(L_\alpha(f)\subseteq L_\beta(f)\). Empty sublevel sets and \(C\) itself count as convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A function is level-set quasiconvex when every one of its real sublevel sets is convex. These sublevel sets form a nested family as the threshold increases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\forall\alpha\in\mathbb R:\quad L_\alpha(f)\text{ is convex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The condition is equivalent to \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
If \(f\) is also lower semicontinuous, every \(L_\alpha(f)\) is closed as well as convex.
special_cases_latex: For an indicator \(\delta_D\) on \(C\), level-set quasiconvexity is equivalent to convexity of \(D\).
A monotone function on a real interval has interval sublevel sets and is therefore level-set quasiconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Feasibility regions of inequalities \(f(x)\le\alpha\) are convex at every threshold.
The minimum-level set is convex whenever a minimum is attained.
boundary_notes: Convexity of one selected sublevel set does not establish quasiconvexity; every real threshold is quantified.
Convex sublevel sets do not imply convexity of the epigraph or the ordinary Jensen inequality.

notation.meaning: Alpha-sublevel set of f relative to C.

children.title: Quasiconvex Strictness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Stronger regimes relevant to minimizer geometry.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict and uniform quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\mathcal H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(f:\mathcal H\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) be increasing and vanish only at zero.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global strict and uniform quasiconvexity on the effective domain of a proper scalar function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex when, for all distinct \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and all \(t\in(0,1)\),
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\]
It is uniformly quasiconvex with modulus \(\phi\) when
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)+t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\]
for all \(x,y\in\operatorname{dom}f\) and \(t\in(0,1)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity replaces the quasiconvex max inequality by a strict inequality between distinct endpoints. Uniform quasiconvexity strengthens it by a positive deficit controlled by the endpoint distance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\text{uniform quasiconvexity}\Longrightarrow\text{strict quasiconvexity}\Longrightarrow\text{quasiconvexity}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strict quasiconvexity says every open segment between distinct domain points lies strictly below the larger endpoint value.
Uniform quasiconvexity quantifies this decrease through \(t(1-t)\phi(\|x-y\|)\).
special_cases_latex: Every strictly convex function is strictly quasiconvex.
A strictly monotone proper function on an interval is strictly quasiconvex, although it need not be strictly convex.
immediate_consequences_latex: A strictly quasiconvex function has at most one global minimizer.
Uniform quasiconvexity excludes nontrivial constant segments in the effective domain.
boundary_notes: Strict quasiconvexity is weaker than strict convexity.
Strict convexity of every sublevel set is not, without qualifications, interchangeable with the displayed strict max inequality.
The local-on-\(C\) versions quantify only over endpoints in a specified subset \(C\).

knowledge_statements.title: Linewise Characterization of Strict Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity can be checked on every affine-line restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A real-valued function \(f\) on a convex set \(C\) is strictly quasiconvex if and only if its restriction to every affine line is strictly quasiconvex on the interval where that line meets \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}\iff\text{ every affine-line restriction is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of the strict segment condition to one-dimensional restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Quasiconvexity Without Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The cubic is strictly quasiconvex but not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x^3\) is strictly increasing and therefore strictly quasiconvex on \(\mathbb R\), although it is not convex on \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex but not convex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp converse failure for the strict-convexity implication.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity Implies Strict Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity implies strict quasiconvexity, but the converse fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is strictly convex, then for distinct \(x,y\) and \(t\in(0,1)\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)<(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\le\max\{f(x),f(y)\},\] so \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Places strict quasiconvexity below the stronger chord inequality.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity requires every interior point of a nontrivial segment to have value strictly below the larger endpoint value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(C\) if, for every pair of distinct points \(x,y\in C\) and every \(t\in(0,1)\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)<\max\{f(x),f(y)\}.\] In particular, strict quasiconvexity implies quasiconvexity, but it does not require the convex interpolation bound \(f((1-t)x+ty)\leq(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex precisely when the strict endpoint-maximum inequality holds on every nontrivial segment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Adopts the standard segment-inequality definition for real-valued functions.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.title: Semistrictness Alone Need Not Imply Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the unequal-endpoint-only definition, semistrict quasiconvexity does not imply ordinary quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) by \(f(0)=1\) and \(f(x)=0\) for \(x\ne0\). It satisfies the unequal-endpoint semistrict condition but is not quasiconvex because \(f(-1)=f(1)=0<f(0)\).
assumptions_latex: Semistrictness uses the packet's unequal-endpoint convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex but not quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Terminology-sensitive boundary for the seed's unequal-endpoint-only convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictness Implication
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict quasiconvexity implies semistrict quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every strictly quasiconvex function is semistrictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relation between the two strictness regimes under the packet's conventions.

knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Semistrict quasiconvexity enforces strict improvement from the worse endpoint only when the two endpoint values differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on \(C\) if, whenever \(x,y\in C\), \(f(x)<f(y)\), and \(t\in(0,1)\), one has \[f((1-t)x+ty)<f(y).\] Equivalently, whenever \(f(x)\neq f(y)\), every interior point of \([x,y]\) has value strictly below \(\max\{f(x),f(y)\}\). No strict inequality is imposed when the endpoint values are equal.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex precisely when unequal endpoint values imply strict decrease from the larger value at every interior point.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the unequal-endpoint convention; some sources call this semistrict quasiconvexity.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.title: Semistrictness Does Not Give Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant function is semistrictly quasiconvex but has every feasible point as a minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On any nontrivial convex set \(C\), a constant function \(f\equiv c\) is semistrictly quasiconvex under the unequal-endpoint convention, while \(\operatorname*{argmin}_C f=C\) is not a singleton.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex and }\operatorname*{argmin}_C f=C.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit witness for the seed's nonuniqueness boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Local Minima Are Global
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a semistrictly quasiconvex function, a local minimum cannot be nonglobal.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be convex and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R\) be semistrictly quasiconvex. Every local minimizer of \(f\) relative to \(C\) is a global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(\bar x\in C\) is a local minimizer relative to \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(\bar x)=\inf_{x\in C}f(x).\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local-to-global consequence of the unequal-endpoint semistrict condition.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimizer-Set Consequences
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The attained minimizer set of a quasiconvex function is convex. Strict quasiconvexity makes it a singleton, whereas semistrict quasiconvexity alone need not imply uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) be finite and let \(M=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\). If \(f\) is quasiconvex, then \(M\) is convex. If \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex, then \(M\) contains exactly one point. Semistrict quasiconvexity alone does not imply uniqueness of an attained minimizer.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
The finite minimum \(m=\min_{x\in C}f(x)\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}f(x)\) is convex; if \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex, this set is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates convexity of the attained minimizer set from uniqueness under strict quasiconvexity.

notation.meaning: Set of global minimizers of f on C

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Closure system generated by quasiconvexity-preserving operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Let \(\mathcal F\) be a collection of quasiconvex extended-real functions on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional scalar quasiconvexity under pointwise supremum, monotone composition, affine precomposition, and partial minimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quasiconvex preservation closure \(\operatorname{Qcl}(\mathcal F)\) is the smallest class containing \(\mathcal F\) and closed under the following well-defined operations: pointwise suprema \(x\mapsto\sup_i f_i(x)\); compositions \(h\circ f\) with nondecreasing \(h\); affine precomposition \(x\mapsto f(Ax+b)\); and partial minimization
\[g(x)=\inf_{y\in D}F(x,y),\]
where \(D\) is convex and \(F\) is jointly quasiconvex in \((x,y)\). Every member produced by these rules is quasiconvex on its induced convex domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quasiconvex preservation calculus is the smallest function class generated from given quasiconvex functions by pointwise suprema, nondecreasing scalar compositions, affine precomposition, and partial minimization over a convex auxiliary set under joint quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[f_i,F\text{ quasiconvex}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \sup_i f_i,\ h\circ f,\ f\circ(A\cdot+b),\ \inf_{y\in D}F(\cdot,y)\text{ are quasiconvex}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a supremum, \(L_\alpha(\sup_i f_i)=\bigcap_iL_\alpha(f_i)\).
For partial minimization, the sublevel set is the projection onto the \(x\)-coordinates of the corresponding joint sublevel set, with closure issues handled by the exact induced-domain convention.
special_cases_latex: A finite maximum of quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex.
Truncation \(x\mapsto\min\{f(x),\eta\}\) is quasiconvex for quasiconvex \(f\).
Every nonnegative weighted maximum of quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex.
immediate_consequences_latex: Many quasiconvex models can be verified entirely through convexity of induced sublevel sets.
Increasing reparameterizations preserve minimizers and quasiconvexity.
boundary_notes: Arbitrary sums and pointwise infima of quasiconvex functions are not general preservation rules.
For partial minimization, joint quasiconvexity is required; separate quasiconvexity is insufficient.
A decreasing outer function generally converts quasiconvexity toward quasiconcavity rather than preserving it.

notation.meaning: Quasiconvex closure generated by the listed operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure for Decreasing Outer Maps
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing outer function can convert a quasiconvex function into a nonquasiconvex one.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=x^2\) and \(\phi(s)=-s\). Then \(f\) is quasiconvex, but \((\phi\circ f)(x)=-x^2\) is not quasiconvex because \[\{x:-x^2\le-a\}=(-\infty,-\sqrt a]\cup[\sqrt a,\infty)\] is nonconvex for every \(a>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is quasiconvex but }\phi\circ f\text{ is not quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that arbitrary scalar outer composition does not preserve quasiconvexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Flat Outer Maps Lose Strictness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flat portions of a nondecreasing outer map can destroy strict quasiconvexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=x\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(\mathbb R\), but the constant nondecreasing map \(\phi(s)=0\) makes \(\phi\circ f\) constant and therefore not strictly quasiconvex on any nontrivial interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is strictly quasiconvex but }\phi\circ f\text{ is not}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes nondecreasing from strictly increasing outer transformations.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotone Scalar Composition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Composition with a nondecreasing scalar function preserves quasiconvexity; strict increase also preserves the stated strict and semistrict regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex and \(\phi:f(C)\to\mathbb{R}\) is nondecreasing, then \(\phi\circ f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\). If \(\phi\) is strictly increasing, composition also preserves strict quasiconvexity and semistrict quasiconvexity under the stated segment definitions.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity, rather than convexity of the scalar outer function, preserves quasiconvexity.

assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space and \(f:C\to\mathbb{R}\) is quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi\circ f\) is quasiconvex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotonicity, rather than convexity of the scalar outer function, preserves quasiconvexity.

If \(\phi\) is strictly increasing, composition also preserves strict quasiconvexity and semistrict quasiconvexity under the stated segment definitions.

knowledge_statements.title: Strictness and Injectivity Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine precomposition preserves strict quasiconvexity exactly when the affine map is injective on the domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be strictly quasiconvex and \(T\) affine on a convex set \(D\). Then \(f\circ T\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(D\) if and only if \(T|_D\) is injective. Indeed, if \(T(x)=T(y)\) for distinct \(x,y\in D\), the composite is constant on \([x,y]\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is strictly quasiconvex on a convex set containing \(T(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\text{ is strictly quasiconvex on }D\iff T|_D\text{ is injective}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine-map condition for preserving strict quasiconvexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Semistrict Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any affine precomposition preserves semistrict quasiconvexity; injectivity is needed only for the strict regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on a convex set containing \(T(D)\) and \(T\) is affine, then \(f\circ T\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on the convex set \(D\). No injectivity assumption is required.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is semistrictly quasiconvex on a convex set containing \(T(D)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\text{ is semistrictly quasiconvex on }D.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine pullback variant for the unequal-endpoint semistrict regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Inverse-Image Level Sets
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every sublevel of an affine composite is the affine inverse image of the corresponding outer sublevel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g=f\circ T\), where \(T(x)=Ax+b\), one has \[\{x\in D:g(x)\le\alpha\}=T^{-1}(\{z\in C:f(z)\le\alpha\})\] for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\alpha(g)=T^{-1}(L_\alpha(f))\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set mechanism underlying affine pullback preservation.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Precomposition
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Precomposing a quasiconvex function with an affine map preserves quasiconvexity on the map's convex natural inverse-image domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) and \(W\) be real vector spaces, let \(C\subseteq W\) be convex, and let \(f:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be quasiconvex. For a linear map \(A:V\to W\) and \(b\in W\), define \(T(x)=Ax+b\) and \(D=T^{-1}(C)\). Then \(D\) is convex and \(f\circ T\) is quasiconvex on \(D\).
assumptions_latex: \(V\) and \(W\) are real vector spaces, and \(C\subseteq W\) is convex.
\(A:V\to W\) is linear, \(b\in W\), \(T:V\to W\) is defined by \(T(x)=Ax+b\), and \(D=T^{-1}(C)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ T\) is quasiconvex on the convex set \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies to affine maps between real vector spaces on the natural inverse-image domain.

knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Infimum Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise minima of quasiconvex functions need not be quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The affine functions \(f_1(x)=x\) and \(f_2(x)=-x\) are quasiconvex, but \(h(x)=\min\{f_1(x),f_2(x)\}=-|x|\) is not quasiconvex because \[\{x:h(x)\le-1\}=(-\infty,-1]\cup[1,\infty)\] is not convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_1,f_2\text{ are quasiconvex but }h\text{ is not}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows that upper-envelope preservation does not extend to lower envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Infinite Suprema May Lose Strictness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arbitrary supremum of strictly quasiconvex functions can lose strictness even though it remains quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(C=[-1,1]\), let \(f_n(x)=(x^2-1)/n\) for \(n\ge1\). Every \(f_n\) is strictly convex and hence strictly quasiconvex, but \(\sup_{n\ge1}f_n(x)=0\) for every \(x\in C\), so the supremum is not strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_n\text{ is strictly quasiconvex for every }n,\text{ but }\sup_n f_n\equiv0.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp distinction between finite maxima and arbitrary suprema in the strict regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite Maxima Preserve Strict Quasiconvexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite pointwise maximum of strictly quasiconvex functions remains strictly quasiconvex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f_1,\ldots,f_m\) are strictly quasiconvex on a convex set \(C\), then \(g=\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\) is strictly quasiconvex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max_{1\le i\le m}f_i\text{ is strictly quasiconvex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strictness variant for finite upper envelopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Intersection Formula for Supremum Sublevels
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A supremum sublevel is exactly the intersection of the corresponding sublevels of all family members.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(g(x)=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)\), then \[\{x:g(x)\le\alpha\}=\bigcap_{i\in I}\{x:f_i(x)\le\alpha\}\] for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(L_\alpha(g)=\bigcap_{i\in I}L_\alpha(f_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact level-set mechanism for arbitrary pointwise suprema.

knowledge_statements.title: Supremum Preservation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pointwise supremum of any nonempty family of quasiconvex functions is quasiconvex, without continuity or attainment assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be nonempty and let \(f_i:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be quasiconvex for every \(i\in I\). Then the pointwise supremum \(g:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\), defined by \(g(x)=\sup_{i\in I}f_i(x)\), is quasiconvex. No finiteness of \(I\), continuity, or attainment of the supremum is required.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is quasiconvex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Covers arbitrary nonempty pointwise suprema, including finite maxima, in the extended-real setting.

notation.meaning: Nonempty index set for the family

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex-Hull Supremum Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduces maximization of a convex function over a generated convex hull to the generating set and preserves the stated direction of attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\) be convex, let \(S\) be any set of points, and let \(C=\operatorname{conv}S\). Then \[\sup_{x\in C}f(x)=\sup_{x\in S}f(x).\] Moreover, if the supremum over \(C\) is attained, then the supremum over \(S\) is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function has the same supremum over a set and over its convex hull. Attainment over the convex hull implies attainment over the generating set.
assumptions_latex: S\text{ is an arbitrary set of points}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{x\in C}f(x)=\sup_{x\in S}f(x),\qquad \operatorname{argmax}_{x\in C}f(x)\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow\operatorname{argmax}_{x\in S}f(x)\neq\varnothing

knowledge_statements.title: Attainment Restores Closed-Level Projection
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fiberwise attainment upgrades the strict-sublevel projection identity to an exact closed-sublevel identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in C_x}f(x,y)\), if every fiberwise infimum is attained, then \[\{x\in D:g(x)\le\alpha\}=\operatorname{proj}_X\{(x,y)\in C:f(x,y)\le\alpha\}\] for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{g\le\alpha\}=\operatorname{proj}_X\{f\le\alpha\}\) for every \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact condition complementing the seed's nonattainment boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Level-Set Projection Boundaries
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite partial minimization preserves quasiconvexity through exact strict-sublevel projection, but projecting closed sublevels can miss points when fiberwise infima are not attained; the exponential example exhibits this failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\), the partial infimum satisfies \[\{x\in D:g(x)<\alpha\}=\operatorname{proj}_X\{(x,y)\in C:f(x,y)<\alpha\}.\] Consequently, \(g\) is quasiconvex on \(D\). Without attainment of the fiberwise infimum, the analogous closed-sublevel identity can fail. For \(C=\mathbb{R}^2\) and \(f(x,y)=e^y\), one has \(g(x)=0\) for every \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), whereas \(\operatorname{proj}_X\{(x,y)\in C:f(x,y)\leq0\}=\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are real vector spaces, \(C\subseteq X\times Y\) is convex, and \(D=\operatorname{proj}_X C\).
For every \(x\in D\), the fiber \(C_x=\{y\in Y:(x,y)\in C\}\) is nonempty and \(g(x)=\inf_{y\in C_x}f(x,y)>-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is quasiconvex on \(D\), but the identity \(\{g\leq\alpha\}=\operatorname{proj}_X\{f\leq\alpha\}\) can fail without fiberwise attainment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact strict-sublevel projection from closed-sublevel projection without attainment.

notation.meaning: Finite partial infimum over the fiber

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Log-convexity, log-concavity, and reciprocal duality
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(f:C\to\mathbb R_{++}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive scalar functions on convex Euclidean domains; zero-valued log-concave extensions are excluded from the reciprocal statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The function \(f\) is log-convex when \(\log f\) is convex, equivalently
\[f(tx+(1-t)y)\le f(x)^t f(y)^{1-t}\]
for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). It is log-concave when \(\log f\) is concave, equivalently the displayed inequality is reversed. Reciprocal duality is
\[f\text{ is log-convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1/f\text{ is log-concave}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-convex or log-concave according as its logarithm is convex or concave. Equivalently, its value at a convex combination lies below or above the weighted geometric mean of its endpoint values. Taking the reciprocal exchanges the two classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\log f\text{ convex}\Longleftrightarrow-\log f=\log(1/f)\text{ concave}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(f\) is log-convex if and only if \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\le f(x)^tf(y)^{1-t}\).
\(f\) is log-concave if and only if \(f(tx+(1-t)y)\ge f(x)^tf(y)^{1-t}\).
special_cases_latex: Every exponential-affine function \(f(x)=e^{a^{\mathsf T}x+b}\) is both log-convex and log-concave.
On \(\mathbb R_{++}\), \(x\mapsto x^p\) is log-convex for \(p\le0\) and log-concave for \(p\ge0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Every positive log-convex function is convex and quasiconvex.
Every positive log-concave function is quasiconcave.
Products and positive powers of log-convex functions remain log-convex whenever their domains are compatible.
boundary_notes: Strict positivity is required for the ordinary logarithm and reciprocal duality.
A nonnegative function that vanishes may be treated as extended log-concave by setting \(\log0=-\infty\), but its reciprocal is then not finite.
Log-concavity does not generally imply ordinary concavity.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-convex if and only if \(\nabla^2\log f\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order recognition of positive log-convex functions.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Sums and Suprema
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive weighted sums and finite-valued pointwise suprema preserve log-convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite nonzero nonnegative linear combination of positive log-convex functions is log-convex. A pointwise supremum of positive log-convex functions is also log-convex wherever it is finite.
assumptions_latex: The functions have a common convex domain and take values in \((0,\infty)\).
For a weighted sum, the weights are nonnegative and not all zero.
For a supremum, the pointwise supremum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The resulting weighted sum or finite-valued supremum is log-convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic closure properties specific to the positive log-convex class.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Convexity Implies Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every positive log-convex function is convex, but a positive affine function need not be log-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:C\to(0,\infty)\) is log-convex, then \[f((1-t)x+ty)\le f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y),\] so \(f\) is convex. The converse fails: \(f(x)=1+x\) is positive and affine on \((-1,\infty)\), but \(\log(1+x)\) is strictly concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is convex, while positive convexity alone does not imply log-convexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison with ordinary convexity and sharp failure of the converse.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Convex Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-convex when its logarithm is convex, equivalently when its segment values lie below the weighted geometric mean of endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is log-convex on \(C\) if the function \(x\mapsto\log f(x)\) is convex. Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)\leq f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t.\] Thus logarithmic transformation converts the multiplicative interpolation inequality for \(f\) into the ordinary additive convexity inequality for \(\log f\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-convex exactly when \(\log f\) is convex on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the positive-valued convention, avoiding extended logarithms at zero.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Taking reciprocals exchanges positive log-convex and log-concave functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-convex if and only if \(1/f\) is log-concave.

knowledge_statements.title: Extended Log-Concavity and Positive Support
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The usual zero-valued convention extends log-concavity to nonnegative functions and forces their positive support to be convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f:C\to[0,\infty)\), adopt \(\log0=-\infty\). Then \(f\) is log-concave when \(\log f\) is extended-real concave, equivalently when \[f((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t\] for \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\). If \(f\not\equiv0\), the positive support \(\{x\in C:f(x)>0\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Extended concavity of \(\log f\) is equivalent to the multiplicative inequality, and \(\{f>0\}\) is convex when nonempty.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard zero-valued extension of the seed's positive-valued convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Quasiconcavity and Its Strict Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-concavity implies quasiconcavity, while reciprocal one-plus-absolute-value has convex superlevel sets but is not log-concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:C\to[0,\infty)\) is log-concave, then every superlevel set \(\{x\in C:f(x)\ge\alpha\}\), \(\alpha>0\), is convex, so \(f\) is quasiconcave. The converse fails: \(f(x)=(1+|x|)^{-1}\) is positive and quasiconcave on \(\mathbb R\), but \(\log f(x)=-\log(1+|x|)\) is strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\), so \(f\) is not log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every positive superlevel set is convex, but quasiconcavity alone does not imply log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Level-set consequence and explicit failure of its converse.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Concave Functions
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive function is log-concave when its logarithm is concave, equivalently when its segment values exceed the weighted geometric mean of endpoint values.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) is log-concave on \(C\) if the function \(x\mapsto\log f(x)\) is concave. Equivalently, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[f((1-t)x+ty)\geq f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t.\] Thus logarithmic transformation converts the multiplicative interpolation inequality for \(f\) into the ordinary additive concavity inequality for \(\log f\).
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-concave exactly when \(\log f\) is concave on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the positive-valued convention, avoiding extended logarithms at zero.

Then \(f\) is log-concave when \(\log f\) is concave as an extended-real function, equivalently when \[f((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t.\] If \(f\not\equiv0\), its positive support \(\{x\in C:f(x)>0\}\) is convex.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Logarithmic-curvature preservation operations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex. Functions are nonnegative and are interpreted using extended logarithms when zero values are admitted. All displayed integrals are assumed finite on their effective domains.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional log-convex and log-concave functions under pointwise multiplication, positive scaling, summation, integration, marginalization, and convolution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The log-domain preservation calculus consists of the following closure rules. If \(f_i:C\to(0,+\infty)\) are log-convex and \(a_i>0\), then \(\prod_i f_i^{a_i}\) and \(\sum_i f_i\) are log-convex. If \(f_i:C\to[0,+\infty)\) are log-concave and \(a_i>0\), then \(\prod_i f_i^{a_i}\) is log-concave. If \(F:\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\to[0,+\infty)\) is jointly log-concave and \(g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^m}F(x,y)\,dy\) is finite and positive, then \(g\) is log-concave. Hence marginals of log-concave densities and convolutions \((f*g)(x)=\int f(x-y)g(y)\,dy\) are log-concave. If \(F(x,y)\) is log-convex in \(x\) for every \(y\) and its integral is finite, then \(x\mapsto\int F(x,y)\,dy\) is log-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The calculus records operations that preserve convexity or concavity after taking logarithms. Positive weighted products preserve both log-convexity and log-concavity; finite sums preserve log-convexity but generally not log-concavity. Integration preserves log-convexity when the integrand is log-convex in the retained variable. Joint log-concavity is preserved by integrating out variables, which includes marginalization and convolution.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is convex and every product, sum, or integral is defined on its stated effective domain.
For the marginal rule, \(F\) is jointly log-concave and \(0<\int F(x,y)\,dy<+\infty\) at the points under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated products, sums, parameter integrals, marginals, and convolutions remain in their indicated logarithmic-curvature classes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: For positive \(h\), log-convexity means \(\log h\) is convex, while log-concavity means \(\log h\) is concave.
The marginal rule is the functional form of the Prékopa preservation principle.
special_cases_latex: If \(p(x,y)\) is a log-concave probability density, then \(p_X(x)=\int p(x,y)\,dy\) is log-concave.
If \(f\) and \(g\) are log-concave, then their convolution \(f*g\) is log-concave.
immediate_consequences_latex: The Laplace transform \(z\mapsto\int p(x)e^{-z^Tx}\,dx\) of a nonnegative function is log-convex on its finite domain.
Positive scaling does not alter log-convexity or log-concavity.
boundary_notes: A sum of log-concave functions need not be log-concave.
For log-concave integration, separate log-concavity in each variable is not a substitute for joint log-concavity.

notation.meaning: A marginal density obtained by integrating out other coordinates.

notation.meaning: Weighted pointwise product with zero-weight factors omitted

knowledge_statements.title: Product Closure Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative powers and finite pointwise products of log-concave functions remain log-concave when zero-weight factors are omitted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt \(\log 0=-\infty\) and omit every factor with \(\alpha_i=0\). The function \(F=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i^{\alpha_i}\) satisfies, for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[F(tx+(1-t)y)\geq F(x)^tF(y)^{1-t}.\] Thus finite pointwise products and nonnegative powers preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F=\prod_{i=1}^m f_i^{\alpha_i}\) is log-concave on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite weighted pointwise products under the extended-log convention.

notation.meaning: Weighted pointwise product with zero-weight factors omitted.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Geometric Interpolation Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Binary normalized-weight form for both logarithmic curvature classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) and \(g\) belong to the same logarithmic curvature class on \(C\), then for every \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \(f^{1-\theta}g^\theta\) belongs to that class, with zero-valued log-concave factors interpreted using the extended-log convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weighted geometric interpolation preserves both log-concavity and log-convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(g\) are both log-concave, or both positive and log-convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^{1-\theta}g^\theta\) has the same logarithmic curvature class.
knowledge_statements.title: Geometric Interpolation Closure
Linear Pushforward Form
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every linear image of a log-concave density has a log-concave density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If an integrable log-concave density on \(\mathbb R^d\) is pushed forward by a surjective linear map \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\), then its pushforward has a log-concave density with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^k\).
assumptions_latex: The original density is integrable and log-concave on \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\) is surjective and linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The density of \(A_\#(F(x)\,dx)\) is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinate-free finite-dimensional form of log-concave marginalization.

notation.meaning: Pushforward of the measure μ through A

knowledge_statements.title: Prékopa Marginalization Theorem
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite Lebesgue marginal of a jointly measurable log-concave function is log-concave in the remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to[0,\infty)\) be measurable and log-concave, and suppose \[g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^m}F(x,y)\,dy<\infty\] for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Then \(g\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to[0,\infty)\) is measurable and jointly log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Foundational finite-dimensional coordinate-marginal preservation theorem.

notation.meaning: Lebesgue marginal over the second coordinate block

knowledge_statements.title: Convolution Closure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite convolution of two measurable log-concave functions is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)\) be measurable and log-concave, and suppose \[(f*g)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x-y)g(y)\,dy\] is finite for every \(x\). Then \(f*g\) is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f*g\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical convolution specialization of Prékopa marginalization.

knowledge_statements.title: Marginalization of Log-Concave Functions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prékopa’s theorem for Euclidean marginal integration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to[0,\infty)\) be measurable and log-concave in the extended sense, and suppose
\[
0<g(x):=\int_{\mathbb R^m}F(x,y)\,dy<\infty
\]
for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\). Then \(g\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R^n\). Thus, for every \(x_0,x_1\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(t\in[0,1]\),
\[
g((1-t)x_0+tx_1)\geq g(x_0)^{1-t}g(x_1)^t.
\]
Joint log-concavity of \(F\), rather than separate log-concavity in each variable, is the required hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integrating a jointly log-concave nonnegative function over some variables produces a log-concave marginal, assuming the marginal is finite and positive.
assumptions_latex: \(F:\mathbb R^{n+m}\to[0,\infty)\) is measurable and jointly log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^m}F(x,y)\,dy\) is log-concave.

notation.meaning: The marginal obtained by integrating out the y variables.
Lebesgue measure on the marginalization space.

source_refs.locator: 3.5 Log-concave and log-convex functions p. 104

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5 Log-concave and log-convex functions p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Linear Pushforward Preservation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional pushforward form of log-concave marginalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)\) be an integrable log-concave density and let \(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\) be surjective linear. Then the density obtained by integrating \(F\) over the affine fibers \(A^{-1}(z)\), with respect to the induced Lebesgue measure and a fixed normalization, is log-concave in \(z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear image of a log-concave density has a log-concave density.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an integrable log-concave density on \(\mathbb R^d\).
\(A:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^k\) is surjective and linear.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The pushforward density \(A_\#(F(x)\,dx)\) is log-concave.

notation.meaning: Pushforward of measure μ through A

knowledge_statements.title: Linear Pushforward Preservation

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convolution Closure of Log-Concavity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical convolution corollary of log-concave marginalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f,g:\mathbb R^n\to[0,\infty)\) be measurable log-concave functions such that \[(f*g)(x)=\int_{\mathbb R^n}f(x-y)g(y)\,dy\] is finite for every \(x\). Then \(f*g\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite convolution of two measurable log-concave functions is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f*g\) is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.title: Convolution Closure of Log-Concavity
Reciprocal and Power Class Exchange
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positive powers preserve logarithmic curvature, while negative powers and reciprocals exchange log-concavity and log-convexity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:C\to(0,\infty)\). A positive power \(f^\alpha\), \(\alpha>0\), preserves whether \(f\) is log-concave or log-convex. A negative power reverses the class: if \(\alpha<0\), then a log-concave \(f\) gives a log-convex \(f^\alpha\), and a log-convex \(f\) gives a log-concave \(f^\alpha\). In particular, reciprocation exchanges the two classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive powers preserve the class and negative powers reverse it.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power transformations of strictly positive logarithmic curvature classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Exponential Parameterizations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exponentiation converts concave functions to positive log-concave functions and convex functions to positive log-convex functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(u:C\to\mathbb R\), \(e^u\) is log-concave exactly when \(u\) is concave, and \(e^u\) is log-convex exactly when \(u\) is convex. Conversely, every strictly positive log-concave or log-convex function has the respective representation \(f=e^u\) with \(u=\log f\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\) is concave iff \(e^u\) is log-concave, and convex iff \(e^u\) is log-convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bijections between additive and strictly positive multiplicative curvature descriptions.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Domain Transformations
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended negative logarithm represents log-concavity as convexity; affine precomposition and positive powers preserve the property.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Adopt \(-\log 0=+\infty\) and define \(\phi:C\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \(\phi=-\log f\). Then \[f\text{ is log-concave on }C\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\phi\text{ is convex on }C.\] If \(D\) is convex, \(T:D\to C\) is affine, and \(\alpha>0\), then \(f\circ T\) and \(f^\alpha\) are log-concave on their respective domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) is log-concave exactly when \(-\log f\) is convex; affine precomposition and positive powers preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-log representation and affine changes of variables.

notation.meaning: Extended negative logarithm of the function.
Affine map whose image lies in the domain of the function.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reciprocal Class Exchange
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Transformation exchanging the two positive logarithmic curvature classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f:C\to(0,\infty)\), then \[f\text{ is log-concave}\Longleftrightarrow f^{-1}\text{ is log-convex},\qquad f\text{ is log-convex}\Longleftrightarrow f^{-1}\text{ is log-concave}.\] More generally, a positive power preserves the logarithmic curvature sign, whereas a negative power reverses it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocals and negative powers exchange log-concavity with log-convexity; positive powers preserve the class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For \(\alpha>0\), \(f^\alpha\) retains the class; for \(\alpha<0\), it belongs to the opposite class.
knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Class Exchange
Addition and Maximum Failures
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two log-affine functions have a sum and maximum that both fail log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The functions \(f(x)=e^x\) and \(g(x)=e^{-x}\) are log-affine, hence log-concave. Their sum \(h(x)=e^x+e^{-x}\) is not log-concave because \(h(0)=2<h(-1)^{1/2}h(1)^{1/2}=e+e^{-1}\). Their maximum is \(\max\{f,g\}=e^{|x|}\), whose logarithm \(|x|\) is not concave. Thus neither pointwise addition nor pointwise maximum generally preserves log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise sums and maxima do not generally preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of two common pointwise aggregation operations.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Power Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reciprocating a Gaussian-shaped log-concave function produces a log-convex, non-log-concave function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f(x)=e^{-x^2}\) is log-concave on \(\mathbb R\), but its reciprocal \(f(x)^{-1}=e^{x^2}\) is not log-concave. Thus negative powers do not generally preserve log-concavity; they reverse logarithmic curvature.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Negative powers do not universally preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp sign boundary for nonnegative-power preservation.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Log-Concavity Is Essential for Marginals
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Slice-wise log-concavity in the eliminated variable can produce a marginal with disconnected support; Prékopa requires joint log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]\) and \(F(x,y)=\mathbf1_A(x)e^{-y^2}\). For every fixed \(x\), the function \(y\mapsto F(x,y)\) is log-concave, but \[g(x)=\int_{\mathbb R}F(x,y)\,dy=\sqrt\pi\,\mathbf1_A(x)\] is not log-concave because its positive support is disconnected. Thus log-concavity only in the integrated variable cannot replace joint log-concavity.
assumptions_latex: Log-concavity permits the identically zero slice under the extended-log convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Log-concavity in the integrated variable separately is insufficient for marginal preservation.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Slice-wise log-concavity in the integrated variable does not suffice.

knowledge_statements.title: Preservation Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive sums need not preserve log-concavity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The sum of positive log-concave functions need not be log-concave. On \(\mathbb R\), let
\[
f(x)=e^{-x^2},\qquad q(x)=e^{-(x-4)^2},\qquad h(x)=f(x)+q(x).
\]
Both \(f\) and \(q\) are positive and log-concave. However,
\[
h(2)=2e^{-4}<1+e^{-16}=\sqrt{h(0)h(4)},
\]
which violates the midpoint log-concavity inequality. Thus positive addition is outside the general preservation calculus for log-concavity, even for smooth strictly positive functions on one dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two smooth positive log-concave functions can have a non-log-concave sum; separated Gaussian peaks give an explicit counterexample.
assumptions_latex: Log-concavity uses the positive-valued logarithmic definition.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\) and \(q\) are log-concave, but \(f+q\) is not log-concave.

notation.meaning: The sum of the two separated Gaussian functions.

source_refs.locator: 3.5 Log-concave and log-convex functions p. 104

source_witnesses.locator: 3.5 Log-concave and log-convex functions p. 104

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum Closure Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of pointwise maximum preservation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f=\mathbf1_{[-2,-1]}\) and \(g=\mathbf1_{[1,2]}\). Both functions are log-concave, but \(h=\max\{f,g\}=\mathbf1_{[-2,-1]\cup[1,2]}\) is not log-concave because its positive support is not convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum of indicators of two separated convex intervals has disconnected support and is not log-concave.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise maxima do not generally preserve log-concavity.

notation.meaning: Indicator of S taking values zero and one

children.top_down_role: Vector-valued convexity relative to generalized inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity relative to a cone-induced order
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a proper cone, and define \(u\preccurlyeq_K v\) by \(v-u\in K\). Let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional vector-valued convexity under the partial order induced by a closed, convex, pointed, solid cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F\) is \(K\)-convex on \(C\) if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), \[F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preccurlyeq_K \theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y),\] equivalently, \(\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y)-F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\in K\). It is strictly \(K\)-convex if the difference belongs to \(\operatorname{int}K\) whenever \(x\ne y\) and \(0<\theta<1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued mapping is cone-ordered convex when its value at every convex combination is below the corresponding convex combination of its endpoint values in the partial order induced by the cone. Strict cone convexity requires the order difference to lie in the cone interior for distinct endpoints and an interior mixing weight.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed, convex, pointed, and has nonempty interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\preccurlyeq_K\theta F(x)+(1-\theta)F(y)\) for all \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if \(w^TF\) is an ordinary convex function for every \(w\in K^*\).
If \(F\) is differentiable on an open convex domain, \(K\)-convexity is equivalent to \(F(y)\succcurlyeq_K F(x)+DF(x)(y-x)\) for all \(x,y\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), \(K\)-convexity is componentwise convexity.
For \(K=\mathbb S_+^m\), the definition gives matrix convexity under the Loewner order.
For \(m=1\) and \(K=\mathbb R_+\), it reduces to ordinary scalar convexity.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every restriction of a \(K\)-convex mapping to a line segment is \(K\)-convex.
Nonnegative dual-cone scalarizations provide scalar convex certificates.
boundary_notes: The induced order is generally partial rather than total.
Strict \(K\)-convexity requires \(\operatorname{int}K\ne\varnothing\); alternative relative-interior conventions are outside this definition.

notation.meaning: Cone order defined by membership of the difference in \(K\).

source_refs.locator: Section 3.6.2, “Convexity with respect to a generalized inequality,” definition of K-convexity and dual characterization

children.title: Cone-Convex Mappings
children.top_down_role: Vector-valued curvature relative to an ordering cone.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Epigraph Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A mapping is cone-convex exactly when its cone epigraph is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[\operatorname{epi}_K F=\{(x,y)\in C\times Y:y-F(x)\in K\}.\] If \(C\) and \(K\) are convex, then \[F\text{ is }K\text{-convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\operatorname{epi}_K F\text{ is convex}.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if \(\operatorname{epi}_K F\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometric product-space representation of cone-convexity.

knowledge_statements.title: Cone-Convex Mappings
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vector-valued mapping is cone-convex when every value on a chord lies below the corresponding chord average in the cone order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mapping \(F:C\to Y\) is called \(K\)-convex if, for every \(x,y\in C\) and \(t\in[0,1]\), \[F(tx+(1-t)y)\preceq_K tF(x)+(1-t)F(y).\] Equivalently, \[tF(x)+(1-t)F(y)-F(tx+(1-t)y)\in K.\] When \(Y=\mathbb{R}\) and \(K=\mathbb{R}_+\), this definition reduces to ordinary scalar convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a convex subset of a real vector space \(X\).
\(Y\) is a real vector space ordered by a convex cone \(K\subseteq Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex exactly when its chord residual always belongs to \(K\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vector-valued convexity relative to a fixed ordering cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

children.title: Scalarization Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Reduction of order convexity to scalar convex function families.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonclosed-Cone Scalarization Boundary
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nonclosed ordering cone, dual-cone scalarizations detect convexity relative to the cone's closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\) be a convex cone in a finite-dimensional space and let \(F:C\to Y\), where \(C\) is convex. Then \[y^*\circ F\text{ is convex for every }y^*\in K^*\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F\text{ is }\overline K\text{-convex}.\] Hence, for nonclosed \(K\), these tests need not imply \(K\)-convexity.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a convex cone in a finite-dimensional real vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: All \(K^*\)-scalarizations are convex if and only if \(F\) is \(\overline K\)-convex.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure boundary for dual-cone scalarization when the ordering cone is not closed.

notation.meaning: Dual cone, which is unchanged upon closing K.

knowledge_statements.title: Scalarization Interfaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a closed finite-dimensional ordering cone, cone-convexity is equivalent to convexity of all dual-cone scalarizations; a conically generating test family suffices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K^*=\{y^*\in Y^*:y^*(k)\geq0\ \forall k\in K\}\). Then \[F\text{ is }K\text{-convex}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y^*\circ F\text{ is convex for every }y^*\in K^*.\] The same test is valid for any subset \(S\subseteq K^*\) satisfying \(\overline{\operatorname{cone}}S=K^*\).
assumptions_latex: \(X\) and \(Y\) are finite-dimensional real vector spaces.
\(C\subseteq X\) is convex, \(K\subseteq Y\) is a closed convex cone, and \(F:C\to Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if \(y^*\circ F\) is convex for every \(y^*\in K^*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dual-cone scalarization in finite-dimensional codomains.

notation.meaning: Dual cone of linear functionals nonnegative on the ordering cone.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-cone scalarization family
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex, let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a proper cone with dual \(K^*\), and let \(F:C\to\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear scalarization of finite-dimensional cone-ordered mappings; the definition concerns convexity certification, not completeness of weighted-sum optimization for every Pareto point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The scalarization interface of \((F,K)\) is the family \[\mathcal S_K(F)=\{\varphi_w:C\to\mathbb R\mid \varphi_w(x)=\langle w,F(x)\rangle,\ w\in K^*\}.\] The family is a complete linear certificate for cone convexity: \(F\) is \(K\)-convex if and only if every \(\varphi_w\) with \(w\in K^*\) is convex. For strict \(K\)-convexity, every nonzero \(w\in K^*\) yields a strictly convex scalarization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The scalarization interface pairs a vector-valued mapping with every nonnegative linear functional from the dual cone. Cone convexity is exactly equivalent to ordinary convexity of all these scalar functions. Thus order-valued Jensen inequalities can be checked through a separating family of scalar inequalities.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a proper cone and \(K^*=\{w:\langle w,k\rangle\ge0\ \forall k\in K\}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\text{ is }K\text{-convex}\iff(\forall w\in K^*)\;x\mapsto\langle w,F(x)\rangle\text{ is convex}.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \(x,y\in C\) and \(\theta\in[0,1]\), cone convexity is equivalent to \(\langle w,F(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)\rangle\le\theta\langle w,F(x)\rangle+(1-\theta)\langle w,F(y)\rangle\) for all \(w\in K^*\).
For matrix-valued \(F\) and \(K=\mathbb S_+^m\), rank-one scalarizations are \(x\mapsto z^TF(x)z\).
special_cases_latex: When \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\), coordinate vectors in \(K^*\) recover the component functions of \(F\).
For a vector optimization objective, a weight \(w\in\operatorname{int}K^*\) produces the weighted-sum objective \(x\mapsto\langle w,F(x)\rangle\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A single scalarization can disprove \(K\)-convexity if it is nonconvex.
The full dual-cone family separates any Jensen residual lying outside \(K\).
boundary_notes: Using only one weight generally does not certify \(K\)-convexity.
Weighted-sum scalarization need not generate every Pareto point in a nonconvex vector optimization problem.

notation.meaning: Family of dual-cone linear scalarizations of \(F\).

source_refs.locator: Section 3.6.2, “Dual characterization of K-convexity”; Section 4.7.4, “Scalarization”

children.title: Partial-Order Comparability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of scalar intuition in incompletely ordered codomains.

knowledge_statements.title: One Scalarization Does Not Detect Cone-Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A single positive scalarization can be convex even though the vector mapping is not cone-convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C=\mathbb{R}\), \(K=\mathbb{R}_+^2\), and \(F(x)=(x^2,-x^2)\). For \(s(y)=y_1+y_2\), \((s\circ F)(x)=0\) is convex. Nevertheless, \(F\) is not \(K\)-convex: the chord residual at \(-1,1\) and \(t=\tfrac12\) is \((1,-1)\notin K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convexity of one positive scalarization does not imply \(K\)-convexity.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete failure of testing vector convexity with one positive scalarization.

knowledge_statements.title: Totality Boundary for Cone Orders
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cone order is total exactly when the cone or its negative contains every vector; pointedness alone does not ensure comparability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the cone-induced relation \(u\preceq_Kv\iff v-u\in K\), every pair of vectors in \(Y\) is comparable if and only if \[K\cup(-K)=Y.\] Thus a pointed cone may define a partial order without defining a total order; for example, \(\mathbb{R}_+^2\cup(-\mathbb{R}_+^2)\neq\mathbb{R}^2\).
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is a cone in a real vector space \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\preceq_K\) is total if and only if \(K\cup(-K)=Y\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic characterization of when cone comparability extends to every pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Comparability, minimum, and minimality in cone orders
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be a proper cone, let \(u\preccurlyeq_Kv\iff v-u\in K\), and let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^m\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order-theoretic boundary between scalar intuition and incompletely ordered vector codomains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Two points \(u,v\in\mathbb R^m\) are \(K\)-comparable if \(u\preccurlyeq_Kv\) or \(v\preccurlyeq_Ku\); otherwise they are incomparable. A point \(u\in S\) is a minimum element if \((\forall v\in S)\ u\preccurlyeq_Kv\), equivalently \(S\subseteq u+K\). It is a minimal element if \((v\in S\text{ and }v\preccurlyeq_Ku)\Rightarrow v=u\), equivalently \((u-K)\cap S=\{u\}\). The comparability boundary is the set of pairs \((u,v)\in S^2\) with \(v-u\notin K\cup(-K)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cone orders generally leave some pairs incomparable. A minimum is below every point and, if it exists, is unique. A minimal point merely has no distinct feasible point below it, so a set may have many minimal points. The comparability boundary consists precisely of pairs whose difference belongs to neither the cone nor its negative.
assumptions_latex: \(K\) is closed, convex, pointed, and solid.
\(S\) is an arbitrary subset of the ordered vector space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u\text{ is minimum}\iff S\subseteq u+K\), whereas \(u\text{ is minimal}\iff(u-K)\cap S=\{u\}\); incomparable pairs satisfy \(v-u\notin K\cup(-K)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Comparability of \(u,v\) is equivalent to \(v-u\in K\cup(-K)\).
Minimality excludes strict improvement in the cone order but does not require comparison with every element of \(S\).
special_cases_latex: For \(K=\mathbb R_+\), the order is total and minimum and minimal element coincide.
For \(K=\mathbb R_+^m\) with \(m>1\), componentwise tradeoffs commonly produce incomparable points.
immediate_consequences_latex: A set has at most one minimum element because the cone order is antisymmetric.
Distinct minimal elements must be mutually incomparable.
boundary_notes: Scalar notions such as \(\min S\) cannot be transferred unchanged to a partial order.
Minimality is weaker than weak Pareto minimality conventions based on \(\operatorname{int}K\); those conventions are not identified here.

notation.meaning: Set \(\{u-k:k\in K\}\) of points no greater than \(u\).
Set of points no smaller than \(u\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lower- and upper-curvature regularity classes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(D\) be a convex subset of a Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\), and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be convex and differentiable where an upper-curvature condition is imposed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Absolute Hilbert-space curvature classes described by a lower modulus and an upper quadratic model; relative-curvature variants require a separate reference function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an increasing function \(\phi:\mathbb R_+\to[0,+\infty]\) vanishing only at \(0\) and a constant \(L\ge0\), define \(\mathcal C_{\phi,L}(D)\) to consist of functions satisfying, for all \(x,y\in D\) and \(\theta\in(0,1)\), \[f(\theta x+(1-\theta)y)+\theta(1-\theta)\phi(\|x-y\|)\le \theta f(x)+(1-\theta)f(y),\] and, whenever \(f\) is differentiable on \(D\), \[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2.\] The first inequality gives quantitative lower curvature; the second gives quantitative upper curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quantitative curvature class fixes a modulus that measures the Jensen deficit from below and a constant controlling the quadratic Taylor remainder from above. Uniform convexity corresponds to a general positive modulus, strong convexity to a quadratic modulus, and gradient smoothness to the quadratic upper model.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is increasing and vanishes only at \(0\).
The upper model is imposed only where \(f\) is differentiable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership in \(\mathcal C_{\phi,L}(D)\) means that \(f\) has lower curvature modulus \(\phi\) and upper quadratic-curvature constant \(L\) on \(D\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Strong convexity with parameter \(\mu>0\) is obtained from \(\phi(t)=\frac\mu2t^2\).
For convex differentiable functions on the whole Hilbert space, the upper quadratic model is equivalent to \(L\)-Lipschitz continuity of \(\nabla f\).
special_cases_latex: \(\phi=0\) formally recovers ordinary convexity, though it is not a uniform-convexity modulus under the stated positivity convention.
If both \(\phi(t)=\frac\mu2t^2\) and the upper model hold, then \(f\) is \(\mu\)-strongly convex and \(L\)-smooth.
immediate_consequences_latex: The parameters are monotone: a valid upper constant remains valid when enlarged, and a valid lower modulus remains valid when decreased.
Quadratic lower and upper control bound the curvature scale between \(\mu\) and \(L\).
boundary_notes: The constants and moduli depend on the chosen norm.
Self-concordance and relative smoothness are distinct nonuniform curvature models and are not implied by this definition.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lipschitz-gradient smoothness
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((\mathbb E,\|\cdot\|)\) be a finite-dimensional normed space with dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), let \(D\subseteq\mathbb E\) be convex, and let \(f\) be differentiable on an open set containing \(D\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Deterministic first-order smoothness on a convex set, with arbitrary primal and dual norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(L\ge0\), the function \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth on \(D\) if \[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\|\qquad(\forall x,y\in D).\] The least admissible \(L\), when attained or interpreted as an infimum, is the gradient Lipschitz modulus of \(f\) on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A differentiable function is gradient-smooth on a convex set when its gradient is globally Lipschitz there, measured from the primal norm to its dual norm. The smoothness parameter is the uniform upper bound on how rapidly the gradient can change per unit displacement.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable at every point of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\forall x,y\in D)\;\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|_*\le L\|x-y\|.\)
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(f\) is convex and differentiable on the whole Hilbert space, \(L\)-smoothness is equivalent to \(f(y)\le f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2\).

In the same convex Hilbert setting with \(L>0\), it is equivalent to \(\langle
abla f(x)-
abla f(y),x-yangle\ge L^{-1}\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|^2\).
special_cases_latex: Affine functions are \(0\)-smooth.
For \(f(x)=\frac12x^TAx+b^Tx+c\) in Euclidean space with symmetric \(A\), the least smoothness constant is \(\|A\|_2\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-Order Taylor Formula with Segment Remainder
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A general multivariable-calculus theorem for twice continuously differentiable real-valued functions on an open set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(f:U\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and let \(x\in U\) and \(r>0\) satisfy \(B(x,r)\subseteq U\). Then, for every \(y\in B(x,r)\), there exists \(\xi\in[x,y]\) such that \[f(y)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)+\frac12(y-x)^T\nabla^2f(\xi)(y-x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a twice continuously differentiable function, each point y in a ball contained in the open domain admits a second-order Taylor formula about x, with the Hessian evaluated at some point on the segment from x to y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists\xi\in[x,y]\) such that \(f(y)=f(x)+\nabla f(x)^T(y-x)+\tfrac12(y-x)^T\nabla^2f(\xi)(y-x)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Hessian Characterization of L-Smoothness in ℓp Geometry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global second-order characterization using the operator norm from the primal ℓp norm to its dual ℓq norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, let \(L\geq0\), let \(p\in[1,\infty]\), and let \(q\in[1,\infty]\) satisfy \(\tfrac1p+\tfrac1q=1\). Then \(f\) is \(L\)-smooth with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_p\) if and only if \(\|\nabla^2f(x)\|_{p,q}\leq L\) for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice continuously differentiable function on all of R^n is L-smooth in ℓp geometry exactly when every Hessian has operator norm from ℓp to the dual ℓq bounded by L.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\text{ is }L\text{-smooth with respect to }\|\cdot\|_p\iff\forall x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \|\nabla^2f(x)\|_{p,q}\leq L.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Lipschitz-Gradient Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Gradient smoothness may hold globally, only on a specified domain, or locally with constants that need not be uniform.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(f\) has an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient on \(C\) if \[\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\qquad(x,y\in C).\] The regime is global when \(C=\mathbb{R}^n\), restricted when the inequality is asserted only on a specified proper subset \(C\), and local when every point has a neighborhood on which the inequality holds with some finite, possibly neighborhood-dependent constant. Global Lipschitzness implies restricted and local Lipschitzness, but neither converse holds without additional uniformity.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex and \(f\) is differentiable on an open set containing \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The global, restricted, and local \(L\)-smoothness regimes are distinguished by where \(\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|\leq L\|x-y\|\) is required.
