knowledge_statements.statement_title: Three-point Bregman defect and identity
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space. Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex, differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and let \(D_h\) be its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiable finite-dimensional geometry. All three points lie in the differentiability region so every displayed divergence and gradient is defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(x,y,z\in U\), define the three-point Bregman defect by
\[\Delta_h(x,y,z)=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).\]
The three-point geometry is the identity
\[\Delta_h(x,y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle,\]
or equivalently
\[D_h(x,z)=D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)+\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The three-point Bregman defect compares the direct divergence from z to x with the two-stage divergences through y. It equals the pairing of the dual-coordinate displacement ∇h(y)−∇h(z) with the primal displacement x−y.

children.title: Bregman Metric-Axiom Boundary
children.top_down_role: Boundaries separating Bregman divergences from metric distances.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-axiom profile of a Bregman divergence
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on a nonempty open convex set \(U\subseteq E\), and let \(D_h:U\times U\to[0,+\infty)\) be its Bregman divergence.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: This definition records exactly where a Bregman divergence agrees with or departs from the axioms of a metric; it does not classify all generators producing metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the symmetry and triangle defects by
\[S_h(x,y)=D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,x),\qquad T_h(x,y,z)=D_h(x,z)-D_h(x,y)-D_h(y,z).\]
The Bregman metric-axiom profile consists of nonnegativity \(D_h(x,y)\geq0\), reflexivity \(D_h(x,x)=0\), separation when \(D_h(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y\), symmetry when \(S_h\equiv0\), and the triangle inequality when \(T_h\leq0\) for every ordered triple. A Bregman divergence is metric-valued on \(U\) precisely when separation, symmetry, and the triangle inequality all hold in addition to nonnegativity and reflexivity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The metric boundary is described by two defects. The symmetry defect compares the two orientations, while the triangle defect compares a direct divergence with a two-leg route. Every convex differentiable generator gives nonnegativity and zero diagonal; strict convexity gives point separation, but symmetry and the triangle inequality are additional properties and generally fail.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq E\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h\) has the metric axioms on \(U\) exactly when \(D_h(x,y)=0\Rightarrow x=y\), \(S_h(x,y)=0\), and \(T_h(x,y,z)\leq0\) for all \(x,y,z\in U\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(S_h(x,y)=2(h(x)-h(y))-\langle\nabla h(x)+\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle\).
\(T_h(x,y,z)=\langle\nabla h(y)-\nabla h(z),x-y\rangle\).
special_cases_latex: For a positive-definite quadratic generator, \(D_h\) is a squared norm: it is symmetric and separating, but \(D_h\) itself generally fails the triangle inequality; \(\sqrt{2D_h}\) is the associated metric.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strict convexity supplies separation but does not supply symmetry or a triangle inequality.
The term “divergence” does not imply that \(D_h\) is a distance metric.
boundary_notes: A squared norm is not itself a metric except in degenerate restrictions, despite being symmetric and nonnegative.
This profile concerns \(D_h\), not transformations such as \(\sqrt{D_h}\) or symmetrizations such as \(D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)\).

notation.meaning: Symmetry defect of the directed divergence.

review_flags: The supplied source hints did not provide an inspected locator supporting the complete Bregman metric-axiom profile.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetrized Bregman Identity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two orientations of a Bregman divergence sum to the gradient-monotonicity pairing of their endpoints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(C\), then for all \(x,y\in C\), \[D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)=\langle\nabla h(x)-\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.\]
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(C\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,x)=\langle\nabla h(x)-\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Algebraic identity measuring orientation dependence.
A one-dimensional negative-entropy counterexample to symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=t\log t\) on \((0,\infty)\). Its Bregman divergence is \[D_f(x,y)=x\log(x/y)-x+y.\] At \(x=1\) and \(y=2\), one has \[D_f(1,2)=1-\log 2,\qquad D_f(2,1)=2\log 2-1.\] These values are unequal, so a Bregman divergence need not satisfy \(D_f(x,y)=D_f(y,x)\), even when its generator is smooth and strictly convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative-entropy Bregman divergence assigns different values to the ordered pairs (1,2) and (2,1), so symmetry fails.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically correct and counterexample is the appropriate kind for this failure leaf, but the record cites no inspectable source with a specific locator. Standard-field rationale alone does not satisfy the citation review requirement.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetric Bregman Divergence Characterization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic characterization proposed under sufficient smoothness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(h\in C^3(C)\) be convex. Then \(D_h\) is symmetric on \(C\times C\) if and only if \(h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+b\) with constant \(Q\succeq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under sufficient smoothness, symmetric Bregman divergences are generated by quadratic functions up to affine terms.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h\text{ is symmetric}\iff h(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+b.
knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Bregman Divergence Characterization

intermediate_metadata.reason: The local inventory is the explicit negative-entropy asymmetry seed and the accepted symmetrized identity. The quadratic symmetric classification was deferred to Metric-Compatible Special Cases; triangle-inequality failure and primal-dual reversal were excluded as sibling scopes.

knowledge_statements.title: Triangle Inequality Forces Affinity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A twice-differentiable Bregman divergence satisfies the global triangle inequality only in the trivial affine, zero-divergence case.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty, open, and convex, and let \(h\in C^2(C)\) be convex. If \[D_h(x,z)\le D_h(x,y)+D_h(y,z)\quad\text{for all }x,y,z\in C,\] then \(h\) is affine on \(C\) and \(D_h\equiv0\). Conversely, an affine generator produces the zero divergence, which satisfies the triangle inequality.
assumptions_latex: \(C\subset\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty, open, and convex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D_h\equiv0\quad\text{and}\quad h\text{ is affine on }C.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp smooth boundary for the triangle inequality applied to the divergence itself.
Failure concerns the divergence itself, not its square root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the smooth strictly convex generator \(f(t)=\tfrac12t^2\) on \(\mathbb{R}\), the associated Bregman divergence is \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^2.\] Taking \(x=0\), \(y=1\), and \(z=2\) gives \[D_f(0,2)=2>1=D_f(0,1)+D_f(1,2).\] Thus even a symmetric Bregman divergence need not obey the triangle inequality and therefore need not itself be a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared Euclidean distance is a Bregman divergence, but at 0, 1, and 2 it violates the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Triangle-Inequality Failure

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The squared-Euclidean calculation correctly demonstrates failure of the triangle inequality for the divergence itself, and counterexample fits the leaf. No source reference or inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Semidefinite Quadratics Give a Quotient Metric
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-semidefinite quadratic yields a Mahalanobis pseudometric; it is a genuine metric exactly for positive-definite curvature, and otherwise becomes one on the quotient by the null space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\langle b,x\rangle+c\) with symmetric \(Q\succeq0\), \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y),\qquad \sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\|Q^{1/2}(x-y)\|_2.\] The square root is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\) exactly when \(Q\succ0\). If \(Q\) is singular, it is a pseudometric on \(\mathbb R^n\) and induces a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\). The affine part of \(f\) does not affect the divergence.
assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{2D_f}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\iff Q\succ0\); for singular \(Q\), it induces a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quadratic metric-compatible cases and their exact point-separation boundary.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_f(x,y):=\sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\sqrt{(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y)}\) is a metric.

notation.meaning: metric induced by the positive-definite quadratic form

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive-definite quadratic generators yield Mahalanobis metric geometry after taking a square root.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be symmetric positive definite and let \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\langle b,x\rangle+c\) on \(\mathbb{R}^n\). Then \[D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y).\] Consequently \[d_f(x,y):=\sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\|Q^{1/2}(x-y)\|_2\] is a metric. The affine part of \(f\) does not affect \(D_f\). The divergence \(D_f\) remains a squared metric and generally does not itself satisfy the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite quadratic generator produces half the squared Mahalanobis distance; its square root is a genuine metric.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Compatible Special Cases

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The positive-definite quadratic case and its induced Mahalanobis metric are stated correctly, and property fits this special-cases leaf. The claim nevertheless lacks a cited source with a section, theorem, definition, or page locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed smooth characterization of symmetric Bregman divergences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On an open convex domain, symmetry of a sufficiently smooth Bregman divergence forces its generator to be quadratic-affine.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth symmetric Bregman divergence has a quadratic-affine generator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(x,y)=D_f(y,x)\ \forall x,y\in U\Rightarrow f\text{ is quadratic-affine on }U\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx+\langle b,x\rangle+c\) with \(Q\succeq0\), \(\sqrt{2D_f(x,y)}=\|Q^{1/2}(x-y)\|_2\). If \(Q\) is singular, it is a pseudometric on \(\mathbb R^n\) and becomes a metric on the quotient \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\).

assumptions_latex: \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) is symmetric positive semidefinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sqrt{2D_f}\) is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n\iff Q\succ0\), and otherwise is a metric on \(\mathbb R^n/\ker Q\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left Bregman projection onto a feasible set
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space, let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and let \(C\subseteq E\) satisfy \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-valued left projection with the feasible point in the first divergence argument. Existence and uniqueness are not built into the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a base point \(y\in U\), the left Bregman projection of \(y\) onto \(C\) is
\[P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y).\]
Its projection value is
\[d^{h,L}_C(y)=\inf_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y).\]
The projection is defined as a set of minimizers; it may be empty, contain one point, or contain several points unless further hypotheses are imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The left Bregman projection of y onto C is the set of feasible points x minimizing the divergence D_h(x,y), where the variable occupies the first argument and y is the fixed base point. The associated projection value is the corresponding infimum.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\{p\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h:D_h(p,y)=d^{h,L}_C(y)\}\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in E}\{\iota_C(x)+h(x)-\langle\nabla h(y),x\rangle\}\), where constants independent of \(x\) are omitted.
\(p\in P^{h,L}_C(y)\) exactly when \(p\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) and \(D_h(p,y)\leq D_h(x,y)\) for every \(x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\).
special_cases_latex: For \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), \(P^{h,L}_C\) is the ordinary Euclidean projector.
If \(C=\{c\}\subseteq\operatorname{dom}h\), then \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\{c\}\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(C\) is convex and \(h\) is strictly convex on \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), then the projection contains at most one point.
Attainment of the infimum is a separate requirement from finiteness of the projection value.
boundary_notes: Closedness of \(C\) alone need not ensure attainment when the generator domain is open or the objective is not level-bounded.
The right projection minimizes \(D_h(y,x)\) and is a distinct orientation.
review_flags: The supplied Euclidean-projection locators do not directly support this Bregman projection definition and its orientation/domain conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The set-valued left-projection definition is plausible and distinguishes attainment from definition, but no cited source supports its domain and orientation conventions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Left- and right-oriented Bregman projections
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\). Let \(C\subseteq E\) and fix \(y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, set-valued formulation distinguishing the two minimization problems created by the directed argument order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The orientation-dual projection pair is
\[P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y),\qquad
P^{h,R}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap U}D_h(y,x).\]
The left orientation varies the evaluation point of the first-order-model error. The right orientation varies its base point, so differentiability requires the variable \(x\) to lie in \(U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: There are two directed Bregman projections. The left projection minimizes D_h(x,y) over feasible x, while the right projection minimizes D_h(y,x). These are different optimization objects because a Bregman divergence is generally asymmetric and because the variable in the right problem must lie where the generator is differentiable.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is proper and convex and differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\).
The left feasible domain is \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\), while the right feasible domain is \(C\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ordered pair \((P^{h,L}_C(y),P^{h,R}_C(y))\) is defined by the two orientation-specific argmin sets above.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}\{h(x)-\langle\nabla h(y),x\rangle\}\), with extended-value conventions.
\(P^{h,R}_C(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C\cap U}\{h(y)-h(x)-\langle\nabla h(x),y-x\rangle\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(D_h\) is symmetric on \(C\cup\{y\}\), then \(P^{h,L}_C(y)=P^{h,R}_C(y)\).
For a positive-definite quadratic generator, both orientations reduce to the same weighted Euclidean projection.
immediate_consequences_latex: Existence or uniqueness of one orientation does not by definition imply existence or uniqueness of the other.
The two projection values can differ whenever the divergence is asymmetric.
boundary_notes: The right projection objective need not be convex in its variable, even when \(h\) is convex.
Points in \(C\cap(\operatorname{dom}h\setminus U)\) may be eligible for the left problem but not for the right problem.
review_flags: No inspected authoritative locator was available for both orientation-specific projection definitions and their distinct feasible domains.
knowledge_statements.title: Left- and right-oriented Bregman projections

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two orientation-specific argmin definitions are mathematically distinct and plausible, but they have no independently inspectable support.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Softmax formula for entropy-regularized simplex maximization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The entropy convention extends continuously to the boundary of the simplex by setting \(0\ln0=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(m\in\mathbb N\), \(\Delta_m=\{u\in\mathbb R^m:u^{(j)}\ge0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ \sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}=1\}\), and \(d_2(u)=\ln m+\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\ln u^{(j)}\), with \(0\ln0=0\). Fix \(\mu_2>0\), and define \(s^{(j)}=f_j+\langle g_j,\bar x-x_j\rangle\). Then \[\max_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}s^{(j)}-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}\] has a unique maximizer \(\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\), whose components are \[\nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{\exp(s^{(j)}/\mu_2)}{\sum_{l=1}^m\exp(s^{(l)}/\mu_2)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear objective regularized by scaled negative entropy over the probability simplex has a unique optimizer, and that optimizer is the softmax of the coefficient vector divided by the regularization parameter.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}s^{(j)}-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}=\{\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\},\quad \nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{e^{s^{(j)}/\mu_2}}{\sum_{l=1}^m e^{s^{(l)}/\mu_2}}

\Delta_m=\left\{u\in\mathbb R^m:u^{(j)}\ge0\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ \sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}=1\right\},
\qquad
d_2(u)=\ln m+\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\ln u^{(j)},
\]

\[
\max_{u\in\Delta_m}\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}s^{(j)}-\mu_2d_2(u)\right\}
\]
has a unique maximizer \(\nu_{\mu_2}(\bar x)\), with
\[
\nu_{\mu_2}^{(j)}(\bar x)=\frac{\exp(s^{(j)}/\mu_2)}{\sum_{l=1}^m\exp(s^{(l)}/\mu_2)},\qquad j=1,\ldots,m.
\]

abla f(y))\quad(x\in C),\] and, setwise, \[P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y)=
abla f^*\!\left(P^{\mathrm L}_{C^*,f^*}(
abla f(y))ight).\] Either side may be empty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y)=\nabla f^*(P^{\mathrm L}_{C^*,f^*}(\nabla f(y)))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Legendre conversion of a right primal projection into a left dual projection.

notation.meaning: gradient image of the primal constraint set

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_f(y,x)\).

notation.meaning: set of right Bregman projections of y onto C

knowledge_statements.scope_note: “Right” means the constraint variable occupies the second divergence argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(x,y\in U\), let \(D_f(x,y)=f(x)-f(y)-\langle\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle\). The right Bregman projection of \(y\) onto \(C\) is the possibly empty, set-valued map \[P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_f(y,x).\] Hence \(p\in P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y)\) exactly when \(p\in C\) and \(D_f(y,p)\leq D_f(y,x)\) for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The right Bregman projection minimizes the divergence over constraint points placed in the second argument.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directional-derivative criteria for differentiability of a convex function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient linearity criterion, together with a sufficient coordinate-partial criterion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let f be convex on \mathbb R^n and suppose f(x)\in\mathbb R. Then f is differentiable at x if and only if the directional-derivative function y\mapsto f'(x;y) is linear. Moreover, f is differentiable at x if all n finite two-sided partial derivatives \partial f(x)/\partial\xi_j exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A convex function finite at a point is differentiable there exactly when its directional derivative is linear in the direction. It is already sufficient that all finite two-sided coordinate partial derivatives exist at that point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ differentiable at }x\iff f'(x;\cdot)\text{ is linear};\qquad \left[\frac{\partial f}{\partial\xi_j}(x)\in\mathbb R\text{ exists two-sided }\forall j\right]\Rightarrow f\text{ differentiable at }x.

source_evidence.locator: Complete book / 25. Differentiability of Convex Functions / Theorem 25.2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Quadratic representation and gradient of an affine-model value function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean partial minimization of a weighted collection of affine models with quadratic regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b^{(j)}=\langle g_j,x_j\rangle-f_j\), let \(A^Tu=\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}g_j\), and define \[\phi(u)=\min_x\left\{\sum_{j=1}^m u^{(j)}\bigl(f_j+\langle g_j,x-x_j\rangle\bigr)+\tfrac12\|x\|^2\right\}.\] Then, for every \(u\in\mathbb{R}^m\), \[\phi(u)=-\langle b,u\rangle-\tfrac12\|A^Tu\|_*^2.\] Moreover, \(\phi\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb{R}^m\) and \(\nabla\phi(u)=-b-AA^Tu\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The quadratically regularized value of a weighted affine model is the concave quadratic −⟨b,u⟩−one half the squared dual norm of A transpose u, and its gradient is −b−AA transpose u.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall u\in\mathbb{R}^m:\quad \phi(u)=-\langle b,u\rangle-\tfrac12\|A^Tu\|_*^2,\qquad \nabla\phi(u)=-b-AA^Tu.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetry Characterizes Quadratic Generators
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth Bregman divergence is symmetric exactly in the quadratic-generator regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open and convex and let \(f\in C^3(U)\) be convex. Then \(D_f(x,y)=D_f(y,x)\) for all \(x,y\in U\) if and only if \(\nabla^2f\) is constant on \(U\), equivalently \(f(x)=\tfrac12\langle x,Qx\rangle+\langle a,x\rangle+c\) on \(U\) for a symmetric positive-semidefinite \(Q\). In this regime the left and right projection objectives coincide.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(x,y)=D_f(y,x)\ \forall x,y\in U\iff \nabla^2f\text{ is constant on }U\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth boundary between orientation-independent and directed Bregman geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Different Minimizers Under Orientation Reversal
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For negative entropy on a two-point constraint set, the two projection orientations select different points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=t\log t\) on \((0,\infty)\), \(C=\{1,4\}\), and \(y=9/4\). Then \[P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{1\},\qquad P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y)=\{4\}.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-set example of distinct left and right projections.

notation.meaning: left and right Bregman projection sets

knowledge_statements.title: Convexity Is Orientation-Dependent
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generator convexity always makes the left projection objective convex, but not the right projection objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For differentiable convex \(f\), the map \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is convex. In contrast, for \(f(t)=-\log t\) on \((0,\infty)\), \[D_f(y,x)=\frac{y}{x}-\log\frac{y}{x}-1,\qquad \frac{d^2}{dx^2}D_f(y,x)=\frac{2y-x}{x^3},\] so the right-oriented objective is nonconvex on intervals containing points with \(x>2y\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and convex for the left-objective assertion.
For the failure regime, \(f(t)=-\log t\) and \(x,y>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\text{ is convex, whereas }x\mapsto D_f(y,x)\text{ need not be convex}.\)
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left-objective convexity and failure of universal right-objective convexity.

notation.meaning: left and right Bregman projection sets

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite constraint set makes the orientation difference explicit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(t)=t\log t\), \(C=\{1,4\}\), and \(y=9/4\). Direct comparison using \(D_f(a,b)=a\log(a/b)-a+b\) gives \[D_f(1,y)<D_f(4,y),\qquad D_f(y,4)<D_f(y,1).\] Therefore \[P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{1\},\qquad P^{\mathrm R}_{C,f}(y)=\{4\}.\] Thus exchanging the arguments can change the projection, and properties of one orientation cannot generally be transferred to the other without additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For negative entropy on a two-point constraint set, the left and right projections of the same point select different elements.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Orientation Asymmetry

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attained, unique, and strongly well-posed Bregman projection regimes
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) generate \(D_h\), let \(C\subseteq E\), let \(y\) be an admissible base point, and define \(F_y(x)=\iota_C(x)+D_h(x,y)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional left-projection problem. The terms classify properties of a fixed triple \((h,C,y)\), rather than asserting that a broad class automatically possesses them.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The left Bregman projection problem for \((h,C,y)\) is called attained if \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_y\neq\varnothing\), uniquely attained if \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_y=\{p\}\), and strongly well posed if it is uniquely attained and every sequence \((x_k)\subseteq C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) satisfying \(D_h(x_k,y)\to\inf_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)\) converges to \(p\). A standard compact-level regime is characterized by lower semicontinuity of \(F_y\), nonempty domain, and compactness of one nonempty sublevel set \(\{x:F_y(x)\leq\alpha\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman projection problem is attained when its argmin is nonempty, uniquely attained when that argmin is a singleton, and strongly well posed when every minimizing sequence converges to the unique minimizer. A compact-level regime records lower semicontinuity, feasibility, and compactness of a nonempty sublevel set.
assumptions_latex: \(F_y(x)=\iota_C(x)+D_h(x,y)\) is defined on a finite-dimensional space.
\(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\neq\varnothing\), and \(y\) is an admissible second argument of \(D_h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong well-posedness means \(\operatorname*{argmin}F_y=\{p\}\) and \(F_y(x_k)\downarrow\inf F_y\Rightarrow x_k\to p\) for every minimizing sequence \((x_k)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Unique attainment is equivalent to \(P_C^{h,L}(y)=\{p\}\).
Level-boundedness means that every sublevel set \(\{x:F_y(x)\leq\alpha\}\) is bounded; together with lower semicontinuity in finite dimensions, its nonempty finite sublevels are compact.
special_cases_latex: A proper lower-semicontinuous coercive projection objective lies in the compact-level regime.
Strict convexity of \(F_y\) on its convex feasible domain is a uniqueness condition, not an attainment condition.
immediate_consequences_latex: Strong well-posedness includes both existence and uniqueness.
Compact-level and strict-convexity conditions address different components of well-posedness: attainment and uniqueness, respectively.
boundary_notes: A unique formal stationary point does not by itself establish attainment.
In infinite-dimensional spaces, bounded sublevels need not be compact, so the compact-level formulation must be changed.
Right-oriented projections require a separate analysis because their objective may be nonconvex.

notation.meaning: The unique projected point when it exists.

review_flags: A source supporting this exact hierarchy of Bregman projection well-posedness notions was not identified among the inspected hints.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Existence Regimes
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous left-divergence objective attains its minimum on a nonempty closed constraint set when its constrained sublevel sets are bounded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(y\in U\). Suppose \(C\) is nonempty and closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and suppose every sublevel set \[\{x\in C:D_f(x,y)\leq\alpha\}\] is bounded for each \(\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\). Since \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is continuous on \(C\), every nonempty sublevel set is compact. A minimizing sequence therefore has a convergent subsequence with limit in \(C\), and the minimum is attained. Equivalently, \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)\neq\varnothing\).
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is open and \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is continuously differentiable
\(C\subseteq U\) is nonempty and closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is level-bounded on \(C\) for fixed \(y\in U\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)\neq\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct-method regime for left projection attainment.

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The finite-dimensional attainment claim is mathematically sound and theorem fits the existence-regimes leaf, but no source is cited. The statement_latex field also contains a proof-style minimizing-sequence argument, which must be removed when a sourced replacement is prepared.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Constraint Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A strictly convex generator need not give a unique projection onto a nonconvex set.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-geometry boundary for strict-generator uniqueness.

knowledge_statements.title: Failure Without Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexity without strict convexity does not ensure uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(U=\mathbb R\), \(f\equiv0\), and \(C=[0,1]\), one has \(D_f(x,y)=0\) for all \(x,y\in U\), and hence \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=[0,1]\) for every \(y\in U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=[0,1]\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generator-curvature boundary for uniqueness of an attained left projection.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and strictly convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)\) is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-convexity uniqueness regime for attained left projections.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(y\in U\), the left objective has the form \[D_f(x,y)=f(x)-\langle\nabla f(y),x\rangle+\text{a constant independent of }x.\] Hence \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is strictly convex whenever \(f\) is strictly convex. Its restriction to the convex set \(C\) consequently has at most one minimizer. If the left projection is attained, then there exists a unique \(p\in C\) such that \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{p\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict convexity of the generator and convexity of the constraint set make every attained left Bregman projection unique.
knowledge_statements.title: Projection Uniqueness Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniqueness theorem is correct for an attained left projection over a convex set, but it has no cited source with a specific locator. The statement_latex field includes derivational proof text that should not appear in the knowledge statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Coercivity Interface
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coercivity of a left Bregman objective is exactly coercivity of the generator after subtracting the linear term determined by the base point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For fixed \(y\in U\), \[D_f(x,y)=f(x)-\langle
abla f(y),xangle+\langle
abla f(y),yangle-f(y).\] The final two terms are independent of \(x\). Therefore \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) is coercive, or level-bounded, on \(C\) exactly when the tilted generator \(x\mapsto f(x)-\langle
abla f(y),xangle\) has the corresponding property on \(C\). In particular, if \(f\) is supercoercive on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), then \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) is coercive for every fixed \(y\).
assumptions_latex: \(f:U\to\mathbb{R}\) is differentiable and convex on open \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) is level-bounded on \(C\) if and only if \(f(\cdot)-\langle\nabla f(y),\cdot\rangle\) is level-bounded on \(C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left-projection coercivity is coercivity of a linearly tilted generator.

notation.meaning: tilted generator for the base point y

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The constant-shift equivalence of level-boundedness is correct, and condition is a reasonable kind for this interface leaf. No supporting citation is supplied, and statement_latex contains explanatory derivation rather than only the mathematical statement.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Variational and Pythagorean Characterization
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a convex target, projection optimality is equivalent to a gradient variational inequality, a normal-cone condition, and the generalized Pythagorean inequality; affine targets give equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(C\subseteq U\) be nonempty and convex, and let \(y\in U\). For \(p\in C\), the following are equivalent: \[p\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y),\] \[\langle
abla h(p)-
abla h(y),x-pangle\ge0\quad( orall x\in C),\] \[
abla h(y)-
abla h(p)\in N_C(p),\] and \[D_h(x,y)\ge D_h(x,p)+D_h(p,y)\quad( orall x\in C).\] If \(C\) is affine, the variational inner product vanishes for every \(x\in C\), and the Pythagorean inequality becomes equality.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is differentiable and convex on an open convex set \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Projection optimality, the variational inequality, normal-cone membership, and the Bregman Pythagorean inequality are equivalent; for affine \(C\), the last relation is equality.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constraint-set characterization of a left Bregman projection; existence is not asserted.

notation.meaning: convex normal cone with convention \(\langle v,x-p\rangle\le0\) for every x in C

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and strictly convex on open convex \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
\(C\subseteq U\) is nonempty, closed in \(\mathbb{R}^n\), and convex
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{p\}\) and \(\langle\nabla f(p)-\nabla f(y),z-p\rangle\geq0\) for all \(z\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closedness supports attainment; convexity supports uniqueness and the variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the stated hypotheses, continuity and level-boundedness give an attained minimum, while strict convexity of \(f\) gives uniqueness. Thus \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\{p\}\) for some \(p\in C\). Since the differentiable objective \(x\mapsto D_f(x,y)\) is convex, its minimizer over \(C\) satisfies \[\langle\nabla f(p)-\nabla f(y),z-p\rangle\geq0\qquad\text{for every }z\in C.\] Conversely, this variational inequality is sufficient for \(p\) to minimize \(D_f(\cdot,y)\) over \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closedness, convexity, and level-boundedness yield an attained unique left projection characterized by a first-order variational inequality.
knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Set Geometry

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The result is fundamentally a theorem or optimality characterization, not merely a condition. The assumptions do not explicitly introduce y as an element of U, the record has no source citation, and statement_latex contains proof-style justification. A sourced revision must correct all three issues without weakening the result.

knowledge_statements.title: Bregman Pythagorean Family
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A left Bregman projection gives a Pythagorean inequality on convex constraints and an exact identity on affine constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The projection optimality condition gives \(\langle
abla f(p)-
abla f(y),z-pangle\geq0\) for every \(z\in C\). The three-point identity then yields \[D_f(z,y)=D_f(z,p)+D_f(p,y)+\langle z-p,
abla f(p)-
abla f(y)angle,\] and hence \[D_f(z,y)\geq D_f(z,p)+D_f(p,y)\qquad(z\in C).\] If \(C\) is affine, both feasible directions \(z-p\) and \(p-z\) are available, so the inner product vanishes and the displayed inequality becomes equality for every \(z\in C\).
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is differentiable and convex on open convex \(U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(z,y)\geq D_f(z,p)+D_f(p,y)\) for every \(z\in C\), with equality when \(C\) is affine.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Left-projection inequality, with the affine-constraint equality regime.

notation.meaning: an attained left Bregman projection of y

enrichment_metadata.review_comment: The Pythagorean inequality and affine-set equality regime are correct under the stated attained left-projection assumptions, and theorem matches the topic role. No source is cited, and statement_latex includes the optimality and three-point-identity derivation, which is proof text.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Bregman Pythagorean inequality and equality relations
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h\) be differentiable and convex on an open convex set \(U\), let \(C\subseteq U\), let \(y\in U\), and let \(p\in C\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The record defines the Pythagorean relations for a candidate projection point. It does not assert that every projection satisfies them without appropriate convexity and optimality hypotheses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The triple \((C,p,y)\) satisfies the left Bregman Pythagorean inequality if
\[D_h(x,y)\geq D_h(x,p)+D_h(p,y)\qquad\text{for every }x\in C.\]
It satisfies the Pythagorean equality if equality holds for every \(x\in C\). By the three-point identity, these relations are equivalently specified by
\[\langle\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y),x-p\rangle\geq0\quad\text{or}\quad
\langle\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y),x-p\rangle=0,\]
respectively, for every \(x\in C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A point p satisfies the Bregman Pythagorean inequality relative to C and y when every feasible x has direct divergence to y at least equal to the sum of its divergence to p and p's divergence to y. Equality is the corresponding exact decomposition. The inequality and equality are equivalently expressed by a dual-gradient pairing condition.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is convex and differentiable on an open convex set \(U\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The Pythagorean inequality is \(D_h(x,y)\geq D_h(x,p)+D_h(p,y)\) for all \(x\in C\), and the equality regime replaces \(\geq\) by \(=\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The inequality is equivalent to \(\langle\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y),x-p\rangle\geq0\) for every \(x\in C\).
The equality is equivalent to \(\nabla h(p)-\nabla h(y)\in(\operatorname{par}C)^{\perp}\) when \(C\) is affine, where \(\operatorname{par}C=C-C\).
special_cases_latex: For a quadratic generator, the equality reduces to the usual orthogonal Pythagorean identity.
For a convex feasible set and a left Bregman projection satisfying the first-order variational inequality, the inequality relation applies.
immediate_consequences_latex: The inequality implies \(D_h(x,y)\geq D_h(p,y)\) for every \(x\in C\).
The equality regime decomposes every feasible direct divergence into two directed legs through \(p\).
boundary_notes: For a general convex set, equality need not hold; the usual projection relation is an inequality.
The displayed orientation is tied to minimizing \(D_h(\cdot,y)\); reversing the divergence requires a different relation.

notation.meaning: The direction space of an affine set C.

review_flags: No inspected source locator was available for the Bregman Pythagorean inequality together with its affine equality regime and orientation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Attainment and nonattainment boundary for a Bregman projection
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be differentiable on \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), let \(C\subseteq E\), fix \(y\in U\), and put \(\alpha=\u200b\inf_{x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h}D_h(x,y)\), with \(\inf\varnothing=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional left-oriented projection. The classification separates feasibility, finite nonattainment, and attainment without prescribing sufficient conditions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The projection datum \((h,C,y)\) is attained if there exists \(p\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) with \(D_h(p,y)=\alpha\). It is finitely unattained if \(\alpha<+\infty\) but no such \(p\) exists. It is infeasible if \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h=\varnothing\). A finite nonattainment sequence is any \((x_k)\subseteq C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) such that \(D_h(x_k,y)\to\alpha\) while \((x_k)\) has no cluster point in \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\). The attainment boundary is the distinction among these three cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Bregman projection is attained when a feasible point realizes the divergence infimum. It is finitely unattained when the infimum is finite but no feasible point realizes it, and infeasible when the effective feasible set is empty. Nonattainment can be witnessed by a minimizing sequence having no feasible cluster point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Attainment is \(P_C^{h,L}(y)\neq\varnothing\); finite nonattainment is \(\alpha<+\infty\) and \(P_C^{h,L}(y)=\varnothing\); infeasibility is \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h=\varnothing\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Finite nonattainment means that minimizing sequences exist but no point of the effective feasible set has objective value \(\alpha\).
Attainment is equivalent to \(\alpha\in\{D_h(x,y):x\in C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\}\).
special_cases_latex: If \(C\cap\operatorname{dom}h\) is compact and \(D_h(\cdot,y)\) is lower semicontinuous there, the datum is attained.
If feasible points approach an excluded boundary point at which the limiting divergence is finite, finite nonattainment may occur.

knowledge_statements.title: Open-Domain Boundary Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A relatively closed constraint curve can approach an excluded domain boundary, causing a quadratic Bregman projection infimum to remain unattained.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The set \(C\) is closed relative to \(U\), but its Euclidean closure contains the excluded boundary point \((0,0)\). For \(x_t=(t,t^4)\in C\), \[D_f(x_t,y)=\tfrac12\bigl(t^2+(t^4-1)^2\bigr)=\tfrac12\bigl(1+t^2-2t^4+t^8\bigr).\] For \(0<t\leq\tfrac12\), this value is strictly greater than \(\tfrac12\), while it converges to \(\tfrac12\) as \(t\downarrow0\). Hence the infimum is not attained, despite relative closedness of \(C\) in the open domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}D_f(x,y)=\tfrac12\) but \(P^{\mathrm L}_{C,f}(y)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative closedness inside an open domain does not prevent escape to its boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Projection Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For negative-logarithmic geometry, projection of a point above one onto the open interval (0,1) has a finite infimum at the excluded endpoint and therefore no minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=-\log x\) for \(x>0\), let \(C=(0,1)\), and fix \(y>1\). Then \[D_h(x,y)=\frac{x}{y}-\log\!\left(\frac{x}{y}\right)-1.\] The infimum over \(C\) is the finite value \(D_h(1,y)\), but it is not attained because \(1\notin C\). Hence \[\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\varnothing.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A one-dimensional open-set counterexample to Bregman projection attainment.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation-Specific Failure
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Entropy divergence permits a boundary point as its first argument, but not as its differentiated second argument, so reversing orientation can destroy feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=x\log x-x\) on \((0,\infty)\), with \(h(0)=0\), and let \(C=\{0\}\). For every \(y>0\), the forward divergence extends finitely to the first-argument boundary and satisfies \(D_h(0,y)=y\), so the forward projection onto \(C\) exists. In the reversed orientation, evaluating \(D_h(y,0)\) requires \(h'(0)\), but \(h'(x)=\log x\to-\infty\) as \(x\downarrow0\). Thus exchanging the arguments destroys classical feasibility even though the forward problem is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\arg\min_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\{0\}\), whereas \(D_h(y,0)\) is not classically defined.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by exchanging the differentiated and nondifferentiated Bregman arguments.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E\) be a finite-dimensional real inner-product space and let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be Legendre. Set \(U=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\) and \(U^*=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Mirror-coordinate duality assigns to each \(x\in U\) the dual coordinate \(\eta=
abla h(x)\in U^*\), and to each \(\eta\in U^*\) the primal coordinate \(x=
abla h^*(\eta)\in U\). The coordinate relations are
\[\eta=

abla h^*(\eta)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad h(x)+h^*(\eta)=\langle x,\eta\rangle.\]
Thus primal and dual coordinates are paired by mutually inverse gradient maps and Fenchel equality.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Surjectivity Without Essential Smoothness
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A half-line quadratic lacks boundary-gradient blow-up, and its gradient misses nonpositive dual coordinates although its conjugate is finite everywhere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h(x)=x^2\) for \(x\ge0\) and \(h(x)=+\infty\) for \(x<0\). Then \(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and strictly convex on \((0,\infty)\), but it is not essentially smooth. Its conjugate is \[h^*(u)=\begin{cases}0,&u\le0,\\u^2/4,&u>0,\end{cases}\] so \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)=\mathbb R\), whereas \(\nabla h((0,\infty))=(0,\infty)\). Therefore the gradient map is not onto the conjugate-domain interior.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h))=(0,\infty)\subsetneq\mathbb R=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the interior-to-interior coordinate correspondence for a closed strictly convex generator lacking essential smoothness.

knowledge_statements.title: Loss of Injectivity Without Essential Strict Convexity
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant convex generator sends every primal point to the same dual coordinate, so essential strict convexity is needed for invertibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=0\) on \(\mathbb R\), \(h\) is proper, closed, convex, and differentiable, but \(\nabla h(x)=0\) for every \(x\). Thus the gradient coordinate map is not injective, showing that differentiability alone cannot replace the essential-strict-convexity part of the Legendre hypothesis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h\equiv0\) is not injective.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the primal-to-dual coordinate bijection when the generator is differentiable but not essentially strictly convex.

abla h^*(u)\). The coordinate maps are mutually inverse: \[
abla h^*(
abla h(x))=x,\qquad 
abla h(
abla h^*(u))=u.\] Equivalently, \(u=
abla h(x)\) if and only if \(x=
abla h^*(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla h:\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\to\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\) is bijective with inverse \(\nabla h^*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Mirror-Map Image
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The image of a Legendre mirror map is exactly the interior of the conjugate function's domain, with conjugate gradient providing the unique preimage.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The mirror map \(M=\nabla h\) is defined on \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\), and its image is exactly the interior of the conjugate domain: \[M\bigl(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h)\bigr)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*).\] Thus the available dual coordinates are generally not all of \(\mathbb{R}^d\); they are precisely those dual vectors at which \(h^*\) is interior-finite. For each such vector \(u\), its unique preimage is \(M^{-1}(u)=\nabla h^*(u)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ran}(\nabla h)=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}h^*)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Formal operator interfaces induced by Bregman geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(h:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be a differentiable convex generator with Bregman divergence \(D_h\), let \(g:E\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be proper, and let \(\lambda>0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A taxonomy of static mathematical operators linking Bregman geometry to optimization methods. It contains no iteration rule, convergence assertion, or rate statement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The principal Bregman method interfaces are the mirror-response map
\[Q_h(\eta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in E}\{\langle\eta,x\rangle-h(x)\},\]
the Bregman proximal map
\[\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda g}(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in E}\{g(x)+\lambda^{-1}D_h(x,y)\},\]
and the Bregman projection map
\[P_C^h(y)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in C}D_h(x,y)=\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda\iota_C}(y).\]
The taxonomy classifies an interface by whether its input is a dual coordinate, a primal base point with a penalty, or a primal base point with a feasibility indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bregman geometry exposes three static interfaces: mirror response converts a dual coordinate into maximizers of a linear functional minus the generator; the Bregman proximal map minimizes a penalty plus a scaled divergence; and Bregman projection is the indicator-penalty specialization. These are set-valued operator definitions, not algorithms or convergence claims.
assumptions_latex: \(h\) is a proper convex generator differentiable at every base point used by \(D_h\).
Each argmax or argmin is interpreted as a possibly empty set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_C^h=\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda\iota_C}\), while \(Q_h\), \(\operatorname{prox}^{h}_{\lambda g}\), and \(P_C^h\) form the dual-response, penalized-primal, and constrained-primal interface classes.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Where \(h^*\) is differentiable and the supremum is attained, \(Q_h(\eta)=\{\nabla h^*(\eta)\}\).
The proximal objective is equivalently \(g(x)+\lambda^{-1}h(x)-\lambda^{-1}\langle\nabla h(y),x\rangle\), up to constants independent of \(x\).
special_cases_latex: If \(g=\iota_C\), the proximal interface is the Bregman projection interface.
If \(h(x)=\tfrac12\|x\|^2\), the interfaces become ordinary Euclidean response, proximal, and projection maps.
immediate_consequences_latex: The projection interface is a specialization of the proximal interface.
Mirror response accepts a dual-coordinate input, whereas the proximal and projection interfaces accept a primal base point.
boundary_notes: The taxonomy does not define an iterative method or prescribe how an operator is evaluated.

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Specialization of the Three Interfaces
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the squared Euclidean generator, mirror translation is an ordinary gradient step and the constrained proximal and projection forms reduce to Euclidean projected gradient.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical generator–domain–divergence geometries
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a finite-dimensional space \(E\), a Bregman geometry is specified by a convex domain \(\Omega\subseteq E\), a differentiable convex generator \(h\), and its divergence \(D_h\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representative finite-dimensional taxonomy defined by standard kernels. Matrix cases use the trace inner product and positive-definite domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A canonical Bregman geometry is a triple \((\Omega,h,D_h)\) belonging to the following standard families: quadratic geometry, with \(h(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx\), \(Q\succ0\); entropic geometry, with \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) on the positive orthant or simplex interior; Burg geometry, with \(h(x)=-\sum_i\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\); and spectral matrix geometry, with \(h(X)=\operatorname{tr}(\phi(X))\) on a spectral domain. In every family,
\[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Canonical Bregman geometries are generator–domain–divergence triples drawn from standard families: positive-definite quadratics, negative entropy, the Burg logarithmic barrier, and spectral matrix generators. Each family uses the same first-order divergence construction but has a different effective domain and coordinate geometry.
assumptions_latex: Each generator is proper and convex on its stated domain and differentiable on the domain interior.
In spectral geometry, \(\phi\) is a scalar convex differentiable function on an interval containing the eigenvalues under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The canonical family consists of the displayed triples \((\Omega,h,D_h)\), with \(D_h\) generated by the common first-order formula on the appropriate domain.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Each geometry may be identified by the pair \((\Omega,h)\), since \(D_h\) is determined by \(h\).
Affine perturbations of a generator leave its Bregman divergence unchanged: \(D_{h+\langle a,\cdot\rangle+b}=D_h\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Q=I\), quadratic geometry gives half the squared Euclidean distance.
On the probability simplex, entropic geometry gives the Kullback-Leibler divergence.
For \(h(X)=\operatorname{tr}(X\log X-X)\), spectral geometry gives the matrix relative-entropy divergence.
immediate_consequences_latex: The domain is part of the geometry and cannot be omitted when logarithmic or entropic generators are used.
Different generators may induce distinct directed geometries on the same ambient vector space.
boundary_notes: The list is representative rather than exhaustive.
Nondifferentiable kernels and infinite-dimensional entropy spaces require other formulations.
The matrix generator requires functional calculus and an explicitly specified spectral domain.

notation.meaning: Domain, convex generator, and induced Bregman divergence.
Spectral trace function obtained by applying φ to the eigenvalues of X.

abla h=
abla h^*=I.\] Hence \[D_h(x,y)=D_{h^*}(
abla h(y),
abla h(x))=D_h(y,x)=	frac12\lVert x-yVert^2.\]

knowledge_statements.title: Euclidean Quadratic Geometry

abla h(x)=x\) under the Riesz identification. Consequently, for every \(x,y\in H\), \[D_h(x,y):=h(x)-h(y)-\langle
abla h(y),x-yangle=	frac12\lVert x-yVert^2.\] In finite-dimensional Euclidean coordinates, \(
abla^2h=I\), so the induced local metric is constant.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-definite quadratic Bregman geometry
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(E=\mathbb R^n\), let \(Q\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric positive definite, and define \(\langle x,y\rangle_Q=x^{\mathsf T}Qy\) and \(\|x\|_Q=(x^{\mathsf T}Qx)^{1/2}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Full-domain finite-dimensional quadratic geometry. The Euclidean specialization is obtained with \(Q=I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The quadratic generator and its Bregman divergence are
\[h_Q(x)=\tfrac12x^{\mathsf T}Qx,\qquad \nabla h_Q(x)=Qx,\]
\[D_{h_Q}(x,y)=\tfrac12(x-y)^{\mathsf T}Q(x-y)=\tfrac12\|x-y\|_Q^2,\qquad x,y\in\mathbb R^n.\]
The resulting Bregman geometry is symmetric, translation invariant, and generated by the squared norm associated with the inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle_Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric positive-definite matrix Q defines the quadratic generator one half xᵀQx. Its Bregman divergence is one half of the squared Q-norm of x−y. The generator has full domain and gradient map x↦Qx.
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(Q=L^{\mathsf T}L\) with invertible \(L\), then \(D_{h_Q}(x,y)=\tfrac12\|Lx-Ly\|_2^2\).
The mirror map is \(M_{h_Q}(x)=Qx\), with inverse \(M_{h_Q}^{-1}(\eta)=Q^{-1}\eta\).
special_cases_latex: For diagonal \(Q\succ0\), the divergence is a coordinate-weighted squared Euclidean distance.
immediate_consequences_latex: \(\sqrt{2D_{h_Q}(x,y)}=\|x-y\|_Q\) is a metric.
Left and right Bregman projections coincide for this generator.
The gradient coordinate map is a linear bijection of \(\mathbb R^n\).
boundary_notes: Positive semidefinite but singular \(Q\) produces only a seminorm and loses point separation.
The squared norm \(D_{h_Q}\) itself generally fails the triangle inequality even though its square root is a metric.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Negative-entropy Bregman geometry on the probability simplex
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(\Delta_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\}\) and \(\Delta_n^{\circ}=\{x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n:\sum_i x_i=1\}\). Adopt \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite probability simplex with the negative Shannon entropy generator. The second divergence argument lies in the relative interior.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the negative-entropy generator on \(\Delta_n\) by
\[h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i.\]
For \(x\in\Delta_n\) and \(y\in\Delta_n^{\circ}\), its Bregman divergence is
\[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i},\]
with each term having value \(0\) when \(x_i=0\). This is the Kullback-Leibler divergence from \(x\) to \(y\). In ambient positive-orthant coordinates, \(\nabla h(y)_i=1+\log y_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On the probability simplex, negative Shannon entropy generates the Kullback–Leibler divergence. The first argument may lie on the simplex boundary, while the second must have all coordinates positive. Zero coordinates in the first argument contribute zero under the convention 0 log 0=0.
assumptions_latex: \(h(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) uses the lower-semicontinuous convention \(0\log0=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,y)=\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\geq0\), with equality exactly when \(x=y\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: On the positive orthant before imposing unit mass, the same generator yields \(D_h(x,y)=\sum_i[x_i\log(x_i/y_i)-x_i+y_i]\).
For simplex points, the linear terms cancel because \(\sum_i x_i=\sum_i y_i=1\).
special_cases_latex: For a vertex \(e_j\) and \(y\in\Delta_n^{\circ}\), \(D_h(e_j,y)=-\log y_j\).
For the uniform point \(u_i=1/n\), \(D_h(x,u)=\log n+\sum_i x_i\log x_i\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The divergence becomes infinite under the extended convention if some \(x_i>0\) while \(y_i=0\).
The entropic mirror coordinate is logarithmic componentwise, modulo the affine normal direction of the simplex.
The divergence is generally asymmetric.
boundary_notes: The gradient of the entropy generator is not finite at zero, so the base point must lie in the relative interior.
The formula is classical relative entropy, not the symmetric Jensen-Shannon divergence.
Simplex mirror coordinates are defined only up to adding a common scalar when viewed intrinsically on the affine hull.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Convexity, Range, and Extremizers
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is strictly convex on the closed simplex, is uniquely minimized by the uniform distribution, and is maximized at its vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\) on \(\Delta_n\), with \(0\log0=0\), \(h\) is strictly convex on \(\Delta_n\) and \[-\log n\le h(x)\le0.\] Its unique minimizer is \((1/n,\ldots,1/n)\), while \(h(x)=0\) exactly at the vertices of \(\Delta_n\).

knowledge_statements.title: Entropy Generator Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is the restriction to the simplex of the coordinate sum x log x. It is strictly convex and relatively smooth in the simplex interior, where its displayed derivative is the gradient of the ambient positive-orthant extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Delta_n:=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^n:\sum_{i=1}^n x_i=1\}\) and \(\Delta_n^\circ:=\{x\in\Delta_n:x_i>0\text{ for every }i\}\). Define the ambient negative-entropy function by \[\widetilde h(x):=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i,\qquad x\in\mathbb R_+^n,\] with \(0\log 0=0\), and let \(h\) be its restriction to \(\Delta_n\). Then \(h\) is continuous and convex on \(\Delta_n\), strictly convex on \(\Delta_n^\circ\), and differentiable relative to the affine hull there. The ambient gradient representative supplied by \(\widetilde h\) satisfies \[(\nabla\widetilde h(x))_i=1+\log x_i\qquad(x\in\Delta_n^\circ).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\) is strictly convex on \(\Delta_n^\circ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative entropy on a finite probability simplex, with derivatives taken from its ambient positive-orthant extension.

notation.meaning: negative-entropy generator restricted to the simplex
ambient negative-entropy extension on the positive orthant

source_witnesses.locator: 8 Convex Functions p. 139

knowledge_statements.title: Square-Root Spherical Representation
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the coordinatewise square-root map, the entropy Hessian metric becomes the round metric on a sphere.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Equip \(\Delta_n^\circ\) with \(g_x(u,v)=\sum_i u_iv_i/x_i\) on \(T_x\Delta_n=\{u:\sum_i u_i=0\}\). The map \[\Phi(x)=2(\sqrt{x_1},\ldots,\sqrt{x_n})\] is an isometric embedding into the positive orthant of the Euclidean sphere of radius \(2\). Consequently, its intrinsic distance is \[d_{\mathrm{FR}}(x,y)=2\arccos\!\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\sqrt{x_i y_i}\right).\]
assumptions_latex: Tangent vectors have coordinate sum zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{FR}}(x,y)=2\arccos(\sum_i\sqrt{x_i y_i})\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global Riemannian representation of the entropy Hessian metric on the simplex interior.

notation.meaning: entropy Hessian, equivalently Fisher information, metric

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Interior Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Inside the simplex, entropy induces the coordinate-weighted tangent metric whose squared norm is the sum of u_i squared divided by x_i.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the negative-entropy generator \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\), every \(x\in\Delta_n^\circ\) satisfies \[\nabla^2h(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(x_1^{-1},\ldots,x_n^{-1}).\] Hence its local squared norm on the simplex tangent space \(T=\{u\in\mathbb R^n:\sum_i u_i=0\}\) is \[\lVert u\rVert_{x,h}^2:=\langle u,\nabla^2h(x)u\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{u_i^2}{x_i},\] which is positive for every nonzero \(u\in T\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\langle u,\nabla^2h(x)u\rangle=\sum_i u_i^2/x_i\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hessian geometry restricted to simplex tangent directions.

source_witnesses.locator: 10 Convex Functions: Variants p. 177

knowledge_statements.title: Empty Finite Subdifferential at Boundary Points
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy is finite at simplex boundary points but has no finite subgradient there.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H(x)=\sum_i x_i\log x_i\) on \(\Delta_n\) and \(H(x)=+\infty\) outside \(\Delta_n\). If \(x\in\Delta_n\setminus\Delta_n^\circ\), then \[\partial H(x)=\varnothing.\] Thus a simplex point with a zero coordinate has finite entropy value but no finite supporting subgradient.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in\Delta_n\) has at least one zero coordinate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial H(x)=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of finite supporting slopes for simplex negative entropy at relative-boundary points.

notation.meaning: negative entropy extended by positive infinity outside the simplex

knowledge_statements.title: Simplex Boundary Behavior
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative entropy remains finite and continuous at the simplex boundary, while the ambient gradient and curvature become singular along every coordinate that vanishes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widetilde h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_+^n\), with \(0\log0=0\), and let \(h=\widetilde h|_{\Delta_n}\). If \(x^{(k)}\in\Delta_n^\circ\) converges to \(\bar x\in\Delta_n\) and \(\bar x_j=0\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then \[(\nabla\widetilde h(x^{(k)}))_j=1+\log x_j^{(k)}\longrightarrow-\infty,\qquad (\nabla^2\widetilde h(x^{(k)}))_{jj}=\frac1{x_j^{(k)}}\longrightarrow+\infty.\] Nevertheless, \(h\) extends continuously and finitely to all of \(\Delta_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\nabla\widetilde h(x^{(k)}))_j\to-\infty\) and \((\nabla^2\widetilde h(x^{(k)}))_{jj}\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary singularity of the ambient derivatives when a simplex coordinate vanishes.

notation.meaning: restriction of the ambient generator to the simplex

source_witnesses.locator: 9 Lower Semicontinuous Convex Functions p. 157

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Metric Symmetry and Triangle Inequality
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is generally asymmetric and does not satisfy the triangle inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p=(1,0)\), \(q=(1/2,1/2)\), and \(r=(1/4,3/4)\), \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\log2\quad\text{but}\quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)=+\infty,\] so symmetry fails. Moreover, \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|r)=\log4>D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|r),\] so the triangle inequality fails.
assumptions_latex: The standard extended-value support convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}\) is neither symmetric nor a metric.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp warning that probability-coordinate relative entropy is a divergence rather than a metric.

knowledge_statements.title: Variational Representation of Relative Entropy
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is the convex dual of weighted log-sum-exp, with a finite maximizing potential exactly when the first distribution has full support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p,q\in\Delta_n\) and \(q_i>0\) for every \(i\), then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sup_{a\in\mathbb R^n}\left\{\langle a,p\rangle-\log\left(\sum_{i=1}^n q_i e^{a_i}\right)\right\}.\] If \(p_i>0\) for every \(i\), the maximizers are exactly \(a_i=\log(p_i/q_i)+c\), \(c\in\mathbb R\). If some \(p_i=0\), the supremum is unchanged but has no finite maximizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sup_a\{\langle a,p\rangle-\log\sum_iq_ie^{a_i}\}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-alphabet Gibbs variational formula and its attainment boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Convexity and Data Processing
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: KL divergence is jointly convex and cannot increase when both probability vectors pass through the same stochastic channel.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability vectors \(p^{(r)},q^{(r)}\) and weights \(\alpha_r\ge0\) with \(\sum_r\alpha_r=1\), \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\!\left(\sum_r\alpha_rp^{(r)}\middle\|\sum_r\alpha_rq^{(r)}\right)\le\sum_r\alpha_rD_{\mathrm{KL}}(p^{(r)}\|q^{(r)}).\] If \(K\) is a finite-state stochastic channel, then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Kp\|Kq)\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q).\]
assumptions_latex: All displayed vectors are finite probability vectors.
\(K\) is a stochastic channel acting on those vectors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Kp\|Kq)\le D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convexity and stochastic-channel contraction of finite-alphabet relative entropy.

knowledge_statements.title: Gibbs Inequality and Pinsker Bound
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Relative entropy is nonnegative, vanishes exactly for equal distributions, and controls squared total variation through Pinsker's inequality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p,q\in\Delta_n\), with \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=+\infty\) when some \(p_i>0=q_i\), \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\ge\frac12\lVert p-q\rVert_1^2\ge0,\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=0\iff p=q.\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\ge\tfrac12\lVert p-q\rVert_1^2\), with equality at zero exactly when \(p=q\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definiteness and total-variation control for finite probability vectors, using natural logarithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Probability-Coordinate Divergence
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On probability vectors, the entropy Bregman divergence is relative entropy, with infinity when the reference assigns zero mass to positive mass.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(h(x)=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log x_i\), \(x\in\Delta_n\), and \(y\in\Delta_n^\circ\), the associated Bregman divergence is \[D_h(x,y)=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}.\] Here a term with \(x_i=0\) equals \(0\). More generally, if zero coordinates are allowed in \(y\), the value is \(+\infty\) whenever \(x_i>0=y_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_h(x,y)=\sum_i x_i\log(x_i/y_i)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entropy Bregman divergence in probability coordinates.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Burg Bregman Geometry on the Positive Orthant
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\Omega=\mathbb R_{++}^{n}\), and the ambient pairing is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_iv_i\). Define the extended-valued negative Burg entropy by \(h(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log x_i\) for \(x\in\Omega\) and \(h(x)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional Burg geometry generated by the logarithmic barrier on the strictly positive orthant; both arguments of the divergence are required to lie in \(\mathbb R_{++}^{n}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: \[\nabla h(y)=(-y_1^{-1},\ldots,-y_n^{-1}),\qquad D_h(x,y):=h(x)-h(y)-\langle\nabla h(y),x-y\rangle.\] The Burg orthant Bregman divergence is therefore defined for every \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{++}^{n}\) by \[D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{x_i}{y_i}-\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}-1\right).\] The pair \((\Omega,D_h)\), together with the generating function \(h\), is the Burg orthant geometry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Burg orthant geometry is the Bregman geometry generated on the strictly positive orthant by negative Burg entropy. Its divergence between positive vectors is the sum, over coordinates, of the ratio of the first coordinate to the second minus the logarithm of that ratio minus one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{dom}D_h=\mathbb R_{++}^{n}\times\mathbb R_{++}^{n},\qquad D_h(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\frac{x_i}{y_i}-\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}-1\right).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[D_h(x,y)=-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log x_i+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log y_i+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{x_i-y_i}{y_i}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(x=ty\) for \(t>0\), then \(D_h(x,y)=n(t-\log t-1)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: \[D_h(x,y)\geq0,\qquad D_h(x,y)=0\Longleftrightarrow x=y.\]
The divergence is invariant under common positive diagonal rescaling: \(D_h(Sx,Sy)=D_h(x,y)\) for every positive diagonal matrix \(S\).
boundary_notes: The divergence is generally asymmetric: \(D_h(x,y)\neq D_h(y,x)\).
Boundary points with a zero coordinate are excluded because the generator is not finite or differentiable there.
This slot does not assert strong convexity with respect to a fixed global norm on the unbounded orthant.

knowledge_statements.title: Burg Gradient and Conjugate Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Burg gradient bijects the positive and negative orthants, and its conjugate is logarithmic on the negative orthant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(b(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\) on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\), \(\nabla b(x)=(-x_i^{-1})_{i=1}^n\) is a bijection from \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) onto \(\mathbb R_{--}^n\), with inverse \((\nabla b)^{-1}(s)=(-s_i^{-1})_{i=1}^n\). Its Fenchel conjugate is \[b^*(s)=-n-\sum_{i=1}^n\log(-s_i)\quad(s\in\mathbb R_{--}^n),\] and \(b^*(s)=+\infty\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla b:\mathbb R_{++}^n\to\mathbb R_{--}^n\) is bijective and \(b^*(s)=-n-\sum_i\log(-s_i)\) on \(\mathbb R_{--}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Legendre and Fenchel-conjugate structure of the Burg generator.

notation.meaning: Fenchel conjugate of the Burg generator

knowledge_statements.title: Burg Generator Geometry
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Burg generator is the negative sum of coordinate logarithms and induces a divergence depending on coordinate ratios.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Burg generator on \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\) is \[b(x):=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i.\] It is smooth and strictly convex, with \((\nabla b(x))_i=-x_i^{-1}\) and \(\nabla^2b(x)=\operatorname{Diag}(x_1^{-2},\ldots,x_n^{-2})\). For \(x,y\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\), its Bregman divergence is \[D_b(x,y)=\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i}{y_i}-\log\frac{x_i}{y_i}-1\right).\]
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_b(x,y)=\sum_i(x_i/y_i-\log(x_i/y_i)-1)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Logarithmic barrier as a Bregman generator.

knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Burg generator decreases without bound along common positive scaling rays.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Orthant Domain
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The extended Burg function is finite exactly on the open positive orthant and infinite everywhere else.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\bar b:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) by \[\bar b(x):=\begin{cases}-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i,&x\in\mathbb R_{++}^n,\\+\infty,&x\notin\mathbb R_{++}^n.\end{cases}\] Then \(\bar b\) is proper, lower semicontinuous, and strictly convex, and \[\operatorname{dom}\bar b=\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\bar b)=\mathbb R_{++}^n.\] Thus the Burg geometry is defined only when every coordinate is strictly positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{int}(\operatorname{dom}\bar b)=\mathbb R_{++}^n\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended-real domain of the Burg generator.

knowledge_statements.title: Burg-Divergence Boundary Blow-Up in Both Arguments
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Burg divergence tends to infinity when either argument loses a positive coordinate that remains positive in the other argument.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix the nonvarying argument in \(\mathbb R_{++}^n\). If \(x^{(k)}\to\bar x\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\bar x_j=0\) while \(y_j>0\), then \(D_b(x^{(k)},y)\to+\infty\). If \(y^{(k)}\to\bar y\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\bar y_j=0\) while \(x_j>0\), then \(D_b(x,y^{(k)})\to+\infty\).
assumptions_latex: The varying argument approaches a finite orthant-boundary point, while the corresponding coordinate of the fixed argument remains positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_b(x^{(k)},y)\to+\infty\), and in the reversed regime \(D_b(x,y^{(k)})\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coordinatewise divergence behavior when either argument approaches a finite orthant boundary.

notation.meaning: Bregman divergence generated by the Burg function

knowledge_statements.title: Coordinatewise Boundary Blow-Up
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a sequence converging to a finite orthant boundary point, the Burg value diverges to infinity, while the gradient magnitude and curvature blow up in every vanishing coordinate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(b(x)=-\sum_{i=1}^n\log x_i\). If \(x^{(k)}\in\mathbb R_{++}^n\) converges to a finite point \(\bar x\in\mathbb R_+^n\) and \(\bar x_j=0\) for some \(j\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), then \[b(x^{(k)})\longrightarrow+\infty,\qquad (\nabla b(x^{(k)}))_j=-\frac1{x_j^{(k)}}\longrightarrow-\infty,\qquad (\nabla^2b(x^{(k)}))_{jj}=\frac1{(x_j^{(k)})^2}\longrightarrow+\infty.\] The derivative conclusions hold for every coordinate \(j\) such that \(\bar x_j=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(b(x^{(k)})\to+\infty\), \((\nabla b(x^{(k)}))_j\to-\infty\), and \((\nabla^2b(x^{(k)}))_{jj}\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singularity along sequences converging to finite positive-orthant boundary points.
